What does this mean for runaway RSI

Will a million or a billion parallel AIs get us to self-sustaining or runaway RSI? Let’s do the math.

Hypothetical software-RSI models assume that a growing number of AI researchers produces a much larger stream of discoveries. Those discoveries make AI cheaper or more productive, allowing the next round of research to grow again.

There’s a strong case for gains in speed and for searching more of a well-defined space. Even speed gains, as we’ve seen, can taper. Intelligence is much harder to boost through parallel agents. In several experiments, peak problem-solving performance (what I’m referring to here as intelligence) rises dramatically more slowly than speed.

Here’s what three software-RSI models assume:

  • Chan and colleagues (2026): doubling effective research labor produces about 2.6 times the rate of software improvement, holding the software level fixed. I find that implausible as a general assumption about adding copies of today’s AI models. The clearest large-team intelligence experiments look nothing like that.

  • Eth and Davidson (2025): their illustrative team produces twice as many papers from twice as many researchers. The accelerating example assumes that the number of researchers grows faster than the work required for each further improvement.

  • Tom Davidson and Tom Houlden (2025): their central exponent for parallel research effort is 0.6. Ten times the labor gives about four times the research pace. They cut that exponent in half, to 0.3, when experimental compute is held fixed and becomes a bottleneck. The benchmark reports above don’t appear to have been limited by experimental compute, so we’re using 0.6 here.

The top half of the next chart shows research-output relationships used in hypothetical RSI models where AI self-improvement can sustain itself or accelerate. The bottom half shows real-world intelligence shapes from the benchmark experiments. Those experiments show dramatically less gain from running parallel agents than the hypothetical RSI models assume.

Hypothetical research curves rise much faster than these benchmark shapes.

Let’s put these onto a single chart. We give every curve the same gain from its first expansion from one to ten agents or researchers, so we can compare their shapes.

The same starting gain, very different later returns.

Now let’s zoom in on the gap. The real-world shapes sit in a very different zone from the gains assumed in those RSI models, even when we let the math-proof curve keep rising slowly.

Zooming in makes the gap clearer. Hypothetical RSI models show much faster gains from adding more agents than empirical models based on real-world experiments.

Today’s hypothetical RSI models assume gains from additional AI researchers that we haven’t seen in these real-world experiments. Removing humans from the loop doesn’t remove shared blind spots or sequential dependencies. Adding more copies of today’s models hasn’t shown the sustained intelligence gains that may be needed for repeated conceptual breakthroughs.

Will agents get better at scaling?

I do expect better AI models to get better at spreading work across agents: dividing the problem, managing collaborators, and combining what they find. We’ve already seen progress in speed on program reconstruction. We haven’t seen a clear trend toward better multi-agent intelligence scaling in the math results. More on that in a moment.

First, an encouraging analogy: single-agent thinking-time scaling. Toby Ord’s analysis suggests that humans get more relative benefit from additional time than these AIs get from additional reasoning tokens. That may surprise people. But newer models are getting closer to the human reference on these cybersecurity tasks.

AI agents can get stuck in cognitive ruts, repeating or refining an approach that isn’t getting them far. Newer models seem to be improving at how they use extended thinking.

Newer models make better use of extra thinking tokens on these cyber tasks. Source.

This isn’t multi-agent scaling, but it’s encouraging. AIs were poor at turning more thinking into harder solved tasks, and that scaling parameter improved. They might eventually pass the human reference. That’s part of why I don’t see runaway RSI as imminent, yet think it could become more plausible as these capabilities change.

We’ve also seen new findings on helping agents escape their ruts and use more thinking time productively. The new Fork-and-Flush study periodically creates parallel branches that keep the accumulated work but start with fresh chat contexts, then continues from the best branch. It improved results across thirteen research and engineering tasks at the same compute budget. That’s a concrete research direction for using additional work more effectively.

So, have we seen a similar improvement in multi-agent scaling? For speed, sometimes. For intelligence, there’s no clear direction, so far, at least on formal math proofs. Opus 5.5 gets more speedup for a smaller cost increase on program reconstruction. But the score gains in the chart below are noisy, and newer models don’t consistently get a larger boost from additional agents.

Newer models don’t get consistently large gains from larger math-proof teams. Source.

That doesn’t mean better multi-agent scaling won’t happen. I expect the labs to work hard on coordination. Improving diversity of thought is a more open research question, but I’m sure it’s at least somewhat tractable given sufficient effort. The structure of the problem may impose the hardest limits: some discoveries have to happen before the next useful step becomes possible. We don’t yet know how much each of these constraints contributes.

Summarizing what we’ve seen, here’s an update on the conceptual limits to multi-agent scaling.

What we’ve learned so far, and where the hardest limits might be.

Can we build minds that think more differently?

Frontier models share many of the same broad training ingredients: overlapping public data, related algorithms, and similar reasoning and coding exercises. So how different are these minds really?

The Artificial Hivemind study found striking similarities in models’ open-ended responses. A creativity study involving 467 people likewise found that adding AI responses eventually contributed less diversity than adding human responses. These experiments suggest that AI agents can bring less diversity of thought than an equal number of humans on these tasks, which may limit how much we get from parallel agents.

Can we make agents more different from each other? Very likely. Here are four ideas. I’m sure there are others:

  • Different training experiences: vary data mixtures, curricula, reinforcement-learning environments, and reward objectives to develop strong agents that favor different useful approaches.

  • Complementary specializations: combine agents trained for conjecturing, finding lemmas, searching for counterexamples, and checking proofs. Test whether their strengths combine into results no member reliably achieves alone.

  • Independent proposals before discussion: let agents develop approaches before seeing one another’s answers, then exchange evidence and criticism. Test whether this reduces early convergence on the same mistake.

  • Teams chosen for complementary errors: select members whose successes and failures overlap less, rather than relying only on individual benchmark rank. Measure whether the team finds more verified solutions as it grows.

How to measure agentic scaling improvements

As we discussed in the previous post, we’re going off of scant data here. This model could be wrong. Or newer AI versions could get sufficiently better at doing parallel work that these diminishing returns would change. If that happens, we need to be aware of it.

How would we track this? I’d propose measuring three things from new AI models across a variety of problem times. Across each task type, and especially across real world AI research, measure three parameters and track how they change as newer models arrive:

  • G - Intelligence scaling: How much verified task performance does each multiplication of agents add? Measure local score gains, slopes, or exponents as appropriate. This is a task-specific proxy for collective intelligence, not a universal intelligence unit.

  • λ - Speed-cost scaling: How much faster does the team reach the same result, and how much more total compute or agent-time does it use? Track the speed exponent λ over successive team-size ranges.

  • N - Where gains weaken or saturate: At what team size do the score or speed curves bend, or approach a ceiling? Does the bend or onset of saturation move outward with newer models?

Track intelligence gains, the speed-cost tradeoff, and where gains weaken or saturate.

G and N answer two different questions. How much extra benchmark score does a defined team expansion buy, and how many agents can we add before those gains flatten? In the illustration below, G is the gain from one to ten agents. N is the agent count where the curve reaches its plateau. A real curve may have a gradual bend rather than a sharp plateau, or no plateau within the tested range.

One hypothetical benchmark curve. G is the added score from a specified expansion of the team; N is the agent count where gains flatten. The illustrated sharp plateau is not assumed for every real task.

Watch these parameters over time, especially G and N. Don’t stop at one to ten agents. Measure the gains from 1→10, 10→100, and 100→1,000 agents, separately, on each benchmark. A newer model might scale better over the first interval and worse over the next. We need to know whether the gains improve and whether the bend moves outward.

Three hypothetical trends for added benchmark score across model generations. Measure each expansion separately: 1 to 10, 10 to 100, and 100 to 1,000 agents. Different intervals can follow different paths.

We especially need to track these trends for actual internal AI research. Are newer models getting bigger gains from larger teams? Are those teams producing more verified discoveries and better successor models? That’s what would tell us whether massive parallel teams are getting closer to the conceptual breakthroughs RSI may need.

The Anthropic test and what would change my mind

Anthropic has given us a concrete test to watch. Its October employment report shows research agents logging about nine hours for every human work-hour by mid-July, and nineteen by late August. The company-wide ratio reached about six.

Research agent runtime rises to about nine hours per human work-hour by mid-July and nineteen by late August. These hours include longer operation as well as parallel agents. Source.

Let’s make a generous assumption: each agent-hour is as valuable as a human research-hour, with the number of human researchers unchanged. Agents can run throughout the 168-hour week. Anthropic’s runtime ratios already count those extra operating hours against a forty-hour human week.

On that assumption, July’s nine agent-hours plus one human hour amount to ten times the labor of humans alone. August’s total is twenty times. But Anthropic already had roughly one agent-hour per human hour in April. Compared with that observed baseline, total labor grew fivefold by July and tenfold by August.

What should that do to research? Treat the added labor as parallel research effort. Davidson and Houlden’s relationships imply about 2–4 times April’s research pace by August, depending on whether experimental compute becomes a bottleneck. Applying the labor exponent used by Alan Chan and colleagues, including Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, gives about 25 times. Log scaling gives about twice the pace. Our sub-log shapes give only about 1.1–1.8 times.

Now translate research pace into the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI). Suppose software research supplies half of baseline capability improvement, while the compute-growth contribution stays unchanged. Then four times the software pace means about 2.5 times the overall ECI slope, not four times. We’re already discounting the software boost. Other obstacles could reduce it further.

Allow six months from research to public release. Here’s what those assumptions imply for January and February 2027. The top group uses hypothetical RSI research relationships; the bottom group extends experimental benchmark shapes.

What different RSI models predict we should see in the pace of AI improvement (using ECI slope), six months after an AI labor increase. Source.

Why do log scaling and Davidson-Houlden’s power 0.3 nearly tie? This is only a tenfold labor increase from April to August. At that scale, both calibrations give about twice the software pace. By 100 agents and then a billion, the hypothetical power law curve pulls far ahead of the experimentally-observed log and sub-log scaling rules.

Around late May, agents were already logging about three hours per human hour: twice April’s total labor on our assumption. With a six-month lag, that earlier signal would arrive around November.

These tests have many different assumptions, including equal value per hour and treating added runtime as parallel labor. I’m open to refining them on how others think about this. In measurement, we should judge the AI pace of improvement as the rate of at which ECI score goes up over successive releases, allowing for development and publication delays.

My expectation - and how I’ll update if I’m wrong

Personally, I don’t expect to see sustained acceleration of Anthropic’s AI progress (as measured by ECI) through the first half of 2027, and certainly not one as large as these simple extrapolations from the hypothetical models of Davidson and Houlden or Chan and colleagues suggest. If anything, I expect acceleration at the low end of the sub-log scaling bar at the bottom of the chart.

I could be wrong for many reasons. Parallel search of different AI training parameters, or use of AI to code new RL environments, or gains from AIs combining existing ideas in the literature could all make a bigger difference than I expect. Or, at the next increment of AI improvement, AIs could start making much more major advances in machine learning theory that allow us to bend the scaling laws and other diminishing returns that AI faces, or to add new axis of scaling, as reasoning models did.

On the other hand, while more parallel search and recombination of existing ideas seems highly likely, they may not bring huge advantages, and the AIs we’re making today might not find conceptual breakthroughs. Atop that, ideas probably really are getting harder to find in AI, and that may chew up some or all of the increased capacity of AI to work on improving itself.

We shall see. If we see the rate of AI improvement increase significantly, I’ll update my views in proportion to what the data show.

In summary, for now, multi-agent scaling shows incredibly steep diminishing returns to model intelligence, or the ability to reach conceptual breakthroughs. I expect those sorts of breakthroughs to be necessary for major AI advances and for self-sustaining RSI, let alone a runaway intelligence explosion. And at the same time, we’re all operating on far too little real world data. The most important thing we can do now and for the months and years ahead is to rigorously collect that data, and use it to update our forecasts of the future.

Donald Trump is Politically Bankrupt. Be Very Afraid

What will he do when he has nothing left to lose?

Paul Krugman
Oct 19
 
READ IN APP
 

According to CNN, all-out war with Iran may be about to resume:

The US military has developed new strike plans that include potentially using the so-called “mother of all bombs” to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites should President Donald Trump give the order to resume combat operations either before or after the midterm elections, according to multiple US officials familiar with the matter.

Trump says that he won’t order a strike before the midterms. But Robert Pape, author of the Substack Escalation Trap, argues that we shouldn’t believe him — that the bombs may well drop before the midterms. And while I am not a strategic expert, I believe that Pape may well be right, because his analysis of Trump’s political position is something I recognize from financial economics.

You see, it’s a well-understood proposition that the owners of businesses that are on the verge of going bust often engage in destructive behavior. And Trump is about to go bankrupt — not financially (he’s made billions through corruption) but politically. So he, like a failing businessman, has strong incentives to wreak havoc.

Pape’s argument is basically a version of the phenomenon — a particular form of moral hazard — often called “gambling for resurrection.” When a company is on the edge of failure, it makes sense for the company’s owner to make highly speculative, even crazy investments that are highly likely to fail but might, just might, make enough money to pull the company back from the brink. After all, for the owner it’s heads he wins, tails his creditors lose.

In Trump’s case, all indications are that his party is heading for defeat in the midterms. And while a normal president might be able to live with a Congress controlled by the opposing party, there has been so much corruption and malfeasance over the past two years that Democratic control of Congress, and the subpoena and investigative power that will bring, will have catastrophic consequences for Trump and everyone around him.

So Trump has an incentive to do something, anything, that might shake up this election. Attacking Iran would probably lead to an even bigger Republican defeat, but it might, just might, rally Trump’s base enough to change the outcome. True, a president who cared at all about what is good for America wouldn’t pursue disastrous policies for the slim chance of saving his own political skin. But this is, after all, Trump we’re talking about.

Pape’s argument, then, makes a lot of sense. But I suspect that Trump’s impending political bankruptcy will have even worse consequences than Pape suggests — and that these consequences will continue and intensify after the midterms.

When I read Pape’s analysis, I found myself thinking about a classic 1993 paper by George Akerlof and Paul Romer, “Looting: The economic underworld of bankruptcy for profit.” Akerlof and Romer were inspired by several historical episodes of widespread bankruptcy, including the U.S. savings and loan crisis of the 1980s. In these episodes, they argued, owners of banks and other companies on the verge of failure didn’t gamble for resurrection. Instead, they simply took the money and ran, transferring as much of their companies’ assets as possible into their own pockets before the hammer came down.

So what would looting by a politically bankrupt Trump administration look like? I don’t mean financial looting — Trump has been doing that all along, on an epic scale. What may be about to happen — indeed, is already happening — is what we might call policy looting: Trump using his remaining power to take actions that are both deeply unpatriotic and deeply unpopular but fit his own preferences and prejudices.

Freedom, wrote Kris Kristofferson, is just another word for nothing left to lose. Once the midterms are over, Trump, with nothing left to lose, will be free to be his worst self — a malignant narcissist who instinctively supports authoritarians and is preoccupied with revenge against anything and anyone that threatens his fragile grandiosity.

We can already see that happening in U.S. policy toward Ukraine. It has long been obvious that Trump loves dictators and despises democracy, and that he has special affection for Vladimir Putin and hatred for Volodymyr Zelenskyy. However, as long as there was some chance of limiting the damage in the midterm elections, Trump was cautious about explicitly taking Putin’s side. Over the past few weeks, however, Trump has grown ever more open about supporting Putin’s attempted war of conquest — buying Russian diesel, canceling sanctions, and most recently by attempting to sabotage Ukraine’s defenses by degrading its access to Starlink.

Something similar has been happening on domestic policy where, for example, Trump has increasingly stopped pretending that he cares about illegal immigration or immigrant crime, and is veering into flat, open racism — so far specially directed against Somalis, but it won’t stop there.

So will Trump resume the bombing of Iran before the midterms? Obviously I don’t know, but Pape is surely right that normal political logic, under which a deeply unpopular president would avoid resuming a deeply unpopular war, no longer applies. And anyone who believes that Trump will become more cautious, more moderate in the aftermath of midterm defeat just doesn’t understand the new political reality.

The truth is that political bankruptcy will free Trump to pursue his true desires. And those desires are horrifying.

The glass is half full for a common sense Democrat revival

Don’t get complacent but also don’t doom

The glass is half full for a common sense Democrat revival

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 19
 
READ IN APP
 

We don’t know exactly what the future holds, but if the current polling is even approximately accurate, then Democrats are going to have a very good election night.

That’s good for America and for the world, but it also raises the risk of an undue level of complacency.

Trump starting a war with Iran that spiked the price of energy was a wild unforced error, but you can’t count on electoral gifts of that scale falling into your lap every cycle. And it’s worth taking seriously a recent Project 270 finding that of 2024 Trump voters who currently have an unfavorable view of the president, a large majority say they still plan to vote Republican in 2028.

This is just to say I think we should take the risk of complacency seriously.

Complacency, I think, is what killed Donald Trump and the MAGA movement’s moment of opportunity. Anger about inflation and border chaos pushed a lot of voters to Trump in 2024 — including lots of younger people and nonwhite people who were once seen as unwinnable by Republicans. But the GOP pocketed those voters, didn’t actually do anything on inflation, and pissed a lot of people off with a very ideological agenda.

Now voters are shifting back by default to the other political party, and I’m worried it’ll lead progressive elites to blow off the idea that there was ever any need to rethink anything.

On the other hand, I read doomer stuff like this from Ruy Teixeira about how Democrats are “deluded” and have fixed nothing, and I think he’s being both analytically wrong and counterproductive in terms of fighting complacency:

Many Democrats are giddy about the likely thumping of Trump and the GOP. The 2024 debacle is fast fading from memory. Between the adoption of the “affordability” campaign trope, a ratcheting up of populist rhetoric, and a carefully curated dose of “heterodoxy” in key races, they are convinced they have found the winning formula to take down the unpopular Trump and his party. The necessary reforms and repositioning have taken place; a “wave” election awaits. Problem solved!

I beg to differ. Here are three reasons they’re deluding themselves.

I think it’s important to understand this in terms of Teixeira’s longer-running dispute with Adam Jentleson and his colleagues at the Searchlight Institute about heterodoxy as a path forward for Democrats. I like both Adam and Ruy, and I think that relative to the bulk of Democrats they are both on the same side, and it’s unfortunate that this has become a narcissism of small differences scenario where they’re feuding rather than cooperating.

I’m half inclined to say that we’re really just watching a dispute over whether the glass is half full or half empty. But really, Teixeira is closer to insisting that the glass is completely empty, even though he acknowledges that James Talarico, Josh Turek, and Mary Peltola have all engaged in a lot of Teixeira-recommended moves to the center.

He dismisses this as inconsequential because Talarico’s current positioning is not entirely congruent with his record. But I think that’s precisely why it’s important to say the glass is half full.

If moderates concede in advance that Democratic gestures toward heterodoxy are trivial or unimportant, then the party as a whole will end up in the delusional failure mode.

The truth is that Democrats have made meaningful gestures, and those gestures have had a real impact on voters. Gestures, though, are necessarily limited in their impact because voters are cynical about politics and politicians. What Democrats need to do is try hard to win, and then if they do win, follow up on their wins by governing in line with the best versions of themselves. There will be a lot of institutional pressure on them to not do that, but the way to fight that pressure is to remember the gestures they made and their importance.

Subscribed

BAAJA in the balance

I would say the best evidence of both real change and also its limits comes from something that Teixeira doesn’t talk about at all: the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

BAAJA, the permitting reform bill, is long and complicated. If you want to learn more about the details, I would recommend reading briefings from Third Way and Searchlight and listening to what Daniel Palken from Arnold Ventures told The Argument’s Milan Singh. Or you could read Baillee Brown from the Inclusive Abundance Initiative or the Niskanen Center writeup or this collection of links from the Abundance & Growth team at Coefficient Giving.

But if you’re at all familiar with those institutions, it’s immediately obvious that the people hailing this legislation are from the “abundance” faction of the Democratic Party.

That’s great. What’s especially great about BAAJA, though, is that while it’s enthusiastically embraced by Josh Harder and the Build America Caucus, it’s not limited to a niche sect of elected Democrats. It was negotiated by Martin Heinrich and Sheldon Whitehouse, two of the senate’s longtime climate champions. Three years ago, Teixeira wrote his three point plan to fix the Democrats and point two was “Democrats must promote an abundance agenda.”

Well, guess what? Leading Democrats are, in fact, promoting an abundance agenda.

But here’s why I think the glass is only half full on energy. From what I understand based on talking to various people who are in the relevant meetings, most of the discussion inside the caucus is purely about climate politics. Everyone is trying to manage their stakeholders, and a great deal of emphasis is on an effort to get the major green groups to stay neutral on this legislation.

In a full glass universe, Chuck Schumer and Brian Schatz would just say to the greens, “Look, I get that this is a mixed bag from your viewpoint, but when you consider the obvious affordability and national security benefits, it’s a total no-brainer and we’re going to do it no matter what you say.” What we have instead is a glass half empty , where they want to take an abundance approach to energy but they also want to be maximally agreeable about it. The climate people still seem to have the upper hand in intra-party debates and the only reason an abundance approach has a shot is that it genuinely makes more sense as climate policy.

But the most important thing is the policy choices, and there’s been a tremendous evolution in the direction of reality-based energy policy, both in terms of the views that Democrats’ frontline recruits have articulated but also in terms of what mainline Democrats seem prepared to do with BAAJA. This is a big deal and worth celebrating.

The cultural mainstream

Teixeira’s point one, “Democrats Must Move to the Center on Cultural Issues,” is more of a mixed bag than abundance.

But in his new piece, Teixeira refuses to give (or take!) any credit at all. He for example doesn’t mention crime at all, except to quote a piece by Dustin Guastella that says reducing crime is the only non-economic issue that ranks as a high priority for working class voters. This is a good point! And it’s worth observing that not moderate Democrats, not mainstream Democrats, but progressive hero Zohran Mamdani has executed a gigantic turnabout on law and order issues as part of his political success. Nithya Raman, running for mayor of Los Angeles on a similar left-YIMBY political platform has been trying to execute a similar pivot, but has been less deft about pulling it off.

In less-lefty precincts of the party, we have Sherrod Brown winning a police union endorsement and actual cop Johnny Garcia as a prized recruit in Texas. There are thirteen senate Democrats cosponsoring a bill to crack down on organized retail theft. It’s been years since anyone who matters in politics was going with the line that policing isn’t an important part of controlling crime.

As someone who took a lot of shit from a lot of people for standing up for common sense on this issue when it was unfashionable, I 100 percent understand the impulse to feel a little churlish about this. Exactly zero people have apologized to me for the shit they gave me. When leftists write articles claiming I’ve been “wrong about everything,” they don’t even put in a to-be-sure graf that’s like “well he was at least right about the politics of defunding the police, as shown by the fact that even Mamdani now agrees with him.” I am annoyed by this! But it’s insane to deny that there’s been a huge shift. We won the argument!

Teixeira notes that Talarico’s moderation on the sex-segregated sports has been a little bit half-hearted. That’s true! But half-hearted moderation is more than anyone was doing in the 2022 or 2024 cycles. And others — Turek, Rob Sand, Amy Acton — have gone further.

What’s even more significant is governance. Abigail Spanberger has managed to serve for a year as governor of Virginia while kind of quietly allowing the Youngkin-era approach to this to stay in place. It’s unclear where Democrats are going to land on these issues — I feel like most in the party are not actually aware that they “shot first” by trying to issue mandatory trans inclusion rules and that “let individual leagues decide” is actually a major moderation.

But the relevant point is that it’s a topic of debate; the era of delusion is over. Now we’re just going to have to see where things actually land.

Known unknowns

My biggest question for the future is about immigration. Here it seems to me that two things have happened simultaneously:

  • It is universally acknowledged that the Biden border situation was fucked up and unacceptable. By the end of Biden’s term, Democrats were all excited for him to issue executive orders clamping down.

  • Democrats have been radicalized against ICE as an institution.

One certainly can make these two points cohere, but there are genuine tensions. I think what most Democrats want, subjectively, is for the border to become an impermeable force field such that it’s literally impossible for anyone to cross without proper authorization. Then with force field in place, we can go really easy on everyone who’s already inside the country — deport them if they’re convicted of crimes, but if they seem like basically sympathetic people, let them stay. I understand the appeal of this force field approach to immigration, and it very much aligns with my moral intuitions.

The problem is that you literally cannot do this. There is no force field.

This is one of a number of issues — along with basic economic management — where the political question facing Democrats is not really one of finding the right message but one of regaining some measure of credibility with the public.

The only way to accomplish that is to actually win an election and then do a good job. It’s clearly possible to back off Trump’s assault on high-skill legal immigration without losing control of the border. It also should be possible to back away from draconian interior enforcement without losing control of the border. But will the next administration actually pull that off? Voters, reasonably, have some doubts, and the only way to dispel those doubts is going to be to actually do it.

A debate not a delusion

There’s a lot I agree with Teixeira about. The risk of complacency in the wake of a good election result is real.

A contrary risk is that the polls are slightly overstating Democratic strength, the real generic ballot is D+6 instead of D+9, Talarico and Turek end up losing narrowly rather than winning narrowly, and leftists say “see they moderated and it didn’t work, but El-Sayed won.” The left ecosystem is frequently dishonest in their presentation of election results, and I worry about this a lot.

I also worry about the genuine collapse of patriotic sentiments among rank-and-file Democrats, which is hard to deal with because you can’t really just decide tactically to love your country.

Subscribed

Teixeira is also right that a big chunk of the party is genuinely deluded into thinking that if you promise everyone more populist economic policy, they’ll just turn off their brains and stop caring that you want to ban plastic straws and let tons of refugees into the country.

Last but not least, I agree that “heterodoxy” as a solution is a bit overrated. It’s good to recruit good candidates to run in the pivotal senate races. But it would be a lot better for the caucus as a whole to accept that American politics is now quasi-parliamentary and it’s the job of every single Democratic Party senator to say and do things that are helpful to winning Alaska, Iowa, Texas, Kansas, Florida, and North Carolina. But heterodoxy is still a big improvement over rigid orthodoxy!

I would say we have a party that is not deluded but debating its future. That’s normal. It would be bad to get complacent about a good midterm result when the party’s overall national image remains in the toilet.

On the other hand, I don’t think it’s realistic to change the overall national image without having a presidential nominee. You need to set a realistic bar. We are seeing in the campaigns which issue-positions make you look better than a generic Democrat and which make you look worse. The task of advocates for common sense shouldn’t be to blindly cheer, but it also can’t be to just doom and complain. Lots of good things are out there happening, and we need to build on them.

The Traitor in Chief

Trump and his allies hate America and what it stands for

Paul Krugman
Oct 20
 
READ IN APP
 

Trump says Russia is being “fine” on Ukraine

Writing in the New York Times, David Sanger highlights the extent to which Donald Trump is going all out to support Vladimir Putin’s war of aggression in Ukraine:

President Trump’s intensifying effort in the past few weeks to rehabilitate Russia and usher President Vladimir V. Putin back into diplomatic society is remarkable for its speed, its characterization of Mr. Zelensky as the primary obstacle to peace, and its brazen denial that Russia is continuing the war that Mr. Trump says he is trying to end.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Mr. Trump said on Monday, speaking to reporters outside the White House as he left for a campaign rally. “They haven’t been doing much,” he said, making no mention of the Russian missiles and jet-powered drones that have been targeting apartment buildings in Kyiv and Ukraine’s surviving electricity grid.

In contrast, he said, “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us. Remember that.”

As Sanger notes, Trump’s support for Putin is unique in American history. Previous administrations have made deals with erstwhile adversaries, as Nixon did with China, and given up on support for failing allies, as the U.S. did in Vietnam and Afghanistan. But never before have we outright switched sides, let alone supported an aggressor while vilifying that aggressor’s victim.

What makes Trump’s support for Putin even more remarkable is that Russia has, by many accounts, been actively aiding Iran against America in the war Trump started. Who says so? Well, among others, Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. And the aid goes beyond intelligence sharing that has helped Iran target U.S. forces. Russia has also reportedly been sending Iran explosives and weapons components.

What would Republicans be saying if a Democratic president were supporting a foreign dictator even as that dictator was helping another nation kill American troops? They would be crying “treason.” But this is all apparently “fine” with Trump.

What’s going on here? It’s important to understand that — as Phillips O’Brien documents — Trump hasn’t “pivoted” away from Ukraine toward Russia. He has been a Putin supporter all along.

Thus when Trump says that “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine,” who, exactly, does he mean by “we”? He cut off all economic and military aid to Ukraine as soon as he took office. Here’s total support for Ukraine, by country, since January 2025:

True, the U.S. continued to share military intelligence with Ukraine while allowing Ukraine to use Elon Musk’s Starshield and permitting European nations to transfer some U.S. weapons to Ukraine. But these actions cost America nothing. The most you can say is that until recently Trump shied away from actively sabotaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself.

And now even that restraint is gone. According to Volodymyr Zelenskyy, U.S. intelligence sharing was blocked “for some period of time,” although it appears to have resumed for now. Ukraine’s access to Starshield has been limited. And the Washington Post reports that the U.S. has been holding up European transfers of Patriot missiles to Ukraine.

There are two questions here. First, why does Trump love Putin and hate Zelenskyy? Second, why has he ripped off the mask and gone full pro-Russia in the past few weeks?

On the first question, Zelenskyy gave a blunt answer in a recent interview with the Financial Times: Trump, he asserted, has an instinctive affinity for autocrats and the super wealthy: “He speaks about it openly that he loves such people and he respects such people.” That’s clearly right.

I would add three points. First, Trump and his inner circle don’t just love autocrats. They hate democracy and rule of law — which means that they hate America and American values.

Second, Putin-worship was widespread on the authoritarian right even before Trump entered the picture, with many celebrating Russia’s anti-wokeness and perceived masculinity. Remarkably, the valorization of Russia’s supposed toughness has survived despite Russia’s repeated military humiliations. So Trump has been following a well-trodden path.

Finally, whatever else you may say about Zelenskyy, he’s a genuine hero, who showed great personal courage by staying in Kyiv when Russia invaded. And Trump surely resents the fact that Zelenskyy is everything he is not.

The second question is, why now? Why has Trump chosen this moment to switch from covert, deniable support for Putin to overtly, explicitly taking Russia’s side?

As I suggested yesterday, the answer lies precisely in Trump’s collapsing support at home. Nothing he does now is likely to avert Republican catastrophe in the midterms. Republican politicians have been going out of their way to avoid being seen with him on the campaign trail. Trump officials are already lawyering up in preparation for the probes a Democratic Congress will launch.

At this point, then, Trump effectively has nothing left to lose on the political front — and his political bankruptcy has freed him to become his worst self, indulging himself by doing what he always wanted to do — which includes supporting corrupt, murderous dictators.

And there will be much more of this to come. Trump can’t and won’t make America great again. But he can betray everything America stands for, and he’s doing it as we speak.

Our culture is way too eager to embrace deception

We desperately need to rebuild an ethic of probity and integrity.

Matthew Yglesias
Oct 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

This post discusses “You Can See Everything” in some detail. If you have somehow avoided spoilers to this point but are also interested in seeing a highly touted three-hour documentary, I would strongly suggest you go see the movie first before reading the article. The upside is that if you haven’t seen the movie and don’t want to or don’t care about spoilers, I think you should understand the article and its argument just fine. Consider yourself spoiler-warned!

At one point in the brilliant new documentary “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder is pressing Elizabeth Holmes on her honesty, and she preposterously proclaims not only that she was honest about everything that happened with Theranos but that she’s never lied, ever, about anything.

In this moment more than any other we can see that she must be a truly sociopathic liar, because nobody would say something that obviously false. And Fielder really presses her: You never told a white lie? You never said you couldn’t make it to a party because you were feeling sick when actually you just didn’t want to go?

She kind of relents at that point, suggesting she didn’t really mean that kind of lie.

Which is striking because her insistence on her own honesty deprives her of the best possible defense of her conduct, namely the clear reality that lots of successful entrepreneurs lie.

Whatever line divides Elizabeth Holmes, a criminal, from any number of successful and celebrated tech C.E.O.s, it cannot actually be that she said things about her product and her company that aren’t true. Just as we’ve all told white lies to get out of awkward social situations, basically everyone in Silicon Valley is telling some whoppers.

In other words, while almost everyone agrees that lying is bad and you shouldn’t do it, it’s also the case that everybody lies. That’s true to the point that the most obviously dishonest thing a person could do, genuinely, is claim to never lie. And yet, despite the universality of this behavior, I think we’ve come to a point where we’re too tolerant of dishonesty — and, even more so, willfully misleading behavior.

Tech entrepreneurs say lots of stuff that isn’t true

I’m wildly more literal-minded and less creative than Fielder or Lance Oppenheim, so if I were to produce something about Holmes, it would be about my obsession with the fact that she was operating in an industry where people are constantly saying things that aren’t true.

I don’t know anything specific about the Alex Gibney documentary on Elon Musk, but it’s by all accounts a very negative portrait of Musk, and I don’t see how any negative portrait of Musk could avoid the fact that he says a lot of things that aren’t true. Musk’s aspirations for self-driving cars, for example, are a notorious cesspool of overpromising and underdelivering:

And yet, it is also true that in 2026, the Tesla self-driving features are extremely impressive. Tesla provides the best vehicle autonomy available in a consumer car product, and it’s second best behind Waymo in terms of developing an autonomous taxi service. It’s not clear to me that Musk is right that his approach to developing this technology will beat the Google/Waymo approach, but it’s also not clear to me that he’s wrong.

Similarly, SpaceX has been consistently behind Musk’s promised timelines. But if somehow Musk had never spoken in public about SpaceX and just released the products, then I think everyone would agree that the rockets work and Starlink works and it’s all very impressive.

As Musk has become an increasingly political figure, his habit of lying has shifted into increasingly political terrain, which makes him seem increasingly villainous.

But Steve Jobs was also a notorious overpromiser who nonetheless really did deliver impressive technology. As a journalist who is aware of the tech industry but doesn’t really cover it professionally, it’s clear that this kind of whopper is an endemic business strategy. I don’t think you’d reasonably say that Apple or SpaceX are fraudulent business enterprises. But it’s also the case that part of how business gets done in the tech field is you need to paint these glorious visions of the triumphant future, and it doesn’t always work out.

This is not to say that Musk’s behavior was identical to Holmes’s — this was actually litigated and a court ruled that a certain amount of “corporate puffery” is an acceptable, non-fraudulent business practice. Musk’s cars and rockets work; Theranos’s product didn’t. But I do think this culture of hype and overstatement is important context for Holmes’s behavior, along with the evident desire not just in the media but among investors to get behind a heroic female founder.

It also made me think about a more recent fraudster, Sam Bankman-Fried, who pulled a con that was if anything more egregiously illegal.

In contrast to Holmes insisting to Fielder that she would never lie about anything, part of how Bankman-Fried tricked people (certainly including me) is that he was pretty open about the fact that he was a bit shady. His infamous explanation to Matt Levine of “yield farming” made smart people (or at least me) trust him more rather than less because it seemed like he wasn’t insulting our intelligence.

Even in retrospect, I find the whole episode extremely vexing because looking back, the Apollo Program for Biodefense that he was trying to get Congress to enact was a really good idea and FTX’s investment in Anthropic would have paid off enormously had Bankman-Fried gotten away with his scam. FTX’s valuation peaked at $32 billion in 2022 and the Anthropic shares it owned would be worth $75 billion today if they hadn’t been sold in a bankruptcy auction.

That’s not to defend Holmes or Bankman-Fried (whose fraud was, if anything, more egregious) but just to emphasize that there’s a wide range of “fake it ’til you make it” practices out there in the business world, some of which are more legal than others and some of which do pay off.

The era of “reality”

The film does not explore any of this wider context. Instead, it dives deeper into questions about the nature of truth.

In the second half of the film, Fielder collaborates with Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Holmes in a Hulu dramatization of the Theranos story. The film includes both Fielder’s (supposedly) real interactions with the real Seyfried and Seyfried re-enacting conversations that Fielder had with Holmes but could not film because she was in prison at the time. Fielder also confronts Seyfried with the fact that the events portrayed in “The Dropout” are not 100 percent accurate, which makes her a little defensive, but she says it’s just television. This, I think, raises the question of whether the re-enactments that Seyfried and Fielder stage are, in fact, accurate depictions of the conversations they purport to be documenting.

We seem to have a consensus in society that what Holmes did (lying for personal gain) is not okay but that introducing fictional elements into a “based on a true story” miniseries for personal gain is totally fine.

I personally am not so sure about this.

I watched and enjoyed “The Social Network” when it came out, but I think the power of the film is considerably compromised by the fact that in the real world, Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan have been dating since before TheFacebook launched. It doesn’t change the fact that it’s a well-made movie on a lot of levels, but to me ranking it the 10th best movie of the 21st century (like the New York Times did) or even the best movie of the century (like “The Big Picture” did) is a little bit crazy. “Citizen Kane” is inspired by the life of William Randolph Hearst, but it does not present itself as a documentary about William Randolph Hearst. It’s about Charles Foster Kane, a fictional character.

I think it’s cheating to add weight and significance to your character study by saying it’s about a real person but then add depth to your character study by making up critical facts.

Part of the strangeness of the documentary is that while co-director Lance Oppenheim is a documentary filmmaker, Fielder just isn’t. “Nathan for You” and “The Rehearsal” are unscripted and feature real people rather than actors, but they’re not news shows or documentaries. They’re closer to the spirit of what we’ve come to know as reality television, which is fake — it just doesn’t involve professional actors or screenwriters.

The current president of the United States, of course, was a very successful reality TV personality before he was a politician. And I’m sort of obsessed with the fact that a guy who is transparently a huge liar is often praised by his supporters for authenticity.

On the left, too, people who want to underplay the importance of issue-positioning often talk about the value of authenticity. Clearly the thing that people call “authenticity” is in fact a relevant political skill. But Donald Trump is a critical illustration of the fact that the actual skill here is not being authentic; it’s acting. Seyfried-as-Holmes seems much more authentic — which is to say relaxed, un-mannered, and natural — than Holmes as herself. That’s because Seyfried has been acting professionally for her whole adult life and she’s very good at it. A normal person’s authentic reaction to being asked questions on camera is to be nervous and weird.

Accurate information is important

Probably my worst take ever was that back in 2010 I defended advocates making overstated ridership estimates for high-speed rail projects on the grounds that investing in high-speed rail was a good idea and that the advocates on the other side were also being dishonest so it didn’t really make sense to insist on unilateral disarmament.

The vast majority of people, I think, manage to avoid ever stating “lying is fine” as baldly as I did.

But I also think it’s pretty clear that the vast majority of the people involved in funding political advocacy organizations — on most sides of most issues — have decided that the stakes of politics are so high and their enemies so low and unprincipled that the only way to succeed is primarily by funding propaganda efforts.

Very little priority is given to trying to support truth-seeking inquiry. You can see this in the generally low quality of the work coming out of political advocacy shops. But you can also see it in the overall shape of the staffing. The teams are too big and too heavily weighted toward relatively cheap people with relatively little experience or technical credentials. And these kinds of attitudes spread. Just as the line between “corporate puffery” or a Jobsian “reality distortion field” (his ability to convince people that the impossible was possible) and an outright fraud can be murkier than we might like to think. Movements that start out doing a little light propaganda, deliberate oversimplification, or aggressive spin eventually start putting out commentary that is completely nonsensical.

The MAGA movement reasoning that cutting imports will increase G.D.P. is a particularly egregious big-picture example. And it’s notable that nothing has done more damage to the MAGA political project than the analytical errors behind the war in Iran and Trump’s trade policy. The basic normative core of Trumpism would be in much better shape if the actual policy analysis had been better.

The ongoing fiasco of California high-speed rail is trivial in contrast to the invasion of Iran, but it’s salient to me because that was the specific thing I embarrassed myself defending propaganda about.

The truth is, a high-speed rail network linking San Francisco, San Jose, and Sacramento to Los Angeles with onward connections going to San Diego, Phoenix, and Las Vegas is a perfectly reasonable idea. If such a train existed, lots of people would ride it and there would be ancillary benefits for the smaller markets on the way like Fresno and Modesto. But building trains turns out to be a somewhat complicated engineering project that involves a lot of tradeoffs. A train like this would be useful but not infinitely useful (people fly and it’s fine), so whether it’s worth it actually depends on the technical implementation details. Pushing ahead with furious political momentum and no real plan turned out to be a recipe for a train to nowhere. Not an administration-killing fiasco like the war in Iran, but certainly a huge waste of money that torched the credibility of rail advocacy and left the whole project further from its goal than it was before.

What these things have in common is that public policy questions are genuinely hard.

The bigger and more important the issue you’re working on, the harder they get. You can’t transform the global energy system or rework all of American health care with a lot of propaganda and nonsense. A logic of superficial sloganeering is how you get reasoning like “if exclusionary zoning is bad, then inclusionary zoning must be good” when, if you actually model it properly, inclusionary zoning makes housing shortages worse.

A culture of probity

If Steve Jobs says Apple is never going to make a stylus and then years later they roll out the Apple Pencil, it’s not the biggest deal. Jobs was notorious to Apple-watchers for pulling this kind of thing.

When the first iPhone launched, it had inferior data speeds and there was no App Store. Instead of saying something reasonable like, “this is an incredibly impressive product in a lot of ways that also has some obvious shortcomings that we will iterate on in coming years,” he made a big deal of insisting that actually the data speed was fine and web apps were way better than native applications anyway.

Then lo and behold, he introduces an iPhone with 3G speeds and it’s way more popular.

I think it’s interesting that successful tech companies have managed to create the kind of corporate culture where they bullshit about complicated technical issues (literal rocket science in Musk’s case) while retaining a reasonable degree of internal discipline around the fact that the products have to actually work. Obviously this does generate the occasional Holmes whose products don’t work or investor enthusiasm for something absurd like WeWork. But products that do work keep emerging from this milieu.

With Jobs, the bullshit was at least cabined to a defined sphere of consumer products. Musk, though, is deeply involved in real-world politics while constantly saying untrue things about public affairs in a way that I find deeply disturbing. Sam Altman is not perpetrating a fraud on the public — OpenAI’s products are incredibly impressive — but he also has a terrible record on honesty that I find very disturbing. Anthropic’s claims to be more ethical strike me as credible, but that is possibly the Bankman-Fried version of ethical rather than the “I’m telling you true things” version of ethical.

Holmes herself probably meant well in some sense. She wasn’t running a smash and grab. She didn’t sell her shares and abscond to Malaysia. Had her machine worked, that would’ve been great for humanity. But it didn’t work. She needed more time and money to keep working on it, and the way to do that was to lie — fake it ’til you make it.

Trump’s supporters think that he is basically right about the need to crush the woke left and that the ends fundamentally justify the means on this score. The climate movement thinks their issue is so critically important that they need to tell everyone that a crash decarbonization program can be executed with zero tradeoffs.

As Dan Williams writes, the idea of “speaking truth to power” becomes an excuse for all kinds of intellectuals to skip the part where you just speak the truth — your allies are the noble underdogs, after all.

In the realm of public affairs, I think these attitudes are toxic. They make it extremely hard to actually govern because you create a group of confused people who don’t understand the levers of power they’re trying to operate. You’re propagating a set of norms in which clear, accurate communication is disparaged and it’s hard to adapt to new questions swiftly. You’re also creating a landscape that is friendly to frauds and grifters. As bad as Trump is, there’s something almost more disturbing about the way that JD Vance and Marco Rubio both explained the mechanics of the Trump con perfectly before deciding to become the two leading succession options.

As a work of art, the nesting doll of Nathan Fielder interrogating Amanda Seyfried in character as Elizabeth Holmes about the nature of truth is fascinating. But the extent to which the very top layers of politics and business now operate on this level of mind-bending dishonesty is disturbing.

And the answer, to be clear, is not to say that the bad guys are so vicious and opportunistic that we need to beat them by any means necessary! It’s to try to rebuild an ethic of basic probity, honesty, and factual accuracy from the ground up.

“You Can See Everything” and the nature of liars

A movie review, plus some thoughts on dishonesty, belief, and human communication.

Noah Smith
Oct 21
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

WARNING: This post contains spoilers for the movie You Can See Everything.

A few days ago, I had the great pleasure of seeing Nathan Fielder’s new film, You Can See Everything. I’ve been a fan of Fielder’s work for a long time, so I basically knew what to expect, but it was still incredible — every bit as good as you’ve heard. Go see it if you haven’t.

The film is a documentary about the notorious fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (of Theranos fame) and her partner Billy Evans. But it’s also sort of a horror movie about liars. That was interesting enough that it made me want to write a post about the movie — about the nature of lying, and of belief, and of human communication in general.

If you read even a little bit about the history of Theranos, there is absolutely no question that Elizabeth Holmes is a deliberate fraudster and a prolific, aggressive liar. Holmes presented potential investors with fake financial results in 2015. She personally added fake logos of pharmaceutical companies to Theranos’ own reports. She flatly stated that Theranos didn’t dilute blood samples, then admitted in court that she intentionally concealed the fact that they did dilute blood samples. Theranos employees detailed the whole deliberate fraud in anonymous online posts years before the story broke.

But You Can See Everything doesn’t cover much of this actual history. Fielder doesn’t bother to indict Holmes and prove that she committed fraud — the court case already did that. Instead, he offers a window into the psychology of someone who could commit such an epic fraud. Holmes and Evans allow Fielder into their home with the goal of proving that they’re just regular, good people trying to improve the world. Instead, Fielder depicts the couple — quite accurately — as monsters of deception and manipulation.

It’s doubtful that any other filmmaker could have done nearly as good a job of this. The blurry line between what’s real and what’s fake has always been a major theme of Nathan Fielder’s work — he loves hiring actors to simulate past and future interactions, constructing facsimiles of whole buildings, and so on. And of course he’s very skilled with the tricks of the visual storyteller’s trade, using deliberate cuts, camera angles, and creative edits to make the audience think and feel what he wants them to.

Whereas many filmmakers would have regarded Holmes as a subject to be studied, Fielder seems to see her as an opponent to be challenged and beaten. If he can shoot what Holmes wants him to shoot, but ultimately seize control of the narrative, then he’s the more powerful storyteller. This, I think, is why he doesn’t bring in outside evidence to show what a well-documented liar Holmes is. That would be cheating. Instead, he has to venture into the monster’s lair alone, and defeat her in single combat. He has to film the movie that she asks him to film, and let her show him only what she wants him to see, and still have audiences walk away having seen the story that he wants to tell.

And of course he succeeds, because he’s very good, but also because he gets to edit the film, and editing is more powerful than acting. Score one for the good guys.

(Major spoilers begin here.)

How does Fielder win the contest? Over the course of You Can See Everything, he captures Elizabeth Holmes saying a number of strange and extraordinary things:

  1. Near the beginning, Holmes tells Fielder that she’s never lied in her life. After he presses her, she half-admits that she may have told small white lies out of convenience. But the audience gets to watch her repeatedly assert something obviously, fantastically false, always with the same sincere, relaxed, wide-eyed expression on her face.

  2. Later on, Fielder shows Holmes the famous “Who’s on first?” comedy routine, which she claims never to have seen. After watching it, Holmes claims not to have realized that the baseball player’s name is “Who” — thus missing the entire point of the sketch.

  3. Fielder recruits Amanda Seyfried, who played Holmes in the miniseries The Dropout, to help him figure out what’s going on with Holmes and her partner. At one point, Holmes is calling on the phone from prison. Seyfried asks Holmes if she knew Seyfried would be on the call, and Holmes says “I’m not sure if I knew.”

It’s moments like these, more than any simple lie, that reveal Holmes’ true character. In fact, Fielder seems like he passes up several chances to catch Holmes in a straight-up lie on camera. After all, what would one lie, or even three lies, really prove? Everyone lies sometimes, and capturing a couple of those instances during weeks of living with Holmes wouldn’t be hard. It would be a cheap trick, and it wouldn’t really prove that Holmes is a liar in general.

Instead, the moments Fielder captures demonstrate something deeper and far more unnerving about Holmes’ relationship to the truth. Holmes is a very special and powerful kind of liar — someone for whom deception and manipulation are as automatic and as continuous as breathing.

Type 1 liars and Type 2 liars

“Maybe it’s something inside/ Maybe it’s something I can’t explain” — Henry Rollins

Suppose you want to tell a lie. Suppose you made a blood test device that didn’t work, and you want investors to believe it did work, so that they’ll give you money, and your parents and your boyfriend and the national press will give you fame and respect. Here are two ways you could tell that lie:

Method 1: Deception

First, assess the truth of the matter. Realize that the device doesn’t work. Then think about which facts you have to falsify or conceal in order to convince investors that the device does work. Concoct a fake story with those specific fake facts, and tell that story to the investors.

Method 2: Fantasy

Ignore the real world completely, and simply imagine the world in which the device does work. Start describing that world to the investors. Watch which details of your description grab the investors’ interest or seem to convince them, and repeat those over and over (adding additional detail and embellishments if necessary).

Ultimately, these two types of lying achieve the same goal — they convince your victims of things that aren’t true, so that you can take advantage of them. But the first method has some distinct disadvantages. It’s very costly in terms of memory — you have to remember not only the fake story you told, but also what’s actually real. You’re carrying around two realities in your head — the truth, and your lies — and you have to keep them separate and consistent.

That’s hard! It’s the reason for the old Latin proverb “Mendacem memorem esse oportet” — “A liar must be good at remembering”.

But what if you didn’t have to be good at remembering? Method 2 lets you dispense with the truth entirely. You don’t have to think about what’s real — you only remember the fantasy world you’ve created. The more you tell your fantasy stories, the better you remember them — the memory of saying the things begins to feel as real, or almost as real, as a memory of the things actually happening would have felt.¹

The downside of Method 2 is that it’s much bigger and more grandiose. You’re not just falsifying a few details; you’re spinning an entire fantasy world. That takes a lot of effort — a lot of narrations and spiels and pronouncements and conversations. The lie has to become your life. You have to actually move into the fantasy world you created, and live there 24/7.

To use Method 2 really well also requires a very unusual type of personality. Most people instinctively go around constructing a model of the truth — they’re constantly thinking “What’s really going on in the world around me?”. This interferes with Type 2 lying — if you have them create a fictitious autobiography for themselves, they won’t actually believe in it, because it conflicts with the model of the real world that they’re always automatically generating.

For the really good Type 2 liars, “What’s really going on in the world around me?” often just isn’t a very interesting or important question. Instead, they’re thinking “How can I get things from this person I’m talking to?”. They’re like a hill-climbing algorithm — a large language model that bullshits people, observes the results, and then learns to bullshit in the direction that achieves more money, more fame, more whatever. These are the pathological liars you’ve heard about.²

Billy Evans, Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, is a Type 1 liar. In the middle part of You Can See Everything, Fielder easily catches Evans in a number of falsehoods. Evans is always clumsily trying to keep Fielder from the truth or conceal information in order to defend Holmes’ reputation. He knows, more or less, what the truth is; all of his lies are defined in opposition to that truth, and so they’re easy to catch, because they don’t hang together in a coherent whole.

But Holmes is the real deal — an incredibly powerful and proficient Type 2 liar. I went to see You Can See Everything with a big group of people, and much of the discussion after the movie revolved around whether or not Holmes actually believes the things she tells people. I argued that “belief” was simply the wrong way to think about it.

Think about this question for a moment: What does it actually mean to “believe” something? For economists, it means that you’re willing to bet on something being true.³ We believe the dining room table exists because we walk around the table when we go through the dining room, instead of trying to walk right through it. For economists, a “belief” is part of someone’s model of reality.

But in a lot of cases, “belief” actually means something else — it means a type of emotion. Go ask a devout Christian or Muslim if they believe that God is omnipotent. They’ll say “Yes.” But as everyone who has taken a freshman philosophy class knows, true omnipotence is a logically incoherent concept. Can God create a rock too heavy for Him to lift? And so on. When people say “I believe God is omnipotent”, what they mean is that when they utter the sentence “God is omnipotent”, they get a warm feeling of rightness — the feeling that they’ve just said something true. They might die for that belief, without ever having a clear grasp of what it meant.

My guess — which is supported by a fair amount of psychological research, though it’s not a consensus — is that Type 2 liars “believe” their fantasies in the second sense, but often not the first. If you forced them to bet on their fantasies being correct in some measurable sense — a medical device producing reliable test results, or Amanda Seyfried being present in a room — they might or might not make that bet. But they feel a warm, good feeling when they utter their fantasies, because those fantasies will presumably get them what they want. To a Type 2 liar, the questions “Do I believe this?” and “Is it to my advantage to say this?” are not different questions.

Human beings talk to each other for many reasons. We want companionship and entertainment. We want people to understand us. We need to gather and convey information about the world. And yes, we need to get each other to do things for us. A Type 2 liar is someone for whom the last of these imperatives dominates the others.

Here’s what I’m guessing is happening with Elizabeth Holmes in the weird moments I described above. When she tells Nathan Fielder she’s never lied, she does so because telling him she had lied seems like it would be contrary to her purposes — it would presumably make the tone of his documentary more negative and accusatory. So she says “I’ve never lied.” And when she speaks those words, she gets a warm feeling of having said something right and good.

When she claims not to understand the “Who’s on first?” sketch, it’s because seeming not to understand it serves her purpose — it paints her as someone on the autism spectrum, implying that she just thinks different, and that the people who sent her to prison for fraud just don’t understand the strange way she thinks. And of course, the sense that she’s successfully promulgating that useful image gives her the warm feeling that religious people get when they say “God is omnipotent.”

The most telling moment, though, is during the phone call from prison, when Amanda Seyfried asks if Holmes knew she was in the room, and Holmes says “I’m not sure if I knew.” This statement seems nonsensical — how could you not know whether you knew something like that? — until you think about it from the perspective of a Type 2 liar. Holmes is actually saying: “I’m not sure whether it’s to my advantage to say I knew or that I didn’t know.”

To the Type 2 liar, uncertainty about your own best interest feels like epistemic uncertainty.

This is what I think is going on, anyway. My guess is that Nathan Fielder saw the nature of Holmes’ personality pretty quickly, or even surmised it in advance, and simply made sure to include scenes that illustrate it to the audience. At one point, he wonders whether she’s “the most manipulative person who has ever lived.”⁴ This is why I see You Can See Everything as a sort of monster movie — a character sketch of a kind of alien that walks unseen among us, insensate to the truth, forever babbling at us in an effort to make us do its bidding.

And Nathan defeats the monster. He beards Elizabeth Holmes in her den, confronts her on ground of her own choosing, lets her do the talking, and still manages to expose her for what she is. And having exposed her, he is magnanimous in victory. In the film’s closing montage, he paints Holmes as a defanged predator — a criminal behind bars, a sociopath who enjoys being a mom, a woman who honestly loves her clumsy liar boyfriend in whatever strange way they both know how.

It’s a very good movie.

2

Actually, the overlap isn’t complete. What I’m calling “Type 2 liars” are actually a subset of what psychologists call “pathological liars”; a different subset are people who lie compulsively with no thought for personal gain. Also, the term “pathological liar” is contentious and disputed, and means different things to different people. Welcome to psychology!

3

Actually, not quite. Several other things affect people’s willingness to bet on outcomes. One of these is idiosyncratic risk — if Trump winning the election would really hurt my business, I may bet a lot of money on him winning even if I don’t think it’s likely, just as a hedge. Another factor is risk aversion, which is different for different people. And a third complicating factor is someone’s portfolio of other bets — I might bet on Trump winning the election just to hedge another bet I made on Trump losing the election. So you can’t actually tell what people believe from how they bet.

4

That’s an exaggeration, obviously — Elizabeth Holmes is in prison, while plenty of master manipulators are still walking free. There might even be one living in the White House right now.

Trump is Destroying Americans’ Healthcare

Twelve million have lost coverage — and it’s getting worse

Paul Krugman
Oct 21
 
READ IN APP
 

On the eve of the midterm election, American families are feeling financially stressed As the chart above shows, the percentage of families who say that their financial situation is good has plunged. For the first time since the post-Covid inflation of 2022, it has fallen below the percentage who say that their financial situation is bad.

Rising prices are the obvious explanation for this stress. And while presidents usually have much less influence on the economy than is generally recognized, the current outbreak of high inflation is all on Donald Trump. He began this with two wars of choice: one, a trade war with his destructive tariffs, and then an unwinnable military war in the most important energy transit point in the world.

There is, however, a third factor behind Americans’ anger, and it isn’t getting nearly as much attention as it should. There has been a catastrophic decline in health insurance coverage combined with sharply rising premiums for many of those who have managed to hang on to their coverage. And this, too, is all on Trump.

Here’s what happened: Trump and his congressional minions refused to renew the expanded subsidies that had made health insurance affordable for millions of Americans during the Biden years. At the same time the One Big Beautiful Bill imposed punitive work requirements that made it far more difficult for families to obtain Medicaid coverage.

And we haven’t felt the full effect of these changes yet — Republicans tried to backload the effects of the OBBB so that much of the pain will come after the midterms. But the consequences of this attack on healthcare have already been dire.

By June 2026 enrollment in Medicaid and the Childrens’ Health Insurance Program had declined by more than 6 million since January 2025; 2.5 million of those losing coverage were children. KFF estimates that enrollment in individual plans, mainly via the Affordable Care Act, was down almost 5 million by June. The redoubtable Charles Gaba, putting these numbers together with other information, estimates that around 12 million Americans have lost health insurance under Trump 2.0.

That’s a lot of lost coverage, even in a nation as big as ours. And because many of the savage cuts Trump and his allies have imposed on healthcare have yet to kick in, the situation will get much worse in the years ahead. It’s worth noting thatkicking children off healthcare coverage is especially personally and socially destructive because it compromises their health and earnings potential for their entire lifetimes.

By the way, Trump, after all these years, is once again promising that he’ll come up with a “truly great” healthcare plan any day now. He’s now saying that he’ll send money directly to Americans, stopping payments to insurance companies — thereby demonstrating that he still has no idea how insurance works.

In any case, we’re now in the midst of an enormous healthcare disaster — a disaster that is receiving surprisingly little media coverage with, as far as I can tell, no recent articles on massive coverage losses in any of the major newspapers. I know that there’s a lot going on, but this seems odd.

Voters, however, have noticed. KFF’s tracking poll finds that the cost of healthcare is near the top of voters’ economic worries:

As an overall issue, health care ranks second only to the overall cost of living — and above the Iran war:

This ongoing healthcare disaster is all on Trump and his party. And again, voters appear to have noticed, giving Democrats a large and growing edge on the issue:

So if there is a blue wave 13 days from now, it won’t just be the result of inflation and Trump’s vainglorious wars. It will also in part be the result of a quiet but massive healthcare disaster.

And ultimately, of course, the political implications are a secondary concern. What really matters is that Trump and his party have done all they can to deny healthcare to millions of Americans. They have done this partly to save money — not to reduce the budget deficit, but to make room for tax cuts for the wealthy. They have also done it out of sheer cruelty.

There are many terrible things happening in America right now, from the debacle in Iran to the depredations of ICE. But the healthcare disaster, which will ruin many people financially and in some cases kill Americans who can no longer afford essential care, deserves much more attention than it is getting.

I’m way more online than I should be, and you probably are too.
