Bernie Sanders did not invent populist rhetoric

All Democrats can (and do) have a little class warfare as a treat.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 10
 
READ IN APP
 

A lot of the Democratic candidates who did well last week say things about the political economy of the United States that sound like things Bernie Sanders might say.

Many on the left have pointed this out in their post-election commentary, and I agree that it’s factually accurate.

But the reason for this is that Bernie Sanders’s rhetoric about the need to unrig a rigged economic system, check the power of billionaire donors, and fight for the little guy rather than for special interests is not distinctive. It’s the kind of language Democrats have used throughout the existence of America’s oldest political party.

That’s why I find it strange that Sanders’s communications director, Jeremy Slevin, insists that pre-2016 presidential candidates did not engage in the kind of non-specific populist rhetoric that we heard from James Talarico. Slevin goes so far as to say that “anyone pretending otherwise is obviously full of shit.”

Jeremy Slevin
@jeremyslevin
Democrats did not sound like this before Bernie Sanders ran for president and anyone pretending otherwise is obviously full of shit
James Talarico @jamestalarico
A young man at our town hall asked if I was pushing class warfare. I told him: “We already have class warfare in this country — billionaires are waging war on the rest of us.”
4:09 PM · Nov 5, 2026 · 127K Views
96 Replies · 1.11K Reposts · 10.9K Likes

This is one of these things where I think a lot of people who are younger than me are genuinely confused about the history of American party politics. It is absolutely true that in the specific context of the 2016 presidential campaign, Hillary Clinton campaigned on some slightly bizarre anti-populist ideas about how breaking up banks won’t end racism, followed by putting forward an unusually character-focused general-election campaign against Donald Trump.

But that is what was unusual. Both the effort to win a primary largely by out-woking Sanders and the effort to win a general election with character attacks rather than issue appeals were idiosyncratic.

Ryan O’Donnell, who graduated from college 19 years ago, says that if I’d been working campaigns 20 years ago like him, I’d know that Bernie innovated specifically by “centering the idea that billionaires and corporations have rigged the system.”

Ryan O'Donnell
@ryanodonnellpa
some of us worked campaigns 20 years ago, and there's a real difference between promising to fight for the middle class and tax the wealthy vs candidates across the party centering the idea that billionaires + corporations have rigged the system and made your life more expensive
Matthew Yglesias @mattyglesias
I think a lot of young people are sincerely confused about this, but it's just not the case that Bernie Sanders invented the idea of campaigning on economic fairness themes — this is the common currency of ~all Democratic Party campaigns.
5:48 PM · Nov 5, 2026 · 15.4K Views
6 Replies · 30 Reposts · 232 Likes

Now, here I think the tragic reality is just that I am 45, and as a result, my political memory goes back further than 20 years.

But even within the O’Donnell window, I recall Barack Obama’s 2008 speech to the A.F.L.-C.I.O. in which he said that “for far too long, through both Democratic and Republican administrations, the system has been rigged against everyday Americans by the lobbyists that Wall Street uses to get its way.” Obama’s 2012 campaign against Mitt Romney was famously populist in its linking of Romney’s regressive tax agenda to his personal wealth and his work in private equity. I’ve often cited Obama’s second term as a break point in Democratic Party thinking, but the difference is that after Obama’s re-election (and especially after the 2014 midterms), Democrats moved left on social issues and energy.

Notably, Sanders, who used to be an immigration moderate and an opponent of gun control, also moved left on social issues.

On economics, though, while Bernie has clearly had a lot of influence within the party since his 2016 run, it’s just not true that his populist rhetorical flourishes are distinctive.

Distinctive Bernie ideas have gained ground

You can’t really talk about Bernie Sanders without talking about Medicare for All.

The concept of single-payer health care is, of course, not original to him. But it was Bernie, distinctively, who in the wake of the Affordable Care Act’s passage said “not good enough” and revived the whole idea of a push for big bang health-care reform.

What’s more, Bernie has literally redefined the meaning of Medicare for All as a slogan. When I started my career, Medicare for All was John Conyers’s H.R. 676, which was more literally modeled on how Canadian health care works — it featured a hard-capped global budget, for example — than Sanders’s version of Medicare for All. I would like to see a Medicare for All initiative that’s modeled on Australian Medicare rather than Canadian Medicare. But unlike Sanders, I do not wield a lot of influence over intra-caucus health-care politics.

Bernie also played an important secondary role to Elizabeth Warren in persuading the Biden administration to ditch a generation of consumer-focused antitrust policy in favor of a neo-Brandeisian approach that emphasizes corporate power and market concentration. While that hasn’t gotten nearly as much mass public attention as Medicare for All, it is, if anything, a clearer example of Sanders’s influence, because his people genuinely did run all the agencies.

Last but not least, Bernie has exerted a lot of influence over the specific idea of a wealth tax.

As one of the few people who actually read his book, I am aware that Thomas Piketty proposed a wealth tax in “Capital in the Twenty-First Century” as a revenue-neutral idea. When I interviewed him, he criticized property taxes as falling heavily on the middle class and for not properly distinguishing between a situation where you have $600,000 in housing wealth and a situation where you have a $600,000 home and $480,000 in mortgage debt. He wanted to replace property taxes with a progressive net-wealth tax to encourage a more equitable distribution of financial assets.

And this is what comes to mind when I think about distinctively Sandersite economic-policy ideas.

These are ideas that Democratic Party nominees have mostly not embraced, and they’re influential enough that it’s plausible the 2028 nominee will embrace one or all of them but also controversial enough that the 2028 nominee might embrace none of them.

This rhetorical stuff, on the other hand, is just how Democrats talk.

Democrats are always doing “populism”

The whole idea of the Democratic Party not only is but always has been that an electoral republic needs a mass political organization the purpose of which is to combat the concentrated power of financial capital. I am aware that the musical “Hamilton” is not a literal work of history, but part of its power is that Lin-Manuel Miranda does a good job of capturing these basic themes of American political conflict.

In the first cabinet rap battle, Thomas Jefferson calls out Alexander Hamilton’s financial schemes as dirty dealing by well-connected political insiders (“His plan would have the government assume states’ debts / Now, place your bets as to who that benefits / The very seat of government where Hamilton sits”) and celebrates productive labor over financial machinations (“In Virginia, we plant seeds in the ground / We create, you just wanna move our money around / This financial plan is an outrageous demand”).

Contemporary Democrats, of course, reject Jefferson as a slaver (Hamilton retorts, “your debts are paid ‘cause you don’t pay for labor”) and no longer hold Jefferson-Jackson Day fundraisers.

But the reason the dinners originally had that name is that Jefferson and Andrew Jackson were the founders of the party. Jackson, like Jefferson, was a slaver and extremely un-woke. But the economic-policy issue at the center of Jackson’s presidency was his effort to kill the Bank of the United States, which he and his allies characterized as a system-rigging hydra of economic and political influence that threatened the true spirit of democracy.

I don’t have time to do the entire political history of the United States, but let’s just yadda yadda yadda to the first presidential acceptance speech that I remember watching. Bill Clinton said:

I was raised to believe the American Dream was built on rewarding hard work. But we have seen the folks of Washington turn the American ethic on its head.

For too long those who play by the rules and keep the faith have gotten the shaft, and those who cut corners and cut deals have been rewarded.

People are working harder than ever, spending less time with their children, working nights and weekends at their jobs instead of going to P.T.A. and Little League or Scouts. And their incomes are still going down. Their taxes are still going up. And the costs of health care, housing, and education are going through the roof.

Meanwhile, more and more of our best people are falling into poverty even though they work 40 hours a week. Our people are pleading for change, but government is in the way. It has been hijacked by privileged private interests.

Clinton, of course, was not a distinctively populist Democrat on economics. What made him distinctive as a candidate was that he embraced the death penalty, criticized Jesse Jackson for hosting Sister Souljah, and otherwise had a moderate approach to culture. There’s a progressive critique of the substance of Clintonomics, but the way this critique worked — former Labor Secretary Robert Reich is its canonical voice — was that Clinton betrayed the promise of his populist campaign with his governance choices.

But then right after Clinton, the nominee was Al Gore, whose campaign slogan was “the people, not the powerful” and whose speeches were full of themes about a rigged system, such as “whether you’re starting out to raise your own family or getting ready to retire after a lifetime of hard work, so often powerful forces and powerful interests stand in your way and the odds seem stacked against you, even as you do what’s right for you and your family.” Next up was John Kerry, whose campaign, of course, talked a lot about national security but whose economic message was focused on the evils of Benedict Arnold C.E.O.s who were shipping your job overseas.

It’s true that Hillary Clinton largely eschewed these themes, but she’s the exception; the populist rhetorical mood is the connective tissue that holds the Democratic Party together across space and time.

Governing matters!

It’s a good idea for politicians to use good slogans and put good zingers in their speeches. But governing actually matters a lot.

I think it’s kind of weird that economic populist types who are way more left-wing than I am are excited about Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, largely on the basis of the way she blasted the data center industry even though she was explicitly disavowing any kind of income tax for Texas.

I am (famously) not that left-wing, and this is too right-wing for me. Texas is a fast-growing, high-inequality state with a high poverty rate and no Medicaid expansion. If they adopted the same 3 percent flat income tax as Louisiana (not exactly a hotbed of leftist politics), they could raise a ton of money while still having a tax competition advantage vis-a-vis Oklahoma and New Mexico, to say nothing of New York and California.

I very, very rarely write articles slamming Democrats for a lack of progressive ambition, but I think this is a real whiff on policy substance — though admittedly she’d have to run harder toward the center on culture to be able to pull it off.

Regardless, the point is that sane people don’t just care what politicians say — they care what they do.

Sanders doesn’t just criticize Obama for failing to invoke populist rhetorical tropes; he embraces a leftist conspiracy theory about Obama’s handling of the financial crisis. Progressives think it was wrong of Bill Clinton to embrace deficit reduction and at the time they were furious about free trade (today Abdul El-Sayed has emerged as a big tariff critic) and the now-forgotten 1996 Telecommunications Act. I am on the side of Obama and Clinton about that stuff, which is part of why I’m not enthusiastic about the idea of a bunch of left-factionalists running economic policy in 2029.

But this is not an argument about whether politicians should vow to fight for the little guy against the rigged system where special interests screw you over. Everyone thinks Democrats should run like that!

And beyond rhetoric, it is genuinely outrageous how Trump has prioritized the interests of his A.I. executive benefactors over the public interest in regulating this industry. That’s something every Democrat should say because the voters agree with it and because it’s true.

As a candidate for office, though, what’s distinctive about Talarico is that he took more moderate positions than establishment Democrats do on oil and gas and on transgender issues while criticizing the Biden record on immigration. He sounds like Bernie on economics in the sense that all Democrats sound broadly populist in their rhetoric and have for literally hundreds of years.

Compact

The Madness of Therapy Culture

By Ashley Frawley • 10 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to be Disordered
By Fredrik DeBoer
Simon & Schuster, 336 pages, $30

Traumatized: The New Politics of Public Suffering
By Catherine Liu
Verso, 192 pages, $24.95

More than a decade ago, I noticed that the walls at the university where I taught were plastered with posters designed to raise “awareness” about mental health. When students began to tell me that they were passionate about mental health, I began to suspect that the word was taking on new meanings. But it wasn’t until one passed me a leaflet in the foyer unhelpfully informing me that one in four people suffer from “mental health” that I understood what was happening. Somewhere along the way, the boundaries between mental health and mental illness had become blurred until the former meant the latter. 

Two new books, Fredrik deBoer’s All in Your Head and Catherine Liu’s Traumatized, draw attention to one of the strangest achievements of contemporary therapy culture. Even as psychological suffering has become more visible, it has become increasingly difficult to speak bluntly about its degrees, causes, and uneven spread. Everything becomes curiously melded together and flattened out. Hence, when the British royals set out some years ago to inform everyone that “we all have mental health,” no one should have mistaken what that meant. Mental health is a continuum or spectrum, we are often told, and somewhere along it sit students with exam stress and people convinced their neighbors are poisoning their water. Everyone is in some sense ill.

Well, not everyone. Even as we are all being told we belong somewhere on the “mental health” spectrum, the World Health Organization is calling for an end to “coercive practices in mental health.” The UN Disability Committee is urging states to pursue “the abolition of substitute decision-making regimes” in favor of “supported” alternatives for those we once called “mentally ill,” but who are now variously “people with mental health conditions” or “psychosocial disabilities.” These are people whose suffering often expressly means they are unable to make decisions for themselves. The rest of us are presumed fragile, but the psychotic is increasingly presumed sovereign. As deBoer writes, it has become “our transcendent obligation to pretend that a man in the grip of psychosis [is] somehow still free.”

DeBoer and Liu both show that attempts to flatten out the experience of suffering, disability, and mental illness fail to accomplish their purported aims, such as “destigmatizing” and expanding access to care. This is because reality, whether in the form of the severity of impairment or of social class, eventually asserts itself, with the consequences falling on those least able to bear them. 

For all the high-level talk of the need for mentally ill people to speak for themselves, it is rarely the severely ill or disabled doing the speaking. DeBoer describes a process whereby the relatively privileged claim conditions once associated with severe impairment, what he calls the “gentrification of disability.” The most egregious example is the expansion of the label of autism from those who will never speak or care for themselves to people who incorporate their diagnosis into a successful professional identity. But it is the latter, deBoer says, who now set the parameters of the debate. The most profoundly affected “have no ability to engage in debates that have profound consequences for them,” he writes, while those “who most actively engage in the effort to define autism and how society should accommodate it are overwhelmingly among the educated professional class and need society’s accommodation the least.” The “autism community” rejects gradations of disability on the grounds that they create a hierarchy, but the hierarchy asserts itself all the same when a mother finds that her adult son who needs round-the-clock care has nowhere to go.

In Traumatized, Liu identifies a parallel “gentrification of suffering,” in which a universalized language of trauma obscures the material and historical circumstances in which people suffer. She points to Oprah Winfrey’s The Me You Can’t See (2021), an Apple TV series that renders the pain of someone like Lady Gaga in the same language as a Syrian boy who lost his home and brother to war. What’s more, war and its causes recede into the background, treated almost like “a natural disaster the young men must endure.” Unpacking the language of trauma, Liu shows how we are invited to wallow in pain as the great equalizer, and to see emotion as the thing that matters most. The good subject must learn to “leverage her suffering for progressive politics and fame and fortune,” which becomes a new kind of bootstrapping for the professional managerial age. 

“Compared to mental health, poverty is tough to deal with.”

Compared to mental health, poverty is tough to deal with, and unpleasant to look at. If you can separate it into these isolable parts (trauma, in Liu’s focus, but elsewhere “adverse childhood experiences,” “toxic stress,” “food insecurity,” and on and on), you can attend to each, and maybe the whole injustice will become so much more tolerable, like a bad piece of furniture that’s really not so bad with just the right throw.

Perhaps the most perverse element of the gentrification of mental illness is the tendency to treat insanity as a “sane response to an insane world.” DeBoer details the onset of his own mental illness, and his experience accords him the authority to acerbically denounce anyone who suggests that madness is a form of liberation. He describes a litany of horrors, including bipolar patients who stab their spouses and coprophagics who “consume their own excrement on public transit,” and asks: “Which of the described behaviors, exactly, constitutes a ‘sane response to an insane world’?”

This romantic viewpoint might seem fringe, but deBoer argues it has seeped into our society’s common sense, tracing much of its influence to the psychiatrist Thomas Szasz, whose The Myth of Mental Illness (1961) recast mental illness as mere “problems in living.” Offering a convincing critique of Szasz’s fundamentalist libertarianism, deBoer details how Szasz’s moral philosophy could only be maintained by a studious avoidance of the truly mentally ill. Of Rebecca Smith, a schizophrenic woman who froze to death on the streets after anti-psychiatry campaigners made involuntary commitment unduly onerous, Szasz wrote, “The sad truth is that Mrs. Smith was a person who did not take care of herself.” 

Liu takes down another sacred cow of anti-psychiatry, David Rosenhan’s 1973 study “On Being Sane in Insane Places,” in which pseudo-patients ostensibly fooled clinicians into admitting them to psychiatric hospitals. If psychiatrists couldn’t tell the difference between the sane and insane, it was claimed, the distinction must be arbitrary. Pointing to evidence that Rosenhan may have suppressed and misused data, she dismisses the study as fraudulent. But the exercise leads her to a different conclusion from deBoer’s: Psychiatry’s claim to be scientific was itself a product of politics, she thinks. For psychiatrist Robert Spitzer, Rosenhan’s study was like “manna from heaven.” Trying to secure “psychiatry’s reputation as an empirical science,” he used it to push the discipline toward a checklist model of disorder much to the “detriment of personal or intrapsychic origins of mental illness.” Life, class, and context were all collapsed into a neat “chemistry of psychic disorder.”

While Liu worries about too much medicalization, deBoer worries that anti-psychiatry and destigmatization campaigns have produced too little where it really counts. He points to Joyce Brown, a schizophrenic woman who became a cause célèbre in the debate over involuntary psychiatric commitment in the ’80s, recounting how after an address at Harvard, she simply ended up back on the streets, on drugs, and exploited. In real life, deBoer concludes, “Joyce Brown acted the way a chronic schizophrenic acts.” 

Campaigners have slipped from the claim “mentally ill people are not bad” to the idea that mental illness itself isn’t bad. When a psychotic person makes antisemitic remarks, for instance, social media users are quick to retort that “mental illness doesn’t do that.” But it does, or society would not grant (in certain narrow circumstances at least) the mentally ill one of their most important protections, the exemption from criminal responsibility. That exemption, I might add, protects our legal and democratic systems too, since to say some people lack capacity implies that most of us have it.

But therapy culture has a tendency to let incapacity seep into the crevices of everyday life, and nowhere is this clearer than in Liu’s treatment of child protection. She shows how spectacular cases of abuse increasingly displaced attention from the ordinary circumstances of poverty. When Sen. Walter J. Mondale introduced the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act in the mid-’70s, abuse was deliberately popularized as “a problem knowing no barriers of class, race or culture.” Child abuse became not a systemic issue, but a kind of illness. Professional class reformers could therefore carry on attending to injuries at a distance from more contentious social and economic questions. 

I would take Liu’s conclusion further. Most children in the American foster care system, for instance, are not there because of serious abuse, but rather because of “neglect,” a category that routinely conflates poverty with poor parenting. When parents see their economic circumstances improve, their involvement with child protective services in turn tends to fall. So often is poverty confused with neglect that a bill currently sits before Congress expressly aimed at amending Social Security to “ensure that child protective services systems do not permit the separation of children from parents solely on the basis of poverty.”

What is more, removing class from ideals of parenting not only obscures poverty, it also opens the door to policing families on the basis of therapeutic middle-class ideals. More than once, in debates over spanking, I have pointed out that corporal punishment remains more common in poor and working class families, only to be told that this fact itself is “offensive.” A form of discipline practiced by most of humanity is recast as a kind of brain damage, which offers moreover, a convenient explanation of poverty itself. If poverty is passed down through bad parenting, the remedy lies in simply adopting expert-approved methods, a fix now prescribed even for global underdevelopment. And so criminalization campaigns continue apace, oblivious to the disproportionate numbers of poor and working-class families who will see stressful investigations added to their plate.

 

DeBoer is most convincing on the need for modern humane institutionalization, and sometimes, involuntary commitment, practices that have been attacked in the name of liberation. But he is less so when he hopes overdiagnosis can be checked by a more assertive psychiatry, policing diagnoses as matters of “objective scientific fact.” Watching the spread of dissociative identity disorder (DID) on TikTok, he is dismissive of young women’s “fake” performances of the diagnosis and laments that clinicians who question them are shouted down. Anyone familiar with the issue will be shouting at the page at this point; this was not the first such wave.

Liu offers what deBoer omits. DID, then called multiple personality disorder, first became a fad in the ’80s and ’90s, spurred on, as Liu describes, by the talk show circuit which acted like an “infectious disease vector, where spectators and professionals could learn about the symptoms and incorporate them into their psychological and professional repertoires.” It was not just teenaged girls, but professionals themselves, who were beguiled by the diagnosis and did much to encourage others to see their pain through its prism. Rubber-stamping self-diagnoses is indeed a problem, but restoring professional authority is an incomplete remedy for fads that professionals have often helped to spread.

“Their belief in their own wellness itself a symptom.”

What neither book quite accounts for is why the current mental-health paradigm persists when it so often fails. Part of the answer lies in what Liu refers to as trauma culture’s “survivor messianism,” in which suffering confers moral authority—the counterpart to deBoer’s liberated madman. But then, what of the well? From this perspective, it is easy to see how the purported normals are complicit, their belief in their own wellness itself a symptom. As a student once summed it up to me: “It’s almost like, if there’s nothing wrong with you…what’s wrong with you?” The outsider has come to be seen as an already liberated subject, whereas the “normal” are held responsible for perpetuating society’s oppressive norms.

As material explanations fall away, ordinary behavior becomes the site of intervention, and confessing your vulnerability becomes a way of signaling that you are one of the good ones. The bad subject still labors under the illusion of autonomy, still perilously choosing to smack their kids’ bottoms while keeping their “trauma” to themselves. Those who still stubbornly believe they can manage their own lives are the last frontier. Therapy culture can accommodate almost anything as madness, except the truly mad and those who insist they are well.

India is quietly doing great

The world’s biggest country continues to defy the skeptics.

Noah Smith
Nov 11
 
READ IN APP
 

My last post was about how for the first time, I’m becoming bearish on China’s continued economic and technological outperformance. A number of people asked me whether I was similarly bearish about India. The answer is no — I’m actually more bullish on India than I have been in a while. In fact, I had been meaning to write a post about that, so this gives me a good opportunity to do so.

The reason I’m bullish on India and bearish on China is that we’re asking the two countries to do two different things. When we think of China’s future success, we think of whether it’ll eclipse the combined economies of the U.S. and its allies, seize the lead in artificial intelligence, reach Taiwan or Korea’s level of income, or dominate Asia. I’m increasingly skeptical about its ability to do all of those things. But India’s job right now is a lot simpler — it just has to escape poverty and become an upper middle income country. And this I think it can do.

In both GDP terms and in terms of the Human Development Index (which combines GDP with education and health), India is around where China was in the late 2000s.

It’s easy to forget, but in the 2000s, people still thought of China as a basically developing country — its cities choked with smog, its rural areas still mired in poverty, its economy driven by cheap labor and lax environmental protections, and so forth. The challenge now for India is to make the leap that China made in the 2010s — to build abundant high-quality roads, trains, housing, and energy, provide decent jobs and livelihoods to the majority of its people, and catch up to the frontier of technology.

A lot of people don’t seem to realize how good of a start India has made. For one thing, extreme poverty in India has mostly been conquered over the last two decades:

This is an incredible accomplishment — a full tenth of humanity saved from deprivation. And what’s remarkable is that — unlike China — India managed to do this incredible poverty reduction while also reducing inequality:

How did India manage this feat? The World Bank says that it was due to the two usual suspects — economic growth and redistribution:

Over the past decade, India has made remarkable progress in reducing poverty across both monetary and non-monetary dimensions, recording one of the fastest poverty declines in the world…This progress was mainly driven by strong consumption growth, rising employment, especially among women, and expanded social transfers, including food subsidies. [emphasis mine]

A strong welfare state is certainly important, but economic growth has to take the lion’s share of the credit here; without growth, there’s simply less of a pie to redistribute in the first place. And India’s growth has certainly been impressive. Ever since the pandemic, India has been growing faster than China:

Now, India isn’t growing as fast as China did when China was at $10,000 of per capita GDP. Back in the late 2000s and early 2010s, China was still growing at close to double-digit rates; it didn’t slow down to India’s current rate until 2014, at which point it was 40% richer than India is now. But 6.5% is still a very healthy growth rate — it represents almost a doubling of living standards every decade.

And Bloomberg expects Indian growth to accelerate even further, to 8% by the end of the decade. Neelkanth Mishra, the executive director of the World Bank, points out that because India’s recovery from the pandemic recession is still incomplete, there’s plenty of room for a growth acceleration.

You’d expect this kind of growth to transform every part of Indian society and culture, and this appears to be exactly what’s happening. Arjun Ramani has a great in-depth report from his travels across India, focusing on how economic development is changing life on the ground:

Economy Class
Dispatches from India
Before starting my PhD, I spent the past three years as a journalist for The Economist. The final year was the best. I was based in India, lived between Mumbai and New Delhi, and travelled across 10 states and over 30 cities and villages as the country carried out history’s largest election. I was responsible for the paper’s India economics coverage, wh…
Read more
a year ago · 167 likes · 11 comments · Arjun Ramani

How is India producing this rapid growth? India is long past the point where you can tell a simple story about the country’s economic progress — manufacturing, finance, real estate, business services, IT, and a bunch of other sectors are all growing at once.

How is India managing to grow so fast? The Economist mostly credits liberalizing reforms and prudent macroeconomic policy:

A programme of fiscal consolidation has cut the budget deficit from 9.2% of gdp in fiscal 2021 (when it was bloated by pandemic spending) towards a target of 4.4% for fiscal 2026. Excluding interest payments, the deficit will be only around 0.9% of gdp…With inflation under control, interest rates have been cut by 1.25 percentage points over the past year…

The decline in inflation is not just limited to food, points out Sonal Varma of Nomura, a bank. Earlier reforms, such as the creation of a digital-payments infrastructure, which made prices more transparent, as well as the RBI’s shift to an inflation-targeting regime in 2016, have helped reduce inflation expectations and are now paying off. The RBI has also built up its stock of foreign-exchange reserves. A banking sector clean-up and reforms to the bankruptcy code have kept the financial system stable…

The longer term looks even more promising, thanks to a vigorous reform effort…A long-mooted cut in the number of labour codes, from 29 to four, was enacted in November. A cap of 74% on foreign direct investment in the insurance industry has been lifted. Nuclear power has been opened up to the private sector. Financial-market regulation has been overhauled…The states have also pursued reforms. Allowing women to work after dark, for instance, means textile and electronics factories can stay open later.

I have to say, I’m skeptical of this story. Fiscal probity is well and good, but India’s long-term borrowing rates haven’t come down all that much:

A stable financial system is very good, but it’s not clear how that automatically accelerates growth. And most of the real structural reform The Economist mentions is in the future. It’s possible for businesses’ expectations of structural reform to drive growth, but as the article mentions, domestic private-sector investment isn’t really driving the boom. FDI is sluggish too (or at least was until this year).

One bright spot is government investment, which has increased by a factor of four since before the pandemic, in spite of the country’s falling debt levels:

The Indian government has been on a tremendous infrastructure-building boom — correcting one of the country’s notorious chronic deficiencies. Highway spending has increased by a factor of five over the last decade. Central government railway spending has risen eightfold.

This is boosting growth in the short term, but in the long term it’ll make both manufacturing and consumption a lot easier in India. It’s also changing the physical look and feel of the country, much as China’s own modernization did in the 2000s and 2010s (if not as rapidly). India is now building its own bullet trains:

Andhra Nexus
@AndhraNexus
🚨 First glimpse of B28, India’s first indigenous bullet train, at the manufacturing facility.
2:01 PM · Nov 1, 2026 · 617K Views
62 Replies · 832 Reposts · 5.32K Likes

I recently saw an example of a Japanese man who declared that he was impressed by how clean and quiet Indian subways were, compared to Japanese ones!

Another important factor in India’s growth story — and another long-standing deficiency that’s now beginning to be corrected — is the growth in Indian manufacturing.

The old story of India’s economy is that it had “leapfrogged” manufacturing and gone straight to services — call centers, business process outsourcing, software outsourcing, and the like. That concealed a quiet disappointment that India hadn’t managed to get on the same industrialization bus that has carried so many other countries out of poverty. But India’s current growth is very broad-based — manufacturing is growing right alongside services. The Economist has some details:

Manufacturing output in August, the most recent figure available, was 9% higher than the year before, thanks in particular to surging production of cars and electronics…India’s rising manufacturing output…reflects its growing appeal as a place to make things. In dollar terms India’s electronics exports were up by 90% in August, year on year, with American-bound iPhones accounting for a large share of that.

Another encouraging sign is the breadth of India’s manufacturing growth. Whereas Bangladesh’s manufacturing boom last decade was powered mostly by the garment industry, India is making and exporting a bunch of different high-tech products:

The strength of India’s engineering exports lies partly in the diversity of its product segments. Automobiles remained the largest contributor in FY 2025–26, accounting for 21.9% of total engineering exports. Industrial machinery followed with an 18% share, while iron and steel products accounted for 16.9%…Electrical machinery contributed 12.5%, other engineering products 12.7%, and non-ferrous metals and products 11.6%.

And keep in mind, this is all in spite of China’s attempts to throttle Indian industrialization by denying them key technological exports and factory expertise. Competitive pressure from a more established economic power is not something China itself had to deal with, since the U.S. wholeheartedly supported China’s industrialization in the 1990s and 2000s.

Whether India’s growth boom can continue past the next couple of years is an open question. Private investment will have to rise, and probably FDI as well. India is also going to need to correct its bigger structural issues at some point — especially bad rural education, female underemployment, and incomplete urbanization.

But for now, India looks like a big economic success story — perhaps the brightest in the entire world right now. It’s less visible than China’s rapid rise two decades earlier, but it’ll be no less world-shaking when it happens. More people should be taking notice.

Twenty-three points on the midterms and the narrative

A sweep that, in retrospect, could have been even bigger

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 11
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Today is Veterans Day, a federal holiday and a day off from school, and normally we wouldn’t run a new piece. But this continues to be a critical moment for shaping public understanding of the momentous electoral events that just unfolded, and we didn’t want to leave you high and dry.

I also think it sometimes does a bit of violence to the complexity of events to sweep everything into a totalizing narrative. The overall composition of the House Democratic caucus is shifting decidedly to the center, but you’ll also see the biggest and most empowered insurgent left group in recent history.

So, because many things are true at once, here are 23 somewhat scattered thoughts on both the results and the narrative. We’ll be back with a full article on Thursday.

  1. Most of the candidate quality debate happens among Democrats, so the focus tends to be on the differences between Democrats. But even in defeat, Susan Collins is clearly a stellar electoral performer. Republican Governors Phil Scott and Kelly Ayotte survived a blue tsunami. If you look up Dem-side 2024 wins-above-replacement ratings, you’d think Angela Alsobrooks is a freakishly bad politician, but that’s actually Larry Hogan being a freakishly good one, even though he also lost.

  2. One of Donald Trump’s largest impacts on American politics has been saddling the Republican Party with a bunch of bad Senate candidates. We remember the ones who lost, like Ken Paxton, Dr. Oz, Herschel Walker, and Darline Graham. But Julia Letlow, who won, also seems very weak, and JD Vance was an underperformer in his one election.

  3. I think the left is on the run in the post-election takes game, largely because they got arrogant about their media echo chamber and made the Bond villain play of explaining their plan in advance. The D.S.A. told people they were hoping for a narrow House majority so they could squeeze Hakeem Jeffries, and A.O.C. told a fundraiser that she was going to spin El-Sayed winning Michigan by any margin as debunking all electability concerns, so analysts were ready.

  4. Some people wonder why I’ve been so dogged about this, but doggedness and preparation matter. There was a good Aaron Blake article in CNN about progressive underperformance, and Nate Cohn also explained it well on Derek Thompson’s podcast. Word is getting out because commonsense Democrats are more organized than before.

  5. As well as the midterms went for Democrats, they could have gone better. Imagine if John Bel Edwards had been the nominee in Louisiana, if Seth Bodnar had just run in the Democratic primary in Montana, and if Gary Peters had run for re-election in Michigan and all the money spent there was plowed into Florida instead. I think that’s very plausibly three more seats.

  6. S.N.L. did a cold open sketch over the weekend where the joke was that it’s funny to imagine anyone giving Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer credit for Democrats’ strong performance — I don’t think that’s fair (they did well!), but it’s a real assessment of where we’re at as a party.

  7. Ultimately, I think Jeffries and Schumer end up being poorly served by not having defeated challengers in order to secure or hold their posts after 2024. If there’d been a contested race where Schumer said, “Here’s my plan, it’s going to work” and then he’d won his contest and then his plan worked, he could say, “See — it worked!”

  8. For that exact reason, I’d love to see an actual challenge this year. It would be great for someone to explain their plan to maximize Democratic gains on the 2028 Senate map and then for Schumer to explain what, if anything, he disagrees with about that plan. Ultimately, I doubt we’d actually see much disagreement, and this whole thing is kind of BS.

  9. When people say the impact of ideology on electability is small, pay attention to the details. My read is that the gap between a progressive and an establishment Dem is small and that the gap between an establishment Dem and a moderate is small but that the prog/mod gap is actually pretty big because it’s a double gap.

  10. Ideology, in my view, is about what positions you actually take, not a kind of ascriptive personal identity. Angie Nixon of the D.S.A. and ex-Republican David Jolly are two very different kinds of people, but they didn’t actually take different positions on the issues except for Israel, so they did pretty similarly. This is what you’d expect — Jolly did better, but not a lot better — if you think ideas matter. It’s not what you would expect if you think “progressive” and “moderate” are fixed personal characteristics.

  11. Halina is too ethical to say this, but Colorado getting Dem supermajorities in the state legislature and electing Phil Weiser as governor is probably bad for the state. Colorado’s residents benefited from a moderate form of Democratic Party governance under Hickenlooper and Polis, and there’s a big risk now of the state adopting some of the more dysfunctional policies of blue states. There’s no electability problem with Weiser, but a more moderate governor would be better on the merits.

  12. Sometimes good politicians are a little bit subpar as electoral performers, and that’s fine! I really like what Kathy Hochul is cooking in New York, but her results were slightly bad. New York is not a swing state, and in fact, beating Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman on Long Island might be enough of a political show of force to shock New York Republicans out of their turbo-NIMBY mode. I wish I could factually say she’s a huge overperformer, since I like her a lot. But it isn’t true, so I don’t say it, because I’m not a dishonest person.

  13. I think the question of which people can say accurate things is ultimately more important than these modest differences in performance.

    The signature substantive problem with progressive governance is that you have a lot of smart people over-indexing on coalition management rather than trying to address the issues clearly. Median voter denialism is a downstream symptom of the underlying pathology.

  14. I don’t think Democratic governors won in Texas, Ohio, and Georgia purely because of the war in Iran. Everyone saying that needs to think harder about what’s going on.

  15. I mentioned trying to help with staffing before, and now I have the links. If you’d like to submit your resume to the Blue Dogs go here, to Third Way’s talent bank go here, and to Majority Democrats go here.

  16. I hope that at some point immigration restrictionists will try to explain to me more clearly why they didn’t even try to pass an immigration bill. Did they think they were going to govern forever? They had a real shot to make a durable change in a policy area they care a lot about, and what happened instead was the Department of Homeland Security posted a lot of edgy memes.

  17. When Jeffries was asked post-election about a D.S.A. summer victory rally for their primary candidates at which he was threatened with a future challenge, Jeffries said, “It was very interesting to me, as observed by others, that there was almost zero diversity in that crowd.” Establishment Democrats love to wield this kind of toxic identity-politics rhetoric against their critics on the left, and I think it’s important for commonsense Dems to criticize them for it and also to remind the world that this is in some sense not our fight. The candidates who flipped seats in states Trump won did so by running to the right of Jeffries and Schumer, not by acting as their allies.

  18. All the moderates (but also Bernie Sanders) are warning Democrats not to spend too much time on investigations when they should be helping the American people with their pressing economic needs. I think it’s important to consider what the real tradeoffs are here. If a good affordability bill like the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act doesn’t pass, it won’t be because Democrats were too busy doing investigations; it will be because progressives didn’t like the bill, because they prefer green purism. I’d love to see our newly elected mods lock in on the bona fide ideological disagreement here and not get sucked into a pointless debate about investigations.

  19. Robert Garcia, who is set to chair the Oversight Committee, said at Crooked Con that “we’re not going to forget” the crimes of former Trump administration officials. “Maybe it’s because I’m gay, but pettiness is a thing.” It’s a decent joke, but I think safe seat members in positions of responsibility need to try way harder than this to not break kayfabe and make sure that everything they say in public is something that helps rather than hurts frontline members. “Do investigations” vs. “pass bills” is a fake tradeoff, but “investigate in a way that’s politically helpful” vs. “get laughs” is a real one.

  20. Ballot measures are a good indicator of policy views separate from partisanship. Conservative initiatives related to trans issues passed in Colorado, Washington, and Arizona. Voter ID initiatives passed in Nevada, North Carolina, and Ohio. Democrats who want to maximize their odds of doing well in 2028 and driving a stake through the heart of the MAGA movement should consider avoiding positions that are too unpopular to prevail in states Trump repeatedly lost. The wealth tax lost in California and a minimum wage hike initiative failed there two years ago — there are limits to the appeal of economic populism.

  21. Ezra Klein wrote over the weekend that “I don’t know any Democrats who are counting on these voting patterns to automatically persist.” I hope that lack of complacency is accurate. But none of the strategists or academics he quotes mention that adopting more conservative views on cultural issues is part of how successful Democratic candidates expanded the map, so I’m concerned that complacency persists.

  22. Krystal Ball says James Talarico talks like Bernie Sanders. Talarico says “I’m a big fan of SpaceX. I’m a big fan of Tesla. [Musk] is a great business leader and entrepreneur and innovator. I want him to stick to those things — I don’t like that he’s trying to buy this Senate seat in Texas. I don’t like that he’s using his wealth to influence our political system. That’s where I draw the line. I will stand up to Elon Musk when he tries to buy our government, but I will work with him when it comes to technology and innovation.”

  23. When I looked at the history of midterms, what’s interesting is that sometimes a big loss prefigures things to come and sometimes it doesn’t. It’s pretty normal for a president to bounce back from a terrible second-year midterm (1994, 2010) and get re-elected. But even a year-six brushback like Democrats scored in 1986 was followed by Republicans’ rare presidential three-peat triumph in 1988. This year was the biggest midterm sweep since 1974, but 1974 led to Jimmy Carter’s narrow win in 1976 followed by basically a failed presidency. I’m not saying that’s what will happen in 2028, obviously, but I do think the collective conventional wisdom keeps failing to appreciate the full range of possible outcomes. What else did we see last week if not that weird stuff happens?

When the Radical Right Loved India

By Mark Sedgwick • 11 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In the run-up to the 2026 midterm elections, the American right was consumed by a conflict over the “Indian question.” The flashpoint came in September, when Bo French, a Republican candidate in Texas, lamented a picture showing South Asian fans at a college football game. This open display of anti-Indian sentiment drew condemnation from mainstream Republicans, but echoed the views of many on the far right, such as the white nationalist streamer Nick Fuentes. Other leading figures on the online “dissident” right endorsed French’s stance, presenting Indian identity as incompatible with a foundationally and essentially white America. 

The irony of all this is that the European rightist thinking upon which today’s American far right draws has more often been Indophilic. A reminder of this legacy came in an earlier phase of the evolution of the far right. Shortly after Donald Trump first won the presidency in 2016, Richard B. Spencer, the founder of the alt-right, held a conference at his National Policy Institute. One of the speakers was Jason Reza Jorjani, an Iranian-American with a doctorate in philosophy who was at that time editor in chief of Arktos, then and now the world’s leading English-language publisher of authors belonging to the “New Right.” Jorjani called for “an affirmation of the Indo-European tradition,” arguing that “Indo-European or Aryan cultures are uniquely worthy of affirmation since they are the roots of every great discovery and world-historical development in spirituality, the sciences, and the arts.” His speech was applauded by the audience.

“Jorjani’s speech reflected a longstanding fascination on the radical right.”

Jorjani’s speech reflected a longstanding fascination on the radical right with India and Iran. Though the European radical right is now committed to maintaining what it calls the European “ethnos,” it was also often taken with the history and culture of “Aryan” civilizations like India and Iran, neither of which are exactly European. 

The contemporary New Right, of which Spencer’s movement was an American offshoot, developed first in France during the last four decades of the twentieth century, and has recently spread worldwide in its “Identitarian” form. Identitarianism distinguishes itself from historical Nazism by stressing not race but identity, by which it means ethnic identity. For Identitarians, there is no hierarchy of races as the Nazis wrongly thought; every ethnicity has its own qualities. What is needed, they argue, is “ethnopluralism:” the right of every ethnicity to remain undisturbed. The conclusion generally drawn from this is that European ethnicity is currently being disturbed by migrants with other ethnicities, and that these migrants should therefore be sent back to wherever they came from. “Remigration is possible” was once the slogan of Identitarians across Europe, and has recently spread into the broader right. The Trump administration has created an “Office of Remigration” within the State Department. 

Jorjani’s use of the term “Aryan” is partly explained by the fact that his father was Iranian, and “Iran” is, quite literally, Aryan. The derivation of the alternative name “Persia” is uncertain, but it may derive from ancient Greek, in which pérthō originally meant “to sack, ravage, or destroy.” This, from an ancient Greek perspective, is what the Persians often did. In 1935, however, the government of what was then called Persia requested the world to use the name “Iran” instead, a name which had been in local use for centuries and which originally meant “of the Aryans.” The name change partly reflected the Iranian government’s enthusiasm for Nazi Germany, itself explained by the way that Iran then found itself squeezed between Britain to the south and the Soviet Union to the north. 

The other term Jorjani used, “Indo-European,” is a synonym for “Aryan.” What we now call Indo-European languages were once called “Aryan” languages, as opposed to Semitic, Turanian, and Chinese languages. The Nazis turned Aryan and Semitic into racial categories that are now recognized as pseudo-scientific, but the Indo-European language group undeniably exists, as does the Semitic language group, in which the most widely spoken language is Arabic. (The Turanian category has been abandoned by scholars.) 

Language is undeniably associated with culture, which is why the term “Indo-European” is now used by the New Right. The founding father of the New Right in France, Alain de Benoist, published a book in 1997 entitled The Indo-Europeans: In Search of their Place of Origin (translated into English as The Indo-Europeans: In Search of the Homeland). The question of the Aryans’ place of origin once worried Nazi theorists, who knew that Persian and Indian languages belonged to the same Aryan family as German, but were not always comfortable with the possible conclusion that the Germans were somehow descended from the Indians. The nineteenth-century German archeologist Heinrich Schliemann briefly explored this possibility, but finally concluded that the Aryan languages came from Bactria, now in Afghanistan, where the currently most spoken language, Dari, is Indo-European. The most popular current theory is that the first speakers of the original Indo-European language came from the Pontic–Caspian steppe, between the Danube and the Urals.

An alternative theory that became popular in Nazi circles was advanced by Herman Wirth, a Dutch-German Nazi who was the first head of the Ahnenerbe Stiftung (Ancestral Heritage Foundation), a research unit within the SS established by Heinrich Himmler. Wirth developed the idea, first proposed in 1903 by the Indian nationalist Bal Gangadhar Tilak, that the Aryans had originally inhabited the Arctic during an era when the weather was warmer, and had migrated south as the Arctic grew colder. The Germans did not descend from the Indians, then: Germans and Indians both descended equally from an earlier group that had inhabited Atlantis, located in the Arctic.

Wirth found much in common between the Old Norse Edda texts and the Hindu Vedas, and saw the Norse god Heimdall (son of Odin) and the Hindu fire god Agni as “local variants of the Atlantean-Nordic mysterium of Yule.” His Indo-European neo-paganism fitted with mainstream Nazi hostility towards Christianity, though relatively few Nazis were themselves neo-pagans. One result was the remarkable composition that still hangs on one wall of the Sky Hall in the Atlantis House in Bremen. This shows a stylized representation of the fire god Agni beneath a gilded disk of the sun. It is the work of the expressionist sculptor Bernhard Hoetger, who was charged with representing Wirth’s conceptions by Ludwig Roselius, the wealthy inventor of decaffeination and founder of Café HAG. Roselius was one of the main supporters of Wirth, the Atlantean model of Norse religion, and the Arctic origins of the Aryans, as well as a patron of Art Deco architecture and expressionism. He was twice refused admission to the Nazi party, largely because Hitler did not approve of his artistic tastes. The Atlantis House is now part of the Radisson Blu Hotel, and the Sky Hall is let out for conferences and weddings. The origins and meaning of the striking composition on the wall are unknown to most visitors. 

 

Although the fall of the Nazi regime buried Aryan racism, some of this worldview’s advocates persisted well after the end of World War II. One of them was Maximiani Portas, the daughter of a Greek father and an English mother, born in Lyon, France, in 1905. She studied philosophy in France, spent time in Greece, and developed views similar to those of Wirth, though without contact with him. Instead, she read Schliemann’s work on Trojan and Indian religious symbolism. Having rejected Christianity, she traveled to India in 1932 in search of the origins of Indo-European religion. She remained there until 1945, taking the name Savitri Devi in honor of the Vedic goddess (devi) Savitri. Her A Warning to the Hindus, published in Calcutta in 1939, presented “Indian paganism” as “the last living expression of Aryan beauty” and India as “the last great country of Aryan civilization.” She regretted that the pagan gods of Greece were no longer worshipped, and warned Hindus about the risk of losing their Aryan paganism.

Savitri’s earlier pro-German positions became pro-Nazi, and she married Asit Krishna, a Hindu nationalist with a doctorate in history from London University who had run a pro-Nazi newspaper in Calcutta, subsidized by the German consulate, until the British closed it down. Savitri remained faithful to Nazism after the German defeat, distributing pro-Nazi leaflets in Allied-occupied Germany in 1948 and 1949. This resulted in six months in a British-run prison. In 1958, she published what proved to be her most important work, The Lightning and the Sun. Here, she combined Hinduism and Nazism, and came to the conclusion that Hitler, as savior of the Aryans, was actually an incarnation (avatar) of the god Vishnu. Savitri was a Nazi, not a Neo-Nazi, but her theories became popular in later American Neo-Nazi circles.

“Hitler, he claimed, was immortal.”

Savitri’s position was adopted by a former Chilean diplomat, Miguel Serrano, who had served as his country’s ambassador to India. Like Savitri’s husband, he had also once published a pro-Nazi newspaper, subsidized by the German mission in Santiago. His Adolf Hitler: The Last Avatar of 1984 added Savitri’s insight to theories he had already developed in 1978 in his The Golden Thread: Esoteric Hitlerism, in which he traced Nazism back to primordial Aryan religion in Atlantis and then forward through the golden thread that led from then, through Hinduism and other esoteric practices, to the present. Hitler, he claimed, was immortal, and had not died in Berlin; he was alive somewhere, probably in Antarctica.

The “Esoteric Hitlerism” of Savitri and Serrano attracted a small following, and Wirth still has a few readers. This is not a major stream within the contemporary radical right, but less esoteric strains of the original Indo-European narrative, shorn of Atlantis and Antarctica, are more popular. They surfaced at the National Policy Institute with Jorjani, and in the work of de Benoist, who concluded that the Indo-Europeans originated in the Pontic–Caspian steppe, a view in line with mainstream linguistic science. De Benoist also rejected the idea that there was an Indo-European race, as opposed to an Indo-European ethnos. What mattered about the “Indo-European dimension,” he told an interviewer, was that it “places our civilization firmly within a long-term historical context—one that is much longer than those who trace its origins to the advent of Christianity, the emergence of the nation-state, or the human rights revolution might imagine.” That the New Right rejects the human rights revolution comes as no surprise, but why the hostility to Christianity and the nation-state? De Benoist, like Wirth and Savitri and, more importantly, Nietzsche, rejected Judaism and Christianity. Like Wirth and Savitri, de Benoist preferred pagan alternatives, going further in this respect than Nietzsche ever did. As to the nation state, the idea of the nation is closely connected with the idea of democracy, which the New Right also rejects.

The relationship of the contemporary radical right with India (and Iran) is paradoxical. On the one hand, especially in the United States, the far right is closely associated with white supremacism, a system that excludes people primarily based on their skin color, and would therefore exclude most Indians. The Nazis were less interested in skin color than in other criteria, as their racism was directed primarily against Jews, a group not distinguishable from other Europeans by skin color. At the same time, it included other groups that American white supremacists would not. 

This view led to Serrano’s vision of Hitler as an avatar living on in Antarctica and Savitri’s dream of a Hindu-Nazi fusion, but also to the more influential Identitarianism of Benoist’s New Right, which preaches an apparently ecumenical gospel of ethnic exclusion. Indo-Europeanism is no longer the predominant view on the radical right. Nevertheless, in their recent anti-Indian invective, American far-right influencers inadvertently recalled the conundrum faced by earlier theorists of the radical right in delimiting the borders of the in-group.

Climates of Treason

Why MAGA is making America weak again

Paul Krugman
Nov 12
 
READ IN APP
 

Transcript

Jensen Huang is a fool who should never again be allowed close to anything involving national security. But the Nvidia honeypot story is about much more than one man. Because the way the Trump administration handled it — basically, its attempt to bury any inquiry into the clear threat Huang’s affair posed to U.S. interests — is part of a bigger story of betrayal at the highest levels.

Hi, Paul Krugman here.

Two years of Trump have led to a catastrophic decline in America’s global role.

Around the world, America is neither loved nor feared. The world has learned that we cannot be trusted to honor our promises or defend our allies; at the same time, we seem unable to punish our enemies. We have essentially lost a military war with Iran and a trade war with China; we may well be losing a technology race with China too.

How did we fall so far, so fast? It’s all about Trump. But I think it’s useful to ask why Trump has done so much to make America weak again.

Part of the answer is the sheer incompetence of the people Trump and his underlings have hired. To take the most spectacular example, we have a self-styled Secretary of War who believes that what our military needs in an age of drones and AI is testosterone shots. You couldn’t make this up.

And the incompetence isn’t an accident. MAGA hates people with expertise, because such people might engage in critical thinking and might care about their reputations. Only the truly hapless can be counted on to be truly loyal.

But it’s not just incompetence. There’s a clear element of betrayal — of key figures in or close to the Trump administration knowingly acting in ways that obviously make America less secure. I don’t know how much of this betrayal meets the legal standard of treason, but morally that’s what it amounts to.

Why do men (and sometimes women) betray their nation? I took the title of this post from a famous 1979 British book, “The Climate of Treason,” about the circle of elite Cambridge graduates who became agents of the Soviet Union. These traitors acted out of ideological conviction: They convinced themselves that Stalinism was the future, and acted on its behalf.

By contrast, the great American spy scandals — Aldrich Ames. Robert Hanssen, and so on — were mainly about corruption: they sold U.S. secrets for personal gain.

The Trump clique’s betrayals, I’d argue, have reflected a combination of these motives.

MAGA’s increasingly explicit support for Russia’s attempt to conquer Ukraine — that is, support for an anti-Western dictator against a pro-Western democracy — is, I believe, largely about ideology. It’s true that Trump and some of those around him may hope for lucrative business deals once Russia wins, and Trump has benefited financially in the past from his Russia connection.

But at base, I believe that Trump, Elon Musk, and many others on the hard right look at Putinism — authoritarian rule under which critics have a tendency to fall out of high windows, male supremacy, social illiberalism, crony capitalism for oligarchs with the right connections — and see it as an exemplar of what they want from a society. The financial payoffs are probably secondary.

By contrast, I don’t believe that there’s a faction within MAGA that sees Xi’s China as a role model, other than the authoritarian bit. The attempt to cover for Huang, the seemingly inexplicable decision to allow significant sales of highly advanced chips — one of America’s few clear advantages in the technology race — to China or buyers close to the Chinese government — are clearly motivated by money, money flowing to Trump and his pet projects. Nvidia itself, for example, gave $25 million to the Trump ballroom. The AI industry as a whole appears to have funneled hundreds of millions in Trump’s direction — and by all accounts people around Trump were covering for Huang in part because they feared that revealing the scandal would hurt an industry that has become a major source of financial support.

And does anyone really doubt that there are many other stories like this? Most obviously, Jared Kushner is being paid huge sums by Middle Eastern potentates. This is a huge scandal even if there weren’t any quid pro quos. And I’ll bet that we’ll eventually learn that there were, in fact, favors exchanged for that money.

The important thing is to realize that the people running this country, while they love to wave the flag — Hegseth is now claiming that to criticize him is to attack the troops — are utterly unpatriotic. They are completely unwilling to make personal sacrifices, no matter how small, or to pass up personal opportunities, for the sake of the nation. And of course at a fundamental level they hate everything this nation stands for, beginning with democracy and the rule of law.

In other words: USA! USA! USA!

The “betrayal” theory of voter rage about the cost of living
