Gasoline isn’t really that expensive

The “betrayal” theory of voter rage about the cost of living

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 12
 
READ IN APP
 

After you finish today’s post, I hope you’ll listen to the latest episode of “The Argument” podcast, where Jerusalem and I continue the conversation about why politicians aren’t listening to voters’ demands for lower prices. Paid subscribers can watch or listen ad free and read the transcript and show notes here. Free subscribers can catch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Voters, clearly, are very upset about the cost of living, and (to be boring) this was an important factor in the midterm elections. Indeed, to the extent that we can tell from surveys, not only do voters think Republicans need to focus much more on the cost of living, but they even make this critique of Democrats to some degree.

Even where you might think other factors are at play, like with Latino voters in Texas, more than 70 percent of those voters cite the cost of living as a top three issue compared with roughly 35 percent for immigration and border security.

People are upset about costs, they’ve been upset for a long time, and the re-acceleration of inflation associated with the war in Iran has been a fiasco for the Trump administration.

But having stipulated all that, now that the election is over, I’d like to observe that voter rage about the cost of living seems somewhat out of proportion to the actual circumstances.

This was the biggest midterm wave since 1974. But on top of Watergate, which was a huge factor in that election, the inflation rate in 1974 was a bit over 12 percent after 8.7 percent inflation in 1973. More recently, we had 7 percent inflation in 2021 followed by 6.5 percent inflation in 2022. As of September, it was 3.7 percent. That’s bad! It’s a legitimate basis for criticism of Donald Trump!

But it’s way better than 1974, and on its face you’d think it would generate a smaller backlash.

Of course, Iran has specifically generated a spike in gasoline prices, which are always particularly salient and particularly annoying. Still, gasoline is way more affordable today than it was not just in the 1970s but in the pretty recent past.

Obviously, it’s completely tone deaf politically to say this, so I encourage the White House to borrow my chart and argue with the voters that things are fine, actually.

But just between you and me … it seems pretty fine? Especially because if you pop over to Jason Furman’s giant dashboard of economic indicators, a lot of other things seem to be going well. The unemployment rate is low at 4.1 percent and has been low for a long time. G.D.P. growth is solid, and the job openings rate is slightly higher than the unemployment rate, indicating a well-balanced labor market. This is not a perfect economy, but it seems genuinely better than a lot of situations I’ve seen play out in my lifetime.

Yet people really hate it, to the extent that they feel the opposition party isn’t focused enough on complaining about how terrible everything is.

Subscribed

The great betrayal

This is vibes rather than data, but after some introspection, one theory I’m partial to is that people feel betrayed by their political leaders.

I, for one, find it strange and annoying that after everyone was clearly furious with inflation in 2021-22, we never got a strong pivot to “It’s time to fight inflation.”

I’m a dork, so I phrase this in technical macroeconomic terms that normal people would not use, but here’s what happened: Inflation surged, we had a period of denial that it was all transitory, and then interest rates went up to keep inflation contained. Inflation then started heading back down throughout the Biden years, but it never returned to its target level. And the Biden administration never made a big policy pivot toward deficit reduction or supply-side regulatory reform to address it. Then Trump won promising not just a return to on-target inflation but an actual fall in the price level. That second part was impossible, but Trump never delivered the return to target that was possible. Instead, he increased the budget deficit in a way that increased inflationary pressures, and then we got a negative supply shock when he started a war with Iran.

The takeaway here is not that the underlying situation is genuinely the worst on record but that the political system is stubbornly averse to addressing it.

Even now, though, if you scour the universe of Democratic Party-aligned think tanks, you don’t see anyone saying, “Now that voters are angry about the cost of living, we need a totally retooled policy agenda to reduce inflation and interest rates.”

What’s happening instead is that everyone has taken the same off-the-shelf ideas from 2019 — neo-Brandeisian antitrust policy, expanded child-care subsidies, fighting climate change — and given them an affordability rebrand.

It would be a little crazy for an ideological movement to just completely abandon its long-held substantive goals in favor of a 100 percent focus on inflation and interest rates. But right now, Republicans are doing less than zero on inflation and interest rates. And the best I can really say for Democrats’ plans is they’re mostly avoiding ideas that would make things worse.

But there has really been shockingly little rethinking of the substance of the policy agenda. The whole idea of the new antitrust thinking, for example, was that the prior generation of enforcement had been overly focused on low consumer prices. It was genuinely bad luck for Lina Khan that she took power right when public concern about low consumer prices exploded — it’s not like the Federal Trade Commission caused inflation — but it seems obvious that when everyone is mad about consumer prices, you pivot back to the “low consumer prices are really important” school of thought.

Taxing wealth or unrealized capital gains is an inflationary mechanism of financing new government spending because you’re increasing overall consumption. Carbon pricing was abandoned as a climate solution in favor of Green New Deal thinking at a time when the economy needed stimulus, but the economy doesn’t need stimulus now and nobody’s gone back. The whole progressive child-care agenda was cooked up when unemployment was high, and it doesn’t make sense in a tight labor market.

Of course, Trump is president right now, and he’s even worse on this score.

It’s not just Iran. And it’s not just that tariffs raise prices — the whole premise of the tariff agenda is that higher prices are a good idea because you’re trying to protect American manufacturers from low-cost competition. Trump is also deliberately shrinking the workforce with his immigration policy, as if there’s some pool of unemployed people who are going to fill the jobs.

Nobody seems to want to sit down and say, “Okay, what is something I believed in but that doesn’t make sense in the specific economic situation we are facing?”

A crisis of politics, not economics

On one level, it seems a little crazy to attribute this level of policy awareness to the American electorate.

But I’m trying to make sense of all the facts. If you want to ask yourself, “How bad is the economic situation, really, in historical terms?” I think the honest answer is that it’s not ideal but we’ve seen much worse, including pretty recently. But if you want to ask yourself, “To what degree have political elites altered their policy priorities to respond to the problems in the economy?” the answer is genuinely not at all.

And that’s kind of remarkable. In 2008, the Bush administration and House Democrats collaborated on a bipartisan stimulus bill. The Obama administration passed a big economic rescue plan in 2009 and then enacted a couple of stimulative deals with Republicans around tax cut extensions and unemployment insurance. During Covid, Trump and Democrats collaborated on the CARES Act.

I don’t want to overstate the extent to which politicians are loyal public servants eager to address the problems of the mass public, but they do normally try at least a little.

I remember being on a briefing call with the Biden economic team, and they were talking about their cost-of-living ideas. Their talking points were pretty uncompelling to me, and I asked a question that I hoped would be helpful, something like: Can you give me an example of something you’re doing to address costs that people wouldn’t normally expect to see from a Democratic administration? Like what’s a policy that you wouldn’t think was a good idea if the economic situation was different but that you have specifically adopted to address the cost-of-living crisis?

And they legitimately had nothing to offer. The agenda wasn’t all bad ideas, but it was stuff Democrats would be inclined to favor in any economic climate.

Then Trump comes in and, again, it’s not like his team has zero initiatives that are helpful on costs. But everything he’s done that’s constructive here is completely generic Republican deregulatory stuff. There’s nothing at all that’s like, “If inflation was 1.9 percent, we’d love to do X, but because it’s 3.7 percent, we’re doing Y instead.”

So while I think the cost-of-living crisis, qua economic crisis, is a bit overstated, it does strike me as a very real crisis for American democracy.

Political parties are supposed to try to advance their coalition’s ideological and interest-group agenda. But they are also supposed to respond to the mass public’s priorities! And for the past four or five years, they just haven’t.

On some level, I think you don’t actually need to understand the whole macroeconomic picture to see this. Everyone knows what it would look like for a president to take on his base or his political allies in order to advance a policy goal. Biden clearly stood up to the left for the sake of a pro-Israel policy that he believed in. Trump stood up to the pro-life movement to reassure residents of blue and purple states about abortion.

But neither of them did anything like that on the cost of living.

Share

People are equally angry everywhere

One piece of evidence for this view is that economic trends impact different places differently, but everyone seems equally angry.

In Alaska and Texas, for example, a negative shock to Middle Eastern energy supplies is arguably good for the local economy since they produce a lot of oil. But Democrats are winning the Senate and gubernatorial races in both those states. That’s in part thanks to four smart candidates who ran smart campaigns, but there’s just clearly no way that Democrats are winning those races without pissed off voters.

I was looking for an example of something that, unlike gasoline, really has become unprecedentedly expensive, and what I came up with is beef.

Now the thing about beef is that unlike gasoline, you don’t really need to go buy beef if you think it’s too expensive. Beef is way less affordable right now than it was in the 1980s, but chicken is cheaper. People need to eat food, but you can always pick another protein. And when Cindy Hyde-Smith made this point, it was so politically toxic that it seems to have reversed the most notorious racial-polarization dynamic in all of American history and gotten a Democrat elected in Mississippi.

I think people aren’t just angry about beef; they’re angry about the arrogance of a political class that refuses to listen when they say this is their top priority.

Political scientist Christoffer Dausgaard did some technical analysis that exploited local variation in gasoline prices to ask whether the swing against Republicans was particularly large in places where gas rose an above-average amount, and the answer is no.

In other words, the level of public anger about prices does not vary with the prices themselves.

Another way I’ve been thinking about this is that northern New England is more exposed to the Strait of Hormuz shock than the rest of the country because people there rely on oil (rather than gas or electricity) for heat and also because gas-fired power plants in New England need to partially use liquefied natural gas rather than rely on cheaper pipeline gas. There was a big swing against Republicans in northern New England, the same as everywhere else, but Republican governors got re-elected in New Hampshire and Vermont, and Susan Collins put up a strong performance (as usual) even in defeat.

I think this all supports a kind of sociotropic account of price-related rage. Rather than mechanically responding to individual variation in the cost of living, voters are aware that inflation concerns are a big deal nationally and that political leaders at the national level are not prioritizing these concerns. They are equally mad about this everywhere in the country and gave some grace to Republicans who have unusually strong brands distinct from Trump and national Republican leadership.

How sure am I that this is what’s going on? Not that sure.

I think the level of voter outrage over modest inflation is genuinely a little bit mysterious. But I don’t think it’s plausible that all the economic data is wrong or that voters are responding to something that’s totally fake. Something that is absolutely real is that we’re now on Year Five of the inflationary episode and first Democrats and now Republicans have declined to genuinely prioritize inflation reduction. And I think Democrats ought to think hard about changing that when they craft their agenda for 2029.

Alex Karp, Cold War Liberal

By Geoff Shullenberger • 12 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Benedikt von Loebell / World Economic Forum
 
 

In the wake of the midterm elections, memes and jokes abounded about Silicon Valley grandees dying their hair blue and adding pronouns back to their email signature lines to signal a strategic rapprochement with the victorious Democratic Party. This week, Palantir CEO Alex Karp seemed to ratify these expectations with an interview in which he declared himself and his company “essentially progressive.” It seemed to many like an abrupt, cynical volte-face for an executive who, perhaps more than anyone other than Elon Musk, personified tech’s rightward turn under the second Trump administration—and benefited considerably from that reorientation.

But such analyses risk mistaking style for substance. Tech leaders’ embrace of right-wing aesthetics, exemplified by Mark Zuckerberg donning a “bro” uniform for his 2025 appearance on The Joe Rogan Experience, has too often obscured the deeper transformations underway in the industry in recent years. Chief among these is Silicon Valley’s open embrace of the state. Karp’s rhetorical vacillations should not distract from the company’s deeper consistency as an early and aggressive champion of this alliance. 

“Karp’s rhetorical vacillations should not distract from the company’s deeper consistency.”

Karp has articulated a broadly consistent philosophy throughout his time at Palantir. Although this outlook was for a long time an unusual one within Silicon Valley, as I have argued before, it would have been recognizable and largely congenial to the Cold War liberals of the mid-twentieth century. For instance, consider the fourth item in Palantir’s twenty-two-point manifesto (presented as a précis of Karp’s book The Technological Republic) published on X in April: “The ability of free and democratic societies to prevail requires something more than moral appeal. It requires hard power, and hard power in this century will be built on software.” Leaving aside the “software” part, any member of the Congress for Cultural Freedom would have likely signed onto this statement. Reinforcing this connection, The Technological Republic favorably cites a principle enunciated by Anne Applebaum, a contemporary spiritual descendent of the Cold War liberals: “There are no rules without someone to enforce them.” 

Such notions, already articulated around Palantir’s founding at the height of the War on Terror, were long at odds with the tech industry’s prevailing worldview, which was explicitly hostile to governments, nations, and borders. This hostility can be traced back to foundational documents like John Perry Barlow’s “Declaration of the Independence of Cyberspace,” which proclaimed the internet “naturally independent” from state power. While there is an anarcho-capitalist libertarian dimension of these views, they also drew heavily on New Left sensibilities; Barlow, a former Grateful Dead lyricist, was echoing John Lennon’s call to “imagine there’s no countries.” During the peak era of globalization, a toned-down version of this utopian vision was congenial to the Democratic Party.  

Conversely, as Michael Steinberger writes in his biography of Karp, “there was nothing utopian about Palantir; if anything, the company was founded on the conviction that we are facing a bleak future.” It was a “dangerous delusion,” Karp argued from the beginning, to think “the end of the Cold War had ushered in an era of irresistible peace and prosperity.” As he reiterated more recently, “no other country in the history of the world has advanced progressive values more than this one,” and only a strong state equipped with the most cutting-edge technological affordances could preserve that achievement. In 2018, he published a Washington Post op-ed singling out Google for withdrawing from a Pentagon machine learning initiative over ethical concerns, framing this as an act of disloyalty or even treason. As he later restated his position in The Technological Republic, “the technology sector has an affirmative obligation to support the state that made its rise possible.”  

Palantir has come to greater prominence during the second Trump administration in part because Karp’s positions have become far less of an outlier. In recent years, as hot wars have flared up once again around the world, a flood of investment has poured into new defense tech initiatives that sell themselves along similar lines to Palantir, portending a possible return to the time when defense contractors comprised the bulk of the tech industry during the Cold War. The burgeoning artificial intelligence industry, even beyond its expansive government contracts, pitches itself as an adjunct to US geopolitical primacy in competition with China. Even if companies like Anthropic still often cast their missions in philanthropic terms reminiscent of the more utopian rhetoric of earlier eras, Karp’s vision of a “union of science and the state” is being embraced de facto by companies whose heavy capital expenditures render them especially reliant on state incentives and favorable regulatory treatment.

Palantir’s X manifesto enjoined readers to “rebel against the tyranny of the apps,” denouncing the frivolity of the prior era of tech, which may have  sold itself in lofty terms (“Don’t Be Evil”) but mostly promised convenience and efficiency. However, the industry changed its tune not primarily due to any change in philosophy but to the end of the era of low interest rates, whose easy money kept so many “app-for-that” startups afloat during the 2010s. An era of tighter money demands different approaches, and Palantir’s project of a rebooted military-industrial complex is finding far broader traction and appeal. Karp’s evolving partisan signalling is a minor detail in comparison to the significance of this shift.

Brad and Noah discuss the reindustrialization of America

The 65th episode of Hexapodia.

Noah Smith and Brad DeLong
Nov 12
 
READ IN APP
 

I was busy with rabbit stuff today, so my next post will be delayed until tomorrow! In the meantime, have another episode of Hexapodia, my revitalized podcast with Brad DeLong.

In today’s episode, Brad and I discuss the question of whether and how to reindustrialize the United States. Brad wrote a whole book on this topic, in fact. Basically, there are three main reasons we might want to boost American manufacturing:

  1. Geopolitical and military reasons: Having a supply chain for defense manufacturing and dual-use manufacturing that isn’t dominated by China would allow us to actually fight a war against China, if we ever had to do that. And since China has shown themselves perfectly willing to use export controls to bully other countries (including ours), we should develop supply chains that China can’t dominate, in order to avoid being bullied.

  2. Economic growth reasons: Having a robust manufacturing sector, in addition to a robust service sector, may make our country richer, by adding agglomeration and clustering effects.

  3. Economic equality reasons: We might want good high-paying blue-collar manufacturing jobs to help revitalize the American middle class.

Brad and I basically think that #3 is a dead end here — it’s not going to work. Especially with the advent of AI and AI-driven robotics, most manufacturing is going to be mostly automated; there will be no way for America to be competitive using human hands in factories when robot hands work so much better. That means the era of mass semi-skilled blue-collar factory employment is simply over and done.

But that doesn’t mean that manufacturing can’t create jobs. They just have to be different kinds of jobs — for example, local service jobs created by the money that the automated factories bring in to a town. That’s called a “local multiplier” effect, and it’s very powerful and important. Of course, it’ll require that the people who run the factories live near them, so they can spend their money locally.

Which leaves geopolitics and security as the main driver of reindustrialization. We note that the one country that we know of that has ever successfully reindustrialized was Ukraine, which built a strong drone and robotics industry out of necessity in order to fight off the Russian invasion. It’s not necessarily the most optimistic example for us to look to, but it may be the most important.

Anyway, Brad and I then spend a long time discussing what, exactly, America needs to reindustrialize. We come to the tentative conclusion that America really lacks only two important things — land use, and bank loans.

Land use, of course, is what the permitting bill currently moving through Congress is meant to address, and it’s important for a whole lot of other things besides manufacturing.

Bank finance seems to be important for manufacturing for a whole lot of reasons (expect more blog posts about this in the near future), and this is one area where America really struggles compared to other countries. My idea is to use America’s moribund megabanks as pools of capital for reindustrialization by giving them selective exemptions from the Dodd-Frank restrictions enacted after the financial crisis of 2008. More on that later.

Elon Still Loves Vladimir

The betrayal of Ukraine continues

Paul Krugman
Nov 13
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

Taking today off, mostly. But amid the furor over Jensen Huang, people may not have noticed that another tech broligarch is betraying national security in another way as we speak. According to Ukraine, Elon Musk has once again disrupted the nation’s military Starlink service. Large numbers of Ukrainians will die as a result.

One might have thought that Musk would be cautious about abusing his power after the midterms. One speculation is that he may believe that he can get away with it because everyone is focused on Operation Honeypot. Another is that he’s aware that the war is tilting in Ukraine’s favor, with Russian casualties spiking and Ukrainian counterattacks gaining momentum. It’s not beyond the realm of possibility that Putin, or Trump officials who support Putin, reached out to Musk to ask for help.

Whatever the specifics behind the timing, the key point is that, as I said the other day, Musk is part of a small but powerful clique that is actively hostile to American values and to any government that shares our values, and actively favors tyranny. As I said,

Trump, Elon Musk, and many others on the hard right look at Putinism — authoritarian rule under which critics have a tendency to fall out of high windows, male supremacy, social illiberalism, crony capitalism for oligarchs with the right connections — and see it as an exemplar of what they want from a society.

And Musk is using his control of Starlink to aid Putin’s war on a Western-allied democracy.

No private individual — and certainly not someone like Musk — should have that power. Starlink must be nationalized.

What a moderate looks like

Plus the trouble with working with Trump, Florida’s blue vibes and red politics, and more

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 13
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

There’s been a lot of talk of G.O.P. “dummymanders” in states like North Carolina, where Republicans drew very aggressive maps that spread their voters too thin and got swamped in the Dem tsunami. Far be it from me to defend election-rigging shenanigans, but I don’t think we should characterize this kind of map as “dumb.”

It’s certainly true that the North Carolina map was not optimal for maximizing G.O.P. seats in a D+13 national environment. But why would you optimize for that? There’s no saving a party that does that poorly and the exact margin in the House isn’t very important. What these nasty partisan gerrymanders do is maximize your seats in the face of a mildly hostile climate.

To take a Democratic example, the party retained a comfortable majority in 2024 with 46 percent of the vote in the lower house of the Nevada legislature. The way this works is that they won a ton of seats in the Vegas suburbs narrowly while the G.O.P. won a bunch of rural seats by Assad-like margins. The same logic applies nationally. If Dems had done 10 points worse, they’d have gotten crushed on the congressional map. These gerrymanders undermine political accountability by making politicians feel immune to normal-sized swings in opinion, and that’s bad.

Person with Internet Access: One of your many Twitter fights this week, was about whether James Talarico was a moderate or progressive, with both sides trying to claim him. Is this more a case of success has many fathers, or an Obama like charisma that , according to Milan’s earlier poll, leads Democratic factions to see what they want in him. And what’s your empirical case for Talarico moderation?

Skillful, charismatic politicians get different kinds of people to like them. But that’s not really what factional politics is about. Rank-and-file progressive Democrats loved Barack Obama, but that didn’t mean progressive movement leaders agreed with them — part of what those leaders hated about Obama was precisely that he was so well-liked by their base. The entire purpose of the Progressive Establishment organizing project is to prevent the emergence of another Obama-like figure who connects with the mass base of the Democratic Party and puts the groups back in the veal pen.

On Talarico specifically.

This guy is a lifelong Democrat. Kate used to work for Mark Strama, who at the time was a Democratic member of the Texas House of Representatives from Austin. Talarico was in high school at the time, interning in that operation, and was by all accounts a standout member of the Strama Campaign Academy program. He is more progressive than the average American and just got elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas, a state that is more conservative than the average state. Having a guy like that win an election there is obviously a triumph for progressive politics, and progressives should be thrilled about Talarico and celebrating his rise. So I don’t particularly want to yuck anyone’s yum about Talarico or Laken Riley Act supporter Jon Ossoff or anyone else. But I do want progressives themselves to think about how they behave in the real world. Adam Hamilton won an election in an even more conservative state in an even bigger triumph for progressive politics, but then he was asked about Medicare for All on television and said he was against it, and progressive media figures have been denouncing him for it.

Here are some positions Talarico has taken that I have been personally dragged for on social media:

  • All-of-the-above energy policy

  • “I oppose trans athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangers safety or fairness.”

  • “I’m a big fan of SpaceX and Tesla. [Elon Musk] is a great business leader and entrepreneur and innovator. I want him to stick to those things.”

Now, again, I’m not asking progressives to stop liking Talarico. I want them to be happy. And I think that part of why they are happy is that Talarico ran a very good social-media campaign that made sure that a national audience of actual and potential small donors was being fed a steady diet of clips of Talarico taking progressive positions and saying progressive things. But the difference between Democrats who progressives like and Democrats who progressives hate isn’t that the hated ones never take progressive positions. Haley Stevens had a lot of progressive positions! You don’t become a Democratic Party member of Congress without having tons of views that are to the left of the policy status quo and to the left of the median voter.

If Talarico had faced a primary challenge from the left, there would be video clips of him disagreeing with his challenger about various things, his challenger and their allies would have circulated those videos widely, and progressive internet users would be marinated in Talarico-hate. But because none of that happened, they’re not.

We’ll see soon enough how Talarico and Hamilton and Josh Turek and all the rest vote and then we’ll see what happens. But I really would like progressive-minded people to try to do some cognitive behavioral therapy. If there’s someone who won and you’re happy that they won and then they say something in office that you don’t agree with, before you get mad check — is what they just said in line with their campaign promises? If they backtracked on a specific progressive commitment, you’re allowed to be mad. If it’s a topic they just managed to stay silent about all throughout the campaign, you can be a little disappointed, but you can hardly be mad. And if it’s something like Hamilton’s remarks on health care, you not only can’t be mad; you need to actually try to convince your fellow-travelers to chill out.

None of these people ran on Medicare for All. Maybe they should have, but they didn’t. So Democrats aren’t going to pass a Medicare for All message bill in 2027-28, and even if Ro Khanna is president in 2029, they’re not going to pass a Medicare for All bill then. It is what it is. Thanks to flipping governors’ mansions in Texas and Georgia, there’s a chance to enact a massive reduction in America’s uninsurance rate via Medicaid expansion. Congress might do health affordability measures related to premium tax credits, a public option, or prescription drug pricing. If Democrats can figure out how to win elections in Florida, they can do even more Medicaid expansion. If you care a lot about health care, I think that’s what you should be focusing on. If what you care a lot about is shit-testing politicians, then by all means keep hectoring newly elected members about Medicare for All and keep getting mad at them. But in that sense, Talarico is not a progressive — he didn’t get elected by taking the leftward side of various intra-party wedge issues.

Share

Joshua: Is there an option for Democrats to triangulate with Trump against the Republican Party? For instance, give him the arch, the ballroom, the reflecting pool, and rename the Lincoln Memorial the Trump-Lincoln monument. Ask in return for statehood for DC and PR, revocation of the new rules and political interference in NIH and NSF, a national anti-gerrymandering bill, restriction on redistricting beyond the decadal pace, and a few other things. I don’t think Trump himself cares about these, and since his veto is the only thing keeping these from becoming law, it could be several major wins.

I am skeptical of this plan on several levels.

Politics is politics, and for a good enough offer there is always a deal to be made. But in terms of what I was saying above, deliberately giving Trump a pass on acts of corruption really would be a betrayal of explicit promises most Democrats made. If we’re just literally talking about the construction of an arch at a traffic circle in Virginia, then, sure, obviously Democrats should be willing to fund that in exchange for substantive policy concessions. But I think what we’re really talking about here is giving him a pass on lawless behavior in general in exchange for some policy wins, and those wins would have to be huge.

That’s where we get to my other layer of skepticism. This idea that Trump is like a naive child who can be persuaded to give away the store in exchange for a shiny object was kicking around all throughout his first term, and it never worked. At one point, Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi thought they had a verbal agreement for some kind of deal to do the DREAM Act in exchange for funding a border wall, but it got scuttled on a staff level. Trump is not a detail-oriented person, he’s not a consistent person, and he’s not a man of his word or deeply committed to honor and integrity — a superficial agreement isn’t worth anything, and a real agreement is going to need to be approved by a very right-wing team.

Which isn’t to say that deals can’t be done.

But if you look at the major bipartisan legislation of the Trump era — ROAD to Housing, the BAAJA permitting bill, the Covid-era CARES Act, First Step criminal-justice reform — it all reflects hard staff work done by Democrats with detail-oriented G.O.P. stakeholders either on the Hill or somewhere in the executive branch. This is work that got done despite Trump’s mercurial nature, not because of it. He in fact nearly scuttled ROAD with some unexpected remarks about private equity and kept spooking people by saying weird stuff about BAAJA. There’s no example of successfully leveraging Trump’s weirdness into doing policy.

Cam Causey: Nate Silver recently remarked in passing that Florida is a weird state because it’s a Red State but has “Blue State Amenities.” I’m born and raised Floridian, so maybe this is a fish-in-water problem, but I have no idea what he was talking about.

I can’t read another person’s mind. But let’s say you’re someone who really enjoys living in New York City — i.e., you enjoy walkable cities and find the consumption amenities available in the city to be so valuable that you are happy to pay the exorbitant price of housing there. What’s more, let’s say you’re the kind of guy who’d strongly prefer living in Chicago or San Francisco to living in Los Angeles. This is a definite kind of guy. I know guys like this. I think I probably am a guy like this.

And I think to these kinds of guys, Miami is a high-tier city in a way that Atlanta and Dallas are not. There’s a reason that when New York finance guys threaten to move to a low-tax jurisdiction it’s almost always Miami and not somewhere in South Dakota.

I don’t know that thinking of these lifestyle amenities in terms of the political lean of whole states is particularly enlightening, though. You could imagine a state of South Florida composed of Miami-Dade, Broward, Palm Beach, Lee, Collier, Monroe, and Hendry counties. This “state” would have a larger population than Arizona, Tennessee, or Massachusetts. And politically, it would have voted for Clinton and Biden before flipping to Trump in 2024 but would have backed Democrats in statewide offices this cycle. It is true that Miami is unusually conservative for a city of its size and character, but what that amounts to in practice is “not super-duper left-wing” rather than “actually conservative.” State politics as a whole is conservative because of the voting behavior in places like the Tampa and Orlando suburbs that I don’t think particularly have amenities that Nate or I would find appealing.

Share

John K: Now, that we know the results, how do you think your pre-scandal case for Platner holds up? Specifically, the idea that Collins would be so hard to beat that we needed to ramp up the variance.

Eyeballing the results, it looks like ME-Sen would’ve been neck and neck if we’d had the D+6 environment many people expected earlier this year, which makes me skeptical, but maybe Jackson was stronger than I think?

If I want to rescue the take, I would say that if Jackson had been running in the first place, we’d have said that he was the high-variance play relative to Janet Mills and that in ending up with the logger from Allagash Democrats basically got the thing that Platner was supposed to have been.

The problem with trying to rescue the take is Jackson didn’t attempt any ideological heterodoxy — not even Platner’s flirtation with being a strong gun-rights guy — and Jackson did terribly in his home region, losing his home town and the district he represented in the State Senate pretty badly. If you look at where Collins ran weaker in 2026 than she did in 2020, the biggest swings are in the Portland suburbs followed by Portland itself and Maine’s smaller cities like Lewiston and Bangor.

If anything, Jackson did worse than Sara Gideon in the more culturally conservative parts of the state.

Bryan T. Mathew: How should democrats in Texas govern? What did Republicans get right that Democrats should leave alone? What should be changed?

The three big ones are that Texas should restore abortion rights, curb the unregulated school voucher program, and expand Medicaid. I am also proud to say that I am much more left-wing on economics than populist Gina Hinojosa — in my opinion, she’s wrong and Texas should create a (low but nonzero) income tax. She’s promised not to do that, and it’s moot with a Republican State Senate anyway, but I think it’s worth saying.

The question becomes “how can you expand Medicaid without a new tax,” and I think the answer will probably be “cut some kind of deal with the data center industry after having campaigned so hard against them.”

In terms of what not to change, my education reform friends are very worried that Hinojosa will go beyond anti-vouchers by wrecking the state’s accountability system and crushing the charter school sector. She should consider not doing that! I think Texas has the most successful electricity transmission and interconnection system in the country and Democrats shouldn’t change that (I see no indication that they will). And I think they should try to double down on housing growth by adopting new pro-infill measures statewide. I would also consider trying to complement housing growth by creating more state parks and the like because Texas is pretty weak on public lands. Again, though, you would need some revenue.

Hank Smathers: Matt, you were concerned that Trump was signaling pre-election a dramatic escalation of the war in Iran after the midterms. In light of Vance’s and other Repubs’ cynical efforts to now blame the war as the sole cause for their defeat at the polls, how do you think this plays out with the war going forward?

I’m not going to claim secret knowledge of the Pentagon’s planning here, but a basic problem facing every president who has ever decided that a war is a political millstone around his neck and he wants to end it is that “just surrender” is not very appealing. The only president who’s ever really attempted “give up” as a strategy, Joe Biden, got hammered for it politically.

And the war in Iran is worse than Afghanistan or Vietnam from the “give up” standpoint because the thing people are angry about isn’t the direct expenditures on the war but the downstream economic cost of the disruption to shipping. Trump does not have a “reopen the strait” button that he can just push. He would need to reach a diplomatic agreement with Iran that would probably involve making a lot of concessions to them. One set of possible concessions would be acquiescing to some kind of Iranian tolling of the strait, but that wouldn’t address voter concerns about energy costs. So if you’re going to do a deal with Iran that secures safe untaxed passage through the strait, you’re going to have to make some other kind of concessions to Iran that could get pretty politically dicey.

So if you’re sitting in the Oval Office thinking, “I need to end this war,” there’s a good chance you end up where L.B.J. was on Vietnam or where George Bush was on Iraq in 2007 or where Barack Obama was on Afghanistan in his first term and saying, “I need to do a big escalatory push to create a more favorable terrain for a diplomatic agreement.”

By Nathan Pinkoski • 13 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In the Realm of the Last Man: A Memoir
By Francis Fukuyama
FSG, 304 pages, $29

The publishing industry is experiencing a surge in memoirs, and the Boomers are to blame. They want to reflect on their lives and describe the vanished world of their youth before they themselves vanish from the earth. It’s a surge in supply, not a surge in demand. Readers are skeptical the Boomers have something to say. But if the memoir of any member of that generation deserves a hearing, it is Francis Fukuyama’s. 

Born in 1952 to a family of first- and second-generation Japanese immigrants, Fukuyama vaulted to fame with his 1989 essay “The End of History?,” becoming one of the world’s most celebrated public intellectuals. His memoir, In the Realm of the Last Man, is marketed as a personal and intellectual autobiography that also provides an apologia for his most famous thesis. The book checks off several boxes of the memoir genre. Fukuyama describes his family origins, childhood, education, and his first professional postings with the RAND Corporation, the CIA, and the State Department prior to publishing his famous essay. He reflects on his personal hobbies (he is an amateur computer coder and carpenter). He reminisces about his intellectual influences: Leo Strauss and his student Allan Bloom, the social scientist Seymour Martin Lipset, and the political scientist Samuel Huntington. Modest and laconic about his political connections, Fukuyama regales readers with amusing anecdotes of an audience with Muammar Gaddafi and a more personal friendship with a senior official in the Chinese government. He also explains why, like most of his generation, he has become less conservative over time.

“The book isn’t really a memoir.”

Yet the book isn’t really a memoir. A few pages in, as Fukuyama recounts his family’s history in America, he abruptly veers off from talking about relatives interned during the Second World War to declare that “in 2025, the US returned to mistreating people—this time, those suspected of being undocumented migrants.” Most of the book is like that. Every few pages, Fukuyama connects an old story, teacher, or lesson learned to some deplorable recent action by Donald Trump or his allies. The book begins with Trump’s second inauguration, casting him as a world-historical figure dismantling the postwar liberal order. It ends by invoking the challenge Christian nationalists and the “strong gods” pose to liberalism. At the heart of In the Realm of the Last Man is Fukuyama’s struggle to explain the success of emerging political movements, particularly Trump’s, which repudiate the consensus he helped define in his youth. What he doesn’t acknowledge is that many of his intellectual shifts mirror those of the movements he despises.

 

Fukuyama is often accused of being a Cold War triumphalist, but his “end of history” argument was more subtle. Liberal democracy, by his account, was an ideology that brought economic and scientific progress, satisfied our material longings, and sought the mutual and equal recognition of all by all. 

This is not supposed to be an inspiring picture. It is a world populated by Friedrich Nietzsche’s “Last Man”: a human type who claims to have discovered happiness, but blinks uncomprehendingly at higher human possibilities. The last men produced by the victory of liberal democracy are fundamentally souls without longing: “Everyone wants the same; everyone is the same,” wrote Nietzsche. “‘Formerly all the world was insane,’ — say the subtlest of them, and they blink.” Encountering this kind of stupor provokes ressentiment from great-souled men. As Fukuyama argued in his original essay, “if the greater part of the world in which they live is characterized by peaceful and prosperous liberal democracy, they then will struggle against that peace and prosperity, and against democracy.”

Since 2016, this demarcation between defenders of liberal democracy on the one hand and the rebels on the other has been used to explain the right’s victories. At its best, it has informed sympathetic treatments of the rebels, while forcing the defenders to examine their own blind spots. But this demarcation has also often degenerated into a caricature in which lovers of freedom are pitted against lovers of fascism. To stay relevant, the cottage industry switches out the antagonists. Yesterday, it was Catholic integralist academics; today, it’s tech entrepreneurs who’ve spent time in South Africa.

Fukuyama often writes in this register, but he intuits its limits. Above all, it imagines liberal democracy as a fixed set of ideas, which generate either assent or revolt. But liberal democracy is an ideology in motion, and Fukuyama’s own reflections on his varying views over the past few decades show this. Long before Trump descended the golden escalator, the inadequacies of the old consensus were prompting him to revise his positions. In the Realm of the Last Man explains why the brand of conservative liberalism that Fukuyama once embraced has failed. It identifies the same problems with liberal institutions that preoccupy postliberals on both the left and the right.

While this has become a subject of regret to the elder Fukuyama, as a young man he was a bona fide 1980s-style conservative. In the book version of The End of History and the Last Man, he stressed the importance of limited state power and an independent civil society. His 1999 book The Great Disruption: Human Nature and the Reconstitution of Social Order, was a neoconservative work in the tradition of Irving Kristol, endorsing America’s trajectory until the late 1960s, then raising the alarm over a country that was veering off course, with rising crime and the sexual revolution. Fukuyama stressed the importance of a strong state enforcing the law and upholding communitarian values, even as he distanced himself from the Christian religious right. His 2002 book, Our Posthuman Future, reflected a similar spirit. He defended natural rights and credited the Western-made conception of equality for placing limits on technological self-modification. Like Kristol, Fukuyama had two cheers for capitalism. He believed in free markets but only up to a point, criticizing libertarianism and excessive individualism. 

Added to this set of mainstream American conservative views was Fukuyama’s liberal universalism. He was confident, like other neoconservatives, in the contagious power of liberal ideas to spread around the world. What chastened this confidence? Fukuyama’s answer is the same that many on the Trump-aligned right give: Iraq. The United States’s failure to bring peace, prosperity, and liberal democracy to the Middle East catalyzed his intellectual shift. 

Iraq certainly revealed the flaw of presuming liberal democracy’s universal reach, leading to commonplaces about America’s inability to spread liberal democracy by military force. But there are more sophisticated lessons to draw. For Obama-era progressives, Iraq taught that nation-building first requires a democratic civil society. Partnerships between the state department and tech platforms, they concluded, might achieve this via the internet, incubating the liberal democratic change that boots on the ground could not. That “lesson” of Iraq accounted for much of the color revolution and Arab Spring stratagems, important in the 2010s.

“Fukuyama went in a different direction.” 

Fukuyama went in a different direction. As he explains, “the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan engendered a major shift in my own intellectual interests and research,” making him more interested in the state. For Fukuyama, the disaster of Iraq was made possible by facile assumptions about how to establish functioning governing institutions. Above all, it was a failure to think seriously about what the state can do well. In this respect, Fukuyama saw himself as repudiating an older conservative-liberal consensus. Americans had long thought of the state as a “cold monster,” and grappled with how “to limit the power of a state, and not how to create power in the first place.” This attitude, he concluded, had ensured that Iraq would fail. “States could be obstacles to growth,” Fukuyama realized, but they also “performed critical functions in making and enforcing the rules under which private companies acted.” An attitude appropriate for warding off a command economy in the mid-twentieth century was inhibiting contemporary Americans from solving their problems. They needed to leave their postwar Hayekian fixations behind and think about how to govern well. 

Fukuyama’s post-2003 interest in the state also brought him to change his views on what had been happening to the global economy in the 1990s. He discovered the critics of neoliberalism. This challenged another Bush-era conservative shibboleth, which taught that the Reagan Revolution, carried on by Clinton, had unlocked a new era of global economic prosperity and stability by encouraging the state to get out of the way. Instead, Fukuyama came to attribute recurring financial crises, from those of the early 1990s in Mexico up to the great financial crisis of 2008, to state weakness rather than excessive state interference. He also explained the success of the East Asian “tigers” by their industrial policies and infant industry protectionism, enabled by their strong states. Countries lacking such state capacity could not launch a similar strategy and would careen from crisis to crisis. Deregulation and privatization were less important than setting up a state that could shield strategic industries and spearhead growth. Fukuyama credits the World Bank’s 1997 World Development Report, which pivoted the bank’s agenda to anti-corruption and governance questions—questions of sound state function—for providing the intellectual foundation for his later pivot. Fukuyama, in short, proposed a paradigm shift in political science and political economy away from postwar liberalism’s anti-statist consensus. 

That paradigm shift suggests that even in 1989, liberal democracy was in crisis. The narrative of a stable ideology bringing prosperity was already misleading, as the embrace of neoliberalism by liberal democracies was contributing to global economic instability and failing to deliver results. Experts in the World Bank and elsewhere were aware of the issues, urging governments to adopt a new course. Long before the great financial crisis, the consensus was already fraying. 

 

Fukuyama’s post-2003 anti-neoliberal orientation tracks closely with how postliberals of the left and the right, from Maurice Glasman to Patrick Deneen, explain the failure of late twentieth-century liberalism. And while Fukuyama regarded his anti-neoliberal outlook as a rapprochement with progressivism, calling for a stronger state and more industrial protectionism was hardly unique to the left, even in the 1980s and ’90s. It echoes the conclusions of other right-wing dissidents who rejected anti-statism after concluding that free trade—a selective protectionism that defended intellectual property and the financial sector but dropped import controls on manufacturing and other strategic sectors—had failed to deliver a stable economic model. For Fukuyama, it’s the critics of neoliberalism rather than conservative liberals who have the best account of what went wrong with liberalism in the 1990s. This contention remains one of the sharpest divides between the old and new right. But Fukuyama’s diagnosis aligns him with the new.

There’s a second shift at play here that likewise mirrors postliberal developments. In the “End of History” essay and thereafter, Fukuyama embraced the “output legitimacy” theory of liberal democracy, which holds that it’s good because of the consequences it brings, not because of the procedures it follows. Liberal democracy defeated communism because it produced consumer goods and delivered technological innovations that communism could not; he called this “The Victory of the VCR.” Fukuyama’s defense of liberal democracy as the ideology that satisfies the thumotic struggle for recognition is a legitimating philosophical veneer that conceals a more pragmatic impulse. Growth is liberal democracy’s real source of legitimacy. As Fukuyama finessed his thinking in the 2000s, he concluded that a strong state was the best guarantor of growth. That meant a strong administrative state. Thereafter, Fukuyama never met a bureaucracy he didn’t like. 

Output legitimacy is at odds with conservative liberalism, which could be accused of a “fetishization of proceduralism”—Fukuyama’s term for one of liberalism’s defects. Pious chatter about parliamentary or senate procedures, representative government, and the Framers’ checks and balances can’t be relied upon to deliver the economic output needed to secure state legitimacy. Yet output legitimacy has been extensively criticized as a repudiation of democracy. If output matters more than process, a monarch—or technocratic elite or caste of judges—could deliver the best results. Output legitimacy justifies elected governments delegating more power to agencies insulated from public accountability, on the promise that they guarantee growth. This has been one of the most important revolutions in late twentieth-century governance, and the reaction against it has fueled populism in Europe, Great Britain, Canada, and the United States. Left and right populists are restorationist in posture, protesting that unelected bureaucrats and judges are acting as legislators and replacing democratically elected representatives. That said, many of these protests have flickered out. Fukuyama’s early bet on output legitimacy in 1989 seems to capture the emerging twenty-first century post-democratic landscape. Voters have generally acquiesced to the transfer of power to unelected bureaucrats so long as the latter deliver material improvements.

“Madisonian liberalism has been superseded.”

Again, Fukuyama’s observations track those of left and right postliberals. Distinct from the populist political movements they are often said to represent, postliberals argued for years that turning back the clock to representative government is impossible. Madisonian liberalism has been superseded. The challenge for a governing party now is to figure out how to deliver positive outputs within the new environment. The clearest strategy is to work within the framework of the administrative state and strengthen executive power.

Dysfunction in the American system stops that from happening. Fukuyama describes the American system as a “vetocracy.” His critique dates from the Obama years, when progressives were frustrated by the GOP-controlled Congress blocking the White House’s big initiatives. But since 2016, a similar critique has emerged on the American right. Even when the GOP controls the presidency and Congress, Republicans still can’t pass anything significant beyond budget reconciliation. Conservative liberals retort by delivering paeans to Senate procedures, from the filibuster to deferring to the parliamentarian. Voters of both parties are unimpressed. 

 

Fukuyama’s diagnoses, as detailed in his other books, are debatable. But In the Realm of the Last Man exposes the unresolved tension in his life work. One side of his thought teaches that since the 1980s, liberal and democratic states have had to adjust their governing institutions and economy, sometimes drastically, to resolve crises of legitimacy. The other side teaches that since the 1980s, an ideology of “liberal democracy” remains victorious, unchanged, and unchallengeable, except by resentful ingrates. 

This determination to cleave to the old source of imagined stability betrays a hint of desperation to hold onto the vanishing certitudes of the late 1980s. As in many memoirs, nostalgia and myopia go hand-in-hand.

We know liberal democracies are still vibrant, Fukuyama argues, because “every year, tens if not hundreds of thousands undertake dangerous and expensive journeys … for the privilege of living in North America or Europe.” He compares this movement of peoples to Cold War migration flowing out of the Iron Curtain. He seems incapable of assessing the mass migration of a wholly different epoch, where the West imports peoples, creeds, and cultures for whom “liberal democracy” means easy access to welfare and women.

With America having fallen from grace in the age of Trump, Fukuyama turns hopefully to the project inaugurated as the Soviet Union weakened—the European Union—as the arsenal of liberal democratic output, which he says has “fully delivered on the promise of peace and prosperity.” Never mind that the EU is a co-belligerent in a war with a great power, the European Commission has ensured that the EU will be a bystander to the AI revolution, a second “China shock” of deindustrialization is underway in Germany, and continental living standards are in free fall. But Fukuyama has a pat answer for these failures in output legitimacy: He blames the populists. “China has been invited into Europe,” he tells us, as “a way of thumbing one’s nose at existing elites.” At last, we know why all those deals were made with China by that anti-establishment icon Angela Merkel.

Yet the greatest failure of In the Realm of the Last Man is Fukuyama’s inability to understand the political changes that are transforming his own progressive camp. Toward the end of the book, Fukuyama accuses the pro-Palestinian protesters who took to the streets after October 7, 2023, of a kind of hypocrisy, on the grounds that “they not similarly outraged at the situation of Ukrainians besieged by Russia or of victims of the civil war in Sudan.” As this framing suggests, he sees the protests as akin to humanitarian campus protests of the 1970s or ’80s. He doesn’t grasp why the Israel-Palestine conflict has become a pivotal drama in Western politics: how it reinforces the oppressor-oppressed ideological framing of the hard left; how it mobilizes so many because of new waves of immigration from parts of the world more closely connected to the conflict, forming the basis for the new red-green alliance that is redefining the left. 

“Fukuyama can’t explain why other alternatives have emerged.”

Determined to maintain the ideology of his youth even when his research reveals how much it has changed and needed to change, Fukuyama can’t explain why other alternatives have emerged. Whether they are in government or the official opposition, the new iterations of the right and left do have daring programs for taking us beyond the vanished world Fukuyama’s generation continues to imagine exists. All Fukuyama can do is keep insisting that they have “no clear, systematic vision.” Faced with concrete alternatives that leave his liberalism behind, he can only blink.

I’m feeling more optimistic about American politics

And it’s not *just* because I prefer the Democrats.

Noah Smith
Nov 14
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

“Partisanship is a helluva drug,” as they say. When your preferred party is in power, the sun seems to shine a little brighter, the birds sing a little more sweetly, and there’s a spring in your step as you walk past the homeless encampments and sterile single-family-home-only neighborhoods of your American city. Foreigners from countries where politics is less contentious, like Japan, will never know this joy.

Anyway, this natural partisan sentiment makes it very hard for me to write about developments in American politics. I would like to give you some analysis that’s more informative than “Yay, Democrats won an election!”. I do consider myself a Democrat, after all (even though I’m registered as an Independent). There has never been a point in my entire life when I’d have told you that the Republican presidential candidate was a better pick than the Democrat (though 2012 was fairly close). I regularly bemoan the state of the Democratic Party, but somehow the Republicans always find some way to be Even Worse.

This has been the unfortunate reality for most people in America for years now. Disgust and dissatisfaction with both parties have grown, as both have become more extremist. But there was little they could do except keep voting for the lesser of two evils, while tuning out political news and expressing anger at the whole system. It got so bad that in my New Year’s essay, I even entertained the notion that liberal democracy itself had suffered a generational failure:

Where does a liberal go from here?

Noah Smith
·
Jan 4
Read full story

To be honest, I still entertain that notion. Reading that essay again, there’s not much I would change. But on the margin, recent events have made me feel more optimistic about where American politics is going.

A lot of this is downstream of the midterm elections. Trump has turned the Republican Party into something truly awful, and it’s refreshing to see America punish the GOP for going along with that transformation:

Croaky Caiman | The Rational Purview
@RationalPurview
MAGA inherited a Republican Party with 54 senators, 247 House seats, and 31 governors. They coopted the tea party that led to these wins and ran on pure populism with no actual guiding conservative principles other than whatever one guy said at any given moment and what his…
Stinson Norwood @snorman1776
Maybe true maga has never really been tried?
3:51 PM · Nov 12, 2026 · 262K Views
31 Replies · 163 Reposts · 800 Likes

But my optimism isn’t just about the fact that Democrats won — it’s also about how they won, and what they seem likely to do with their victory. Here I’ve been pleasantly surprised so far. And there are also some scattered signs that our leaders are starting to take our substantive policy challenges more seriously, instead of just relying on partisanship and culture wars. Basically, I see three broad positive trends:

  1. The Democrats are not becoming extremist at the rate I had feared.

  2. There is some real bipartisan movement on good policymaking at the federal level.

  3. The nation is waking up to the problem of corruption, and holding the perpetrators to account.

Liberals, not leftists, are leading the anti-Trump charge

Over the past few years, I’ve watched the emergence of a leftist faction within the Democratic Party, which I’ve likened to MAGA on the right. This faction had its roots in the Bernie insurgency of 2016-2020, but it has grown beyond that. The Palestine movement both invigorated the leftists and radicalized them, shifting the locus of power in left-of-center activism away from Black activists, identitarian movements, and anti-capitalism, and toward explicitly anti-American “decolonial” ideas.

As recently as this summer, I believed that a Democratic victory in the midterms would be led by this hard-left vanguard:

Are the Democrats going to save us this time?

Noah Smith
·
Aug 6
Read full story

Here’s what I wrote:

Democrats have spent their political capital moving to the left…[They are selecting] candidates who are so far to the left that they end up frightening and/or offending many voters, and then basically daring people to keep voting for the Republicans…

When DSA-type candidates were just winning in deep blue cities, it was possible to think that they would remain a small, limited faction within the party. But Francesca Hong is going to be the Democratic nominee in a statewide race. So is Abdul El-Sayed, who, while not a member of the DSA, is closely aligned with them (especially on Israel, which he focuses on a lot)…This, increasingly, is who the Democrats are now.

Well, happily, I was wrong about this. Francesca Hong was actually defeated in the Democratic primary race just a few days later in a stunning upset, showing that even partisan Democrats aren’t sold on the DSA faction.

Even more importantly, the hard left didn’t end up leading the anti-Trump charge in the midterms, as I had expected. Despite the blue wave, most of the high-profile DSA-faction candidates performed significantly worse than their normie Democrat counterparts. Jeff Maurer has great data on this:

I Might Be Wrong
How Leftists and Moderates Did in the Midterms
Three months ago, I wrote a post “setting up the goal posts” to measure how individual candidates did in the midterms. I did that for two reasons: First, I did it to be a dick. I feel that liberals can be too polite, and we bite our tongues in response to the hate and idiocy that DSA types are trying to smuggle into the mainstream — I see a role for a t…
Read more
10 days ago · 307 likes · 140 comments · Jeff Maurer

And the same voters who powered the big Democratic victories also endorsed a lot of centrist policies at the ballot box. Here’s the Washington Post:

Voters in North Carolina elected a Democratic senator…giving former governor Roy Cooper an overwhelming win. At the same time, they approved three [Republican] measures…The first would add a constitutional requirement for a levy limit on property taxes…The second would cap the state income tax at 3.5 percent…The third would require photo ID for voting…

In Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley won the gubernatorial election…Those same voters approved an initiative…to ban affirmative action in state institutions…Iowa voters elected Democrats as governor and senator while amending their constitution to make it substantially harder to raise state income taxes…Ohio….went blue for Senate and governor. At the same time, two-thirds of voters backed an amendment to require photo ID for voting…

Moderates and independents drove Democratic gains in all these places.

Voters in several blue and purple states also approved measures to restrict women’s sports teams by biological sex.

There’s also a general indefinable “vibe shift” in the air. Anecdotally, people I talk to are less ashamed to voice full-throated support for the kind of liberalism that Barack Obama typified in the early 2010s. Meanwhile, liberal influencers online are beginning to push back more strongly on leftist shouters.

And in Congress, the sheer scale of the Democrats’ victory means that the DSA faction will be effectively disempowered. Because marginal victories tend to be won by moderates in purple states, the leadership in both the House and the Senate is likely to be held by moderates like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer. If they fail to find a candidate for 2028, and if Democrats take back the White House with a normie liberal, the leftist faction faces the real possibility that the window of America’s decade of unrest will limp to a close without them. That would, of course, be good for the nation.

Smart policy is starting to win (and “the groups” are starting to lose)

Even moderate politicians, of course, often support unworkable or inadvisable policies. On the Democratic side, the worst problems are anti-development policies at the state and local level. “Progressive” policies have made it prohibitively difficult and/or expensive to build housing, roads, trains, power stations, and transmission lines across much of the country, freezing our built environment in the 1970s. I’ve been loudly complaining about this for years now:

The Build-Nothing Country

Noah Smith
·
February 27, 2023
Read full story

This was a big part of my pessimism about politics. What’s the use of kicking out the Republicans, if the Democrats are just going to decide that “open space” and historic gas stations are more important than giving the middle class a place to live and power for their homes?

Now there are signs that at long last, America’s leaders recognize this problem and are taking action to fix it.

In July, Congress passed the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, without Donald Trump’s signature. The law streamlines federal requirements for environmental reviews (one of the biggest barriers to development), makes it easier to build prefabricated and modular housing, and makes it easier for local banks to make housing-related loans. It’s far from a complete fix for the NIMBY problem, obviously, and most of the heavy lifting will still have to be done at the state and local level, but it’s a very positive sign.

Now it’s being followed up — finally!! — with action on permitting. The “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act” (BAAJA) may have a slopulist-sounding name, but it’s actually a very smart bill that would make it easier to build infrastructure. Once again, streamlining the review process — i.e., making it harder for NIMBYs to delay infrastructure projects for years by suing them and making them do a bunch of paperwork — takes center stage. Here’s Alex Mechanick on what the bill gets right:

Much of the coverage has focused on the implications of the bill for energy transmission buildout…Expert analyses have estimated that it will make energy cheaper and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. All of that work is important. But, in my view, [BAAJA] is first and foremost a state capacity bill…

[T]he most important way that BAAJA cuts through the morass is by changing what happens when an agency violates only NEPA or NHPA alone. (That is, when the agency does not violate a substantive regulatory statute, the Administrative Procedure Act, or any other law.) Instead of voiding the permits and sending everything back to square one, the project continues as the analysis is fixed…

That means that it is not just energy generation and energy transmission projects that will be sped up (and made cheaper) by BAAJA. It’s transportation projects like rail, congestion pricing, and port deepening. It’s projects that will expand water reservoirs, restore lakes, and thin forests to prevent wildfires. It’s even federal housing projects, presidential libraries, and broadband buildout.

While we don’t yet know how big of an impact this bill will have, the history of permitting reform is encouraging:

Why is this happening now, when it failed to happen for so many years? The AI boom is the obvious reason. Companies are building a ton of data centers, and this is putting strains on the electrical grid, making local consumers angry. On top of that the U.S. is in a technological race with China, and being able to build energy infrastructure will be crucial to winning that race.

The confluence of these three imperatives — the needs of businesses, consumers, and national security — brought together an extraordinary alliance across the political spectrum, including Democrats like Jeffries and Schumer, Biden appointees like Janet Yellen, Republicans like John Thune and Mike Johnson, and Trump appointees like Stephen Miran. The speed with which this bipartisan group came together and took action — including all of the necessary horse trading — is highly encouraging, because it shows that our leaders are still responsive to the imperatives of the outside world, and not just wrapped up in a bubble of culture wars and personality cults.

It also shows the waning power of the special interest pressure groups known collectively as “the groups”. Although most environmentalists support making it easier to build green energy infrastructure, a loud minority of obstructionist groups like the Sierra Club basically oppose making it legal to build anything at all. But a high-pressure campaign by these groups to stop BAAJA failed. That’s a highly encouraging sign, because it means our politics — and especially Democratic politics — aren’t quite as dominated by special interests as we had feared.

Our tolerance for corruption might not be infinite

That’s what the Jensen Huang affair is really about. I’m not particularly interested in the Nvidia founder’s personal life or marital infidelities, and I bet most people aren’t that interested either; if he had just been sleeping around, it would barely make the headlines, and I doubt he would have been forced to resign. The reason people are interested in this particular scandal is that it’s directly tied to the corruption of the Trump administration.

Basically, U.S. export controls, enacted by the Biden administration but so far mostly kept in place by Trump, forbid Nvidia from selling powerful AI chips to China. But the Trump administration relaxed the rules and allowed Nvidia to sell some of these chips, either to China directly, or to data centers in countries like Singapore that turned right around and let the Chinese make use of them.¹ Some of those sales were facilitated by Alice Huang, one of Jensen’s many lovers, who has also been linked to the Chinese intelligence services.

Why did Trump poke loopholes in the export control regime on Nvidia’s behalf? Writing in The Free Press, Matt Pottinger and Lila Tobin suggest that corruption was involved, and focus on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick:

The U.S. Department of Commerce could reverse [Nvidia chip sales to China] with a few strokes of a pen. Instead, the department, led by Howard Lutnick, the former CEO of a major Wall Street firm, has slow-rolled, stymied, and undermined efforts by his own officials to constrain China’s access to chips, according to numerous people with direct knowledge of the department’s affairs. On Friday, The New York Times reported that “Mr. Trump’s close relationship with Mr. Huang has also made department officials wary of taking aggressive steps to rein in sales of Nvidia chips, out of concern about angering Mr. Lutnick or the White House.”..

Congressional investigators will have questions for Lutnick too. Did he or his family benefit from the loopholes staying open? Did his old firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, benefit? Cantor’s public filings show it is a sales agent for Bitdeer, an Nvidia cloud partner that is expanding its data centers into Southeast Asia. Bitdeer is a spin-off of Bitmain, which has been the subject of a national security probe over fears its machines could be remotely controlled to disable the U.S. grid or for espionage. Rules designed to close these loopholes have been blocked by the Department of Commerce on multiple occasions, even after the president ordered them closed, according to recent reporting by Axios.

But although Lutnick’s role certainly deserves more scrutiny, it seems overwhelmingly likely that this one goes all the way to the top. Before Trump relaxed export controls, Huang cultivated a close relationship with the President, and contributed tens of millions of dollars to Trump’s White House ballroom project:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has spent the past two years cultivating an unparalleled relationship with President Donald Trump, gaining extraordinary access and influence over federal artificial intelligence policy as his company has pushed for looser restrictions on selling advanced chips to China…Nvidia has committed at least $26 million to Trump’s pet projects, including $25 million toward his White House ballroom and $1 million to his 2025 inaugural fund.

Trump, meanwhile, purchased millions of dollars of Nvidia’s stock just before he changed the export controls to allow Nvidia to sell more to China.

The exact shape of this scandal is still forming, and it’ll take many months of dogged Congressional investigations to get at something resembling the truth. But fortunately, it looks like we’re going to get those investigations. Thanks to the Democrats’ resounding midterm victory and the salience of the corruption issue, someone is finally going after the rot at the top.

That’s a very hopeful sign for American politics, for several reasons. First, it means that Democrats have something positive and unifying to focus on — fighting corruption — that’s also popular with the electorate. This will take attention away from more divisive culture-war issues. Second, a rolling series of corruption scandals and investigations might both disempower Trump and force the White House’s next occupant to be scrupulously clean and honest, as happened after Watergate.

It’s also possible that general disgust at corruption will inaugurate an era of more moderate politics and national calm, as it did after Watergate. Corrupt politicians often hide behind ideology as a smokescreen against public outrage; cutting through the fog and focusing on corruption itself will take away an incentive for manufactured extremism.

Ultimately, any reason for hope about American politics has to come back to moderation. We’ve just lived through over a decade of roiling unrest that enabled some of the country’s worst actors to rule over the rest of us. Anything that tamps down or soothes the remnants of that unrest — and gets rid of the bad actors who rode that unrest to power — is good for our country. And recent events make me a little more optimistic that our country is finally crawling back toward collective sanity.
