Will AI crash? How bad will it be if so

Paul Krugman
Nov 14
 
READ IN APP
 

A conversation with Jared Bernstein and Jason Furman

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo, Bookshop, and Nook.

. . .

TRANSCRIPT:
Paul Krugman in Conversation with Jared Bernstein and Jason Furman

(recorded 11/12/26)

Paul Krugman: Today I’m talking with Jared Bernstein and Jason Furman, both of whom have been writing, as I have, about AI. Is it a bubble? If it is a bubble, what happens when it bursts? What’s it doing to the economy? All things AI. Hopefully, we can stay off of honeypots for the most part. But is it a bubble? I am surprisingly uncertain in my own judgment here. So, we can talk about the scope of it, but what can we make of this huge, huge investment in a very new technology?

Jared Bernstein: Well, when I’m being disciplined, I describe it as probably a bubble. I should start out by saying almost everything I’m going to say for the next X minutes is going to be speculative. And also, I’d like to underscore that, for all my concerns about a bubble and a bubble bursting, I think AI is likely to be a significant productivity enhancer, perhaps even transformational in that regard. So I don’t want to lose that. But in terms of your basic question, my work on this is with Ryan Cummings, and we started sniffing a bubble in the sector over a year ago, and we had a piece in The New York Times to that effect. We thought that the gap between the spend of the hyperscalers and the labs—the actual spending that they were doing and the expected spending—the gap between that and plausible earnings projections suggested bubble dynamics. So in later work, we were able to roughly quantify that gap. And others did a similar exercise. And I know you, Paul in particular, you’ve written about that. There’s a Brookings paper on this, which further raised our bubble antennae.

Actually, at this point, the diagnosis is pretty widely agreed upon, although there are doubts. And I share yours as well, Paul, with the added worry—now, this wasn’t quite there when we first started writing in October of last year—of leverage, that is. A lot of the spend was initially financed through cash flow. And some of these companies have big cash flows—not the freestanding labs, but the Metas and the Amazons—and now there’s the added worry of leverage because there’s so much more borrowing.

Last point on this: I do think it’s a good question for people who have the position I have as to whether you’ve personally divested in the sector. And I will say that I partially have, in that there is no SpaceX in my portfolio at this point in time.

Krugman: Let me ask you, Jason, for your take. I have some thoughts also.

Jason Furman: Well, first of all, I’ll do the investment advice first. All of my financial assets are basically in Vanguard Global ETF. So I have every single company on the planet Earth, or at least I aspire to have every single company on planet Earth. And so in that sense, I think with the sort of “your money’s where your mouth is” test, I’m implicitly saying it’s not a bubble.

I wake up different days taking different sides of this argument. It doesn’t feel like this is the type of network that previous technologies were—like Google Search becoming the best, or Facebook becoming the best. Everyone basically needed to use it, and they could end up with, in the case of Google, 90% of the search market. For this, I can use Claude, you can use ChatGPT, and I know Jared is just obsessed with Grok—maybe I wasn’t supposed to tell people that, Jared?—but it all works just fine. Moreover, if you go to Claude and say, “The bills are too high, what should I do?” it’ll say, “Try ChatGPT, and here’s a file to download and instructions for how to upload it to ChatGPT.” So there just doesn’t seem to be anything keeping people on these.

Moreover, the more they improve, the more for most purposes you can use older models. It’s like cars that used to go 200 miles an hour and now they go 1,000 miles an hour. For race car drivers, that’s a great thing; they want the latest car. For most of the rest of us, the old one is perfectly fine. So that is the “it’s a bubble” story.

On the other side, though, I have two reasons why I’m cautious about going too far with that. One is, I first personally called the Tesla bubble in April 2017. That is when Tesla’s market cap exceeded both Ford and General Motors. At the time, Tesla was making fewer than 100,000 cars, and these other companies were making like 10 million cars. And it seemed insane to me. It seemed like a massive bubble. Tesla’s up about 2,000% since I made that bubble call. And yes, it may collapse one day, but there’s no collapse that’s going to make me correct in my April 2017 call. And that’s happened over and over again with people.

And then the second thing that gives me pause is small probabilities of infinity, which is: you don’t need that high a probability of Anthropic taking over everything in the world to justify its valuation. So bottom line: I would not be at all surprised if it was a bubble. I would not argue strongly against it being a bubble, but I’m just too humble to believe any of my analysis or act on it.

Krugman: So, I’ll give you my take. I kind of look at the size of the CapEx and the experience that we had from the dot-coms, which was that it was a really big technology, but the big spenders didn’t capture much of the gains. So it is hard to understand the valuations. On the other hand, people who understand the technology better than—well, it’s not hard to understand better than I do, because I understand very little of it, something about matrices—but Azeem Azhar, whom I’ve talked with, has all of these reasons why it actually does make sense.

And there’s a funny thing: I kind of look for the sociological correlates. I’m certainly older than you, Jason, and I remember the late ‘90s when bars had CNBC on the TV instead of sports—that sort of popular enthusiasm. And I remember the housing bubble when there were shows like Flip This House, and I don’t see that now. There doesn’t seem to be the same kind of popular obsession with investing in this stuff. And the actual CapEx is being undertaken largely by established companies, where their cash flow is no longer enough to pay for the investment, but it’s not the little guy in the street who’s driving this.

Sometimes I look at the scale of this, and instead of this being naive individual investors, one possibility is that, except for Jensen Huang and so on, most of the people doing this have been in the tech business and have been billionaires for a long, long time, and sometimes I think that what’s actually happening is just they’re trying to repeat their former glory. One interpretation of the whole AI boom is that it’s basically a tech-bro midlife crisis. But anyway.

Bernstein: I’ll throw a couple of numbers here and take the bubble side of the argument, with the strong caveat that it’s all speculation, and I think we’ve all been clear and will continue to underscore that. So today, the CapEx for the industry basically has been north of $1 trillion. That’s since 2024. And the planned CapEx is around $6 trillion through 2030. And by the way, the chips wear out after five to six years. So this is what we did in some of our analysis. If you assume a break-even of about 10% of the cost of capital, or even a lower hurdle—a 3% to 4% hurdle rate, which is pretty standard—you quickly get numbers like the fact that their revenues so far appear to be a little bit south of $300 billion. And to justify that spend, given the assumptions I’ve mentioned on returns, they need to be $2 trillion to $3 trillion. So they’re off by multiples relative to where they need to be.

If you look at their operating losses, they’re much higher than other firms like Amazon when it started out, or Google, or Uber, or whatever. And so just in historical context. And again, the gap between spend and revenues or earnings—it’s plausible and suggestive of a bubble. And then the other point is just how much economic activity—I know we’ll get into this, because when we’re worrying about the bubble trouble, it’s a simulation of what happens if that activity goes south—it’s so pervasive. It’s playing such a large role in markets, in investment, in growth. A lot of that is imports, as you’ve pointed out, and so you have to net that out. But I don’t think there’s any question that the AI trade is playing a disproportionate role in the broader economy.

Krugman: Okay. I want to come back to that. But Jason, you made a point just now that is something I really had not thought of, which is normally when there’s a sort of catastrophic, far-tail risk out there, it’s something that is a bear case: “this might all disappear.” And you’re saying that actually the catastrophic risk here is that, in fact, AI takes over everything. And so it’s actually a bull case.

Furman: Yeah. No, I think that’s exactly right. And I think we think of rare disasters, and there’s a real disaster here too, right? But there’s a rare boom here, and I don’t think you need a lot of mass there to make sense. And by the way, if that’s right, it might mean that we play the world 80% of the time, 90% of the time, and Jared is right. But on average, he’s still wrong, and it’s worth investing in this. Yeah.

Krugman: And the other part of what you’re saying is—this is very much not, I think, the way that most of the sort of tech guys are thinking about it—but you’re thinking that this does not look like a technology where you get to build moats, that it’s not like Google where everybody uses Google because everybody uses Google, or everybody uses actually pretty bad products like Microsoft Word or Excel. But this is one where...

Furman: I mean, that’s what I tend to think. And I think paradoxically, the better it is, the worse the moats might get. There’s this idea where if I’m the first company to RSI—recursive self-improvement—I get to infinity quickly, and now everyone’s going to be using my product. If somebody is at infinity, half of infinity is still a pretty large number. A quarter of infinity is a pretty large number. You don’t need to use the infinity; you can use just part. So in some ways, the better it gets, the more being behind the curve is fine. Not for everything. If you’re doing cybersecurity, if you’re doing national defense, there are certain things where you’re going to be willing to pay. Maybe Jane Street hedge fund would be willing to pay. But for me? Fable II comes out. I’m pretty intense on these models, and there’s very little in my life that I think Fable II changes very much relative to things that came out a few months ago.

Bernstein: I think I’m a little confused about this part of the rap, and I think you could clarify it for me. So if we’re talking about a sort of winner-take-all—or couple-winners-take-all situation because somebody figures out how to do RSI and get to infinity quickly, then you have this big overbuild and a lot of investors will lose a lot of money, because, just like fiber optics [25 years ago], there are too many data centers. Meanwhile, you’ve got competition from open-source, open-weight models from China, which I also think is a potential competitive problem for our firms. So how does that square with what you’re saying, Jason?

Furman: I was giving your side of the argument. This whole thing—the “no moats,” the better it gets, the more you can switch to other things—is your side of the argument. And intuitively, that seems right to me. Except it also seemed intuitively right to me that Tesla shouldn’t be worth more than GM in 2017. So it’s sort of my humility without being able to explain it versus my rational analysis. But then the one rational analysis I have is the sort of rare boom. And by the way, it might be that one of these companies really is worth nothing, but the other’s worth $10 trillion. And so you invest in all three of them and it’s still worth doing.

Krugman: But I mean, the three companies are the frontier models. And there’s also the hardware. Basically, there’s the compute. And those are somewhat different questions. All that being said, if the bubble bursts in the next two years, I am not going to go out on a limb and try to predict what Donald Trump will do. He is an unbelievably unpredictable person. COVID was a huger thing; he acted in a big way there. George Bush did stimulus as a lame duck in 2008. He might want his name on the checks, and Democrats might be willing to let him put his name on the checks so they can have more checks. So I wouldn’t write off a fiscal response to this. But yeah, beyond that, I am worried less about our numbers and more about our political system’s ability to respond and change in response to those numbers.

Bernstein: Yeah, I’m sympathetic to the point that one definition of a Keynesian is a Republican in a recession. I’ve seen that lots of times. That said, we’re basically running recessionary-level deficits right now. I mean, our deficit is north of 6% and it should be half of that given the economic growth. It’s just that we’ve debauched our revenue function with all these ratcheting tax cuts to the point where there’s just this very structural disconnect. So, I would be concerned.

I will say the following, just putting on my fiscal hat: it isn’t the temporary stuff that hurts you in the long run; it’s the structural stuff. So, yes, if we were to go from a 6% of GDP deficit to 8% or 9% because we had to, that would show up as even higher debt going forward than we’d like, but it would go into the system and go out of the system. So I would advocate for fiscal responses. I’m sure we all would, whether that would be met by deaf ears, I don’t know.

Krugman: What I take from this is we all kind of think it’s probable, but not certain, that it’s a bubble, but are less concerned than you might be about the bubble bursting because this is such a weird form of investment where most of the money is going overseas, and we’re worried about wealth effects, but those don’t look enormous.

I mean, my take on this is that extra spending, even a higher level of debt, wouldn’t necessarily be a problem. Britain came out of World War II with debt of 250% of GDP, but no crisis, because everybody said, “They are a reasonable, responsible country that will in the end do what needs to be done.” And my question is, do we look like a reasonable, responsible country at this point? That’s where I get hung up.

Bernstein: We look more reasonable and responsible than we did a week and a half ago.

Krugman: Yeah, true.

Bernstein: Just to end on an optimistic note.

Voodoo Economics, MAGA Style

The latest attack of the usual zombies

Paul Krugman
Nov 15
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

I don’t buy the widespread claim that the Republicans’ midterms shellacking was simply a show of voters’economic discontent. According to exit polls, voters were also deeply angry about the unbridled corruption endemic to this administration. Hispanic voters swung back hard to the Democratic party, motivated by rage at Trump’s vicious deportation policy. Black voters surged to the polls in response to Trump’s naked racism and Republicans’ attempts to negate their votes through gerrymandering. And young white men turned out against the Republicans in force to protest the war on Iran.

Still, economic issues were clearly important to voters — especially the contrast between Donald Trump’s big promises and his utter failure to deliver.

The most conspicuous area of failure has been inflation. During the 2024 campaign, Trump promised to cut grocery prices starting on “day one”. According to the most recent data, food prices are up 4 percent since he took office. He promised to cut energy prices in half within six months. But thanks to his war of choice, prices of refined products — gas and diesel — are up 45 percent. Overall inflation, which was running below 3 percent when he took office, is now 3.9 percent over the past year. This acceleration of inflation, which is lowering the average American’s living standards, is entirely the result of Trump’s tariffs and his war.

While Trump’s faceplant on inflation understandably gets most of the attention because it directly affects voters’ pocketbooks, we shouldn’t forget that he also made big promises on economic growth. Trump’s economic apparatchiks officials explicitly predicted that his One Big Beautiful Bill, which cut taxes on the wealthy while slashing aid to the poor and middle class, would deliver a huge boost to economic growth.

In so doing they were following in a long, dishonorable tradition. I’ve written many times over the years about zombie economic ideas — economic ideas that should be long dead, having been refuted by experience again and again, yet keep shambling along, eating people’s brains. The most important of these zombies is the claimthat tax cuts will deliver miraculous economic growth — dubbed “voodoo economic policy” by George H.W. Bush when he was running for the 1980 Republican presidential nomination. Despite an unbroken history of Republican tax cuts leading to larger deficits and no sustained increase in growth, the cult of miracle tax cutsfor the rich is official G.O.P. doctrine. Perhaps this has something to do with the fact that wealthy Americans disproportionately give to Republicans and Republican-affiliated causes?

While Trump has chosen to betray the conventional Republican view by imposing tariffs, which are effectively a tax on Americans, he has been a staunch practitioner of the standard Republican voodoo, insisting that lower taxes on the rich will supercharge the economy. And we can be sure that when a future Democratic president tries to raise taxes in order to lower the federal deficit that has become unsustainable due to Republican tax cuts, that the Republicans will cry “job destroyer,” as they did with both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama

So today’s primer will be devoted, first, to deconstructing Republican voodoo economics — and then to demonstrating that Trump, the so-called populist, has, like his Republican predecessors, gone full voodoo.

Beyond the paywall I will address the following:

1. The Reaganomics legend

2. Taxes and growth: a broader view

3. Trump’s rosy growth scenario

4. The longer-term harmful consequences of the Republican tax-cut zombie

5. What Democrats must do now...

Bumbition

An alternative route to success in life.

Noah Smith
Nov 16
 
READ IN APP
 

“Hey, I’ll get a job…when I hear the true call.” — Slacker (1990)

About 10 years ago, I met a woman who worked as a mid-level software engineer at Facebook. She didn’t work on machine learning, but just for fun, she read a bunch of papers and got into the subject as a hobby. Later, in the pandemic, she quit her boring corporate job and spent a few years unemployed, contemplating the meaning of life. She made her own clothes, learned ballet, made cute Instagram videos, dyed her hair, and went to a bunch of hackathons (almost all of which she won).

Also in the late 2010s, I knew a man who had been a promising software engineer and data scientist, and before that a top performer on the International Math Olympiad. But when I met him, he was spending a few years unemployed — crashing at his girlfriend’s place, playing Hearthstone (and becoming one of the top-ranked players in the world), learning to skateboard, going on hippie retreats, and contemplating the meaning of life.

Both of those people are billionaires now. They are Sasha Sheng and Diogo Almeida, two of the three founders of TypeSafe AI, a startup that was recently valued at $7.5 billion (and in which I invested a small amount of money). TypeSafe invented Jev, an all-new kind of AI model that bypasses human language, and so is able to make decisions much faster and more cheaply than Claude or GPT. It was an incredibly creative idea — one that the big labs are racing to copy — and it took an incredible amount of hard work to realize.¹

Sasha’s and Diogo’s roundabout, seemingly improbable route to stunning success is actually more common in the tech world than you might think. Steve Jobs is the most famous example — he famously dropped out of college, not to start Apple, but to do psychedelic drugs, crash on friends’ floors, immerse himself in hippie spirituality, live on a commune, and travel around India looking for enlightenment before eventually inventing the personal computer and becoming the most beloved tech icon in American history. Jack Dorsey, Larry Ellison, and Mitch Kapor all had their own periods of aimlessness.

Nor is this sort of life path confined to the tech world. History is full of examples of people who looked lackadaisical until they suddenly rose to greatness:

  • Ulysses S. Grant drank copiously, worked as a clerk in a leather store, engaged in various failed business ventures and was said to lack ambition — until one day he rejoined the military and became the most successful and important military commander in the entire Civil War, as well as President of the United States.

  • Charles Darwin neglected his medical studies and turned in a mediocre performance on his exams at Cambridge, routinely going hunting and riding instead of studying, before becoming a naturalist, signing up for an ocean voyage, and inventing the theory of evolution.

  • James Cameron was a college dropout and a truck driver, before seeing Star Wars prompted him to quit his job and teach himself how to make movies, ultimately becoming one of the most commercially successful movie directors of all time. (Kevin Smith had a similar path to success, except his inspiration was the movie Slacker.)

  • Haruki Murakami ran a jazz bar and had little ambition, before suddenly deciding to become a novelist, and eventually becoming one of the most celebrated writers in the world.

I like to tell these stories because they demonstrate an approach to success in life that I believe is overlooked and deserves more recognition. I call it “bumbition”.

“Bumbition” is an obvious portmanteau of “bum” and “ambition”. In general, we think of ambitious people and slackers as polar opposites — ambitious people work hard, set goals for themselves, and are constantly motivated, while slackers drift aimlessly, laze around, or fail to apply their talents. A lot of our culture is oriented around pushing young people to be ambitious instead of turning into bums.

Bumbition, however, defies placement on the ambitious/bum spectrum. It exhibits elements of both. For a significant portion of their life, a bumbitious person doesn’t strive hard, or apply themselves to definite goals…until a clear and compelling opportunity presents itself. When that opportunity to do something really interesting or impactful does come up, the bumbitious person is quick to recognize it, and works very hard to exploit it.

The key here is that bumbition is not simply intermittent ambition. It’s a fundamentally different approach to life — it has different goals and motivations, and when it succeeds, it succeeds for different reasons.

An ambitious person is always working toward a set of goals — either those they define for themselves, or those defined by the people around them. Those goals could include:

  • “Make partner by age 30”

  • “Start a unicorn startup”

  • “Get a tenured job at a top 10 research university”

  • “Make a hundred million dollars”

  • “Conquer Central Asia”

…And so on. The purpose of achieving those goals — the motivation that drives ambitious people — is to feel a sense of personal success.

A bumbitious person does not automatically have a goal at all times,² because they tend to be motivated less by the need to feel successful than by the desire to do something intrinsically interesting or worthwhile. Such projects are inherently in short supply, in part because what constitutes an inherently “interesting” or “worthwhile” project is highly subjective. An ambitious person can always identify some brass ring that would make them feel like a success; a bumbitious person will often wait years or even decades before finding that one magical opportunity or life calling.

In fact, this is bumbition’s inherent limitation. Sitting around waiting for the right opportunity to present itself is a highly uncertain, risky endeavor. There’s always the possibility that it won’t come until you’re old, or that it’ll come but you’ll fail to see it in time.

The other problem with bumbition is that waiting around for the right opportunity comes with a bunch of costs and risks. Your technical skills and work ethic can decay over time. You can get caught up in life’s various stumbling blocks — bad relationships, drug addictions, depression, etc.

But bumbition also has some big advantages over the ambitious life. One is that ambition can keep people overly busy. If you’re the kind of person that always has to be working toward a goal, and you can’t find a truly great project to work on, you’ll end up working on a modest or mediocre one. If Steve Jobs had become distracted by getting a perfect GPA at Reed College, he might never have had time to start Apple. If Ulysses S. Grant had focused on owning his own leather goods store, he might not have leapt at the chance to join the U.S. Army. If Sasha Sheng had focused on climbing the corporate ladder at Meta, she wouldn’t have founded TypeSafe.

Paul Graham talks about this in his essay “How to Do Great Work”:

Ambition comes in two forms, one that precedes interest in the subject and one that grows out of it. Most people who do great work have a mix, and the more you have of the former, the harder it will be to decide what to do…The trouble with planning is that it only works for achievements you can describe in advance. You can win a gold medal or get rich by deciding to as a child and then tenaciously pursuing that goal, but you can't discover natural selection that way.

In his book Zero to One, Peter Thiel — who I’d classify as an ambitious rather than a bumbitious person — recounts a vivid example of how his ambition almost prevented him from becoming a tech titan:

[A]fter a conventionally successful undergraduate career, I enrolled at Stanford Law School, where I competed even harder for the standard badges of success. The highest prize in a law student’s world is…a Supreme Court clerkship…I was invited to interview for clerkships with Justices Kennedy and Scalia. My meetings with the Justices went well. I was so close to winning this last competition. If only I got the clerkship, I thought, I would be set for life. But I didn’t.

At the time, I was devastated…With the benefit of hindsight…winning that ultimate competition would have changed my life for the worse…Had I actually clerked on the Supreme Court, I probably would have spent my entire career taking depositions or drafting other people’s business deals instead of creating anything new.

Nor is this bumbition’s only advantage. The “bum” phase — the time spent traveling in India, or working at a convenience store, or playing Hearthstone on a couch — isn’t just a holding pattern. The seeming aimlessness of this period of life can serve several important functions that facilitate rapid success once a good opportunity gets spotted.

First, and most importantly, time away from the grind of constant striving allows people to broaden their perspective. A lot of unique and original ideas come from recombinant innovation — from combining insights and perspectives from vastly different fields.³ Even something as simple as changing the context of your surroundings can improve creativity. For an intelligent person with a restless mind, the “bum” phase of life leads to a lot of play and exploration that can end up sparking novel ideas. Here’s a fun example from Richard Feynman:

I used to enjoy doing physics. Why did I enjoy it? I used to play with it. I used to do whatever I felt like doing - it didn't have to do with whether it was important for the development of nuclear physics, but whether it was interesting and amusing for me to play with…Now that I am burned out…I'm going to play with physics, whenever I want to…

Within a week I was in the cafeteria and some guy, fooling around, throws a plate in the air. As the plate went up in the air I saw it wobble…I had nothing to do, so I start to figure out the motion of the rotating plate…I went on to work out equations of wobbles. Then I thought about how electron orbits start to move in relativity. Then there's the Dirac Equation in electrodynamics. And then quantum electrodynamics.

Steve Jobs’ study of calligraphy, during his hippie period, famously helped him to think about what would make the letters on a personal computer look beautiful to the eye.

A related advantage is that the “bum” phase also allows people to develop their interests. Paul Graham talks about how “excited curiosity” will often lead people to their most important life’s work. Bumbitious people aren’t just waiting around; they’re playing around, actively searching for something that sparks their interest. In contrast, if you’re constantly grinding away, it can be hard to develop that curiosity.

A “bum” phase also gives people a chance to broaden their human networks. When you’re working hard towards a goal, you usually don’t have much time to meet a lot of people outside work — i.e., outside your narrow current field of endeavor. Ambitious people are always working toward a goal, and thus get relatively little time to go meet interesting people from other walks of life. But the “bum” phase gives bumbitious people time to meet all kinds of folks. This can lead to hearing about radical new opportunities, getting insights from other fields, or even meeting useful partners for a new venture.

Broadly speaking, the “bum” phase of bumbition serves two purposes. It represents waiting and exploration time, as people patiently wait for the big opportunity that will define their career. But it also represents personal development time, either deliberate or unconscious, that helps bumbitious people to better see the big opportunities when they come along.

Now, I don’t mean to claim that bumbition is better than ambition, or vice versa — either in terms of personal success, or in terms of changing the world. Among the greats of any field — politics, business, academia, literature — you can find plenty of examples of both ambitious and bumbitious people.

But I think our society underemphasizes bumming. We have a tendency to frown on people who spend years unemployed, neglecting work in order to play video games or make Instagram videos. We assume that these people are being lazy or squandering their potential, and we tell them to get back to the grind and make something of themselves. Other societies, of course, tend to be even worse on this score — China treats its slacker generation as a national security threat.

In the AI age, this could be even more consequential. AI algorithms are consummate hill-climbers — set them to a task, give them some data, and they’ll be more ambitious than the hardest-working Stanford law student. In a world of abundant AI, setting AI on the right goals will be an increasingly central human task. Figuring out the right goals requires exploration, unique perspectives, and curiosity — all things that bumbition facilitates. We should be teaching our young people to be more bumbitious.

At the same time, we should remember that being bumbitious isn’t just a matter of sitting around on the couch. Just because you tell yourself you’re waiting to hear the true call doesn’t mean you’ll actually hear it when it comes. You have to actually want to do something great — whatever that means to you — and you have to be ready to work incredibly hard for years when that something presents itself. Bumbition isn’t the same as ambition, but it also isn’t the same as being a lifelong bum.

Subscribed

Share

1

Diogo’s rise as an AI researcher didn’t start with TypeSafe. He was also a key researcher for OpenAI, creating key features of the original ChatGPT and GPT-4 that kicked off the AI boom.

2

There are actually a few bumbitious people who somehow manage to always find huge passion projects — David Holz of Midjourney comes to mind.

3

An example I like to cite is a college friend of mine, who ended up adapting a camera technique he learned from his photography hobby to create a novel method of neuroimaging.

Republican Ideology Ruined Your Weekend

Decades of underinvestment, then two years of DOGE vandalism and destruction, grounded American air travel

Paul Krugman
Nov 16
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo,Bookshop, and Nook.

Early in the morning on Ground Stop Day I flew to Chicago to speak to economics educators. It was supposed to be a day trip, with an evening flight back to NYC. So like many others, I got caught in the nationwide flight chaos. I got through it relatively unscathed: I found a hotel room near the airport and got home only 24 hours late. It was much worse for many others – families with children, the elderly, those who couldn’t afford a hotel room, and so on.

How did we get to the point where an unforced error — it wasn’t weather, it wasn’t a terrorist attack, it was simple incompetence — could inflict so much damage on a rich, technologically advanced nation? To use the old line: Gradually, then suddenly.

According to federal officials, the immediate cause of the problem was a failed router upgrade at a remote radio facility in Arkansas, combined with a so far unexplained issue at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas. So far there is no specific reason to doubt this story, just the fact that Trump officials lie about everything. But in any case, the real question is not the specifics of what happened Friday but how a basic federal function like air traffic control could have deteriorated to the point where minor, local problems could bring the whole system crashing down.

Remarkably, the sudden disruption of air travel was a disaster foretold. Just two months before the ground stop, the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office warned that the ongoing effort to modernize air traffic control was a rush job that was all too likely to go wrong:

The Federal Aviation Administration has struggled for decades to modernize its outdated air traffic control systems, which are critical for safe and efficient flight operations. In May 2025, it launched an initiative to accelerate these efforts.

FAA has made progress implementing this initiative, but it could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions. For example, FAA doesn’t have a lifecycle cost estimate or master schedule for related projects. Without them, the agency could end up causing air traffic disruptions or prolonging reliance on severely outdated systems.

And sure enough …

But why are the FAA’s systems so outdated? And I mean outdated: The agency is planning to phase out floppy disks by 2028.

The answer is that the FAA isn’t unusual. In the U.S., government at all levels — federal, state and local — runs on outdated software and hardware, with legacy systems basically held together with paper clips and rubber bands. During the Covid crisis, as states scrambled to provide temporarily enhanced unemployment benefits, we learned that many states were still administering benefits using systems running on COBOL, a programming language introduced in 1959.

This reliance on antiquated technology isn’t because government workers are stupid. It’s because for many decades they haven’t been given the resources to upgrade their equipment. America used to have a government that invested in the future. But ever since Ronald Reagan declared that “…government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem”, critical government functions have been starved of funds for investment.

Here’s federal nondefense investment spending as a percentage of GDP:

Indeed, Republicans have often opposed paying for even the most obviously necessary government investments. For example, in 2019 a Republican Congressman from Wisconsin voted against a bill that would have provided badly needed funding to the Federal Aviation Administration. His name was Sean Duffy andhe’s now Trump’s Transportation Secretary. When Americans needed reassurance that this mess would be sorted out quickly, Duffy held a press conference in which he blamed the Democrats and lavished sycophantic praise on Donald Trump.

The truth is that the foundations were laid for a revival of federal investment under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, enacted in 2021 under Joe Biden. This law included $25 billion for the FAA. But days after taking office Trump issued an executive order pausing spending under that bill. And Duffy then tried to implement a rushed renovation, ignoring warnings that this uncoordinated renovation, carried out without, among other things, consulting aviation employees, risked exactly the kind of disruption we just experienced.

Government in America is not only underfunded; it is also seriously understaffed. I know that this runs counter to popular mythology — a mythology carefully promoted by Republican politicians and their mouthpieces like the Heritage Foundation. Under this mythology, America is besieged by a vast, useless federal bureaucracy. But the truth is that even before Elon Musk’s DOGE came along with its chainsaw, federal employment had been on a long downward trend as a share of national employment. That trend accelerated after Republicans took control of the House in 2010 and forced President Obama to impose austerity policies:

In case you’re wondering, the 2020 spike in federal employment reflected two factors. First, there’s a spike in employment every 10 years as the federal government hires temporary workers to carry out the Census. In 2020 there was also a temporary hiring surge because extra workers were hired to deal with the Covid crisis. But this temporary rise in government employment quickly faded away, with just the beginnings of a recovery under Biden.

And then came DOGE. DOGE utterly failed in its promise to reduce federal costs by trillions of dollars and, in fact, it almost surely worsened the budget deficit by, among other things, slashing the number of IRS auditorsand hence undermining tax collection. Elon Musk and his gang of twentysomething vandals did, however,manage to fire or drive out an astonishing 13 percent of the federal work force in a matter of months.

These drastic job cuts weren’t based on careful evaluation of which jobs could safely be eliminated, based on consultation with experts who actually knew how government agencies worked. Instead, the Muskovites came in with an attitude of arrogant ignorance: They knew nothing about the agencies of which they became temporary overlords, but believed themselves to be so much smarter than the people working at those agencies that they didn’t need to check with those people before wielding their chainsaws.

In the end, they disrupted many essential government functions, and in some cases agencies scrambled to rehire the workers who had been laid off.

Did DOGE help cause the air travel disaster? My guess is that we’ll eventually find out that it did, but we’re just beginning to piece together exactly what happened.

What’s already clear, however, is that DOGE’s attitude of arrogant ignorance was central to the FAA modernization program. That GAO report makes it clear that there were strong reasons to worry that the program was being rushed without adequate thought or consultation. It’s also clear that Duffy and his subordinates ignored these warnings, presumably believing that whoever was advising them was smarter than all those timid experts and bureaucrats — those who had survived the DOGE cuts.

Or to put it differently, tech broligarchs — who are still highly influential in the Trump administration even though Musk has left and DOGE is no more — still love the motto “move fast and break things.” And that’s exactly how the Trump administration operates. On issues as small as repairing the Reflecting Pool and as big as going to war with Iran, the administration has moved fast — ignoring normal procedures and expert advice — and ended up breaking things.

And one of the things it broke over the weekend was U.S. air travel.

View in browser

What I got wrong about the midterms

Complications avoided, a big turnout advantage, and some candidates I underrated

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 16
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

I got a lot right about the 2026 midterms, and I feel like many Slow Boring positions have been vindicated — most notably the argument that winning a Senate majority is possible if and only if Democrats make some moves to the center on cultural issues.

We also called some small, specific things correctly, such as that nominating Matt Dunlap would cost Democrats ME-2 and that Josh Turek was the right candidate for the Iowa Senate race. There’s been an incredible amount of beefing on the internet about the fact that Abdul El-Sayed won comfortably in Michigan while putting up a mid-sized underperformance, but this is exactly what I said all along would happen.

That said, it’s my job to comment on issues in the news despite uncertainty, and when you do that, you get things wrong.

My view is that the only way to improve your judgment is to try to be honest with yourself about errors. There are prominent members of the media who I see out there every day full of bluster claiming to have been right about everything. To me, people like that are basically Elizabeth Holmes telling Nathan Fielder she’s never lied — it’s a huge red flag that means your heart and mind are completely closed and you’re not learning anything.

Obviously, in a sense, basically everyone was “wrong,” and the final national popular vote was about D+13 rather than D+9 as the polling averages said.

What I would say is that even though this was a decent-sized polling error, it was still a victory for the general concept of trusting the polls. Not because polling is precisely accurate but because errors happen in both directions — they don’t always underestimate Republicans — and it’s not possible to predict in advance which way they will be off. Nobody has come up with a reliable way of doing better than looking at polling averages. What I want to focus on today, though, are more interesting mistakes: things that destabilize my worldview a little and will cause me to adjust my takes going forward.

This focuses mostly on the role of turnout, the success of a particular way of ducking inconvenient issues, and the ways that these two things maybe interacted in putting a few races on the table that didn’t seem winnable to me.

Turnout seems to have mattered a lot

Everyone is aware that turnout matters in politics. But my sense is that after almost every election, many people massively overstate its significance in explaining the outcome. The facts are not currently 100 percent known yet, and we’ll get a better picture in the weeks and months to come, but that seems to have not been the case this year.

As my friend and fellow turnout skeptic Charlotte Swasey says, the big thing the polls missed this year is they were trying so hard not to undersample Republicans that they missed Republicans legitimately just not voting.

Spooky Charlotte Swasey
@charlotteeffect
I am marveling at the level of turnout effects this election. I am a known turnout skeptic, but Republicans do seem to have lived the nightmare of "your base just straight up stays home"!! Obvi we'll know more as more data comes in, but wow.
3:17 PM · Nov 6, 2026 · 6.76K Views
5 Replies · 5 Reposts · 49 Likes

Slow Boring readers knew that Democrats had been benefiting from differential turnout in special elections, but my dominant interpretation of that was that the advantage would evaporate in a higher-profile midterm. That does not appear to have been the case. Instead, at least in Texas and Georgia, where we have the most complete data, Democrats essentially got to run in a special election environment. Fewer Kamala Harris voters showed up this year than in 2018, but dramatically fewer Trump 2024 voters showed up.

We’ll have to find out more about the details, but obviously this shaped the battlefield in an important way. Interesting nuance!

Democrats end up talking a lot about turnout any time they lose, which generally strikes me as a kind of cope, and it’s one reason I’m generally so dismissive of people who just want to talk about turnout. For some reason, though, both JD Vance and Ted Cruz wrote long tweets recapping the election in which they specifically disavowed turnout-based explanations, even though turnout really did explain why the blue wave turned into a tsunami. I don’t know what the deal with that is.

The optimistic take for Republicans is that turnout is always higher in a presidential year, so these voters should show back up again. The optimistic take for Democrats, though, is that non-participation is often a halfway house on the road to converting. If Democrats can put up a fresh face in 2028 who people don’t have a years-long relationship with (i.e., not Harris, Newsom, or A.O.C.), then we could see a bunch of these demoralized, disengaged Trump voters actually flip blue.

The politics of evasion

For years — for decades really — Democrats have been dogged by the idea that they can navigate culture war politics not by moving to the center but by just ducking the question or pivoting, arguing that these topics are distractions from the real economic issues of the day. My bias is toward believing this evasion strategy almost always fails and that candidates need to either defend their views in a way that persuades people (very hard but clearly possible in some cases) or else just adopt the more popular view.

But Gina Hinojosa in Texas seems to have really pulled off the evasion strategy in a pretty effective way.

She did her “Pronouns” ad to signal moderation on transgender issues without committing herself to anything specific. She indicated opposition to Texas’s draconian abortion ban without addressing any details about how far she’d go with this — again using a personal story to signal some sympathy with culturally conservative sentiments without making any policy concessions to the right. On the death penalty, she made a Slow Boring move and implied that she has no desire to change Texas’s laws. And she had some praise for Trump’s work to shut down illegal border crossings but stood by her fairly liberal record in the Texas legislature.

Greg Abbott hit her hard as a gun grabber, and she just didn’t say anything about gun control. She was asked at the Texas Tribune Festival specifically about stuff like Texas rules barring pride clubs at public schools and public-school bathroom issues, and she simply refused to answer.

That’s sort of exactly why I think these evasion strategies don’t work. Whether or not Hinojosa is “focused on” culture war issues versus economics, she’s running for governor, and these K-12 school management topics are within her area of responsibility. She should just pick some progressive changes to promise (so L.G.B.T.Q. activists view her as more progressive than Abbott) and some to disavow (so swing voters are reassured).

Instead, she ducked — and it worked really well!

If she’d asked my advice about this (which of course she did not), I would have added that not only was evasion unlikely to work, it was pointless because if she won, the G.O.P. legislature would obviously just jam her up with message bills on these issues. But Democrats flipped one house of the legislature. That means both conservative and progressive bills stay off her desk.

She really will be able to focus on what she wants to focus on — though she’s still going to have to address these school management questions.

Randy Villegas

The situation in CA-22 was, in some ways, structurally similar to ME-2 in that it pitted a moderate candidate backed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (Jasmeet Bains in California, Joe Baldacci in Maine) against a Progressive Establishment candidate (Randy Villegas in California, Matt Dunlap in Maine).

I like Bains more than Villegas on the merits, and I still wish she won. But I collapsed these two cases in my mind and wrote Villegas off on electability grounds.

He actually did fine-to-great depending on how you want to account for district demographics, making it one of many races where a Latino Democrat in a heavily Latino district rode a huge Latino wave to victory.

I don’t think there was any good reason to doubt that he could pull this off, and I would even go so far as to say that this was an inappropriate D.C.C.C. intervention. The national party should intervene selectively to get moderate nominees in critical races — like Baldacci in ME-2 or Johnny Garcia in TX-35, who they backed against an antisemitic conspiracy theorist. But progressives are always going to worry about dirty pool here, and it makes everyone look bad to intervene against a Villegas and then have him win.

South Carolina and Mississippi

I thought it was silly that people were asking national Democrats to invest money in the South Carolina and Mississippi Senate races. I really liked Scott Colom, but my take was more that Democrats should try to run candidates like that in the Carolinas and in Florida than that Democrats should play in Mississippi.

And Annie Andrews in South Carolina honestly struck me as a borderline grift. Some of the stuff she’s put out on social media over the years is squarely in “not even trying to win” terrain. I looked at this and thought, “There is absolutely no way someone like this is going to win in a state where Trump won 58 percent of the vote.”

Dr. Annie Andrews
@AnnieAndrewsMD
“We’re Republican Women Politicians”
4:48 PM · Apr 26, 2024 · 3.21M Views
723 Replies · 3.12K Reposts · 25.6K Likes

In Mississippi, Trump got 61 percent. I thought maybe if you took Colom and his campaign and transposed it to a less red state and also blessed him with a terrible opponent like Darline Graham, he’d be viable. But Colom in Mississippi and Andrews in South Carolina? My view was let’s just spend in Iowa.

But Andrews, it turns out, kind of locked in down the stretch.

She called for an all-of-the-above energy strategy, disavowed socialism, argued that sports teams should be based on biological sex rather than gender identity, and said “Democrats have failed” on border security.

So there was certainly an opportunity here for me to be prescient and say, “Actually, Andrews could win because she did a lot of last-ditch moderation in response to polls showing it was kinda close and got over the top.”

But I did not say that and was not actually prescient, in part because I thought this was probably too little too late, given that South Carolina voters would likely be skeptical and her new positions didn’t really reflect her record. I think the 2026 midterms should cause most of us to update broadly in favor of flip-flopping as a strategy, and I include myself in that, even though I think I’ve always been more favorable to flip-flopping than most.

As for Colom, I am still shocked he won.

He ran a really smart campaign and seems great, but it’s still Mississippi, and I had previously believed the level of racial polarization in that electorate was impossible to overcome absent some huge scandal. I wonder if, when the data is in, this will turn out to be an epic collapse of white turnout.

The mystery of the groups

If you just paid attention to the 2026 campaigns, you’d think that the power of “the groups” over the Democratic Party had been completely obliterated.

Forget about the Slow Boring candidates and just look at El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, Peggy Flanagan, and other progressive winners.

None of these people talked a ton about climate change or promoting electric cars. They were viciously critical of ICE and Trump’s approach to interior enforcement, but none of them called for reopening asylum claims at the southern border. None of them “centered” racial justice in their campaign or used terms like BIPOC. Everyone seems to have agreed that Woke 1 was crazy. On the front lines, things were even bolder in terms of blowing off “groups”-think. Even Hinojosa, who didn’t really moderate on culture, did at least a little bit, and nobody tried to cancel her over it.

On the one hand, I feel semi-vindicated by this. On the other hand, I am genuinely surprised that any of this occurred without an actual fight. Only El-Sayed, in an interview with Ross Douthat, articulated what I think the actual issue is:

Douthat: Why didn’t the Biden administration enforce the border? What was the problem?

El-Sayed: I think the politics of it at the time were complicated.

Douthat: Complicated by what?

El-Sayed: I mean, complicated by a lot of advocacy, right? And I think we’ve learned the lesson. And I also think that it’s important for us to realize that — the idea that politicians don’t learn from what comes before them, because it was done by a different party, is kind of ridiculous. There are things that some Republicans have gotten right. It’s just that they also get a lot of things wrong. So learn from the things that they get right. And fix the things that they get wrong.

This is a much clearer articulation of not just the specifics of border security but of the broader structural dynamic than I heard from any of the candidates with a more moderate positioning.

What surprises me isn’t that El-Sayed can see the issue clearly — he’s probably the smartest of the new class of senators — but that the advocacy dogs just chose not to bark during the 2026 cycle.

I thought, based on my interactions with them, that they were unrepentant and that Democrats would need to learn the lesson that they need to tune these guys out. But because they chose to just shut up, it’s not clear to me whether El-Sayed is right that “We’ve learned the lesson.” The question — what do you do in the face of a lot of advocacy complicating your decision-making? — simply wasn’t posed.

I didn’t believe Democrats would be so lucky as to avoid that complication this cycle. And even after it happened, I don’t really believe it will happen again, given the realities of a large presidential primary field. But I’ve been wrong before, and maybe I’ll be wrong about this.

Compact

Houellebecq Saw This Coming

By Louis Betty • 16 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

Michel Houellebecq’s novels are our age’s most profound and devastating studies in what it means to be godless. Pascal wrote that “nothing more surely underlines an extreme weakness of mind than the failure to understand the unhappiness of someone without God.” Houellebecq’s body of work is, in some sense, simply the working out in fiction of this observation. The godlessness he depicts is not only personal and social but (as explored in Submission) political and civilizational as well. 

Considerations like these make what is now happening to Houellebecq feel all the more revealing. The author is accused of making statements liable to “incite racial and religious hatred,” a crime under French law, for claiming in a 2022 interview that native Frenchmen were arming themselves to resist the future Muslim domination of France. In particular, Houellebecq likened potential nativist violence to so many “Bataclans in reverse,” a reference to the 2015 Islamist terror attack in Paris that left nearly one hundred people dead. Muslims, he added, were not likely to respond to attacks against them by lighting candles and carrying bouquets of flowers.

In the same interview, Houellebecq also used the term “the Great Replacement” to describe statistically demonstrable changes in European demography over the last fifty years. “The Great Replacement” is often understood to denote a deliberate effort to replace the white populations of Europe with non-white foreigners. The term’s originator, Renaud Camus, has always denied this charge, but to little avail.

Leave aside the obvious political opportunism of the case leveled against Houellebecq, a naked attempt to censure a speaker of inconvenient truths going into a presidential election year in which those truths favor the nationalist right. Leave aside, too, the tendentious nature of the charges against him. His comments on Muslim violence were not a call to arms, but a prediction of what might happen were French nativists to engage in their own acts of terrorism. What is really significant about the charges against Houellebecq is that they suggest he has been right along. In the name of “the rights of man,” the rights of this man are being curtailed. 

In the world of Houellebecq’s fiction, France’s revolutionary battles were won long ago, but the reward gained is social atomization, nihilistic consumerism, spiritual despair, and the suicidal worship of youth. The cult of reason inherited from the Enlightenment is no longer experienced as a thrilling liberation, secularism no longer as an exhilarating exercise in snubbing authority. Houellebecq writes the obituary for a French Baby Boomer generation that has exhausted these impulses, leaving their children and grandchildren with an existential void.

The protagonist of Whatever, Houellebecq’s 1994 debut novel, describes a Sunday morning as “warm but a little sad, as Sundays often are in Paris, especially if one does not believe in God.” In The Elementary Particles, Desplechin, a researcher at the French National Scientific Research Center, laments that in its pursuit of rational certainty, the West has “sacrificed everything … religion, happiness, hope—and, finally, its own life.” For Florent-Claude Labrouste, the protagonist of Serotonin, the third millennium is “one millennium too many” for a civilization that “had previously been known as Judeo-Christian.” Houellebecq’s fiction places us in the midst of materialist horror, the monsters conjured by a society that has banished the divine. 

Is Islam the only force strong enough to save this society, as Submission suggests? Robert Rediger, the president of the Islamic University of the Sorbonne in the novel, thinks so. Explaining the reasons for his conversion to Islam, he says that the old Europe is dead. “That Europe, which was the summit of human civilization, committed suicide in a matter of decades ... it all came to an end with the unjustifiable madness of the First World War.”

There is reason to believe that Rediger’s conclusion is premature. The pope’s visit to Paris in October, for example, showed the world that La France éternelle is still alive and well, even if it is no longer demographically dominant. Next year’s presidential election will, however, pit this France of Clovis, Charles Martel, Joan of Arc, and Charles de Gaulle against the “New France” of Jean-Luc Mélenchon and his left-wing party France Unbowed, which draws much of its support from Muslims in the country’s suburbs. Should Le Pen prevail, as appears likely, violence greater than what the world witnessed this fall might well break out.

Until then, it will not be surprising if other writers and public figures are treated to the same persecution that Houellebecq is enduring. Indeed, the author of Submission is not the only outspoken Frenchman to have lately run afoul of his country’s censors. Renaud Camus, for instance, is scheduled to appear in court in March to answer charges of inciting racial hatred. His alleged crime is having made a post on X calling the city of Saint-Denis “le négropole des rois,” a punning allusion to the resting place of France’s kings and the Africanization of the city’s  population. Éric Zemmour, who is running for president in 2027, was reported last month to public prosecutors by Arcom, France’s audiovisual regulator, for referring to October 17 rioters as “hordes of North African and African barbarians” on live television. Desperate to suppress mass discontent over decades of failed immigration policy, the nation of the rights of man is increasingly willing to send free speech to the scaffold.

Houellebecq, meanwhile, may find himself observing the political events of next year from a prison cell, depending on the outcome of his case. Were this to happen, one could only hope for a kind of Bastille à l’envers—a reverse Bastille Day—that would see France’s most famous living author freed from the petty tyranny that now threatens him.

The Trump Administration Has DOGEd the IRS, Too

Fixing it can help pay for Democrats’ agenda

Paul Krugman
Nov 17
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo,Bookshop, and Nook.

Tell me if you’ve heard this one before: There’s a federal agency, one that fulfills a critical function, that is still using extremely outdated technology. Notably, decades of underinvestment have left it still reliant on legacy software — and even, in some cases, hardware — from the 1960s.

The Biden administration made a start on upgrading the agency’s technology. But soon after Donald Trump returned to power, these efforts were put on hold. Meanwhile DOGE moved in, reducing the agency’s IT staff by 40 percent and removing almost 80 percent of its senior technology leadership.

But not to worry: The Trump administration insists that it can greatly improve the agency’s effectiveness, even with a decimated work force, by using artificial — sorry, “super” — intelligence, and by bringing in corporations, notably Palantir.

Am I talking about the Federal Aviation Administration? I could be. While there’s a lot we still don’t know about last weekend’s air travel nightmare, we can be fairly sure that the stage for that disaster was set by the Trump administration’s decision to abandon Biden-era plans for systematic upgrades, instead engaging in a perilous rush to modernize the technology quickly and on the cheap. They relied, of course, on AI and ignored warnings from experts and long-term employees that this rush job would risk exactly the kind of disaster we just experienced.

But I am not talking about the FAA. In fact, I’m talking about the Internal Revenue Service. You know, the agency responsible for collecting the revenue that allows the federal government to function and pay for things like air traffic control.

Yesterday I wrote about how many state governments still run on COBOL. So, it turns out, does the IRS — COBOL and 60s-vintage Assembly code. I don’t know enough about the technology to compare the backwardness of IRS systems with those at the FAA. But we do know that the IRS has been long targeted for destruction by Republicans.

You see, even Republicans want air traffic control to work — they just don’t want to pay for it. But they don’t want the IRS to be effective at doing its job collecting taxes – in particular, taxes on high-income Americans and corporations. Through underfunding and understaffing year after year, the Republicans have undermined the agency’s ability to identify likely tax cheats and audit them. And tax cheats are the modern GOP’s type of people. (Let’s not forget that the Trump Organization was found guilty of criminal tax fraud stretching back 15 years.)

The IRS’s severely weakened ability to track down wealthy individuals who don’t pay what they owe is a serious national problem on several counts. First, there’s the moral rot caused by a system in which crime pays — because cheating on one’s taxes is a crime. Second, there’s a lot of money involved. The last official estimate of the “tax gap” — the difference between the amount taxpayers owe and what they pay — was $606 billion in 2022. In 2022 that was more than 2 percent of GDP. If the current gap is of comparable size, it accounts for around a third of the budget deficit.

Unfortunately, I can’t give you a current estimate of the size of the tax gap. The IRS was scheduled to produce an updated estimate of the tax gap last fall, but that update has been delayed. At this time, there is no indication of when, if ever, the estimate will be released. And without that estimate, we can’t know how DOGE’s staffing cuts at the IRS and the attempted IT push have affected the agency’s performance.

But it’s a safe prediction that Trump’s “reforms” at the IRS, like every other major project the administration has undertaken, from the Reflecting Pool to the Iran war, will be a bust. So we’ll eventually learn that the tax gap has grown even wider.

This is bad. But the exploding tax gap also presents an opportunity. If Democrats retake the White House in 2028, there are a number of measures they will want to take almost immediately to deliver on their affordability agenda — starting with restoring Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, health insurance subsidies and food stamps. These measures will cost money at a time when there is already large concern about budget deficits. And there is a debate about whether the Democrats should propose tax increases to help cover their agenda’s costs.

They should. But they can also raise a lot of money simply by getting rich people and corporations to pay the taxes they already owe under existing law.

So if Democrats reclaim the White House in 2028, a critical part of their agenda should be to adequately fund and modernize the IRS — real modernization, not the delusions peddled by the Trump administration. This would not only achieve a major reduction in the tax gap and lower the deficit, but it would also make a significant contribution towards paying for their affordability agenda.

And making the IRS effective again would also help fight the rising tide of inequality.

The biggest myth about American immigration policy

Surging Hispanic migration had nothing to do with the 1965 immigration law.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 17
 
READ IN APP
 

For a while now I’ve been wanting to write about a widespread misunderstanding about the history of American immigration policy. Fortunately, Donald Trump’s decision to respond to the blue wave by promoting Stephen Miller to chief of staff gives us a news hook, because he is a frequent purveyor of this misunderstanding.

This is from an April profile of Miller in the New York Times, and even though the authors quibble with Miller, they actually miss his biggest mistake:

Mr. Miller has blamed many of the country’s problems on a landmark 1965 law that paved the way for more Hispanic and Asian immigrants, a shift from primarily allowing in Europeans.

Despite decades of data showing that immigrants outperform native-born Americans on major indicators, including crime rates and use of welfare, Mr. Miller contends that those who entered after the 1965 law, as well as their descendants, have largely been unsuccessful.

“If you bring those societies into our country and then give them unlimited free welfare, what do we think’s going to happen?” he told Fox News in December. “We need a moratorium on immigration from third world countries until we can heal ourselves as a nation.”

Here’s the issue: While it is true that the United States enacted a major change in immigration policy in 1965 and it is also true that Hispanic immigration to the United States increased significantly after 1965, it’s simply not the case that the 1965 law paved the way for more Hispanic immigrants. It’s actually the complete opposite — the 1965 law imposed quantitative restrictions on immigration from Latin America that didn’t exist previously.

It would probably be going too far to say that it’s a total coincidence that these things changed at around the same time, but the relationship is indirect and unrelated to the text of the immigration law.

What Hart-Celler did

The law at issue is the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, also known as the Hart-Celler Act after its main authors.

This law was a major reversal of immigration policy from the National Origins Formula adopted back in 1921. These 1921 immigration quotas were not adopted to keep out people from the “third world” as Miller would understand it. The point of the 1921 law was to prevent people from Southern and Eastern Europe — people like Miller’s ancestors or First Lady Melania Trump — from coming to the United States.

It also restricted immigration from Asia, though Asian immigration was already severely limited by laws such as the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and the 1907 “Gentlemen’s Agreement” with the Japanese government to stop giving passports to U.S.-bound Japanese laborers. The Naturalization Act of 1870 made it impossible for immigrants from Asia to become American citizens while for the first time explicitly creating a process of naturalization for “aliens of African nativity and to persons of African descent.”

Which is just to say that this was all happening under a very different political paradigm than the contemporary immigration debate.

You often hear restrictionists express nostalgia for the midcentury immigration system. But they’re really just saying they liked the low level of immigration — or maybe that they approve of the broad principle of discriminating on the basis of nationality — not that we should replicate the specific details of the quota system. Nobody today thinks the United States should prefer immigrants from Western Europe over immigrants from Eastern Europe.

At any rate, the impetus for the Hart-Celler Act was to create a non-discriminatory immigration system in which your ability to get a visa would be based on individual-level criteria rather than nation of origin.

But in the case of Latin America and the Caribbean, that meant making policy more restrictive.

The old National Origins Formula didn’t apply any cap at all to migration from within the Western Hemisphere. Which isn’t to say the border was per se “open” — there were border controls and often intrusive sanitation procedures at the U.S.-Mexico border, along with literacy tests and other qualitative controls. Legally speaking, you needed a visa to work in the United States, and the ability to get those waxed and waned over time. During the Great Depression, there was a big push to repatriate Mexicans back south of the border, but then during World War II, the Bracero Program was started up to bring in more seasonal workers.

Hart-Celler neither intended to increase Latin American immigration nor had any provisions to increase Latin American immigration. In 1965, when the law passed, there were just under 150,000 legal immigrants admitted from the Western Hemisphere, and 37,000 of these were Canadians. The new system capped Western Hemisphere immigration at 120,000 per year, and the Bracero Program ended in 1964. So in theory, there should have been a modest cut in permanent immigration from Latin America as a whole and a large cut in temporary labor migration from Mexico specifically.

So what happened?

It’s kind of funny that immigration restrictionists forget this, but what happened was illegal immigration.

The Hart-Celler law created a more restrictive environment for legal migration, but it didn’t actually do anything about the fact that the U.S.-Mexico border is extremely long and sparsely populated in many places. Even during the Bracero years, there was a good amount of illegal agricultural and other casual labor happening, and with the legal temporary migration channel shut down, more people started coming illegally.

Scholars seem to disagree as to why the volume of illegal immigration was so much higher than the prior volume of legal immigration. But part of the issue is clearly just that Mexico had a huge baby boom and there were literally more people around who could migrate. The United States was also becoming richer, meaning plenty of opportunity for people willing to do unpleasant jobs like agricultural work.

Still, the really big surge in Mexican immigration to the United States took off quite a bit after the 1965 law’s passage, because it was basically unrelated to those policy changes.

Ironically, the 1996 Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act, which was supposed to clamp down on illegal immigration, seems to have accelerated the growth of the Mexican-born population in the United States.

That’s because by making it substantially harder — but still doable — to cross the border, it shifted the balance of illegal workers toward “cross once and stay” rather than “go back and forth seasonally.” Eventually, the cratering of Mexican population growth plus ever-hardening border security plus the collapse of the American labor market in 2008 brought this to an end.

Then as the economy started to recover in 2014, you started to see a very different set of immigration problems largely driven by people (mostly not from Mexico) making asylum claims rather than trying to sneak past the Border Patrol.

Long story short, though, the transformation of American demographics driven by immigration from Mexico was not the result of the 1965 immigration bill or of any other deliberate shift in immigration policy.

The other large Hispanic populations in the United States (Puerto Ricans and Cubans) also don’t have anything to do with the 1965 bill. Puerto Ricans are American citizens who can move to the mainland as they wish. Meanwhile, until around 2016, the United States maintained a policy of welcoming basically anyone from Cuba as a refugee.

Real debate and real reforms

Who cares about all this history except pedants? Maybe nobody. But I always do hold out vague hope that a clearer understanding can create space for better policy, more compromises, and a happier outcome.

Donald Trump, for example, in his interview with Ross Douthat seemed to float the idea of an amnesty program for people who’ve been living and working illegally in the United States for a long time.

AF Post
@AFpost
Trump endorses an amnesty deal with Democrats, saying immigration maximalists are on the “pretty far right” and suggesting that illegals who have been in the US for 10-15 years should have an opportunity to stay. Follow: @AFpost
12:22 AM · Nov 9, 2026 · 1.89M Views
1.93K Replies · 974 Reposts · 7.98K Likes

This is not the first time that Trump has seemed to embrace the logic of comprehensive immigration reform. Part of the power of Trumpian immigration politics is that he’s been happy to just lie and say that the typical person who immigrates to the United States illegally or tries to exploit loopholes in asylum laws is a criminal or a terrorist. Whenever he’s confronted with the reality that it’s mostly people just trying to make more money and that millions of them have been quietly working in restaurants or cleaning houses or doing casual construction labor, he kind of glitches out.

It’s not good to expend a large amount of resources on rounding these people up and kicking them out, and it drives political backlash to interior enforcement in general.

Obviously, though, Republicans aren’t going to flip and give Democrats what they want on this. The old concept was that a deal would include lots of measures on border security, but Republicans aren’t going to want that now, because they’ve already achieved what they wanted on border security through partisan bills. What I can imagine, though, are changes to real features of the Hart-Celler system.

One potential area for negotiation is that a very large fraction of America’s immigration visas are allocated on the basis of “family reunification” — i.e., you get in based on having relatives in the United States. Conservatives reasonably believe that immigration should be selective, aimed at bringing over people who are most likely to make large positive economic contributions to the United States. Cosmopolitans reasonably want to make room in the system for refugees and others with strong humanitarian claims. Family reunification is neither of these things and seems ripe for reform in favor of mostly skills-based immigration, spousal visas, and some number of refugees.

Another is that asylum law should be tightened on a permanent basis. But Trump hasn’t even tried to pass an immigration bill, so there’s been no discussion during his second term of what conservatives actually want out of immigration policy and what they might be willing to give up to get it.

But I think that starts with setting aside this paranoid and inaccurate view of immigration history where somebody decided in the mid-1960s to dramatically increase immigration from the “third world.” There was a ton of illegal immigration specifically from Mexico in the 1980s and 1990s for reasons that are basically unrelated to official acts of Congress. Excavating the political history of why the federal government was relatively slow to crack down on this could be interesting, but the crackdown really did happen, and over the past 10 years, immigrants have been coming from different countries through completely different channels.
