The Forgotten Socialist

By John B. Judis • 17 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

American Socialist: The Life and Legacy of Eugene V. Debs
By Shawn Gude 
Simon & Schuster, 416 pages, $30

Eugene V. Debs was the founder and four-time presidential candidate of the American Socialist Party. In 1920, while in jail for opposing US entry into World War I, Debs received almost a million votes for president. That election, however, marked the last hurrah for Debs and the Socialists. The Socialist Party crumbled and ceased to be a force within American politics. Debs became, at best, a footnote in history textbooks. In 1978, Bernie Sanders, out of work and politics, began a rough-hewn documentary on his hero with the apt warning: “It is very probable, especially if you are a young person, that you have not heard of Eugene Victor Debs.”

But Debs’s name is being heard again amid a revival of American socialism for which Sanders can take considerable credit. The last biography of Debs, by the outstanding labor historian Nick Salvatore, was published forty years ago. This year, Simon & Schuster has brought out a 400-page biography by Jacobin contributor Shawn Gude, who has done his homework.

The book is noteworthy for highlighting Debs’s support for racial equality and for its portrayal of his prison years. Gude gives Debs his due for being an early supporter of industrial unions and for putting socialism on the American agenda before World War I, but he also recognizes Debs’s failings as a party leader and politician. He does justice to his subject’s courage and conviction as a public man without eliding his struggle with alcohol and his troubled marriage. I have bones to pick with some of Gude’s interpretations, but that is to be expected when addressing the question of why Debs and the party ultimately failed and what can be learned from these failures.

 

Debs’s career can be divided into the periods before and after he became a socialist, with a dramatic transition from one to the other that spanned the 1890s. He was born in 1855 and grew up and lived in Terre Haute, Ind., then a hub of industry and transportation. His parents ran a grocery store. His father passed onto Debs an enthusiasm for French Romantic novelists Eugène Sue and Victor Hugo, from whom he got his first and middle names. Sue and Hugo were anti-clerical republicans concerned about the plight of the poor. In The Silver Cross, Sue envisioned Jesus as a social revolutionary—an identification that Debs would reiterate after he became a socialist, and that was central to his conception of how he should conduct himself as a leader.

Debs dropped out of high school at age fourteen to work on the railroads. In 1875, he joined the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, where he rose to become the editor of the union’s magazine and a national figure. His outlook on labor issues during those years was conservative. He opposed the rail strike of 1877. “A strike at the present time signifies anarchy and revolution, and the one of but a few days ago will never be blotted from the records of memory,” he wrote.  He regarded the union itself as a social insurance organization, not as a vehicle by which workers could exercise power against owners and managers. “Capital and labor united. That is our motto,” Debs proclaimed in 1883. He blamed joblessness on individuals lacking “industry.”

The only signs of his later radicalism came in his early support for women’s suffrage—in 1880, he invited feminist Susan B. Anthony to speak in Terre Haute—and in his opposition to racism.  Elected to Indiana’s state legislature as a Democrat in 1884, he was one of handful of Democrats who joined Republicans in putting forward a bill that would have repealed Indiana’s law against interracial marriages. Opposition to racism and support for women’s suffrage would remain Debs’s commitments throughout his life. When D.W. Griffiths’s Birth of a Nation opened to rapturous crowds in Terre Haute in 1916, Debs wrote in the Terre Haute Post: “If the author’s studied purpose was to insult the black race and to revive and intensify the bitter prejudices which grew out of the war, he couldn’t have better succeeded.”

Debs began turning away from conservative unionism and rugged individualism in the late 1880s, a shift that was driven by what was happening to the workers he represented. The last three decades of the nineteenth century saw economic growth punctuated by repeated financial crises and recessions culminating in the depression of the mid-1890s. Owners were cutting wages, and workers fought back by joining unions and going on strike. The owners responded harshly with the support of the federal government and the courts.

“Debs emerged from the strike a changed man.”

In 1888, Debs’s firemen and the engineers of the then-powerful Burlington Railroad went on strike for better wages and union recognition. The company replaced the workers and brought in the Pinkertons—detectives and armed guards—to police the rails. The company also got an injunction against other unions joining the strike. After a year, the unions admitted defeat. Debs emerged from the strike a changed man. He no longer believed in a harmonious relationship between labor and capital.  He railed in the union’s magazine against “an age of greed and grab, an age of monopolies, trust, syndicates, and combinations, in which the opulent few, by processes of chicane and legerdemain, seek to make the toiling many pay them tribute money.” 

Debs also changed his view of craft unionism. During the strike, the firemen and engineers had failed to get the other rail unions to back them. Debs concluded that in order to succeed, the craft unions would have to band together. In 1893, he left the firemen’s union and founded the American Railway Union (ARU). The new union successfully struck on the Great Northern Railway the next year, but then was drawn, despite Debs’s misgivings, into a nationwide strike against the powerful Pullman Car Company, which built and staffed the sleeper cars on trains.  Debs’s doubts were confirmed when, at the Pullman company’s behest, the federal government sent in the National Guard and obtained an injunction against the strike on the dubious grounds that it was obstructing US mail delivery. The union was crushed, and Debs was sent to jail for six months for violating the injunction.

Between 1894, when he was jailed at Woodstock, Ill., and 1897, when he folded the American Railway Union into the Social Democracy of America, Debs became a socialist. There were two sides to what Debs described as his “conversion.” From his experience in the Pullman strike, Debs wrote, he learned “the workings of the capitalist system, the resources of its masters and the weakness of its slaves.” Milwaukee socialist Victor Berger, who would later become the Socialist Party’s first member to serve in Congress, brought him a copy of Marx’s Capital, but Debs was most impressed by The Class Struggle, by German Social Democratic Party leader Kaul Kautsky. Kautsky described “the irresistible and inevitable nature of the social revolution” that would result in substituting “common, for private, ownership of the means of production.”  Debs learned, in other words, the rudiments of what became orthodox Marxism.

Debs combined this orthodox Marxism with the appeal of the Protestant Social Gospel and Christian Socialism, even if his relation to Christianity was complicated. His father disliked organized religion, and Debs did not attend church as a child. In 1878, he became an admirer of the “Great Agnostic,” Robert Ingersoll, whom he heard speak in Terre Haute. Gude writes that Debs “got religion” at the same time he “got socialism,” but I think well before he read Kautsky and Marx, he retained a deep appreciation of Jesus as a moral figure. He had also absorbed the Christian aspiration, commonly voiced in those years, to create a kingdom of God on earth.  

In August 1890, Debs called in his magazine, United Labor, for the “setting up of the Kingdom of God,” but he identified the kingdom with “fraternity” and the recognition of “the interdependence of men,” rather than with socialism. That changed during what he called his “baptism” into socialism. After he was released from jail, as Gude recounts, Debs fell under the influence of the Denver minister Myron Reed, who identified socialism with the achievement of the Kingdom of God. Debs praised Reed for recognizing that “Christ was always and everywhere a friend of the suffering poor.”

Debs initially joined Reed’s effort to establish colonies that would combine socialist and Christian principles. At a rally in Newark in November 1897, Debs declared: “What is socialism? Merely Christianity in action.” But the next year, under Berger’s influence, he backed away from Reed’s utopian socialism and embraced a more conventional electoral path to socialism, while retaining a commitment to Christian socialism. His running mate when he ran for president in 1900 was Job Harriman, a Christian socialist, and one of his greatest admirers and influences was George Herron, a Christian socialist minister. Herron, who joined the Socialist Party, nominated Debs for president at its 1904 convention. Debs was fond of quoting Herron saying, “Cain was the author of the competitive theory, while the cross of Jesus stands as its eternal denial.” When Debs was jailed in Atlanta in 1920, the only picture that adorned his cell was that of Jesus.

 

The two sides of Debs’s socialism were manifested in the two sides of the Socialist Party’s politics. One side consisted of practical politicking. After succeeding the Social Democratic Party in 1901, the Socialist Party ran candidates across the country in addition to running Debs for president, and it enjoyed considerable success. By 1912, it boasted over 1,200 local officials, including over 100 mayors. It would send two members of Congress. Its membership grew from 10,000 in 1901 to 118,000 in 1912. That year, Debs won 919,000 votes for President, 6 percent of the total.

The other side of Socialist politics was its proselytizing for socialism as the coming Kingdom of God, an equation that appeared frequently in party writings and speeches. The party held days-long encampments throughout rural America and notably in states like Oklahoma, a center of socialist support, and Texas. These encampments were like religious revivals. Participants would gather under the skies or under a big tent to sing and dance and hear speeches. The highlight would be “Debs day,” when Debs would speak for as long as two hours. Debs measured his success in these events by the “converts” he had made.

Within the Socialist Party, a debate raged between those like Berger, who believed the party should focus on immediate demands like ending child labor, adopting unemployment compensation, and a minimum wage, and those like journalist Angie M. Simons, who thought that focusing on immediate demands was a betrayal of the ultimate goal of socialism. Debs, as Gude recounts, disliked factional fights and stayed above the fray, even refusing to attend conventions. He let others, like Herron, work out compromises between the factions.

Debs’s role in the Socialist Party was more like that of a preacher than an organizer or politician. He was a splendid orator who, without the aid of a microphone, could hold hundreds spellbound.  He conducted his public life in a way that reinforced a message of Christian sacrifice. He went to jail for the Pullman strikers and in protest of American entry into the war. He made a decent salary as a public speaker, but he was known to give it away to those he saw as being in need. “Gene Debs,” wrote the socialist journalist Oscar Ameringer, “was the only through-going Christian I have met. Money meant nothing to him.” His followers often compared him to Jesus. Debs was a “social savior,” one Ohio minister wrote, “the vicarious victim of society’s sins, and his life is a continual crucifixion.”

“In his private life, Debs was only human.”

In his private life, Debs was only human. He suffered from periodic depression and exhaustion. He drank excessively. Upton Sinclair described him as being “in the grip of John Barleycorn.”  He was initially devoted to his wife, Kate, whom he married in 1885. But in his travels, he frequented houses of prostitution, and in 1916, he fell in love with another woman, Mabel Dunlap Curry, with whom he carried on an affair to the end of his life.

In spite of his limited schooling, Debs was well read in literature and history. He was not a theoretician of socialism, but he had a sense of the challenge he faced. He spelled out his own conception of the road to socialism in an interview in 1908 with the journalist Lincoln Steffens.  Prior to the 1900 and 1904 elections, Debs had held out hopes of immediate success for the Socialist Party as displacing the Democratic Party as the party of the working class arrayed against the capitalist Republican Party, but by 1908, he held a more sober view. “I am in a hurry, but socialism isn’t,” he told Steffens.  When Steffens asked him about his aspirations in running for office again, Debs gave a wonderfully revealing answer, saying that “if there were any chance of my election I wouldn’t run.” Instead, he explained, “I am running for president to serve a very humble purpose: to teach social consciousness and to ask men to sacrifice the present for the future … When Socialism is on the verge of success, the party will nominate an able executive and a clear-headed administrator; not—not Debs.”

In his interview with Steffens, Debs assigned to unions a joint role with the Socialist Party of preparing workers’ minds for socialism. Three years later, in the midst of a strike wave, Debs articulated the role that unions would play in the evolution to socialism. He saw industrial unionism as “laying the foundation and erecting the superstructure of the new revolutionary economic organization, the embryonic industrial democracy.” Debs continued to reject the AFL’s craft unionism and put great hope in the formation of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW) in 1905. But the IWW, which refused to sign contracts with employers, began to fall apart after it failed to maintain the gains it won in the 1912 Lawrence textile strike.

The period from 1910 to 1912 marked the high point of the Socialist Party’s impact on American politics. After that, many of its local candidates failed to be re-elected. Of the seventeen socialist Ohio mayors elected in 1911, only two won re-election. Debs let his membership in the IWW lapse, and with it the dream of one big industrial union underpinning the Socialist Party. The party did not run a presidential candidate in 1916. Its brave stand against American entry into World War I won it some support in local and state elections in 1917. But the federal government, determined to quash dissent, used the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918 to jail antiwar Socialists, including Debs, and to block Socialist literature in the mail. The Socialists lost 1,500 locals from wartime repression. Debs’s support in 1920 was for his antiwar stand and a protest against his imprisonment. It was not an indication of underlying support for the Socialist Party. After the war, the party’s membership plummeted to 11,000. The party was over.

 

Why did the American Socialist Party decline? Gude focuses on business opposition to working class organization. “The United States had the most powerful, most virulently anti-union business class in the capitalist world,” he writes. “The doors to a mass working-class politics were repeatedly slammed shut.” That was undoubtedly a factor, particularly after 1912, when business organized opposition in elections to Socialist Party candidates. The power of business discouraged the creation of industrial unions. Gude also cites the “extraordinary heterogeneity” of the American working class as a bar to organizing.

But there were other factors that contributed to the Socialist Party’s decline. The first was the difficulty faced by third parties in America’s two-party system. Third parties have arisen and enjoyed some success when both the major parties have either ignored or dismissed large public grievances and concerns. The third party then distinguishes by addressing these concerns.   Debs’s own model for the Socialist Party was the birth of the Republican Party in the 1850s, which by opposing the westward expansion of slavery replaced the Whigs as one of the two major parties. But Debs’s party was unable to play a comparable role.

Debs and Berger conceived of a Socialist third party in the wake of Democratic President Grover Cleveland suppressing the Pullman strike and William McKinley, with business backing, defeating William Jennings Bryan in the 1896 election. By championing the grievances of workers and farmers, Debs and Berger imagined they could supplant the Democrats as the opposition to the Republicans. But by 1912, progressives in the Republican and Democratic parties had begun to oppose child labor and support the minimum wage. In 1912, Theodore Roosevelt’s Progressive Party, which temporarily split off from the Republicans, had a very similar platform to the Socialist Party. A cartoon in Harper’s Weekly suggested that Roosevelt had gone off with Debs’ clothes—that is, his program. Woodrow Wilson, too, espoused some of the same issues as the Socialists. Under Wilson, Democrats outlawed the use of antitrust legislation and other varieties of injunctions against unions. The final death knell to the idea of a Socialist third party came during Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal.

“Socialism remained a distant and largely undefined objective.”

Some socialists, like Simons and even Debs himself, believed that it was possible to build a socialist movement and party simply on the appeal of socialism. But socialism remained a distant and largely undefined objective comparable to the Kingdom of God. In his book, Marxian Socialism in the United States, Daniel Bell pointed to “the religious, chiliastic origin of modern socialism.” Its appeal, absent immediate relief, was religious rather than political. Such an appeal could attract thousands, as religious denominations were able to do, but not national majorities.  

The other factor that doomed the Socialist Party was, to put it simply, the development of American Communism. As described in James Weinstein's book, The Decline of Socialism in America, the success of the Russian Revolution in 1917 convinced many socialists in Europe and the United States that the revolution was nigh. They disdained electoral politics for general strikes and even armed struggle. They clamored to join the Soviet Third International. Debs himself was initially swept up in the fervor. In March 1919, Debs wrote in the Illinois Comrade, “Comrades, the call comes to us all ... to ... do everything that in our power lies to face... the duties and responsibilities that the impending revolution imposes.”

Within the Socialist Party, Berger and New York City leader Morris Hillquit faced a rebellion from party members who imagined that the revolution was imminent. In 1919, the rebels formed the Communist and the Communist Labor parties, splitting the parties’ membership. William F. Dunne, a founder of the Communist Labor Party, warned that labor organizing was “out of date” and “mass action” was on the agenda.  He predicted that “unemployment will increase, there’ll be starvation, and someday the banks will fail, and the people will come pouring out on the streets and the revolution will start.” Debs initially thought the Socialists and the Communists could be reconciled, but by June 1920, he cast his lot with Berger and Hillquit and rejected calls to join the Communist International. “The Moscow program would commit us to a program of armed insurrection,” Debs wrote.  

After Warren Harding commuted his sentence in December 1921, Debs returned to Terre Haute. He participated fitfully in socialist politics, but he already suffered from the heart ailments that would kill him five years later. The two Communist parties joined hands in 1921 to form the Communist Party USA, which enjoyed some success in the 1930s in covertly aiding the growth of industrial unions. However, its identification with Soviet autocracy and terror defiled the image of socialism for the rest of the century and made it inconceivable that a socialist movement could regain even the limited success that Debs’s party had enjoyed. In the United States, the collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the Cold War was a precondition of the revival of socialism—socialism with the adjective “democratic” attached to it. 

There are lessons to be learned from this history, some of which have not been absorbed by today’s socialists. There are still socialists who fantasize about building a third party; who have a quasi-religious view of socialism that is not grounded in practical possibility; there are even socialists within the Democratic Socialists of America who describe themselves as “communists” and as “Marxist-Leninists”—a term popularized by Joseph Stalin.  Gude’s book should serve as a corrective to this foolishness. It is also a good read about a great man.

Someone can be extremely effective at pursuing a goal while giving insufficient thought to whether that goal is worth pursuing. Exploration has an opportunity cost, but so does committing prematurely to a career that consumes all your attention. Conventional career advice often notices only the first cost. There’s also research supporting something close to your proposed sequence. A 2021 study of artists, film directors, and scientists found that periods of unusually successful work were associated with exploration followed by focused exploitation…

Roundup #91: Rocketing into the technofuture

Teen happiness; AI capabilities; Inflation; Inclusionary zoning; Cloud laws; Pronatalism; The Democrats

Noah Smith
Nov 18
 
READ IN APP
 

Howdy, folks! Welcome to the future where science fiction becomes reality every day. Where AI-powered cyberattacks paralyze air travel one day and banks the next. Where shadowy billionaires make fortunes illicitly selling America’s enemies the technology to create artificial gods, while you slave away for $150 a day hoping to get half a day off. Where it seems like a new rare disease is cured every week, even as measles returns to America thanks to an anti-science cult that somehow made it to the highest rungs of power. Where self-driving cars whizz past people hunched over dying of fentanyl in the street. I mean, look at this:

In such confusing times, it’s all your friendly neighborhood economics blogger can do to keep up with it all. But I’m trying my best, so that I can help you understand these crazy times just a little bit better.

First, podcasts. Here’s the latest episode of Hexapodia, in which Brad DeLong and I discuss morality and technology with Ryan Avent:

DeLong's Grasping Reality Weblog
Live with Brad DeLong


Listen now
10 hours ago · 22 likes · 1 comment · Brad DeLong, Ryan Avent, and Noah Smith

And here’s a conversation between me and the streamer Destiny, in which we talk about how liberalism can resist rightism and leftism at the same time:

Anyway, on to this week’s roundup.

1. Good news on teen happiness

For years, we watched America’s young people — and young people throughout the world — become less and less happy. They told surveys they were unhappy. They attempted (and committed) suicide more. They were more socially isolated. They formed relationships less.

The most plausible candidate for a cause for all of this was smartphone-enabled social media, which replaced in-person small-group interaction with impersonal arm’s-length interactions with huge numbers of potentially hostile strangers — something the human animal never evolved for.

But human beings are resilient and adaptable, and I always expected young people to find new ways to be happy in a hyper-connected world. Now, there are some signs that things are starting to turn around:

Jonathan T. Rothwell
@jtrothwell
U.S. teens saw notable declines in self-reported sadness and suicidal ideation from 2021 to 2025. Relative to 2021, they were also more likely in 2025 to: 1) play sports (49% to 58%) 2) do strength training (45% to 51%) 2) eat fruit >=twice/day (19% to 28%) 3) eat at least one
6:05 PM · Nov 9, 2026 · 258K Views
44 Replies · 197 Reposts · 1.35K Likes

A word of caution: This is just one data source, the Youth Behavioral Risk Survey. Other sources, like the CDC, continue to show high teen suicide rates. It’s far too early to conclude that general teen happiness is on the upswing. But the YBRS data is a very positive sign.

If the trend is indeed turning around, what’s the cause? One possibility is that even as the online world became more all-consuming and alienating, the offline world was becoming kinder and gentler. Here’s Rothwell again:

Another possibility is that teens are moving away from the toxic public platforms — X and Facebook — and moving toward either private discussions or passive video apps like TikTok:

Other surveys show that teens are trying to cut back on social media use in general, realizing that it’s bad for them.

This is why I’m a long-term techno-optimist. The downsides of technology can sometimes dominate in the short run, but eventually people figure out how to handle it and turn tech to their advantage.

2. Is AI getting less bang for the buck?

As the Anthropic IPO approaches, various analysts are trying to figure out if the incredible rate of AI progress is going to slow down, speed up, or continue at a steady rate. A number of data sources show that progress has sped up recently, around either late last year or early this year:

One popular theory is that the speedup was due to the advent of AI coding tools. But economists Luis Garicano and Alex Imas argue that what actually accelerated was spending on AI research. They show data showing a smooth deceleration in the amount of AI capability that each dollar of research spending buys:

On the other hand, should we really think of a linear increase in the ECI as a linear increase in capability? Some people argue that each point of increase in the ECI multiplies AI capabilities by a constant factor — like points on the Richter Scale.

Whether that’s true in any meaningful sense is hard to assess. But at the end of the day, what really matters is AI’s ability to generate economic returns. And some people argue that it’s here that we see the true acceleration, as AI hits critical thresholds for economic usefulness:

But it’s also possible that this increase in usefulness doesn’t cleanly map to increases in raw capabilities, and that human beings are simply finding new uses for AI capabilities that already exist.

So the jury is still out on whether AI progress is slowing down.

3. The return of inflation

One of the great accomplishments of economic policy in the last few decades was the conquest of the post-pandemic inflation. The Fed raised rates, and the economy didn’t tank, and inflation went down anyway. But that victory might prove ephemeral; inflation is creeping back up. Though there’s some volatility, most recent months have come in at around 5%:

The rise in oil prices due to the Iran War is an obvious contributor, but in fact the new inflation is remarkably broad-based:

It’s just not possible to play the old game of “Well, inflation is just X and Y and Z, so it’s not really a problem.” There are various possible causes of this broad-based price acceleration — budget deficits, Trump pressuring the Fed to be dovish, cost pressures from the data center buildout, and so on. Teasing these out deserves a longer post.

And just as basic economics would expect, a burst of unexpected inflation is causing real wages to go down:

In other words, Americans are getting poorer this year, because the cost of living is going up and their paychecks aren’t keeping up. It’s not as bad as it was in 2021, but it’s going to be enough to make a lot of Americans very angry at the people in power.

4. Inclusionary zoning is bad

A lot of people mentally divide housing into two types: “luxury” or “market-rate” housing, and “affordable” housing — as if the price of a house or an apartment is built into its walls and floors. The assumption is that if developers aren’t forced to build “affordable” housing, normal people won’t be able to afford housing.

That assumption is totally wrong — building market-rate housing drives rents down and makes housing more affordable. But because lots of people believe in the “luxury”/“affordable” distinction, they embrace policies that try to force developers to offer some units at below-market rates. These policies are called inclusionary zoning. Basically, inclusionary zoning says that some percent of the apartments in a new building have to be rented out for very cheap. The policy is attractive because it doesn’t have any direct fiscal costs — the cost of subsidizing cheap apartments comes out of the pocket of a corporation, rather than the taxpayer.

But this kind of policy ends up backfiring. Forcing developers to take a loss on some of their housing units simply makes it less financially possible to build new housing. And when they do build new housing, they end up raising rents for all the non-“affordable” units in order to try to recoup some of their losses. Here’s what Kouchekinia (2026) finds:

In California, more than a third of localities have adopted [inclusionary zoning ordinances]. Mandatory inclusionary zoning acts as a tax on construction and, all else equal, reduces the overall supply of housing. This potentially reduces affordability in the aggregate…I find the typical inclusionary zoning ordinance reduces annual new residential construction by nearly a third (31.8%). Additionally, I find the policies relocate multi-family developments within jurisdictions to lower rent areas, where the policy is effectively less severe…I estimate the cost of generating an affordable unit with inclusionary zoning to be approximately $800,000 in “excess rents” paid by market rate renters as a result of the policy’s constraint on supply.

As Kouchekinia points out, making housing more scarce acts as a shadow tax on everyone in the area. Inclusionary zoning looks costless, but it’s actually extremely costly.

California cities and other places that use inclusionary zoning are starting to realize that the policy doesn’t do what it’s supposed to do. Some have actually started cutting inclusionary zoning mandates:

M. Nolan Gray 🥑
@mnolangray
The evidence is by now clear and policymakers/planners are slowly starting to respond to it: unfunded inclusionary zoning programs ultimately hurt housing production and affordability.
9:16 PM · Aug 13, 2026 · 25K Views
5 Replies · 22 Reposts · 112 Likes

Matt Yglesias also has a good recent post about inclusionary zoning in D.C., and why the District should scrap it.

Basically, it’s time for this policy to go. There’s really no salvaging it, it’s making our cities worse for no good reason, and we need to stop viewing it as just another inevitable cost of doing business.

5. More on Cloud Laws

For years, I’ve been arguing that AI is going to cause a scientific revolution. My hypothesis is that there are a bunch of “laws of nature” — i.e., exploitable stable causal relationships — that are too complex and diffuse for the human mind to comprehend, but which AI can learn and exploit on our behalf. I call these “cloud laws”, because I envision them as diffuse clouds of weak but densely interrelated causal effects — the kind of thing that human minds will never be able to either grasp in their entirety or bite off into little separable chunks.

Well, here’s a little bit of evidence that cloud laws exist…in the clouds. Yohan Iddawela writes about Google DeepMind’s new weather forecasting AI model:

A single GPU can now calculate hundreds of global weather scenarios in under 60 seconds. The exact same task requires a supercomputer and hours of brute-force physics.

Google DeepMind recently released WeatherNext 2. The model beats the previous state-of-the-art system on 99.9% of weather variables across a 15-day forecast window. It achieves this massive jump in accuracy using a new modelling approach called a Functional Generative Network.

Meteorologists categorise weather data into two buckets:

1. Marginals are isolated data points, like the precise temperature at a specific location or the wind speed at a certain altitude.
2. Joints are the massive, interconnected systems that form when all those individual elements interact.

The researchers hid the joint systems from the model during training. They only taught it the isolated marginals. When they turned it on, the model skillfully predicted the massive, complex systems anyway…The model gives forecasters a full 24-hour advantage in tropical cyclone tracking compared to the previous leading system. It maps extreme wind speeds and heatwaves with unprecedented precision.

We’re watching a pretty big shift in predictive capabilities. The machine is deducing the structural reality of planetary weather from isolated fragments of data.

Normal weather forecasting is reductionist. We take the basic physical laws of motion, model the atmosphere as a bunch of little chunks of air that sort of behave like independent units, and apply the laws of motion to those units. What Google is doing is something else; it’s letting an AI model look at a bunch of weather data and then predict how the whole system is going to behave.

The AI approach ends up working better than the typical reductionist brute-force approach. Why? My guess is that weather has cloud laws — principles that no human could ever intuit from staring at masses of weather data, and which could never be explained in any graduate textbook, but which AI can just grasp holistically.¹

What other phenomena might we be able to predict and control with AI this way? Patrick Collison has a fun list:

Patrick Collison
@patrickc
Which are the most common everyday phenomena that we don't properly understand? Off the top of my head: • Lightning (how does it happen?) • Sleep; dreams (why do they exist?) • Glass (thermodynamics of formation) • Turbulence (when does it start?) • Morphogenesis (how does…
Patrick Collison @patrickc
Some progress in lightning: https://t.co/i7mlLQnYK4.
1:22 PM · May 9, 2026 · 1.27M Views
466 Replies · 225 Reposts · 3.48K Likes

We know these effects have some sort of regular causes, but reductionist science has so far been unable to characterize any of them very effectively. But perhaps AI will, because they might be governed by cloud laws.

If so, we’re in for the most rapid and dramatic scientific revolution in our entire history.

6. Paying people to have kids works (just not enough)

Plummeting fertility is a problem, and nobody knows how to fix it. There are a few people who deny this obvious and disheartening truth. One of those is Lyman Stone, whose own research has cast doubt on the efficacy of paying people to have kids, but who stubbornly insists that such pronatal policies can act as a “crowbar” with which to pry open the door of child-rearing.

Well, they probably can’t do that. Here are Hartley and Jaros, evaluating a Michigan “baby bonus” program that paid people to have kids:

This paper studies the fertility effects of the Rx Kids program, the first baby bonus introduced in the United States. Beginning in 2024, the program was launched in Flint, Michigan and subsequently expanded to additional municipalities across Michigan, creating staggered variation in treatment timing across places….[W]e estimate the effect of Rx Kids on birth outcomes. We find that live birth growth rates increase in treated municipalities…We find that Flint’s $7,500 baby bonus generates a small but statistically significant fertility response: actual 2024 births exceeded a three-year pre-treatment baseline by roughly 7.5%, implying $107,000 in program spending per induced birth. These results provide the first U.S. evidence that direct cash transfers tied to childbirth can measurably affect fertility behavior.

The issue isn’t that these programs don’t work. They do. The problem is that their effects aren’t very large. The United States’ current total fertility rate (TFR) is about 1.6 children per woman; replacement level is between 2.0 and 2.1. That would require at least a 25% increase in fertility rates. The program Hartman and Jaros study resulted in only a 7.5% increase, and was forced to spend $107,000 per child on that paltry increase. That’s not nearly enough, but you can bet that if it were scaled up to the national level, you’d hear a lot of anger directed at the “welfare queens” who benefited from the policy.

And if it’s not nearly enough for the U.S., it’s utterly, laughably inadequate for a country like South Korea, which has a TFR of 0.8. To increase that to replacement level would require a 150% increase — 20 times the size of the increase generated by Michigan’s extremely generous program.

In other words, we’re not going to buy our way out of the baby bust by paying people to have kids. I still think paying people to have kids is a good idea, but the main thrust of effective pronatal policy will have to be something else.

7. Democrats can’t be the Second Party of Tax Cuts

When I was a kid, everyone knew that Democrats were the party that wanted to raise your taxes to spend more on the poor, while Republicans wanted to cut your taxes and spend less. Those days are long gone. America now has two parties who are both dedicated to cutting taxes on the vast majority of Americans — including most wealthy and high-earning Americans — and raising spending at the same time.

This is a big problem for the country, because there will be no getting out of our debt problem until this political equilibrium changes. When I was a kid in 1992, all the presidential candidates were stumbling over themselves to tell America how they were going to fix the deficit, so I know a different equilibrium is possible. We just have to figure out how to get there.

But Democrats’ fiscal profligacy is also a political problem for them. Higher deficits and debt contribute to faster inflation; we’ve already had both Biden and Trump be punished for failing to tame inflation, and Democrats are deluding themselves if they think it can’t happen to them again.

Eric Levitz writes about how the incoming Democrats’ economic policy program is incoherent:

To seize this historic opening, Democrats will need to formulate a platform that effectively advances their core goals. Unfortunately, this will be harder than it sounds — because the party’s current economic priorities appear incompatible with each other…During the midterm campaign, Democrats promised to:

  • Bring down inflation and interest rates.

  • Dramatically expand the welfare state.

  • Raise taxes on the very wealthy — but no one else — while cutting taxes for millions of Americans…

Democrats’ goals…aren’t necessarily coherent.[I]t probably won’t be possible to create large new social programs, avoid tax hikes on anyone but the rich, and drive down inflation and interest rates…

The party’s congressional leaders have signaled support for a social welfare agenda at least as ambitious as President Joe Biden’s unpassed Build Back Better Act, which contained $4.73 trillion of new spending…Add up the estimated fiscal costs of all these programs and the bill comes out to nearly $5 trillion…Critically, America is already on track to run an average annual deficit of $2.4 trillion over the coming decade…[A] greater than $2 trillion deficit will put upward pressure on interest rates and prices.

Democrats do want to raise some taxes, but only on the ultra-mega-super-duper-giga-rich. I’ve written that this approach of “just tax the billionaires” is insufficient to fund all the other economic policies that Democrats want. Levitz concurs.

In time, fear of the deficit will grow to a level that enables the kind of fiscal hawk equilibrium that obtained in 1992. Until then, Democrats need a more modest economic agenda. The American people can be satisfied with an anti-corruption drive, tariff repeal, and policies to spread the wealth generated by AI. They don’t need infinite government largesse in order to be satisfied. Democrats need to stop chasing the Bernie Sanders dream, at least for a while.

Share

1

Also note that the model Google used here wasn’t an LLM. This suggests that AI is more general than the specific techniques the frontier labs are currently focusing on.

Don’t ICEwash or Griftwash the Midterms

Yes, cruelty and corruption matter to American voters

Paul Krugman
Nov 18
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo,Bookshop, and Nook.

After the Democratic sweep in the midterms, some commentators and politicians rushed to declare that theblue tsunami was all about affordability and nothing else. This diagnosis was paired with the political advice that Democrats should focus overwhelmingly on kitchen table issues. Thus NBC News, to take just one example, declared flatly that “Democrats won on affordability,” while Hakeem Jefferies declared that his party will be “laser-focused on addressing the affordability crisis.” According to this mind-set, voters were uninterested in Trump’s autocratic use of the presidency and his bottomless pit of corruption.

This “don’t-rock-the-boat” reaction to Democrats’ historic midterm success was in stark contrast to the way many commentators reacted to the 2024 election. That election was, in fact, mainly about the cost of living. Yet it was widely heralded as signaling a fundamental shift in the cultural and political landscape towards MAGA.

While I’m not a professional voting analyst, it seemed clear to me that an affordability-is-all-that-matters interpretation of the midterms was wrong. First, the historic scale of the Democrats’ victory indicated that voters weren’t just motivated by the issue of affordability. In 2024, which was in fact largely a cost-of-living election, Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points. This year Democrats have won the popular vote by roughly 14 points.

In addition, the demographic evidence – especially, the huge leftwards swing of Latinos – provides strong evidence that Trump’s vicious deportation policy cost the Republicans badly. Third, a number of polls showed that corruption had also become a major issue among voters.

Now G. Elliott Morris, my go-to poll analyst, has a detailed statistical analysis of polls and voter interviews, under the headline “ICE may have cost Republicans more votes than inflation did in 2026.” Furthermore, his evidence documents the importance of corruption in the election.

It’s a fascinating and impressive analysis, and I urge people to read it. Let me just add a few points.

First, Morris — quoting his colleague David Nir — advocates a “smorgasbord theory” of the election: It was lots of things, not just one thing. I’ll expand on their analyses and propose a “gestalt theory” of the election results.

Here’s what I mean: Voters aren’t calculating machines who assign a certain number of points to Trump’s handling of inflation, a certain number of points to his handling of immigration, etc., add up these scores, and use the sum to decide how to vote. Instead, their perceptions on different issues interact. Trump’s corruption and self-dealing made voters more sensitive to how their living standards were falling behind; ICE’s brutality made them more willing to believe Democrats’ claims about Trump’s authoritarianism; Trump’s pandering to the tech broligarchy magnified their sense that he didn’t care about ordinary Americans. Perhaps most important, the Iran debacle made voters skeptical of administration promises and competence on every other issue. And so on.

So when Trump proclaimed that voters should vote as if he was on the ballot, according to my gestalt theory they took him at his word. Republican candidates who tried to distance themselves during their campaign fared no better than those who stuck by his side. What voters had come to believe, based on the Administration’s performance on several fronts, was that Trump and his lackeys were primarily responsible for the multiple deep crises besetting the country.

Why, then, have so many pundits and politicians tried to downplay the role of everything except affordability? Why the rush to ICEwash and griftwash the midterms?

Here is my explanation. Many people in the pundit and political class – particularly older members of that class – are in a reflexive cringe mode due to losing twice to Donald Trump. They don’t fully trust that American voters care about issues beyond their own pocketbooks. Thus they fear that acknowledging the sheer evil of MAGA will come across to swing voters as extremist and pandering to their “woke” base.

But however reasonable the strategy of “it’s all about affordability” may appear, I think it is wrong — as the evidence from G. Elliott Morris and David Nir clearly indicates. Affordability is no longer the sole motivator as it was in the 2024 election. Instead, in voters’ minds it is now part of a constellation of failures and outrages perpetrated by MAGA.

To be clear, Democrats should by all means push an affordability agenda. But they most do this in a way that is honest with the American people, acknowledging publicly the fact that it is much harder to bring prices down and real wages up than it is to do as Trump did, raising prices and lowering real wages.

True, there are ways to gain several quick affordability wins by reversing Trump’s policies: eliminating the tariffs, reinstating the Obamacare subsidies, normalizing immigration, ending the war on Iran, and so on.

A long-term affordability agenda, however, is doable but it will be a legislative slog. For example, Democrats can raise taxes on the rich and corporations to generate tax revenue for programs to help ordinary families, they can pass a Medicare-Buy-In Option, they can subsidize renewable energy, they can raise the federal minimum wage and make unionization easier.

But holding Trump and his accomplices accountable can and should be done swiftly. Not only that, it should be done along with adopting a strong anti-corruption and anti-grift agenda that applies to both Democrats and Republicans. For Democrats need to build their own gestalt with American voters that governance by the Democratic Party will be of, for and by the people.

In short, there’s more to life and politics than the kitchen table. That’s the true lesson of the midterms, and Democrats would be foolish to ignore it.

What does it mean to be “laser-focused on affordability”?

Policy consensus is harder than agreeing on a slogan.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 18
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

As a naturally disputatious person, I was a little bit annoyed by how good the vibes were at last week’s “What’s Next” conference from the Majority Democrats. Annoyed in particular because I suspect that many of the Democrats who believe they’ve reached consensus around ideas like Democrats need to be “laser-focused on affordability” don’t actually agree with each other.

Or, rather, that what they have agreed upon is a slogan rather than a plan.

Words are, after all, tricky things and full of different kinds of ambiguities that clever sloganeers exploit. The way that politics works is that participants in political debates talk about highly technical policy areas while simultaneously trying to communicate with normal people who are not versed in technical jargon.

Doing this effectively is a real skill. But a lot of the skill resides precisely in not being clear about exactly what you mean.

For example, back in John Fetterman’s 2022 campaign, when he was a progressive hero, he used to say that he was determined to “make more shit in America” as part of his solution to inflation. Part of what made this turn of phrase so good is that it’s ambiguous between an abundance-flavored agenda of supply-side reforms and a protectionist agenda of tariffs. If a writer turned in a piece to me that was ambiguous in that way, I’d ask them to try to be clearer about what they’re saying. But in politics, it’s good to be unclear. And while obviously Fetterman has fallen out of favor with the left, the consultants behind him also worked on the Zohran Mamdani, Graham Platner, and Abdul El-Sayed races and continue to be quite skilled and influential, not least in popularizing “affordability” as an alternative to “inflation.”

What’s good about this term, though, is precisely that it’s less clear.

In a campaign speech or ad, it’s optimal to find terms that resonate with large groups of people while being vague in their specific implications. But if you’re trying to reach consensus on a policy agenda, you need to actually work through the disagreement, not find turns of phrase that cleverly paper over it.

Multiple approaches to affordability

If we took the term “affordability” literally, I think it would mean something like what economists call “real income.” In America, for example, cars are broadly affordable — it’s more common for a family to own two cars than to own zero — even though cars are expensive. Incomes are high enough that people can afford them. And, indeed, Americans of 2026 can afford more (and better) cars than they could afford in 1986 or 1956. In India, by contrast, incomes are low, so most people can’t afford cars.

This definition has two virtues. One, I think, is that it makes a lot of sense as a question of technical economics. Would you prefer a world where you earn $250,000 and a burrito costs $20 or a world where you earn $65,000 and a burrito costs $9? Rationally, it’s clearly better to be in the former world.

The other is that in terms of progressive politics, “affordability as real income” lends itself to some obvious policy fixes.

These include reversing Donald Trump’s tax cuts for the rich and using the proceeds to reverse his cuts to SNAP and Medicaid, which would make real incomes higher for more (and more sympathetic) people than it would lower them for. But in addition to welfare state expansion, “affordability as real income” also suggests YIMBYism and other supply-side, pro-growth reforms.

On the merits, I think it would be great if Democrats would coalesce around an affordability agenda that meant rising real incomes. But is this what resonates with voters? The fact is, real median household income was higher in 2024 than it was in 2021 and voters still seemed pretty mad.

Real median household income has fallen in 2026 thanks to the war in Iran, so it’s understandable in those terms why voters are furious about affordability. But real median household income soared to an all-time high in 2025, and my recollection is that voters were already pretty cranky pre-Iran.

I think that voters are probably looking for relief in terms of actual prices and that policymakers almost certainly can’t deliver a general fall in the price level. But they could deliver a rate of inflation that returns us to the customary 2 percent annual rate (or even slightly lower); we just keep not doing that. And America could also have lower interest rates, which don’t show up in inflation statistics but are certainly a price that people see and care about.

My advice to a politician who wanted to deliver that outcome would be to support the Fed hiking rates until inflation returns to target and then to ask Congress to pass deficit reduction bills to help bring interest rates down. Then pair that with supply-side reforms to make sure that real incomes keep rising.

On this interpretation, what the United States needs is essentially an International Monetary Fund structural adjustment program. If Democrats win total control of the government in 2028, they could reverse Trump’s tax cuts for the rich but not his spending cuts. Instead, they could add new cuts to Medicare graft and implement all the Government Accountability Office’s recommended program-integrity stuff. They could kill off ineffective federal programs and try to appoint some kind of commission to look into politically sensitive topics such as the explosion of questionable veterans’ disability claims. This is tough stuff. Not, I think, because the voters would hate it, but because the activists and donors and volunteers who brought the next president to the White House would hate it. They want to see progress on their key issues, not an I.M.F. structural adjustment program.

The other approach to nominal prices, the one that elected officials seem to prefer, is to do stuff that won’t work.

For a while, trying to address housing affordability by cracking down on algorithmic rent-setting was in vogue. This did not succeed anywhere that it was implemented, but there are lots of different things that have prices and lots of different organizations trying to use computers and data to set prices, so there’s a lot of politician whack-a-mole happening around different pricing strategies. This is appealing because, in contrast to anything budgetary, it doesn’t involve tradeoffs. A trillion bucks of deficit reduction is a trillion bucks you can’t use for something else. A crackdown on personalized pricing is free. The problem is it won’t make prices lower, and if you’re in office, people will notice that.

Ideas that don’t work have obvious limits as a policy agenda. On the other hand, ideas that don’t pose tradeoffs have an obvious appeal. But the aversion to tradeoffs raises the question of what it means to “focus” on something.

Focus on affordability … as opposed to what?

One of the huge triumphs of the 2026 midterm campaign is, per this Blue Rose Research polling, that Democrats managed to persuade voters that they — just like the electorate — were very focused on the cost of living.

In the context of a midterm campaign, this mostly comes down to good ads and solid message discipline. It’s also a huge shift from two years ago when Democrats were seen as focused on other stuff. If you’re a campaign consultant, I think this gives you a happy story to tell, which is something like, “hire us and we’ll portray you as laser-focused on affordability and it will work.”

But I think the problem is that the 2024 ads were also good. When you govern, though, you get judged on your governing agenda.

I know a lot of Biden-era Democrats were very frustrated that polls kept showing them as very focused on L.G.B.T.Q. issues when their perception was that they spent a large share of their workweek dealing with economics and almost no time “focused on” L.G.B.T.Q. issues. But that’s not the only way to think about the idea of focus. I would say that Biden-era Democrats were treating L.G.B.T.Q. issues as moral absolutes that were beyond compromise. It’s totally fine and appropriate for people working in politics to hold to certain moral principles in an uncompromising way. But it is also fair for voters to notice which issues you feel that way about and to see them as the focus of your politics.

My sense is that the phrase “laser-focused on affordability” is being used to describe two opposite approaches to this. One group of people thinks that by exclusively talking about affordability, they can make it politically viable to remain completely uncompromising on non-economic issues. Another group thinks Democrats should prioritize affordability by adopting softer views on non-economic issues.

During a campaign, these ideas can seem similar. But when governing, it gets tougher. Suppose there’s a mass shooting next April that gets a lot of media coverage. Will House Democrats pass an assault weapons ban and pass it to the Senate because the vast majority of urban/suburban liberals think the widespread availability of these weapons is morally scandalous, or will Hakeem Jeffries say that he personally supports such a ban but he’s “laser-focused on affordability” and isn’t going to waste the House’s time on a message bill with no chance of being signed into law?

My guess is that most of the people who currently agree that Democrats should be “laser-focused on affordability” would be very frustrated with Jeffries sticking to that pledge the second it means giving up on something they feel strongly about.

2027 vs. 2029

Because Democrats like to discuss internal party strategy in public, it’s sometimes hard to know if people are giving their real thoughts about tactics or if they’re just making the tactically wise choice to say things that are publicly palatable. I’ve heard a bunch of newly elected members of Congress say that Democrats were given a chance by the public but not a strong vote of confidence, and that’s true. I’ve also heard a bunch of newly elected members of Congress say that the public will reward or punish them based on whether they can deliver big relief on the cost front.

That flies in the face of everything we know about the operation of American public opinion. Donald Trump is the president, and this is the Donald Trump economy no matter what Hakeem Jeffries says or does.

I don’t think Democrats should deliberately sabotage the economy, because that would be immoral. But in political terms, there is absolutely nothing wrong with passing a bunch of bills that sound good, and then Trump either signs them or he doesn’t, and you complain about the ones he didn’t sign.

But this completely flips if Democrats win in 2028. In 2029, Democrats badly need to implement policies that actually work.

I saw Rob Flaherty say on Twitter recently that “policy is downstream from message,” which is thinking like a candidate rather than thinking like a governing regime. The Biden administration was aware that they had a big cost-of-living problem on their hands, and they had plenty of smart people working there who had ideas that could help in small ways.

But those people were not empowered to override interest group opposition. So the administration was left with basically messaging gimmicks that would be great for a Senate campaign but didn’t help a sitting president.

The next administration needs to not do that. They need to empower the smart people and prioritize cost-effectiveness over green demands or labor union demands or farmer demands. That’s the laser-like focus. And they need to accept that a lot of the substance of a laser-like focus on costs is going to be a little bit tedious and technical and that the opponents of the policy may not always be bad guys out of central casting. That’s a hard messaging problem, and they’re going to need really smart communications professionals to help them make stuff sound exciting and give advice on what to emphasize and what to downplay.

The point, though, is that not in this Congress and not in the 2028 campaign, but in the actual White House in 2029, the laser-like focus on affordability very suddenly and discontinuously stops being an exercise in showing how much you feel normal people’s pain and becomes an exercise about doing policy analysis correctly.

Needing to care a lot about the merits of technical questions is sort of everyone’s worst nightmare in politics, since it makes it very hard to achieve consensus and politicians are natural people-pleasers. But the focus on affordability ultimately has to mean more than just repeating the slogan, and that means caring about the merits.

Why the Democratic Party Dominates

By Carlos Dengler • 18 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

In the midterm elections, the Democratic Party secured the most decisive political victory by any party since Barack Obama’s 2008 election. Democrats are now poised not only to reshape ongoing conversations about policy, but also to enact previously unthinkable measures, such as the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would transform the nature of political campaigning. The fleeting “vibe shift” that seemed to push the country rightward around Donald Trump’s return to power now looks like a temporary aberration. 

But the whipsawing of the past decade, culminating in Trump’s popular vote victory in 2024 and then his party’s crushing defeat this year, risks obscuring a deeper reality: the perennial dominance of the Democratic Party. The “changing of the guard” between parties gives the periodic impression that elections determine which party is in power, but this is a fiction. The Democratic Party, irrespective of whatever that toggle seems to show us, has been and remains the establishment party, which is to say the dominant party, in US politics. 

This has been the case for almost a century, dating back to the first election of Franklin Delano Roosevelt, when the Democratic Party overcame its backwater, post-Reconstruction malaise. Evidence of Democratic Party struggle and implosion over the years, whether during the triumphs of Nixon, Reagan, or Trump, should not overshadow the extent to which the political dominance of the “losing” party remains intact. 

The legacy of the 1932 Rooseveltian victory manifests itself as an unerring grip on institutions created and fostered by the New Deal and which, in the years since, have grown immensely powerful. Most of these institutions—principally the federal bureaucracy, but also the nonprofit sector, media, academia, and military-industrial complex—lie outside the realm of democratic contestation. What is now spoken of among political scientists as “state depth” (a polite rebranding of the infamous “Deep State”) is nothing more than this relationship between powerful institutions that lie outside the purview of democratic mediation and have been dominated by a single party for more than ninety years. 

“Republican victories should be seen as expressions of impotence.”

If Democratic electoral defeats obscure the party’s continued dominant status, Republican victories should be seen as expressions of impotence. This is because the chief function of the Republican Party since the time of FDR has not been to acquire power, but to run interference—to serve as the official opposition party to the establishment party. 

The Republican Party’s function is not to govern, but to complicate the fact of political dominance of the other side with an illusion of symmetric partisanship. For an illustration of this fact, one need look no further than the now waning political career of our current president. As is well known, his appearance on the political scene in 2015 galvanized existential opposition from both parties. To this day, the given explanation for this has been that his brand of nationalist populism was so “un-American” and proto-authoritarian that it had to be resisted from the right and the left. Trump was an aberration, but not in the way Democrats and Never Trump Republicans claimed. His real break with “norms” lay in his attempt to get behind the line of state depth. His presidency will come to be seen by future historians as a rogue efflorescence of populist discontent that induced a crisis in the dual-party structure, but did not unravel it. 

Only the opposition party, as the weaker of the two, was vulnerable to such a takeover. The fact that Bernie Sanders was twice routed by the party whose nomination he was seeking for president provides evidence of the underlying reality of Democratic Party dominance. Control of that apparatus was never going to fall to someone interested in upsetting the status quo.

The famous quote by former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere—“The United States is also a one-party state, but with typical American extravagance, they have two of them”—is correct. But there is no symmetry between the power of the two. The theater of electoral politics is oriented and enforced by actual dominance by one side. That dominance is located in the Democratic Party, which relies on the Republican Party to provide the appearance that voters are able to make a genuine choice. No matter which party holds the presidency, however, the Democratic-dominated network of government agencies, non-profits, and media companies remains intact. Vote for whoever you want, but don’t expect change.

How to fight monopoly

It’s the barriers to entry, stupid.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 19
 
READ IN APP
 

After you read today’s post, I hope you’ll listen to the latest episode of “The Argument” podcast, where Jerusalem and I talk with economics commentator Kyla Scanlon about why young people are so pessimistic about the economy, even when the economic data looks relatively good. Paid subscribers can watch or listen ad free and read the transcript and show notes here. Free subscribers can catch the episode on YouTube here or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts

Thanks to Skydance’s rapid acquisition of both Paramount and Warner Bros., Hollywood is dramatically more concentrated than ever, especially since Fox and Disney merged several years ago.

And yet the movie industry — which has been teetering since the pandemic thanks to competition from home streaming and the proliferation of social video content — is wrapping up its healthiest year in a long time.

So far in 2026, domestic moviegoers have spent about $8.76 billion at the box office, which is more (in nominal terms) than the totals from 2021, 2022, or 2024. Once the December haul — which will include both “Avengers: Doomsday” and “Dune: Part Three” — comes in, everyone expects this year to shatter 2023’s $8.9 billion box-office haul and be the best year since the pandemic by a decent margin.

While that box-office haul is led by big studio pictures (“Spider-Man” is a Sony/Disney collaboration and “The Odyssey” is from Universal), part of what’s striking about this year’s top 10 is how diverse it is.

We have mini-majors Lionsgate and MGM (which is only a midsized movie studio even though it’s owned by Amazon, which is a giant company overall) with the #5 and #6 movies and specialty label Focus and independent studio A24 coming in at #7 with “Obsession” and #9 with “Backrooms,” respectively. Notably, those two horror hits, while not as large in revenue terms as the biggest movies of the year, are spectacularly more profitable due to their dramatically lower production costs and lack of dependence on expensive intellectual property. “You Can See Everything,” also from A24, was a massive artistic achievement, drove incredible amounts of discourse, and made spectacular sums of money for a low-budget documentary.

This is not to say that we should have zero concerns about the regulatory process around the merger — I have big concerns that I really hope the new Congress will investigate. But the threat of a movie studio monopoly turns out to be pretty illusory. It’s just fundamentally very difficult to monopolize this industry because, thanks to the First Amendment, there are very few barriers to entry into the world of making movies, similar to the problem facing us journalists. The incumbent studios can’t stop A24 and Neon from growing their market share. They can’t stop Apple from getting into the movie business. They can’t stop Netflix from competing asymmetrically via streaming or from putting “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” into movie theaters and competing with them directly.

If they could block competition, of course they’d try, and in tons of industries, established companies succeed. And in most cases, if you want to fight monopoly and take on system-rigging corporations, what you need to do is dismantle barriers to entry.

The captured economy

Health care costs are a big deal. A lot of people end up focusing their mental energy on insurance companies because you pay money to them directly in premiums and then they annoyingly don’t always cover what you want them to cover. Ultimately, though, the availability of health care services is downstream of the actual availability of medical facilities and personnel. And when it comes to facilities, most states have a range of certificate-of-need laws on the books that set up processes where you have to beg permission before opening a new facility.

In terms of personnel, the number of residency slots to train new doctors is capped by law in a way that creates a structural shortage of physicians.

In many states, this shortage is ameliorated by nurse practitioners having full scope-of-practice rights, meaning they can evaluate patients; diagnose, order and interpret diagnostic tests; and initiate and manage treatments, including prescriptions. But in lots of states, they’re subject to rules that are much more restrictive.

The same is true of dental medicine, where hygienists are often prohibited from offering tooth-cleaning services without cutting dentists in on the deal. Tesla successfully fought state-by-state battles against monopoly rights for car dealerships, but those fights were often won in a limited way that has meant Rivian now needs to re-fight the battle to legally sell cars directly to consumers without cutting a dealership owner in as a middleman. But even if Rivian wins this battle, it’s still a relatively small thing compared to a world where old-line car companies — Ford, GM, Toyota, Volkswagen, Kia — could just sell directly to consumers.

In the housing space, not only do land use regulations often serve as a quantity limit on the supply of housing, but a preference for discretionary processes also serves as a barrier to entry.

After all, on some level you might ask yourself what a “real estate developer” is anyway. A construction company builds buildings. An architect designs them. A developer in some sense encompasses those trades but adds in a layer of detailed competency in navigating local permitting processes. A guy who rose up through the ranks in the construction industry might know perfectly well how to build an apartment building. But he can’t really go out on his own and start a business, because he doesn’t know how to get a zoning variance or navigate a Planned Unit Development process.

The point, though, is that these kinds of barriers to entry aren’t unique to health care or housing or auto sales. They’re pretty typical of the American economy.

How the system gets rigged

Something you’ll note about this is that car dealerships aside, most efforts to rig the system against competition are mixed up with plausibly useful regulatory ideas.

It is very easy to understand why there would be occupational licensing of medical doctors and other health care providers. The existence of safety concerns surrounding this makes a lot of sense! My considered opinion is that land use regulations are an all-around bad idea, but I understand why people in good faith believe they’re beneficial.

By the same token, I think it’s pretty obvious that if not for the First Amendment, we in the United States would have had a major push starting way back in the blog era to license journalists in order to keep a lid on misinformation. This would have been incredibly misguided, but it is true that journalists behaving unethically and people publishing things that are false or misleading are real problems in our society. I think that due to Americans’ cultural respect for free speech, an unusually wide range of people understand that a journalist licensing regime intended to improve the quality of information would in practice be used to (at best) stymie competition and (at worst) suppress inconvenient or undesired information.

But while speech is in some respects special, the exact basic dynamic exists in other areas.

Back in October, I mentioned in the New York Times that “new American commercial jet pilots generally must have 1,500 hours of training flight time before they can qualify to co-pilot a plane — over five times as much time as required by perfectly safe European airlines.”

For my trouble, I got some leftists accusing me of wanting to see more people die in plane crashes. The point, though, is that while there are clearly good reasons to regulate aviation safety, doing so also creates opportunities for system-rigging.

When Colgan Air Flight 3407 crashed in February of 2009, the American aviation industry was already in rough financial shape because of the recession — demand for air travel was plummeting, and nobody was very interested in hiring new pilots. Lobbyists pushed Congress to enact this dramatic increase in training requirements not because this would have prevented the crash — the pilots of that plane would have qualified under the new stricter standard — but because they saw an opportunity in the crash to do something pretextual. Congress went along with it because in the economic climate of 2009, a pilot shortage didn’t seem worth worrying about.

Today, though, we have a profitable airline industry, albeit one that’s achieved profitability by adopting some consumer-unfriendly practices. What we’d like to see is profitable airlines seeking further profits by expanding service, either by offering new direct flights between city pairs that don’t currently enjoy service (a win for consumers) or by competing on routes that are already served (a different win for consumers).

Major airlines are in fact doing this, but it’s a slow process. If it were faster to get pilots trained up and hired, we’d have more intensive competition and a better economy.

Here in Washington, the Council is using safety concerns as a pretext to prevent Waymo from competing with Uber and Lyft. And does anyone think beauty salons in Iowa and Wyoming are genuinely safer than ones in New York and New Jersey thanks to their more onerous licensing requirements? That’s silly. I don’t understand the sociology of why state legislatures in the Great Plains and Appalachia (and I guess Oregon) seem unusually susceptible to unreasonable rules on this subject, but there’s no way this is a bona fide consumer-protection rule.

What would benefit both workers and consumers more is more competition, just as cinema continues to thrive as a medium despite the best efforts of corporate M&A specialists to consolidate.

The case for populist liberalism

It’s worth understanding all of this because it is definitely true that there’s political merit to populist rhetoric about how the little guy is getting screwed by the system.

It’s also true that as a matter of habit, the kinds of people who talk about the kinds of issues I’ve raised here tend not to use populist rhetoric in our internal discussions. For starters, we’re mostly people who believe in positive-sum economic growth, so we don’t love populist framings, which tend to reflect a negative-sum worldview.

Secondarily, it’s generally true that the “villains” in stories about barriers to entry and rent-seeking, though they are richer than the average American, are not literally the very richest people in the country. That’s not because an Elon Musk or a Jeff Bezos is above lobbying for anti-competitive rules — everybody tries to work the angles available to them. But the way to become multi-billionaire rich is to found a company in a space that is open to competition and then win the competition. The people owning and operating businesses in heavily protected spaces tend to be “everywhere millionaires” rather than ultra-billionaires. But these people are very wealthy in aggregate.

Mostly, though, it’s just happenstance. People operating in spaces that I’ve seen labeled at different times as “neoliberal,” “pro-growth progressive,” “liberaltarian,” or more recently “abundance” tend to use words like “barriers to entry” rather than “monopoly” and usually say “rent-seeking” rather than “rigging the system.”

But these are the same ideas. When traditional stick-built housing interests imposed onerous regulations on manufactured housing to ward off competition, that was monopolists rigging the system for profit. When the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act finally repealed those rules, it was a triumph for the little guy against the power of concentrated special interests.

I do not personally have very strong feelings about which rhetorical mode should be used. When I wrote “The Rent is Too Damn High” way back in 2011, I thought that co-opting left-populist rhetorical framings was a promising idea. I wanted to use the phrase “land reform” to mirror populist political demands from rural Latin America, just applied to urban and suburban areas. The YIMBY movement has prospered in the years since then and has mostly not gone in that direction, and so I think its choices have probably been correct.

I do believe, though, that both operatives and journalists who are less policy-focused have gotten confused about the actual stakes at issue and that’s the fault of those of us more on the abundance side of things for not articulating the populist window into our message. People who think they’re getting a raw deal from the system are making good points, and the obligation of policymakers is to fix real problems rather than feed people slop that doesn’t work.

The perils of slop politics

Back to where this piece started, though: The merger of Paramount and Warner posed no serious problems for competition due to the lack of barriers to entry in the movie business.

But I do have serious antitrust concerns about the way the merger went down.

My concern is that from the moment Warner went on the auction block, the Trump administration acted as if merger approvals were not a question of law but of the president’s whim. There is some reason to believe that a rival bid from Netflix was ultimately shot down by signs that the White House would look less kindly on such a combination than on one that would give a political ally control over CNN. It’s not totally clear that this is actually what went down, but there are some indications — including the fact that Trump interfered with legitimate antitrust enforcement specifically to influence CNN back in his first term.

This is just one in a long list of things that I hope the new Congress will look into because there’s smoke around it and it deserves to be seen as a major scandal if that’s what Trump did.

I’m concerned, though, that this entire angle has been lost to Democrats because they’ve embraced too much unsound neo-Brandeisian thinking. On the view that basically all mergers are bad, the question is whether it was bad to approve the Paramount bid. On the more sound view that monopolies normally require barriers to entry and that the general market for video entertainment is very competitive, the inappropriate action was threatening to block a Netflix bid.

Note, though, that either way, we’re talking about a rigged political and economic system, corrupt people in power, and the machinations of billionaires. The general populist rhetorical frame does not uniquely point toward either perspective on competition policy. The reason to prefer the correct perspective is just that it’s correct and that it will let us make good policy choices that help people and improve lives. But either way, you’re fighting monopolies and unrigging a crooked system.
