A Norwegian Pop Star Embraces a Medieval Mystic

By Matthew Schmitz • 19 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

Norway is one of the world’s least religious countries, but the spirit is moving some of its most interesting artists. Jon Fosse, the Nobel-winning novelist, is a Catholic who writes of lonely men’s encounters with divine providence. Karl Ove Knausgaard, a writer known for minute realism, has turned to supernatural themes. And now Susanne Sundfor, an independent musician known for snappy dance numbers and tales of heartbreak, has released Revelations of Divine Love, a record whose lyrics are drawn entirely from the writings of the fourteenth-century mystic Julian of Norwich.

Some religious artworks are the expressions of broadly believing cultures—think Bach’s Mass in B Minor or the cathedral at Chartres. But today, religious art often has a different character. Rather than giving voice to the dominant outlook, religion becomes a site of resistance to mainstream values. In this way, it can prove attractive to people who normally would not be drawn to dogmatic belief.

“Religion becomes a site of resistance to mainstream values.”

“There is a mysticism wave happening among artists in Europe,” Sundfor tells me. Her new album, co-written with the organist Kit Downes, exemplifies this trend. Though Sundfor is not Catholic or avowedly Christian, she has produced a remarkable piece of sacred music, her supple voice lending poignancy to the unexpected affirmation that God is what “Holy Church preacheth and teacheth thee.”

Sundfor came across Julian’s writings at a time when a friend of hers was suffering from breast cancer—and joining the Catholic Church. What she found surprised her. “It felt like something a guru in the ’60s New Age movement would write, but it was Christian. And I hadn't really been introduced to that kind of Christianity before.”

Part of the attraction was feminist, though not in the conventional sense of that word. In Julian’s writing, and in Catholic piety generally, Sundfor finds compelling images of womanhood. “The religious story that makes the most sense to me is Jesus and Mary,” she says. “I think it's what a society should be based on, mother and child.”

This vision of womanhood is especially attractive in a society that is at once prurient and censorious. “Sex is very distorted,” Sundfor says. “It’s either Puritan or porn.” She views sex in religious terms as something positive. “To me, sex is sacred. I think that's a problem we have around sexuality today, that it's become sort of secularized, for lack of a better word.”

Sundfor’s high view of sex and motherhood explains the album’s cover art. It shows a woman giving birth, her face lit with ecstasy. Based on a photo from the natural birth advocate Ina May Gaskin, it depicts a phenomenon reported by midwives, in which the woman climaxes during delivery.

Unsurprisingly, the cover art has been censored by music platforms such as Apple and Spotify. Sundfor hesitated before using it, but she finally decided that it was necessary to convey her meaning. For her, the image has a specific theological resonance. “In the Scripture, they say that Mary gave birth without pain,” she notes. “There’s a theory within Christianity that Jesus reversed Adam’s sins, Mary reversed Eve’s sins”—a reference to the patristic idea of Mary as the “new Eve.” This reversal entailed the lifting of a curse described in Genesis. “What was the consequence of Eve's misdoings or errors? She had to have pain in childbirth. And then Mary didn’t.”

In this way, an explicit image drawn from an alternative birth manual comes to express a spiritual longing for the restoration of motherhood—so that it ceases to be painful or despised, and becomes instead an unmixed blessing.

Sundfor’s own experience of childbirth helped her understand the words of Julian. The mystic’s great theme is trust in divine providence—God’s control over all that happens. Thus her famous words, “All shall be well.” As Sundfor notes, midwives often tell mothers to “trust the process” in order to avoid anxiety — a kind of lesson in relying on providence.

That trust can be seen on her album’s cover and in Julian’s writing. “Here is a woman who is in complete trust of the wonder that is about to happen,” Sundfor says. “And only then can you sort of give birth to someone in such ecstasy. So it's like the ultimate image of love, really.”

Sundfor understands her exploration of faith as a response to a universal longing. “I think we're supposed to be religious. I don't think it's natural for human beings to not be religious,” she says. “It creates a vacuum in us, and we need to fill it with something.”

If Sundfor is right, people in secular societies will continue to search for some source of spiritual meaning. Where will they find it? Ever since she was a child, Sundfor says, she has been “searching for something bigger.” She has found intimations of that something in the words of a medieval mystic and in the relationship between Jesus and Mary. “Love really is bigger,” she tells me.

Does it really matter if there’s an intelligence explosion?

Maybe this is the wrong frame for the AI safety discussion.

Noah Smith
Nov 20
 
READ IN APP
 

Vernor Vinge is possibly my favorite science fiction author of all time.¹ The Singularity, which he famously predicted would happen somewhere between 2005 and 2030, features heavily in most of his stories. It usually happens the same way: an Intelligence Explosion, of the type envisioned by I.J. Good — the smarter AI gets, the faster it’s able to make itself even smarter, meaning that AI becomes godlike nearly instantaneously once it reaches a certain threshold of capability.

Almost every discussion about AI safety that I hear in San Francisco or read in the tech blogosphere centers around this sort of event. The discussions are all about whether recursive self-improvement (RSI) is near, and whether we should “pace the frontier” — i.e., deliberately slow down or pause AI progress — to stop RSI from creating an intelligence explosion.

As I’ve listened to these arguments, I’ve grown increasingly skeptical that this is the right discussion we should be having. But before I explain why, let me quickly summarize the debate itself, to give an idea of what the arguments look like.

The intelligence explosion debate, in brief

In fact, I’ve published some pieces of that discussion on this blog. Back in September, Ramez Naam wrote a guest post arguing that an intelligence explosion is not imminent:

Where’s the “intelligence explosion”?

Ramez Naam
·
Sep 27
Read full story

His basic arguments were:

  • OpenAI data show that AI is still only able to automate short chunks of the AI research process.

  • AI research is subject to diminishing returns, so that each increase in AI capability should buy less of a speedup in the pace of automated research.

  • Diminishing returns also mean that accelerating AI progress will require exponentially more of other resources, such as compute and money.

  • There’s no sign yet of an acceleration in the rate of AI progress.

In a follow-up post, Ramez did a deeper dive on the topic of agent swarms, arguing that they’re not as effective as many people believe.

Theo Jaffee echoed these arguments, noting that OpenAI’s data shows that AI hasn’t even been able to fully automate smaller research tasks yet:

Luis Garicano and Alex Imas also wrote a post downplaying the likelihood of an intelligence explosion:

Silicon Continent
Are we approaching an intelligence explosion?
(Dear reader: this is an unusual post; it gets a bit technical. Alex and I are trying to do something hard here: look at the data and try to understand what they tell us about the intelligence explosion. There is math, Greek letters, and two models. So please bear with us, and if you are bored, apologies. We think it is worth making an exception here…
Read more
7 days ago · 65 likes · 13 comments · Luis Garicano and Alex Imas

Their arguments are more economic in nature. They show that although AI progress has accelerated, it also shows diminishing returns in terms of research spending, meaning that every unit of progress has come with a higher price tag:

They also estimate an economic model of RSI,² and conclude that ideas in AI research are probably getting harder to find, reducing the likelihood of an intelligence explosion.

On the other side of the debate, we have the recent METR report about Anthropic’s internal progress in automating AI research. The report uses Anthropic’s own internal measure of AI capability, AECI, rather than the better-known public ECI. It also relies on data that aren’t public, meaning that deciding how much of the report to believe requires a lot of guesswork and assumption-making. But the basic story METR tells is that Claude is already speeding up Anthropic’s research process by a lot:

As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration [of AI progress in late 2025] was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute…We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current…acceleration is due to AI.

Dwarkesh Patel, meanwhile, argues that AI research isn’t that different from math, and that the same factors that made AI suddenly go from useless to godlike at math will happen soon with AI’s own self-improvement:

Dwarkesh Podcast
The avalanche that hit math is coming for AI development


Read more
7 days ago · 547 likes · 103 comments · Dwarkesh Patel

He writes:

It’s crazy how fast we went from, in 2023, “This model can’t reliably add four-digit numbers,” to…about a month ago, “Okay, it fucking solved a Millennium Prize problem in 88 hours.”…

AI research is actually surprisingly similar to the type of mathematical progress that current AIs are disproportionately good at: unlocking a ton of low-hanging fruit by applying a combination of incredible persistence and a superhuman capacity to connect ideas from lots of adjacent domains…In every domain where we can check answers and give AIs thousands of rounds of practice—for example, competitive programming contests, or well-scoped open math problems—they’ve gone from worse than most humans to better than the best humans within a few years…AI research has those same verifiable properties…

Once AI is as good as the best humans at AI research, algorithmic progress will get radically faster…Today’s AIs already do work at about 10 times human speed. And automated researchers would also be working around the clock, nights and weekends included. As a result, each individual automated researcher will be cramming in roughly 50x more work every calendar week than a human researcher can do…During the intelligence explosion, automated engineers will build tens of thousands of times more [reinforcement learning] training environments than we have currently.

So that’s the debate. Basically, it depends on whether ideas get harder to find faster than AI gets better at finding ideas, and only time will tell which one wins.

But as I said, while this debate is intellectually interesting, I’m not sure how much it matters.

How useful is this debate?

Whether an intelligence explosion happens is obviously very important. A sudden unfathomable leap in AI capabilities to godlike levels would be, to put it mildly, a very big deal. But that doesn’t mean an intelligence explosion is the thing we should be thinking and arguing about.

First of all, if an intelligence explosion is possible, it’s going to happen, and there’s probably just not much we can do to affect how it all shakes out.

Although people disagree about AI’s contribution to its own uplift, everyone agrees that AI capabilities are improving at a steady, rapid rate. Here’s Epoch AI’s ECI number, the most common measure of AI capabilities:

Most discussions about AI safety policy revolve around the idea of “pacing the frontier” — i.e., using government policy and AI labs’ own decisions to bend that trendline of progress downward. The usual reason given is that this will allow alignment research time to catch up, so that more powerful AI is safe by the time it arrives.

But this approach simply can’t deal with an intelligence explosion. If there’s some threshold at which AI gets good enough to start an intelligence explosion, that threshold will be reached. Even if we “paced the frontier” and slowed the rate of AI progress down by half, that would mean we’d hit the intelligence explosion in 2037 instead of 2032, or 2030 instead of 2028, or something like that. It would only buy us a few extra years.

I guess two years or five years isn’t nothing — we could use it to hang out with our loved ones and try some cool new restaurants while we waited for the arrival of the computer gods. But ultimately, it seems like small potatoes, especially if you’re an AI safety type who thinks an intelligence explosion would be a catastrophic event for humanity.

If an intelligence explosion is possible, the only way to prevent it is to halt AI progress completely, rather than just slow it down. In 1993, Vernor Vinge made a powerful argument as to why that’s impossible:

But if the technological Singularity can happen, it will. Even if all the governments of the world were to understand the “threat” and be in deadly fear of it, progress toward the goal would continue. In fiction, there have been stories of laws passed forbidding the construction of “a machine in the form of the mind of man”. In fact, the competitive advantage -- economic, military, even artistic of every advance in automation is so compelling that passing laws, or having customs, that forbid such things merely assures that someone else will get them first.

I’m a little more optimistic than Vinge here — I think we could engineer an AI slowdown if we got sufficiently scared — but I don’t for one minute believe we could engineer a complete halt.

Nor do I believe that alignment research will be able to make an intelligence explosion safe. “Pacing the frontier” so that alignment research can catch up might be effective in a world of steady linear AI progress.³ But in a world of sudden superexponential progress, AI alignment research will immediately be left behind. Even if there is a Singularity for understanding alignment, in a world with an intelligence explosion it will be the superintelligent AI, not us, that carries out that Singularity and decides on its alignment for itself.

A second point is that it’s not obvious why an intelligence explosion would be more dangerous than — or even distinguishable from — the type of rapid, non-explosive progress we’re already getting. Remember, AI going from “can’t add two numbers together” to “solves problems too hard for all human mathematicians combined” in three years is not counted as an intelligence explosion!

It’s clear that at the current rate of steady progress, AI will become superhuman in most domains in a fairly small number of years. Even robotics and other physical tasks look conquerable with the current type of AI that powers Claude and GPT. This means that AI will basically look like a god within our lifetimes, whether or not it looks like the kind of infinitely self-improving gods that populate Vernor Vinge novels.

This is why I’m not sure what an intelligence explosion means for our economy. It’s easy to write down a model in which smoothly increasing AI capabilities drive a smooth increase in GDP. But why should we believe a model like that? Other technologies haven’t really worked that way.

Usually, technologies reach some threshold of usefulness where adopting them makes economic sense. When they hit that threshold, their local contribution to productivity growth becomes very rapid, but also finishes fairly quickly. Fiszbein et al. (2024) shows this for electrification, Bartel (2005) shows it for IT-enabled machines. Each new invention creates a whole bunch of little local Singularities. It’s only when you add all these up across the economy that you get something that looks like a big smooth wave of growth.

A suddenly superintelligent AI isn’t really limited by locality — it could, essentially by definition, take over all or most human tasks if it wanted to. Whereas if an intelligence explosion doesn’t occur, these takeovers are likely to be staggered and irregular. But they will still happen, and the economic effect after the first few years probably won’t be that different.

In other words, I think:

  • The AI we’ll get from our current trend of improvement will look about as godlike — and as economically important — as an AI that suddenly bootstraps itself to godhood.

  • It’s not possible to stop AI improvement completely, and so if an intelligence explosion is possible, it’s going to happen to us soon.

  • Slowing down the rate of AI progress will not help us deal with post-Singularity superintelligence.

This is why I think this whole debate is misplaced. We need to be thinking about how to deal with the AI we already have, and the one we’ll almost certainly get soon — an AI that’s smarter than all humans at most economically important tasks. We need to think about how to regulate that actually existing superintelligence, how to prevent AI-enabled bioterror, how to make sure the economic benefits of AI are widely shared, and so on. We need to think about competition policy, to make sure the benefits of AI don’t exclusively go to one company.

I think we need to accept that nobody is “pacing the frontier” enough to prevent the emergence of superintelligence — and that nobody is likely to do so. If the machine god awakes, then it awakes, and we’ll simply deal with it. In the meantime, we need to focus on dealing with the AI we have now.

Why Are Tech Lords Rallying Around a Man Who Sold Out America?

The Jensen Huang story keeps getting worse

Paul Krugman
Nov 20
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo,Bookshop, and Nook.

You might think that billionaires are completely self-interested, that their attention is exclusively focused upon making themselves richer. But that’s unfair. Because quite a number of the wealthiest men in America are now banding together and advocating for the greater good — that is, the greater good of the billionaire class. Billionaires such as Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Bill Ackman and Greg Brockman have been showing vociferous support for Jensen Huang, the disgraced former CEO of the chip giant Nvidia, and demanding that he be given his job back.

It’s true that Huang’s fall has been particularly shocking. Before his fall, he was a virtual potentate in the world of AI. He controlled access to the most sophisticated chips for AI data centers and, critically, the financial backing that his customers needed to purchase those chips. More so that any other single person, Huang both engineered the chips that made AI possible and inflated the AI financial bubble that looms over the economy.

But as we now know, Huang had an extended affair with Alice Huang (no relation), who has been identified by U.S. intelligence as a likely Chinese asset. Alice Huang is the controlling shareholder of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company that provides compute to Chinese companies and, quite possibly, to entities tied to the Chinese military.

Yet the focus on Huang’s apparent fall into a Chinese honeytrap obscures the fact that Nvidia was systematically undermining U.S. security for financial reasons, not just carnal ones.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are one of the few major advantages America has in its technology competition with China — a nation that is not an outright enemy, yet has consistently worked to undermine America’s interests globally, including providing significant technological and financial support to Iran. Moreover, China is an autocratic surveillance state that has bolstered anti-democratic forces around the world. The U.S. has had a policy, initiated by the Biden administration, of denying China access to the most sophisticated chips, Nvidia’s in particular.

Then Jensen Huang intervened. Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration for a relaxation of Biden’s export restrictions, after contributing $25 million to Trump’s hideous ballroom. Howard Lutnick, the Commerce secretary, appears to have played a special role in undermining U.S. sanctions. Members of Congress have leaked data showing that Commerce approved the sale of hundreds of thousands of advanced chips to Chinese companies, including some with known ties to the Chinese military.

Furthermore, Nvidia also sold chips to third-party buyers — Megaspeed in particular — which appear to have smuggled these chips to China. On Monday the Justice and Commerce departments revealed that they have launched a criminal investigation into Megaspeed. Announcements of investigations in progress are rare; obviously Trump officials are scrambling to contain the political damage from the Huang revelations. Scott Bessent, the Treasury secretary, said in an interview last week that he had been pushing for months to have Megaspeed on a trade blacklist, but that Commerce — “which has the pen” — failed to act.

Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial company run by Lutnick’s sons, reportedly has a large financial stake in Nvidia, and Congressional Democrats are investigating. Lutnick looks like a prime target for impeachment once Democrats take control of Congress.

For a lot of money was involved in Nvidia’s dubious dealings: In fiscal 2025 customers with a billing location in Singapore, which accounts for only around 0.5 percent of world GDP, accounted for 18 percent of Nvidia’s revenue. Presumably the bulk of those purchases went to other nations, especially China.

So regardless of whether you want to frame it as a honeytrap or a moneytrap, Huang was effectively selling out U.S. national interests. (Democracy too.) Yet rather than make it clear that they would never betray America the way Huang (and apparently Lutnick) has, the tech oligarchy has rushed to his defense.

As the Wall Street Journal reported, at the latest New York Times Dealbook conference, “the technorati” — notably including Elon Musk — “took turns praising Huang.” David Sacks, the former White House technology czar, has defended Huang and argued that the “real story” is the leak of intelligence concerns to the New York Times. And of course Donald Trump himself has expressed support for Huang.

What’s going on here? As a number of observers have pointed out, many people in the tech-bro elite believe that corporations should be run in “founder mode,” in which one Big Man basically gets to do whatever he wants. And this is regardless of whether the company is publicly traded and thus legally obligated to act in its shareholders’ best interests.

As a recent op-ed by Amit Seru and David Larcker puts it, “some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies are basically authoritarian realms.”

So when these corporate strongmen see Huang fired for bad behavior that compromises national security, they see it not as a necessary corrective but as an implicit threat to their own authority. In their Ubermensch world view, only the little people need to obey the rules — including the rule of law. And of course they have an ally in Trump, the ultimate example of someone who revels in breaking rules and laws.

But do they realize how dangerous this kind of arrogance is about to become? Josh Marshall of Talking Points Memo, who has been writing along similar lines, doesn’t think so:

[I]t does not seem like any of these guys have entirely absorbed just how staggeringly unpopular they and their entire industry has become. They also don’t seem to have grasped how unpopular Trump — with whom they’ve cast their lots — has become.

Indeed. YouGov’s latest poll finds that Americans who believe that Huang’s affair compromised national security outnumber those who believe it hasn’t three to one. And most people probably don’t know how much Nvidia appears to have profited from chip-smuggling; if they did, their anti-Huang views would surely be even stronger.

In the aftermath of the midterm blue tsunami, quite a few tech lords will soon find themselves testifying before Congressional committees, as well as their businesses under greater regulatory scrutiny. So it’s a hell of a time for them to publicly rally for autocratic impunity. But, hey, that’s what they did when their tied their fates to Donald Trump.

Going forward, just as in the case of Elon Musk and Starlink, the Jensen Huang debacle shows that critical national security assets cannot be controlled by one person, no matter how impressive a businessperson he or she is. Just as the midterms results signaled the death throes of MAGA, let’s hope that the Jensen Huang debacle, along with Democratic investigations, will mark the beginning of the end of autocratic founder syndrome — and the self-dealing that so often goes with it — in the tech world.

Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer convicted of murdering George Floyd in 2020, was stabbed twenty-two times while in federal custody.

Due Process for Derek Chauvin

By Scott Yenor • 20 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

American Scapegoat: 
How a Corrupt Justice System Sacrificed Derek Chauvin to the Mob
By T.J. Harker
Passage, 400 pages, $34.95

Derek Chauvin, the former Minneapolis police officer convicted of murdering George Floyd in 2020, was stabbed twenty-two times while in federal custody. Though he survived, he has become America’s scapegoat—the title of T.J. Harker’s meticulous new book on the Chauvin trial. Harker, a former assistant US attorney, has prosecuted many such cases. Drawing on his experience, he shows where the conventional narrative goes wrong.

As a strict legal matter, Chauvin’s case is not about race relations, patterns of police conduct, or any of the other controversies for which it was taken as evidence. It is about whether Chauvin, in fact, committed a crime and received a fair trial. In the American system, justice requires clear, rebuttable charges brought before a neutral magistrate and an impartial jury that decides on the basis of clear evidence, not hysteria or fear. The prosecution must charge only what the evidence can bear, while giving the accused fair notice of how the evidence will be organized. Exculpating evidence or material that would impeach the state’s own witnesses must also be given to the defense. 

In the mob-like atmosphere that surrounds high-profile and politically charged cases, these safeguards come under assault. Prosecutors playing to the crowd can act unethically. Judges can bow to the mob too. No number of peremptory challenges will change the fact that jury pools can hate the accused, refuse to listen at trial, bow to the crowd, and preordain a conviction.

Initial toxicology and autopsy reports did not provide evidence that Derek Chauvin caused George Floyd to die. As Chief Medical Examiner Andrew Baker wrote in the immediate aftermath of the events, “there were no medical indications of asphyxia or strangulation” and, as Harker adds, “no mention of asphyxia, neck compression or back compression.” No bruising either. County prosecutors on the case were reluctant to pursue the most serious charges.

Instead, politicians from across the state and the country jumped into action. Mike Freeman, the Hennepin County Attorney, said public pressure was “immense” and, in internal communications unearthed after the trial, told the county prosecutors to “get back to work ... you’re f**king this up.” Gov. Tim Walz put Attorney General Keith Ellison in charge of the prosecution. At a press conference a day after the Floyd video went viral, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey demanded retribution. “Why is the man who killed George Floyd not in jail? If you had done it, or I had done it, we would be behind bars right now.” He demanded that the country “charge the arresting officer” since the city “could not turn a blind eye” to Floyd’s killing. He also imputed a racial motive, insisting the next day on television that Floyd would be “alive today if he were white.” Minnesota Department of Public Safety Commissioner John Harrington, around the same time, said: “We’ll call it a murder; that’s what it looked like to me.”

As a result, the initial prosecutors were sidelined and the charges were upped to second-degree murder. Prosecutors may have pressured Baker to change his story in a highly irregular meeting where no independent observers were present. The prosecutors were later removed from the case for meeting with witnesses without a third party present. 

Baker was also pressured to change his testimony by one Roger Mitchell, then a DC chief medical examiner. “You don’t want to be the medical examiner who tells everyone they didn’t see what they saw,” Mitchell told Baker privately. When that failed to persuade him, Mitchell threatened to criticize Baker in a Washington Post op-ed. Baker yielded and, ambiguously, added neck compression to the cause of death. Mitchell sat on the op-ed. Later in the trial, expert defense witness Dr. David Fowler testified that Floyd died from a sudden heart attack resulting from heart disease, combined with fentanyl use and other contributing factors. Neck compression, he said, played no role at all. Mitchell wrote an open letter, published right after the verdict, to Attorney General Merrick Garland and Maryland Attorney General Brian Frosh, Fowler’s former superior. Mitchell called Fowler’s testimony “disingenuous” and “baseless,” and demanded an “immediate review of ALL the deaths in custody” investigated by Fowler’s Maryland office. Maryland followed the advice. As a result, dozens of police-restraint deaths were re-classified as homicides. One family shook Maryland down for $5 million, and Fowler faced a civil suit. In the environment of those years, any medical examiner had good reason to worry about the power of professional criticism.

Baker asked the county prosecutor, Amy Sweasy, in a conversation she recorded in a memo: “Amy, what happens when the actual evidence doesn’t match up with the public narrative that everyone’s already decided on?” and worried that “this is the kind of case that ends careers.” None of her memos complaining of the lack of evidence for the most serious charges were handed to the defense during the trial. 

Baker received hundreds of private threats when he first held that there were “no physical findings that support a diagnosis of traumatic asphyxia.” The defense was not notified of these threats, so they could not ask about how they shaped his views during the trial.  

On May 29, 2020, the county prosecutors charged Derek Chauvin with third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter even though, as Harker notes, “the autopsy revealed no physical findings that support a diagnosis of traumatic asphyxia.” On June 3, the Hennepin County prosecutor at Ellison’s direction upped the charge to second degree murder. The cause of death was now “cardiopulmonary arrest complicating law enforcement subdual, restraint, and neck compression.” (The word “complicating” here means “occurred in the setting of” being subdued, restrained, and having the neck compressed.) 

The charges against Chauvin assumed the existence of an assault as the predicate to the second-degree murder charge. On this theory, at some point the lawful, normal way Chauvin restrained Floyd became an unlawful assault. Because Floyd died as a result of the “assault,” Chauvin could, under Minnesota law, be charged with second-degree murder, without ever intending to do Floyd any harm. Sweasy and the other county prosecutor, as Harker documents, papered “memos to file” with concerns regarding the theory that Floyd died of asphyxiation. (“Memos to file” are essentially contemporaneous notes designed to create a record around problematic decision-making or interference in the case.) Sweasy worried that Chauvin was being charged in a way that “violated professional and ethical rules, and withdrew from the case. These memos, like her notes about her meeting with Baker, were only made public in 2023, when Sweasy was suing the county for sex discrimination. 

Jury selection started relatively quickly. On the Minneapolis-based PowerlineBlog, attorneys Scott Johnson and John Hinderaker provided contemporary coverage. Scott Johnson wrote that “the fair trial challenges” were “beyond the capacity of the judicial system” and that protecting Chauvin’s rights in “the lynch mob atmosphere that pervades the case” would be extremely hard unless the venue were changed. The atmosphere was, Johnson concluded “one step removed from the territory of The Ox-Bow Incident,” a story about a lynch mob killing three innocents. Powerline catalogued juror responses, almost without exception showing hostility to Chauvin and a desire to convict. 

The city of Minneapolis announced a $27 million settlement with Floyd’s family during jury selection, implying the city’s view of Chauvin’s guilt for all who had ears to hear. In other high-profile cases, the city waited until after the criminal trial to announce settlement with the victim’s family. Juror 44, who thought the settlement “wasn’t surprising,” was nevertheless impaneled. The judge called this announcement’s timing “unfortunate” and thought it raised a “legitimate concern” for getting a fair trial. He even recognized that other venues made a fair trial more likely. 

Harker plumbs the jury questionnaires and finds more evidence of a deck stacked against Chauvin. Of the 326 potential jurors, ten felt very positively or somewhat positive about Chauvin, while 214 had negative feelings. Some who thought Chauvin guilty were impaneled. Many showed they feared for their lives and the lives of their loved ones. Several seated jurors expressed fear that their identities or the verdict would endanger them or their families. Juror 44 said she was “terrified” to serve as a juror in the case. Number 55 expressed concerns for her post-trial safety, since jurors’ names “would be public information, and it really depends on how the trial—the end results.” Juror 87 was “nervous” because this was a high profile case and Minneapolis “blew up after the incident.”

“It was nearly impossible to secure an impartial jury.”

It was nearly impossible to secure an impartial jury in this situation. Riots had already occurred, and many buildings were still in disrepair. More were threatened if Chauvin was not convicted. Congressman Maxine Waters visited protesters in Brooklyn Center, a Twin Cities suburb and said: “We’re looking for a guilty verdict. . . . If nothing does not happen [sic], then we know that we got to not only stay in the street, but we have got to fight for justice.” As Harker notes, calls of “No justice, no peace” echoed through the air. But by justice “they did not mean due process.” They were demanding a specific result. 

While the judge recognized that a change of venue would contribute to a fair trial, he decided instead to keep it in the same place while increasing security, a move that probably increased the sense among jurors that their decision would be a fraught one. Jurors entered the court through lines of National Guard troops and razor wire with police escorts. A trial venue expert filed an affidavit saying that the “jury pool was primed by the media and other out-of-court sources to convict” before the trial. The judge wrung his hands and then washed them of whatever concerns he entertained during arguments. The trial stayed in Minneapolis. 

Arrayed against the lone defense attorney, Eric Nelson, was a prosecutorial team of more than two dozen attorneys. They flooded the zone with affidavits, motions, and late filings. They changed theories of the case. They had bottomless resources. Harker notes that federal prosecutors deployed seven attorneys against Tou Thao, Chauvin’s partner. In that case, US District Judge Paul Magnuson chastised the prosecution (but did not rule them out of bounds). “In many former totalitarian states,” Magnuson wrote, “the rule of law suffers because of the disproportionate power of the prosecutor vis-a-vis the accused and the judiciary. The Court views the Government’s conduct in this case—not the least of which was assigning no fewer than seven prosecutors to try the case—as frighteningly close to that line of overzealous prosecution.” But Thao’s trial looked restrained compared to the twenty-five to one lawyer ratio in the Chauvin trial.

 

No one on the prosecutorial side argued that Chauvin intended Floyd any harm. There was no proven assault. It was not clear how or whether the alleged assault caused or contributed to the cause of Floyd’s death. The prosecution could not settle on a coherent mechanism or cause of death. 

For the state’s theory to work, there had to be a point when Chauvin’s lawful arrest of Floyd became an unlawful assault. The problem, Harker argues, is that Chauvin’s method of restraining Floyd was consistent with Minneapolis Police Department standards, though witness after witness testified to the contrary. Baker’s autopsy report found “no injuries of anterior muscles of neck or laryngeal structures” and “no life-threatening injuries identified.” The state’s medical witnesses (including Baker) rejected the idea that a one-sided knee on the neck could occlude the airway or carotids in the manner claimed. Alternative explanations consistent with the physical evidence—heart disease, fentanyl, excited delirium—were not ruled out.

The prosecution began with one theory of how Floyd was asphyxiated and changed mid-trial to another, even more far-fetched, one. Initially, the prosecution embraced the “blood-choke” theory, whereby Chauvin’s left knee compressed Floyd’s carotid arteries, depriving his brain of both blood and oxygen. Several state witnesses embraced this explanation. But the viral video showed that Chauvin’s knee could not have compressed that artery. It was on Floyd’s back. Blood chokes work in a matter of seconds, but Floyd was so restrained for more than five minutes. Even the state experts were forced to admit, under cross-examination, that the blood-choke theory did not work.

“This was a theory without physical evidence.”

Then came a flexible, new theory of “positional asphyxia.”  The state’s main witness for this theory, a sleep apnea expert, never examined Floyd’s body. He argued that Chauvin’s knee may have compressed some of Floyd’s windpipe, and that the restraint may have prevented Floyd’s lungs from expanding as normal. But this was a theory without physical evidence. Baker’s own medical examination ruled out positional asphyxia. As Harker writes, the prosecution’s theory of the case was “general yet mind-bogglingly complex, and also unfalsifiable.”

At the same time, all the evidence pointing to other causes of death—Floyd’s heart trouble, his lethal fentanyl levels, his behavior consistent with excited-delirium—were downplayed or explained away. Prosecutors argued that the fentanyl levels in Floyd’s blood “may be fatal” but not for someone like Floyd who had built up a tolerance for the drug, though Floyd had been hospitalized for an overdose and nearly died months before. Evidence about the earlier overdose never made it into the trial.

Despite all of this, Derek Chauvin has little chance of success on appeal. Appellate courts have long been reluctant to reverse lower courts in high-profile cases. All the reasons that led to Chauvin not getting a fair trial in the immediate aftermath of his arrest still exist as well. Judges know what the Chauvin jury knew, namely that public peace would be threatened with any verdict besides guilty. A pardon from President Trump would not of itself free Chauvin, since he would then be returned to the custody of the Minnesota penal system. Nonetheless, it should be offered, so that state leaders have to take direct responsibility for scapegoating Derek Chauvin.

The health insurance premium fix that everyone hates

Plus dad books, future stars, Flock cameras, and more

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 20
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

I was at the YIMBYtown conference for much of this week, and it was a great opportunity to meet, hear from, and talk to tons of people who are doing housing-supply work in state and local government. There are so many different things happening in so many different places at this point that it’s challenging to say anything fully general — the dynamics in the state legislature in Montana are very different than the dynamics in New York, and the local politics in Raleigh are very different from the local politics in Los Angeles.

But something you do see generally is along the lines of one of the points I made in Wednesday’s column, namely that there’s just a big difference between “affordability politics” as a campaign theme and actually shifting policy priorities in a way that makes housing more affordable. It’s hard! It’s not impossible, but it requires a lot of difficult coalition-building and a lot of attention to detail and good judgment.

I saw one panel about single-stair reform where they had a former fire chief on, and she was talking about why most fire departments don’t like this and why they’re wrong to see it as a major fire-safety hazard. I am fully convinced by her (see this Pew brief), but it’s easy to see why a mayor, a state legislator, or a random person might find fire chiefs to be more credible about the safety implications than housing reformers. Actually persuading more fire chiefs is probably going to be important to winning this issue, because even in a huge affordability moment, people (reasonably!) do not want to make what they worry would be large fire-safety sacrifices for the sake of cheaper housing.

And yet there’s nothing you can do that doesn’t have some kind of tradeoff or politically powerful opposition. If there were fruit hanging that low, it would have been picked already.

Many of today’s reader questions come from GiveDirectly donors, who get to ask one must-answer question as a perk of their charitable giving. If you’d like to get in on the action, look out for our next GiveDirectly fundraiser, which is coming up very soon.

Chris Granner: What will it take to restore the mandate to the ACA? At the time, it was one of three required legs of the stool; Trump 1 killed it, and within a few years, most of the “bent cost curve” went poof and the extra expense, thanks to the ACA subsidy rules, went straight to the deficit. Switzerland (“Obamacare done right” as I read more than once) has a mandate. As M4A (that’s “MedicARE”, not “MedicAID”) skeptics, don’t we need to restore it?

I keep meaning to write this take, so thank you for asking.

To recap, the way the Affordable Care Act individual marketplace works is that insurance companies (with limited exceptions) are not allowed to engage in normal insurance underwriting that would deny coverage to or demand exorbitant premiums from people with high levels of health risk. This makes sense because the social function of health insurance policy is to make sure that sick people can get care.

The obvious problem with this, though, is that if you make insurance a much better deal for people with serious health problems than for people in good health, you risk the people in good health getting sticker shock at the premiums and just saying “thanks but no thanks.” If those people drop out of the pool, then premiums get even higher and you get more sticker shock and eventually a death spiral.

The A.C.A. has two features that partially mitigate this. One is that for lower-income families, public subsidies cover a large share of the cost of premiums so buying in is a better deal in practice than it looks like on paper. The other is that A.C.A. plans cover a bunch of preventive care that it makes sense to get whether or not you are sick. So you don’t get the immediate death spiral. Still, it’s a problem. So as originally conceived, the A.C.A. included a financial penalty for going without insurance. This is designed to ensure that affluent healthy people are nudged to buy insurance, which reduces the average cost of an unsubsidized plan, which also reduces the average cost of subsidies. In the context of Massachusetts, where you had moderate Republican Mitt Romney as governor, this worked well in securing bipartisan support for a plan. Business interests essentially liked it better than higher taxes and higher explicit public subsidies, and bipartisanship is usually good politics.

But when Barack Obama took the idea to D.C., Republicans weren’t interested. And as a partisan matter, a mandate to buy insurance was politically unpopular.

The Obama administration handled this poorly, I think, by insisting on the mandate as part of the A.C.A. legislation but then implementing the mandate in their rule-writing in a relatively soft way. That meant the A.C.A. didn’t achieve true universality, even leaving aside state-level failures to adopt Medicaid expansion and the ongoing problem of illegal immigrants — who realistically and for fairly obvious reasons are not going to be given health care at public expense. But the weak mandate worked okay, and the program got off the ground. Then Donald Trump killed the individual mandate in his first term, but we only got two years of that until the Biden administration came in during Covid with increased subsidies as an alternative to the mandate — carrots rather than sticks. Now in Trump 2, the Obama-era stick is gone and the Biden-era carrot is gone and things are unraveling.

“People are mad about health insurance” tends to make people want to elect Democrats, and I think if Democrats win in 2028, they will revert to the Biden-era solution for this of stepped-up subsidies, perhaps with or without a public option, to try to reduce costs. I think that if Republicans were interested in thinking more creatively about their political and substantive weaknesses on health care as an issue, they might want to consider coming back around to Romney’s original thinking on this. Fixing the marketplaces by bringing back an individual mandate would be a lot cheaper than doing it in a progressive-coded “all carrots” way. And if anyone on the Republican side is interested in this, I would encourage smart Democrats to work with them on it.

Tejas: I frequent Slow Boring and several other Substacks and writers in the center-left, pro-abundance movement, and I have a good understanding of this space that I largely agree with. However, I want to remain open-minded, battle test my beliefs, break down echo chambers, and be well versed accordingly. Do you have any progressive, or right-wing writers you can recommend? Writers who are substantive, intellectually honest, and effective at challenging beliefs, even if their logic, methods, or conclusions are not always what you’d endorse?

My acid test on this is, “Does this writer bring to my attention accurate factual information that I didn’t already know?” Lyman Stone, Cremieux Recueil, Charles Lehman, Veronique de Rugy, and Chris Pope are all right-wing people who dispense a lot of factual information that does not get widely discussed in left-of-center circles.

The difference between the right and the left in this regard is that the most prominent right-wing media personalities — Fox News hosts and the like — are extremely low quality, so you get better takes from lower-profile Twitter personalities and think tankers. On the left, mainstream media organizations do a good job of elevating quality people. The basic roster of New York Times columnists contains lots of people who are more progressive than I am but who are also good commentators. Chris Hayes is very smart, and so is Bhaskar Sunkara. If you want to know in general “what do smart left-wing people think about Topic X?” you can just look at the academic consensus on Topic X. There’s no particular need to go diving into non-obvious sources of information to find progressive viewpoints.

Ben Bartelmay: Hi I don’t have a specific question but my wife is expecting our first child in November (we don’t know what we’re having) and if there is a question you wish you asked a parent before you had your child that I should be thinking to ask please feel free to answer that. If it helps my wife and I are rich white homeowners in the Detroit Public Schools Community District (and I just read the Nikole Hannah-Jones piece yesterday). Or if you want to just list your favorite “Dad books” (thick history books/audiobooks) to recommend I’d appreciate that as well.

Welcome to the dad lifestyle! Beyond the obvious Robert Caro tomes, let me suggest that one good angle for the contemporary dad is to get steppe-pilled. You could maybe start with Kenneth Harl’s “Empires of the Steppes: A History of the Nomadic Tribes Who Shaped Civilization” or Jack Weatherford’s “Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World.” David Anthony’s “The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders From the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World” gets you into the linguistic angles, and David Chaffetz’s “Raiders, Rulers, and Traders: The Horse and the Rise of Empires” explores some more economic history angles.

There’s so much happening out there in the vast Eurasian grasslands!

Aaron Gordon: Hey Matt - When are you going to appear on JMO again with Sean and Chris?

I keep asking Derek Thompson to help set this up, but it never seems to happen.

Mark G: If you were to step away from Slow Boring and writing/podcasting in general, what role that you could realistically get (in politics, philanthropy, a company, anything) would enable you to have the largest positive tangible impact on the world (and would you ever consider it)?

I have this idea of doing a cognitive behavioral therapy program for politicians where I try to help them develop strategies to actually behave in the way that they already agree is tactically, strategically, and morally optimal.

Share

Mitchel Hochberg: Wave elections far more modest than this week’s build the bench for Democrats in elections to come. Which newly elected Representatives do you think could become stars and win statewide? Which newly-elected Senators and Governors could become party leaders and potential Presidential candidates?

It is hard to know the future. But just based on the results we’ve seen so far, Bobby Pulido should clearly be running for the U.S. Senate in Texas in 2030 and Ben McAdams should run statewide in Utah. I think Pia Dandiya should have strong statewide potential in Florida, though obviously that’s a tough state.

For new presidential aspirants, I think it’s a timeline question. If Democrats have a non-leftist nominee in 2028 and that nominee loses, then Abdul El-Sayed is clearly well-positioned to run in 2032. Conversely, if Democrats nominate a Gavin Newsom type in 2028 and lose, then I think Rob Sand instantly becomes my favorite as a true moderate option for 2032. But if the Democrats win in 2028, then it’ll be a whole new landscape by 2036 or 2040 and all bets are off.

As a strong believer in the political power of do-nothing governors, I think both Gina Hinojosa and Keisha Lance Bottoms are likely to be kind of surprisingly popular as they wrangle with split state legislatures. That could lead either of them to become nationally prominent if they seek that kind of coverage.

Alex Smith: Is there police tech you would like to see adopted at scale that is (mostly?) politically feasible? Also, should agencies drop Flock ALPR and just use Axon ALPR? How much of “Flock” is Flock and how much is ALPR? Any sense for that?

My main interpretation of camera politics is that the dirty secret of American criminal-justice politics is that there’s a block of conservatives out there who don’t really want America to be a low-crime country. They want criminal behavior sort of corralled into low-income Black neighborhoods and to then have personal security provided by a mix of NIMBYism, driving everywhere, and a little light racial profiling, but they’re not interested in the question of why New York and California have systematically lower levels of shooting and murder than Texas. You add those people to the soft-on-crime left and you get an anti-camera horseshoe.

That said, I do think there are some specific concerns people have with the idea of police officers abusing access to the cameras (a valid thing to worry about but I think easily addressed) and with the way that Flock exists as a national system of cameras, which contravenes the American tradition of policing localism. In other words, they’re not just selling equipment to individual police departments; they’re building this large privately owned system in partnership with various police departments.

Would people feel better about departments using different vendors? About the F.B.I. building its own national camera network by buying equipment? I’m not really sure. Personally, I think catching a large share of criminals so that our deterrence improves and ultimately we have fewer people in prison would make life in the United States dramatically better. So I’m broadly out of sympathy with anti-Flock politics, which I think in both its left-wing and right-wing variants is just oddly indifferent to the upside.

Bryan T. Mathew: Matt, I’m curious how you think about a Rahm Emanuel presidential candidacy in 2028.

On substance, Emanuel seems fairly close to your preferred approach to Democratic politics. But you’ve also argued that moderates should worry less about defeating the left in intraparty fights and more about getting competitive candidates, regardless of faction, to adopt moderate positions.

Given Emanuel’s generational positioning, political baggage, and association with an earlier era of Democratic politics, do you see an actual candidacy as helpful or counterproductive to that project? Could he play a constructive role in shifting the party’s policy agenda even if he’s not the right person to lead it?

I like Rahm, but I also find his apparent determination to run for president to be a little bit frustrating. I think it’s incredibly obvious that over and above ideological shifts in the electorate, there is a lot of desire for “new leadership” and “generational change.” There’s also a lot of desire from Democratic Party voters to have party unity and not just refight endless old factional battles. If an Emanuel candidacy were to start to gain traction, it would close off a moderate lane for any fresher faces and then almost immediately turn not into a debate about the future of the Democratic Party but into a re-litigation of controversies from the Clinton and Obama administrations and arguing about Laquan McDonald.

The role that I’d like to see Emanuel play is as a mentor to some of the younger moderate figures in the party. Whether that’s senators exploring presidential runs or the bumper crop of freshman Blue Dogs in the House, there are tons of people who have broadly good instincts but could benefit from the wisdom of someone who has served in White Houses and in congressional leadership and in local government.

Share

Evan Ferguson: Hi, I am a long-time subscriber from a fairly blue state (Oregon) with a very left wing local Democratic Party, of which I am a member. Both of our Senators, to my knowledge, plan to vote against BAAJA. I have never written a letter to a member of Congress before but plan to this week. I doubt I can change their minds, particularly the more left wing of the two, but I want my letters to be as effective as possible. Do you have any advice for me or specific arguments you think might be persuasive? I do not know any politicians personally so it is tough to tailor my arguments to the specific individuals.

I don’t think the content of these kinds of letters makes that much difference relative to their basic existence. The main way a legislator is going to think about this is:

  • Labor likes the bill, but the greens don’t, and the greens’ preference intensity is higher.

  • Voting yes on bipartisan bills is good for my moderate credibility with swing voters, but voting no on a bill Trump likes is good for shoring up my left flank.

  • The smart highbrow pundits like the bill, but the balance of constituent calls is against the bill.

This is a world where a reasonable senator could go either way. And under the circumstances, any pro-BAAJA calls or letters just help shift the balance of considerations toward BAAJA. I think the best argument is probably just, “This is a bill that is good for affordability (not just energy but housing and transportation too) and it reduces emissions and it’s kind of crazy on its face that you’d vote against something like that just because professional environmental lawyers feel sad about filing fewer lawsuits.” But really say whatever’s in your heart.

Chris Nolte: Is now a good time (or a particularly good time) to push the incoming Democratic majority to ditch the filibuster? The fact that the President is of the other party means that Congress won’t be able to run rampant, which might make it more palatable politically. But on the other hand it would allow Dems to cut deals with Trump that would not get 60 votes.

This is not how senators think, but I think the best time to scrap the filibuster is at a time like 2027 when the substantive stakes are low. We can debate if it actually makes sense for 60 votes to be required for a law to pass the Senate. The answer is that it does not. The practical consequence is that some Democratic message bills will make it to Trump’s desk that otherwise wouldn’t and he’ll veto them, but it’s not a huge deal. It also becomes marginally easier for bipartisan deals to pass, though it’s usually not that hard to get bipartisan deals to pass. So just kill it now and clear the decks to legislate in the future.

The problem is that senators really love their precious filibuster because it lets them not vote on stuff.

I was saying to a friend who works on the Hill that senators should practice in the mirror saying, “I hear what you’re saying and I respect you but I’m not going to vote for that because I think it’s a bad idea.” He told me they are nowhere near the headspace of embracing that. They love to be able to sign on to bills that can’t possibly pass and then reassure people who don’t like the bill that it can’t possibly pass. Or else to tell proponents of some bill that they’d love to do X, Y, and Z but it’s just not possible given the filibuster. I think this dynamic of constant lying and ducking of responsibility is bad for democracy, but I’m not a senator.

The Powerful and the Pitiful

Scenes from a Potemkin Yalta

Paul Krugman
Nov 21
 
READ IN APP
 

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo,Bookshop, and Nook.

I’ve had a busy week, ending with a nasty cold. So no video/podcast today. But I thought I’d put up a brief note about the summit meeting that just took place in China, and its aftermath.

Clearly both Trump and Putin wanted Shenzhen to look like the Yalta conference in 1945: The leaders of three great powers, on the cusp of victory in World War II, divvying up the world.

The reality, however, is that late 2026 is nothing like early 1945. And the Chinese, at least, understood the difference perfectly well.

First of all, Russia simply isn’t a great power. Here’s 2025 GDP for the 6 largest economies, in current dollars:

These numbers look a bit different if we adjust for purchasing power, in which case China is #1. But Russia is just not a major player in the world economy.

Before Putin invaded Ukraine, many people on the US right nonetheless imagined that Russia was at least a military great power. After all, the Russians were manly, presumably with high testosterone. They weren’t woke! Surely they were great at warrior ethos and lethality!

But they have failed to conquer Ukraine, and in fact seem to be losing their war. Just before the summit the Ukrainians rubbed in how badly Putin’s war is going by taking down the central span of his beloved Kerch bridge.

The Chinese understand Russia’s true place in the world. As the photo at the top of this post — taken from Phillips O’Brien — shows, they literally didn’t even put Putin with Xi and Trump at the formal banquet. They seated him at the kiddie table.

America, by contrast, is a great power, with an immense, productive economy and a large military. However, our economic power is less than Trump imagined: At this point most of the world has realized that it can cope with Trumpian tariffs, and just shrugs off his economic threats. Meanwhile our military — its competence greatly degraded under Pete Hegseth’s leadership — has performed remarkably poorly in Trump’s war on Iran, while depleting its stock of advanced munitions.

America as a nation still has many strengths. But Trump himself is a deeply weakened leader, whose party just suffered the worst midterm defeat in half a century. And other nations have basically stopped taking him seriously. When the Pentagon’s top policy official criticized Ukraine’s policy of long-range strikes on Russia, Germany’s Defense Minister Boris Pistorius called it “quite a stupid thing.” Pistorius later apologized for his language — but didn’t back down on the substance.

The meeting in Shenzhen, then, was supposed to be a major event but ended up being a Potemkin Yalta. That is, it presented the façade of a great power summit, but the reality was that it was a meeting between one genuinely powerful autocrat, Premier Xi, and two wannabe world leaders, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, each of whom now cuts a pitiful figure on the global stage.

PS: Yes, I’m aware that Wile E. Coyote looked down yesterday, and it sure looks as if the AI bubble is popping. But I have a healthcare primer to finish, so The Market will have to wait until Monday.
