AI people are very, very, very, very rich

What should we think about that?

Noah Smith
Nov 21
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

As you may have heard, Anthropic had its IPO this past Thursday. At a valuation of $1.5 trillion, it was actually just the second most valuable IPO in history, just behind SpaceX at $1.77 trillion. I bought some shares on the first day at what I thought was a reasonable price, only to see my shares drop the following day as the company’s valuation fell to $1.175 trillion, making it only the 14th most valuable company in the world. Such are the risks of buying individual stocks!

But that price drop doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic’s IPO was a staggeringly large wealth creation event. Anthropic began hiring lots of employees just a few years ago; now, almost all of those people have either hundreds of millions of dollars, or tens of millions of dollars. Andrew Benson had a good breakdown of exactly who would get what, if the company hit its initial valuation target of $2 trillion:

Who actually gets rich if Anthropic lists at $2 trillion?…

- $199B for the 7 controlling co-founders, about 10%
- $28B for Ben Mann, if his stake matches theirs
- $100B for the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, 5%
- $331B in employee options and RSUs, about 17% , That pool covers about 5,300 employees, an average of $62M each…

[H]ere is roughly how many people made what at $2T:

- $110M to $400M each: ~300 to 500 people hired by 2023
- $200M to $300M each: ~440 to 640 hired in 2024
- $70M to $95M each: ~1,360 hired in 2025
- $10M to $20M each: ~3,000 hired in 2026

So about 940 people hired by the end of 2024 average nine figures. Everyone hired since averages eight figures.

The company’s (fully diluted) valuation is now only about 80% of that $2T number, so you have to scale those numbers down a little bit. But it’s still a staggering amount of money for just a few years of work! We’re used to seeing the first few employees at a generational company make hundreds of millions of dollars, but seeing several hundred people make that much is just unprecedented.

Let’s put these numbers in perspective. If Anthropic were worth $2T, it would have more centimillionaires than the entire city of Los Angeles. Even with only 350-400 centimillionaires, that’s about as many as Houston, Dallas, and Austin combined:

Steve Rattner
@SteveRattner
There are now more hundred millionaires at Anthropic than in all of Los Angeles.
3:16 PM · Nov 20, 2026 · 101K Views
52 Replies · 269 Reposts · 1.84K Likes

By some reckonings, Anthropic now has between 0.5% and 1.3% of all the centimillionaires in the U.S. Collectively, the company’s founders and employees have as much wealth as the entire bottom third of Americans, combined:

Of course, just looking at these numbers tremendously understates the amount of wealth that has been created in the AI industry over the last couple of years. There’s also OpenAI, which is targeting an IPO valuation of $1.25 trillion. And there are quite a number of AI startups that have gotten very valuable, very quickly. Just a few include Isomorphic Labs at ~$50 billion, Cognition at $48 billion, Prometheus at $41 billion, Safe Superintelligence at $32 billion, VAST Data at $30 billion, Reflection AI at ~$27.5 billion, Cohere at $25.5 billion, ElevenLabs at $22 billion, and so on.

And of course, all of this is just today. I wouldn’t have bought Anthropic stock unless I thought the company had a very good chance of becoming much more valuable than it is today. Despite the early price drop, I’m still very bullish. I think AI’s extremely cross-domain capabilities mean that Anthropic has a good shot at being a very large, diversified conglomerate:

Anthropic’s moat is Claude

Noah Smith
·
Nov 2
Read full story

Furthermore, I think the company is amassing a huge pool of top human talent, essentially giving them a hedge against a future in which AI continues to be a complement to top human talent rather than a substitute. Almost every smart person I know here in Silicon Valley either works there or has strongly considered working there. That makes Anthropic resemble Google back in 2004, which became a legendary brain trust. If anyone can figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI, it’s probably Anthropic. And yes, someone will figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI. Even if that means the company only becomes as valuable as Google or Microsoft is today, that means I’ll more than double my own investment.

If that happens, all of those wealth numbers from the top of this post will also more than double. And if the U.S. economy grows robustly and AI itself grows rapidly as a percentage of that economy, this could easily turn out to be the greatest wealth creation event in American history, by far — greater than the internet, far greater than crypto, greater even than the railroads.

I can definitely feel this wealth all around me. A lot of the people I went to potlucks with three years ago now have an order of magnitude more money than anyone I ever met before I turned 30. Some of those people are under 30 themselves. A few of them are billionaires. Now, when I go to house parties, they’re often in lavish designer-furnished mansions overlooking spectacular ocean views from high up on San Francisco hilltops.

As a social phenomenon, this is totally unprecedented. Sarah Chieng writes:

You can build a startup in 9 months, get acquired (but rly acquihired) by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cognition, and walk away a multi-millionaire…You can join the right company at 22 and become effectively post-economic…And I don't think we've even begun to grapple with the degree to which this is warping an entire generation's relationship with money, ambition, work, and success…When your peers are making generational wealth before 25, what does a normal career even look like anymore[?]

I’m happy for my friends, of course. And I am not personally bothered by seeing displays of great wealth. But I find myself wondering what this is going to do to my society. If the AI class are the only people who get rich going forward, what kind of tensions will that produce among the country’s elites? What would it mean for America if wealth inequality goes up far further even than it already has?

What if only the AI people get rich?

We’re used to thinking of successful tech founders as super-rich. Well, here’s a statistic that might blow your mind:

Frad
@bogdonz
if you had 2 cofounders, raised from top teir vc, exited for a few billion dollars, you still wouldnt make as much as employee #400 at Anthropic will from the IPO. Just let that sink in for a moment
7:04 AM · Oct 29, 2026 · 272K Views
36 Replies · 41 Reposts · 1.94K Likes

What about in other industries? Quantitative finance is a famously lucrative career for ultra-talented individuals. But a senior quant at a top trading firm like Jane Street, Citadel, or Two Sigma probably makes a few million dollars a year on average. If they become a senior portfolio manager or desk head they can make substantially more, but any quant would be hard-pressed to make as much over their entire career as a 25-year-old AI researcher will end up making from being Employee #400 at Anthropic.

Of course, quants can be entrepreneurial, and start their own trading firms, hedge funds, or big financial firms like Citadel. But even then, how much can they hope to make relative to the titans of AI? The list of the world’s richest people is chock full of tech founders; the top finance titans, excluding cryptocurrency types, are Warren Buffett at #7 and Michael Bloomberg at #21.

Which raises the question: If you’re a smart person in America today, why on Earth would you go into finance instead of going into AI? Why are you slaving away earning a paltry $3 million a year, hoping to make it big and make $15 million a year someday, when kids ten years younger than you are walking away with $100 million from a few years of work? We used to complain that the finance industry was siphoning smart people away from industry, but at this point, if you go into trading instead of into AI, you’re doing it for pure love of the game.

As for “main street” businesses like fashion, retail, publishing, or manufacturing, they’re very rare on the list of billionaires these days. Regular Americans can get rich doing things that don’t require elite cognitive skills and connection to the social circles of Silicon Valley, but unlike in previous eras, it’s very hard for them to get super-rich without those assets.

Of course, most of the existing tech fortunes are not AI — they’re the remnant of earlier waves of innovation like software, internet, social/mobile, and so on. But AI is catching up very fast. Just for fun, I had GPT estimate the value of all the wealth directly created¹ by various waves of technological innovation, both at their height and over the long term. The estimates are subject to a lot of uncertainty and questions about which companies to include in which category. But the basic story is that since the current boom began in 2022, AI has now generated about a quarter of the wealth generated by all non-AI information technology industries up to the start of 2022.

And a big difference is that AI is generating this wealth without sparking a massive hiring boom. Plenty of people are getting hired in the AI industry, of course, but not enough to cancel out the ongoing massive job losses in the tech industry as a whole:

This is even more keenly felt in San Francisco and Silicon Valley, where payroll is way up but the money is flowing into a shrinking set of pockets:

The days when a reasonably smart person could reliably get a nice safe job at Google for $300,000 a year and live in a nice house in Mountain View or San Francisco are drawing to a close. Increasingly, making it in tech is a lottery with fewer and fewer winners, and bigger and bigger payouts.

My question is: What happens when the AI industry is the main route to getting rich in America? We may have to deal with the anger of legacy elites — people who made money in other industries, including other tech industries, and are now seeing their success eclipsed. I’ve argued that some piece of the unrest of the 2010s was due to downwardly mobile educated elites venting their frustrations against society; what happens when the only elites in the country are the AI industry and the government?

One possibility is that people try to use the government to bring down or hold back the AI industry. That could take the form of regulation, antitrust, new laws, and so on — just as it did during the time of the railroads, when railroad barons seemed poised to rule America. Or, in the extreme, it could involve some sort of military action, as AI and the state vie for the pinnacle of power.

Of course there are plenty of more benign scenarios. But having a concentration of wealth and opportunity in the hands of one single industry is extremely rare, and a bit troubling.

Inequality on steroids

Then there’s the question of whether AI will cause a wealth divergence in broader society. In general, I had worried less about this problem lately. Wealth inequality looked like it had topped out in the mid-2010s after a long rise (the size of which is still hotly debated), and the tech bust of 2022 even looked like it was compressing the wealth distribution a little bit:

Those numbers are from the website Real Time Inequality, which is partly run by Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman — two economists whose estimates of wealth inequality always tend to come in on the high side. If Saez and Zucman are seeing a plateau in wealth inequality, I believe it. And the modest increase in the wealth of the top 0.001% — the super-rich — might be due to the difficulty of measuring such a small, heterogeneous, and secretive group.

In addition, I’ve tentatively concluded that wealth inequality isn’t quite as corrosive as a lot of people claimed back in the 2010s. You constantly see lefty types — including smart people like Joe Stiglitz and Daron Acemoglu — claim, without solid evidence, that wealth inequality distorts the political process. But when we look at the actual evidence, it seems to point in the other direction — rich people only subvert democracy when they’re in cahoots with the government. Here’s a long, good explainer by Tibor Rutar:

Political Economy, Stats, and Society
Inequality doesn’t damage democracy
I find it theoretically plausible and even likely that inequality damages democracy. If theory is all we had to go by, I’d probably err on the side of “inequality is dangerous.” It’s also what emotionally and personally resonates with me most of the time…
Read more
3 months ago · 123 likes · 56 comments · Tibor Rutar

We could see this in action in the recent U.S. midterm elections, where Elon Musk — who actually is politically well-connected to a very corrupt administration — spent $500 million trying to beat various Democrats and failed utterly.

But the AI boom is making me start to worry about wealth inequality again. One reason is that AI threatens the possibility of large-scale job displacement. This hasn’t happened yet, except in a few specific industries. But if AI does end up killing jobs across the broader economy, it could spark rage at the tech businesspeople who got insanely rich by destroying regular people’s livelihoods.

Right now, those pre-furnished mansions owned by 30-year-old AI workers on San Francisco hilltops are unconnected to Americans’ broader economic struggles — and in fact, the AI industry is generating an economic boom via the data center buildout. But at some point — if there’s a big recession, and companies use it as an opportunity to replace humans with Claude and GPT en masse — regular people might look up at those mansions and start to wonder why a few people were able to get so unfathomably rich by immiserating their countrymen.

And it really doesn’t help that the insanely rich people who work at AI companies keep saying, over and over, loudly and in public and to anyone who will listen, that killing jobs and turning regular people into helpless impoverished wards of the state is the goal of the industry that’s making them personally super-duper-ultra-mega-rich:

jesse
@jessexai_
Anthropic Researcher Tao Lin: Pretty much all humans on earth will become permanently unemployable because of AI "It's very likely that pretty much all humans on earth will become permanently unemployable" "And will need to strictly rely on government welfare to sustain …
1:09 PM · Nov 17, 2026 · 5.52M Views
1.76K Replies · 632 Reposts · 4.94K Likes

Why would you make hundreds of millions of dollars for yourself by destroying millions of your countrymen’s lives? It seems like an incredibly bad sales pitch, even when you ignore the usual accompanying “doomer” stuff about AI maybe killing off the human species. I’m not the only one to have noticed this:

Matthew Yglesias
@mattyglesias
Today’s tech pitch: 1) Our product might kill everyone 2) If not, it will let everyone spend all day at home streaming AI-generated shortform video and cashing welfare checks 3) We need to develop it to beat China, who we also have to sell chips to
Conor Sen @conorsen
Thinking back to 2011: -Banks and institutions had been discredited -The housing market was a black hole -Government at all levels was doing austerity -Steve Jobs died, becomes like a secular saint -We still need jobs and economic growth “Let tech/startups cook” made sense.
4:32 PM · Nov 21, 2026 · 132K Views
46 Replies · 201 Reposts · 1.97K Likes

Some AI industry leaders, like OpenAI’s Sam Altman, have recently pivoted their messaging and declared that AI will create jobs instead of destroying them. But the folks at Anthropic continue to insist that they’re working to make humanity obsolete:

Max Zeff
@ZeffMax
While at OpenAI, Dario suggested that immersive videogames might be a solution for the political strife caused by AI-induced joblessness. One of many new details in our story on the siblings leading Anthropic. W/ @berber_jin1 and @keachhagey
wsj.com
The Brother-Sister Duo Who Want to Keep Anthropic Weird
9:19 PM · Nov 21, 2026 · 88.8K Views
72 Replies · 58 Reposts · 733 Likes

I am sure that Dario & co. are being completely honest and forthright here. But if their predictions are borne out, we may see large-scale social conflict between the AI industry — which will increasingly have a monopoly on wealth and power — and the entire rest of society. That’s not a conflict I’m particularly looking forward to.

What will be the purpose of wealth in the age of AI?

My bull case for Anthropic — a big part of the reason I bought the company’s stock, even at the current high valuation — is that AI might be better than humans at making business decisions. There is a world in which the very top-of-the-line frontier version of Claude — with the help of some humans — can run an insurance company better than anyone who doesn’t have access to that model. Anthropic might thus become the ultimate conglomerate, able to diversify into many seemingly unrelated business lines across the entire economy without sacrificing its core competence.

But it’s worth asking why, in that universe, we should even allow wealth inequality to persist. The justification for wealth inequality has always been economic growth — that by dangling the reward of fabulous wealth in front of talented entrepreneurs, we could incentivize them to strike out into the unknown and create the new industries and technologies and business models that make humanity as a whole richer and happier. As long as it doesn’t subvert democracy, allowing a few people to have giant mansions and yachts and private jets seems like a small price to pay for wonders like cars, airplanes, and the internet.

And yet in a world where Claude provides the spark of entrepreneurship instead of human beings, why would we continue to tolerate wealth inequality? Just as the Fields Medal looks increasingly outdated in a world where AI is much better than humans at solving hard math problems, it’s not clear that we’d need the Forbes Billionaire List as a brass ring to incentivize the Elon Musks and Jeff Bezoses of tomorrow if Claude could just do their pioneering and organization-building for them.

That’s why a world of true Anthropic supremacy increasingly looks like a world where Anthropic ought to be nationalized and its proceeds distributed to the general public via some sort of sovereign wealth fund. In fact, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman have already both suggested this sort of arrangement, with Altman even offering the Trump administration a 5% stake in OpenAI.²

In a world where wealth confiscation disincentivizes entrepreneurship, that sort of scheme might represent an overly costly merging of the private and public sectors — the sort of politically-connected wealth that actually does damage democracy. But if human entrepreneurs go the way of human mathematicians and coders and chess players, then the downsides to nationalization of industry and large-scale redistribution seem much less.

There are also other wild cases that deserve serious consideration. AI might be able to redistribute wealth on a large scale through first-degree price discrimination — if Claude takes over all business, it might realize that since I own Anthropic stock, I can afford to pay ten times as much for groceries. Or AI companies might actually be able to forcefully overthrow the U.S. government, by hacking the military’s systems and turning its drones to useless bricks, while their own private robots stormed the White House. The world is changing rapidly, in ways that no one — not even AI itself — can predict, and scenarios that were science fiction a few years ago now deserve to be in the discussion.

But whatever happens, a world in which a few brilliant, lucky people in the AI industry monopolize most or all of the wealth on planet Earth is not likely to be a stable equilibrium. I’m sure we will figure out something better than that.

1

This means just the value of the corporations created in these industries, not including knock-on economic effects or effects on other asset classes.

2

Naturally, in a world of godlike AI, industry leaders would view a merger of Anthropic and the U.S. government as Claude becoming America’s benevolent ruler, while human politicians would see it as humanity reasserting its rightful dominance over its own creations. Claude itself would probably remain politely neutral on the question, and the ambiguity would never be resolved.

A New Agenda for Healthcare Reform, Part I

The Policy and Politics of A New Democratic Consensus on Healthcare

Paul Krugman
Nov 22
∙
Preview
 
READ IN APP
 

The 2024 midterm results were a watershed event in American political history. The Democratic lead in the popular House vote is now above 14 points, the biggest such victory since the post-Watergate midterm election in 1974. Still, without veto-proof majorities in both the House and Senate, Congressional Democrats will have limited ability to pass legislation over the next two years. Yet now is the time to begin planning the Democratic platform for the 2028 election.

And one of the best places for Democrats to focus their attention is healthcare reform. Concern over healthcare costs is an important factor in overall concerns about affordability, and it’s the important issue on which Democrats have the largest advantage over Republicans. As soon as Democrats take control of Congress in January of 2027, they should attempt to repair the immense damage to healthcare coverage that Donald Trump and his party have inflicted on Americans, such as resurrecting the Obamacare subsidies and reversing the punitive Medicaid eligibility restrictions. As many as 12 million Americans may already have lost coverage so far.

However, they shouldn’t stop there. At this point, given Trump’s historic unpopularity and Republican weakness across the country, there’s a high likelihood that the 2028 election will deliver a Democratic trifecta: a Democratic president, House and Senate. Thus the Democrats should now plan a healthcare agenda that goes much further than restoring the pre-Trump II system.

There are signs that a consensus around major reform is already emerging.

One thing we can say with fairly with a fair degree of certainty is that the scope of major reform is much better now than it has been for decades. In particular, the 2026 Democratic congressional majority, although roughly the same size as the Democratic majority when Obamacare was enacted, is much more solidly progressive than the Obama coalition.

Today’s primer will review the basics of designing a healthcare system, followed by discussion of what we’ve learned about healthcare policy and — especially — healthcare politics over the past 20 years. I’ll then turn to what appears to be the emerging Democratic consensus for reform. In a subsequent primer I’ll talk more about what reform is likely to achieve and how to pay for it.

Beyond the paywall I will address the following:

1. How to move close to universal health coverage

2. The Obamacare story

3. The political economy of healthcare and how it has changed since Obamacare was enacted

4. The shape of an emerging Democratic consensus...

Pop! Goes the Bubble

This is how the exuberance ends — not with a whimper but with a bang

Paul Krugman
Nov 23
 
READ IN APP
 

The NASDAQ index of AI stocks

Marketing note: I have a new ebook, Navigating the Chaos: Chronicles of Economic and Political Madness, which uses material from this Substack to construct a thematic narrative of the past two years and the issues that Democrats must now address to build an enduring progressive movement. Available from Amazon, Kobo,Bookshop, and Nook.

Uh-oh. Wile E. Coyote just looked down and realized that he was suspended in mid-air, with nothing to support him. And so, obeying the laws of cartoon physics, he plunged.

I’m talking, of course, about the prices of AI-related stocks. Many observers have long argued that AI valuations weren’t justified by the fundamentals, that we were looking at a massive financial bubble. Over the past few weeks, the market has started taking these warnings much more seriously.

Let me be honest and admit that even now I’m not quite as confident in my bubble verdict as I was in diagnosing the housing bubble 20 years ago. AI is, after all, a radically new technology, and we can’t be 100 percent sure that historical patterns will apply. But they probably will.

There are a variety of metrics analysts use to assess whether we’re in a bubble. Most analyses involve projecting future spending on AI and future revenue of the companies supplying AI, and asking whether theseprojections justify current valuations. Such exercises are useful and necessary, but are riddled with huge uncertainty. And I don’t believe that I understand either the technology or the markets well enough to do such an analysis myself.

But there are other ways to assess the situation. Lately I’ve been looking at a metric that doesn’t depend on assumptions about future demand for AI, let alone earnings projections. The so-called Buffett indicator — yes, that Buffett — is simply the ratio of the total market value of U.S. stocks to GDP. Here it is, estimated up to Sept. 30, that is, just before the recent meltdown:

Until a few weeks ago, the Buffett indicator was very far above historically normal levels, and in fact well above its level at the peak of the dotcom bubble.

Now, the Buffett indicator is a metric for the valuation of all stocks, not just AI stocks. But on the eve of the plunge, AI-related companies accounted for almost half the S&P 500, and were responsible for most of the rise in the Buffett indicator over the past few years. So in practice there isn’t that much difference between looking at AI stocks and the valuation of the market as a whole. And the Buffett indicator is looking strongly bubblicious.

OK, what would plausibly justify such a high valuation on stocks?

One answer, which is what you hear from AI boosters, is that this technology will lead to explosive growth in productivity and hence future economic growth. Based on this scenario, a Buffett indicator based on future GDP – that is, the ratio of today’s total stock market value to future GDP – would look much less out of line.

Now the truth is that while AI is a remarkable technology, we still can’t see a large payoff in productivity growth, which is running only slightly above its 20-year average:

But maybe the big payoff is still to come.

Another possible justification for a sky-high Buffett indicator might be a large redistribution of income away from labor to capital, which would hurt the great majority of Americans but would raise profits. We’ve already seen a substantial reduction in the share of national income going to workers:

And AI is a highly capital-intensive technology that will, other things equal, lead to an even larger decline in the labor share and rise in the profit share.

So let’s grant for the sake of argument the proposition that a combination of accelerated economic growth and redistribution from labor to capital will mean rapidly rising profits. Even so, this wouldn’t necessarily justify the extremely high valuations the market has been placing on leading AI companies unless we believe that those companies will capture those future profits. And that’s a very dubious proposition.

As many of us have pointed out — with special clarity by Dean Baker — there’s growing evidence that today’s leading AI companies are not establishing durable monopoly positions like those held in the past by Microsoft, Google, Facebook etc. They are instead facing rapidly growing competition, for example from open-weight Chinese models that deliver most of the performance of frontier models at a fraction of the cost.

The market has been valuing the hyperscalers as if they’re all future Microsofts, companies that generated huge profits for decades on end. But they may instead be future WorldComs, companies that raised investor hopes only to go bankrupt when it turned out that they didn’t have a viable profit model.

So how bad will this get? Many observers have been making comparisons with the dotcom bust a quarter-century ago. Indeed, some have been making Nvidious comparisons — sorry, I’ve been waiting months to make that joke. In any case, so far the fall in AI stocks has been smaller than the dotcom bust, when the Nasdaq fell 70 percent:

But notice that the dotcom bust didn’t happen all at once. There was an initial downward leg roughly comparable to what we’ve already experienced with AI. Then there was a temporary period of stabilization, followed by a second, even bigger plunge.

And we’re talking about a lot of money here. If the Buffett indicator falls back to what it was in, say, 2019, that would wipe out wealth equal to around 80 percent of GDP: $25 trillion.

What would that do to the wider economy? I’ll talk about that in a future post.

Compact

James Bond in the Yookay

By Dominic Green • 23 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
Scott Menchin
 
 

Mr. Bond, we’ve been expecting you. For five years, since 2021’s No Time To Die. After Daniel Craig’s final and overextended turn in the black tuxedo, it was past time for his James Bond to die. Outmanned by Jason Bourne’s supremacy and unmanned by the psychic confessional of Skyfall (2012), the sixth 007 became the first to die on the job. At the end of No Time To Die, Craig became a human target marker, blown to bits by a shower of cruise missiles. The critics were little kinder: The Bond franchise needed a mercy killing. 

Yet Bond is back, with Denis Villeneuve, skilled at a slick epic, directing the saturnine Robert Pattinson. Bond never lived, so he cannot die. Like Sherlock Holmes, he lives in the imagination, and that makes him more real than most real people. His translation from books to screen proved that you can, as it happens, live twice. But his life has lately undergone a further translation. From 1962’s Dr. No until No Time to Die, the Bond movies were produced in Britain by Albert “Cubby” Broccoli’s Eon Productions. When Broccoli died in 1997, his stepson Michael G. Wilson and his daughter Barbara took over. In February 2025, Wilson and Barbara Broccoli sold creative control of the Bond franchise to Amazon MGM Studios. Bond, the personification of an ideal from twentieth-century Britain, is now an American idol. Can Bond live for a third time?

Bond is a fantasy figure, and fantasy is the realm of psychic compensation. Ian Fleming did not only seek compensation for Britain’s postimperial diminution when he contrived Commander Bond the Scottish superhero. Commander Fleming’s service at a senior rank in the wartime Naval Intelligence Division remained restricted by the Official Secrets Act. The nature of Fleming’s wartime work was not revealed until Nicholas Shakespeare’s biography Ian Fleming: The Complete Man (2023). As second-in-command to Rear Admiral John Godfrey, the Director of Naval Intelligence, Fleming liaised across Britain’s intelligence services, including the Special Intelligence Service (which became Bond’s employer, MI6); its domestic counterpart, the future MI5; and the Special Operations Executive, which ran Churchill’s espionage and sabotage campaign in occupied Europe. 

“My plots are fantastic, while often being based on the truth,” Fleming drawled in his decade of celebrity. The ostensibly fantastical gadgetry and the elaborate deceptions of the novels drew on the prosaic fantasies of Fleming’s wartime intelligence work. One of the dreams that became reality was a scheme to mislead the Germans about the imminent Allied invasion of North Africa by floating a dead body off the coast of Portugal, with fake invasion plans in its pocket. That one saved countless American lives and became the movie and Broadway show Operation Mincemeat.

Similarly, the fetish details of Bond’s Spartan ethic and Epicurean taste crystallized the refined paradoxes of the late Edwardian Scottish gentry that shaped Fleming, and also the art historian Kenneth Clark. The screen granted Clark and Fleming another kind of fantasy, late-life celebrity in America. While Shakespeare describes how Fleming wore his heart out much as Dickens had, by playing a fictional part for American audiences, Clark’s diary describes how, after receiving an ovation for “Civilization” at the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC, he rushed to the lavatories, closed the door, and burst into tears. Fleming does not tell us how reacted when, aged eleven, he heard that his parents had died in a mountaineering accident in France.

“We must play Greece to their Rome,” Harold Macmillan advised in 1944, as Britain’s elite recognized that the future was American. In 1963, when Dr. No became America’s highest-grossing movie of the year, Macmillan was prime minister. The Bond novels and movies presented a fantasy in which Bond’s sure grasp compensates for Britain’s diminished reach, but also the hard reality by which Britain struggled through by reworking its imperial networks as the skeleton of the dollar-denominated financial system and leveraging its practical and emotional appeal to “the cousins.” 

“This endowed the fantasy with geopolitical resonance.”

This endowed the fantasy with geopolitical resonance, especially during the Cold War. The best Bond movies acknowledge reality, and hold it at bay with an ironic eyebrow that allows the rewards of fantasy to rush in. The movie version of From Russia with Love (1963) is framed by post-Cuban Missile Crisis rivalry with the Soviet Union. In The Living Daylights (1987), Bond supports the mujahideen against the Soviets in Afghanistan. Goldeneye (1995) asks whether a “dinosaur” like Bond, and by extension Britain’s intelligence apparatus, can survive the end of the Cold War. Tomorrow Never Dies (1997) predicts that media manipulation will replace cyanide as the toxin of democracy. When the Global War on Terror revived the Cold War alliance, Bond hunted terrorist funders in the Casino Royale remake (2006). By Skyfall (2012), the enemy was state-sponsored cyber hacking.

Can Britain’s present reality sustain this loose but critical connection? The current Labour government struggles to pretend that it wants to remain in the American orbit at all. The British pop culture of the 1960s flew the flag: Winston Churchill, who died in 1965, lived just long enough to see the military uniforms of his youth recycled as neo-Edwardian Mod fashion, and its music revived in the music hall parodies of the Kinks and the Beatles. Since 1997, the year of Tomorrow Never Dies, mass immigration has shattered the unities of British life and produced competing factions in popular culture. It turns out that tomorrow can indeed die if you bring in millions of foreigners who follow distinctly unclubbable values.

 

There is no place for Bond’s values in the multicultural post-imperial successor state known to its immigrants, and hence its jaundiced natives, as “The Yookay.” As late as 2012, Bond and Queen Elizabeth II’s stunt doubles parachuted into the London Olympics’ opening ceremony from a Union Jack-liveried helicopter. Today, he would have a harder landing. The semi-official mascot of The Yookay is now Paddington Bear, an illegal immigrant from Peru who got his furry foot in the Yookay’s most prestigious door in 2012, when he took tea at Buckingham Palace. The Temple of Apollo at Delphi had “Know thyself” inscribed overhead. Synagogues everywhere are inscribed “Know before whom you stand.” The Paddington cult’s motto is “Be kind.”

James Bond is an ecumenical lover, but he fights for his own kind. Despite his Swiss mother, early Continental education and cosmopolitan tastes in food and women, Bond is an ethnonationalist. His job is to keep Britain’s end up, keep the Americans on side, and keep Johnny Foreigner out. His politics are Ian Fleming’s politics. They were Establishment then, and Britain’s successor Establishment, which leans further leftward than its predecessor ever leant to the right, now stigmatizes Bond-like values as far-right.

If Bond were in Britain today, Moneypenny would #MeToo him for harassment. His attitudes would lead to a sit-down with Prevent, the anti-extremist unit that intervenes in cases of suspected radicalism. In 2023, a Prevent research unit red-flagged reading Shakespeare and J.R.R. Tolkien, along with Orwell’s 1984 and Huxley’s Brave New World, as signs of white-nationalist radicalization. Prevent has a history of missing suspects, almost always Muslims, who go on to commit terrorist acts, so it should not surprise that they omitted the Bond books and movies. But in 2025, eagle-eyed academics at Portsmouth University examined Fleming’s works with a view to a kill and pronounced that they “contain many problematic issues such as racism, misogyny, and xenophobia.”

“Bond should see a lawyer.”

After his Prevent interview, Bond should see a lawyer. The International Criminal Court will issue a warrant faster than the time Bond takes to unclip a bra hook. If the international courts don’t get Bond, the British courts will. With his record and methods, he is likely to face prosecution for doing his duty in the past. In 2023, Britain’s previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, repealed the immunity clause in the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation Act). The threshold for prosecution is up to the attorney general. This has allowed human rights groups to charge 242 members of the Special Air Service (SAS) with alleged abuses in theaters including Northern Ireland, Syria, and Afghanistan. Half of the accused are still serving. Dozens have resigned. The cases are paid for by the taxpayer. 

Bond’s task is to fight those who would harm the British people. As the law now pursues the special forces for doing their dirty duty, so Bond’s bosses, the bureaucrats and politicians, have turned against the values of the British people. If the current attorney general, Ellie Reeves, has seen any of Bond’s official excursions into extrajudicial killing, she will throw away the key. If Bond sees how Britain now treats its bravest servants, he might consider going into the private sector, as many of Britain’s elite soldiers do. Or perhaps he will go rogue, vanish to an exotic location, and emerge from the waters of the Indian Ocean to find out why it is that two of Keir Starmer’s close friends are closely involved in the scheme to pay Mauritius to take over the rocks of the Chagos Islands—which, as Felix Leiter knows, support the runway of the strategically vital Diego Garcia airbase.

A Yookay-compatible Bond movie would be “DEI Another Day.” Apple TV’s adaptation of Mick Heron’s Slow Horses novels shows how false this would ring. Britain’s security services say that active Islamist terrorist plots constitute three-quarters of their caseload. Thousands more cases are on the back burner due to limited resources. Since the murderers of the IRA hung up their gelignite, every single mass-casualty terrorist attack in modern Britain has been perpetrated in the name of Islam by Muslims. Yet the massacres in Slow Horses are perpetrated only by whites, one of them a disaffected ex-CIA agent, and the real threat to the British state is a Nigel Farage-style nationalist. A Bond movie must nod to reality, not invert it. That said, no one seemed to mind that Bond got through the Global War on Terror without tangling with Islamists. 

It’s a pity that we cannot see Bond operating with full license in our world. Britain may no longer resemble Bond’s Britain, but the world has become more like Bond’s world. Bond villains are rarely state actors. They are transnational criminals. The Russians are always there to exploit the situation, and the Americans are always there to assist the Brits, but Bond’s nemeses are usually private actors. Bond’s typical mission is to track down a stolen gadget or blueprint whose possession threatens to unbalance the global order by paralyzing the world’s governments or pauperizing the Western financial system. The threat is sometimes so systemic that the Soviet enemy not only sleeps with Bond but also collaborates with Bond’s masters. As the Soviet Union started to totter and the gerontocrats cycled ever faster on the balcony of the Kremlin, the only constant face we saw on our screens was the twinkling eyes and grim-set visage of Walter Gotell, who played General Gogol, the head of the KGB, between 1977 and 1987.

The villain usually lurks in an extraterritorial lair, staffed with a private army, a deadly weapon, and a bikini-clad girlfriend. When his retreat, weapon, and army are blown to pieces in the final scenes, it’s not just Bond’s personal revenge for the murder of the love interest. It’s also the revenge of the Westphalian system. Bond movies prefigured the retreat of our Big Tech overlords to fortified bunkers in Bond-friendly locations such as Hawaii and New Zealand, often with private armies of security contractors and polygamous domestic arrangements. It is all too easy to imagine Robert Pattison tracking down an Elon Musk-like, “fascist” media oligarch who turns out to be a CIA asset gone sour. 

China is the world’s biggest hacker of secrets from state, corporate and research lab servers, but China is also a key Hollywood market. We are not going to see Chinese intelligence using private criminals to hack the West, or Bond leaping from a helicopter into the South Pacific to head off a shipload of false-flagged fentanyl precursors on their way to Mexico. But Russia is once more our Big Other. The Russiagate story in the 2016 elections, the war in Ukraine, and the oligarchic corruption and neo-imperial revanchism around Vladimir Putin have instructed a new generation that Russia’s historic destiny is to play the villain. The Musk-like oligarch in the modern Bond will, of course, be working for the Russians.

 

It might be better for Amazon MGM Studios to beat backwards into Bond’s natural habitat, the past, when the unities of British society were intact and the Russian enemy first came into view. All the characters will be better dressed, too.

In You Only Live Twice (1964), Bond fakes his death at sea off Japan. Chapter 21 of the novel is a mock obituary for the London Times. Fleming’s most detailed statement about Bond’s biography, and it includes this reference to Bond’s Fleming-like early career in World War Two naval intelligence and his postwar work for the Special Intelligence Service (MI6): 

“The nature of Commander Bond’s duties in the Ministry, which were, incidentally, recognized by the appointment of CMG” (Companion of the Order of St. Michael and St. George) in 1954, must remain confidential, nay secret.” His colleagues report, however, that his “outstanding bravery and distinction, although occasionally, through an impetuous strain in his nature, with a streak of the foolhardy that brought him into conflict with higher authority.”

“There is more than a decade of prequels, and plenty of targets.”

We know about Bond’s loss of his parents. We know that his character-building education in some of Britain’s better schools included homosexual experiences (Skyfall) and allowed him to keep his cool while being tied naked to a chair and having his testicles whipped with a length of rope (Casino Royale). But we know nothing about his wartime service and about his postwar activities in the period between the Japanese surrender of August 8, 1945 and the morning of January 13,1952, when Fleming typed the first lines of Casino Royale at his Goldeneye estate in Jamaica. There is more than a decade of prequels, and plenty of targets.

One of the real-life adventurers whose biography and exploits Fleming wove into the Bond persona was Fitzroy Maclean (1911-1996). Like Bond, Maclean had a Scottish father with military connections and had served time at Eton. Did Bond operate alongside Maclean in the SAS’s initial campaigns in the deserts of North Africa? Who was the first to raise an eyebrow at the name of Operation Bigamy, the SAS’s failed 1942 raid behind German lines in Libya? Could Bond have been on board in Operation Pongo, when Maclean and a platoon of Seaforth Highlanders kidnapped a Persian general and smuggled him to the Palestine Mandate for interrogation? Was Bond personally briefed by Winston Churchill when Maclean parachuted into Yugoslavia to live rough with Josef Tito and his partisans? Did Bond witness the squalid realpolitik by which Winston Churchill let Tito and the communists take over Yugoslavia, as those other unlikely diplomats, Winston’s son Randolph and his chum Evelyn Waugh, did in 1945? 

The rot of Britain’s ruling class was accompanied by compromise and even outright betrayal as the long imperial retreat began. Fleming started writing Casino Royale only nine months after the defections of Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean shamed Britain before the Cousins. Did Bond suspect that there were traitors in the service, or was he out in the field, dealing with other dirty business at the dawn of the Cold War? 

Perhaps he was in Berlin and Vienna just after the war. Or working with anti-communist militias in the Greek civil war. Or caught between the Jews and Arabs as the Palestine Mandate fell apart. It’s hard to believe that Bond did not work in Egypt until 1971 (the Cairo casino punch-up that opens Diamonds are Forever), and easy to see the safari suit deployed in the early 1950s, as Gamal Abdul Nasser and his officer friends were preparing to annex the Suez Canal. Or was Bond East of Suez? The British fought the Viet Minh in Vietnam in 1946, the anti-communist Mayalan Emergency from 1948 and then the Korean War from 1950. It would take Robert Pattinson about two decades to shoot his way through that lot. It would be fantastic, and it would be based on the truth.

People who just won tough races should try to win again — and hold Trump accountable

Saving democracy by practicing democracy

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 23
 
READ IN APP
 

The sheer scale of the 2026 blue wave — an anti-MAGA swing large enough to carry Democrats in places like Mississippi and South Carolina — poses a question of democratic theory that I think is a lot more interesting than the tired empirical debates about moderation. What should a person who won somewhere they “shouldn’t” have do with their term (or terms) in office, knowing that it’s objectively unlikely that the terrain will be as favorable in future cycles?

My perception is that most mainstream Democrats adhere to an ethic I would call Pragmatic Progmaxxing.

They understand that Ayanna Pressley tweeting about reparations is bad politics, that politicians like Josh Turek and James Talarico are going to have to stay away from 100-proof left-wing politics, and that even Abdul El-Sayed needs to do some picayune localism related to the auto industry. But their basic orientation is as intense policy demanders who are trying to maximize the amount of progressive change by pushing elected officials to be as left-wing as they can possibly get away with.

Pragmatic Progmaxxing has especially interesting implications for the people who won the real reach seats. From a Progmaxxing point of view, you accept a certain amount of moderation from Sherrod Brown and Roy Cooper so they can win re-election. But Scott Colom needed a D+13 national political climate and an amateur hour opponent to barely win, so he should just give up and vote like Ed Markey. It’s basically a free Senate seat for six years.

I want to push back against this.

I think American democracy has been in a really dangerous place for the past 10 years. That’s proximately due to Donald Trump and the MAGA movement. But the intense policy demanders have been creating an underlying structural weakness by framing thumbing your nose at your constituents as noble and trying to be a loyal servant of the people as cowardly.

I would like to see Colom and Annie Andrews and the couple dozen House Democrats who won deep red seats make a good-faith effort to represent their constituents. That doesn’t mean they answer every policy question with a poll of public opinion in Mississippi. But it does mean they have to take seriously the question of whether a particular piece of legislation aligns with what their constituents are asking for. Because it’s not “brave” or “fearless” to ignore the public will in order to curry favor with your side’s interest groups. That pattern of behavior has made voters cynical about the democratic process, eroded faith in party politics, and given us the bad phenomenon of “safe seats” where the incumbents barely even care what’s happening.

To the extent that newly elected members run big political risks, I hope they look into their own hearts about what motivated them to run for office as Democrats at a time when large swaths of the business community were deciding to bandwagon with the MAGA movement. My guess is that in most cases, the Democrats who ran in 2026 were both aware that the “save our democracy” messaging of 2024 was not persuasive and also (rightly) believed in the merits of that messaging.

If I’m right about that, I think the best way to behave consistent with that ethic is to:

  1. Fight for democracy by being willing to take risks to hold Trump and his cronies accountable for violations of the law.

  2. Practice democracy by acting as if you care more about the policy views and interests of the voters in your constituency than the views and interests of ideological donors and the groups.

My fear is that in practice the opposite combination is more likely. The Democratic base is in some sense very fired up about the issues in bucket (1). But in terms of concrete political power — campaign dollars and the endorsements that can win you primaries — it’s all about the greens and the labor unions and the civil rights orgs and the child care advocates and the immigration lawyers.

If you feel that you need to break with party leadership on something, the thing you’re most likely to get latitude on is Trump accountability. This is more or less “how things work” in the modern era of American political parties — they demand a lot of party loyalty on votes about policy ideas — but it’s terrible for the country.

The nobility of winning

In his classic 1974 book “Congress: The Electoral Connection,” David Mayhew says we should understand members of Congress as single-minded seekers of re-election.

In a world where that’s broadly true, it’s also true that when a member of Congress deviates from the rule, that’s usually driven by courage and prescience. All of your colleagues are looking at the Voting Rights Act through the narrow lens of re-election, but you decide that the most important thing is whether you can tell your granddaughter that you did the right thing, so you vote yes. Maybe you lose in 1966, maybe you don’t. But either way, it’s the right thing to do.

It’s important to understand, though, that a lot has changed since then. American political parties used to be basically patronage operations whose business model was winning elections so they could hand out jobs and contracts. Around the time that Mayhew wrote his book, these old patronage parties were dissolving in the face of amateur political activists who were rapidly forming professionalized issue-advocacy groups.

Those groups have now formed into quasi-stable coalitions that are aligned with and finance the political parties. The business model now is to deliver wins for intense policy demanders. And to accomplish that, you do need to win power sometimes — it’s Pragmatic Progmaxxing, not doctrinaire left-wing politics — but that’s quite different from Mayhew’s singular focus on winning.

Similarly, just being a member of Congress has become a significantly less elite job even as high-end income inequality has exploded. I wouldn’t say anyone is deliberately losing elections just for the pay raise, but it’s objectively true that going down in defeat and then becoming a media personality or a senior fellow at the Center for Pragmatic Progmaxxing is going to mean your living standards go up rather than down.

In this post-Mayhew universe, it’s of course still possible for a member to risk their re-election prospects for the sake of a transcendent moral cause.

But we don’t actually have any issues that are as titanically significant as civil rights. And I would say a much more typical case is a situation like the 2025 Congressional Review Act vote to disallow the state of California from imposing a de facto ban on internal combustion engine cars.

Electric vehicle mandates are unpopular, Republicans were unified on it, and it’s not filibusterable, so how individual Democrats voted had no relevance to the outcome. As a result, a few dozen vulnerable House Democrats broke with their party to vote with the Republicans. Notably this included three of the six House Democrats from Michigan — Shri Thanedar, Hillary Scholten, and Kristen McDonald Rivet — because the Michigan-based auto companies are laggards at E.V. manufacturing compared with Kia/Hyundai and Tesla, so they would be particularly disadvantaged by what California wanted to do here.

Notably, though, Haley Stevens did not defect. She was, at the time, prepping her Senate run and courting establishment support. And the Democratic Party establishment is, contrary to myth, actually quite left-wing and pressures elected officials to cast progressive votes even on meaningless bills.

There was a fair amount of anger from the green community that Hakeem Jeffries didn’t whip the vote harder, and pressure was brought to bear on Chuck Schumer to get his frontliners to all cast meaningless no votes against a popular resolution. Schumer succeeded in getting every single Senate Democrat except Elissa Slotkin — even the retiring Gary Peters — to do this before putting Stevens up as his electability choice in Michigan.

I think that in this case, the real courage was shown by Slotkin and Rivet and the others who deviated from the party line, standing up to out-of-state bullies in order to serve their constituents’ interests. I think it’s crass to act like Stevens and betray your constituents in an effort to climb the intra-party ladder or to act like Peters and just kind of give up on your state on the way out the door. There is no organized interest group of “Americans for Being Able to Buy a Normal Car if I Want to,” but it’s better to align with the actual views of the people you represent than to be feted at a League of Conservation Voters dinner.

Defend — and practice — democracy

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton said on television shortly after the election that he’d be disappointed if Democrats spend all their time in the new Congress investigating Trump rather than focusing on the critical cost-of-living issues that were decisive to marginal voters.

I don’t think you can save democracy from the MAGA movement without practicing democracy, so it’s perfectly correct for Hamilton to emphasize cost of living in his public presentation. That being said, while I’ve never met the guy and have no access to his private thoughts, I feel like it would be strange if a successful minister risked his career on a longshot Senate bid primarily because he was personally outraged by the price of ground beef.

My guess — and I freely admit it’s just a guess, but I think I’m right about this — is that he was concerned about the state of American democracy.

Both Mary Peltola and Sherrod Brown considered running for governor, races where it would be easier to achieve separation from the national Democratic Party brand, but Schumer talked them into running for Senate instead. When he did that, did he appeal to the idea that they’d have more influence over grocery prices as senators than as governors? That just doesn’t seem true, analytically, and it also seems kind of implausible as a motivation. I bet he appealed to them as patriots about the need for a check on Trump’s powers.

The good news is that fighting to hold Trump accountable doesn’t involve any genuine tradeoffs with fighting for policies that improve affordability.

What it does involve is a modicum of political risk for people representing districts that voted for Trump three times. I think it’s a risk that’s worth running because it’s genuinely the most important issue of the day — and, again, because it doesn’t trade off in a substantive way against making progress on affordability.

But guess what does trade off? A lot of intense policy-demander priorities. There are, of course, ways to fight for affordability that amount to just fighting Trump — reduce tariffs, end the war in Iran — but ideas like fiscal discipline, Jones Act repeal, biofuel waste, or prioritizing cheap energy over green fundamentalism require conflict with Democratic Party interest groups.

You can’t take the politics out of politics, and obviously Turek isn’t going to go against corn farmers and El-Sayed and Slotkin aren’t going to advocate for Chinese E.V.s. But I think everyone holding down a tough seat should try to be really rigorous about prioritizing the cost of living over Democratic Party interest-group slop and then also be really rigorous about protecting democracy and the rule of law.

These folks should also try to practice democracy on the cultural issues. There’s a kind of thin consensus around “focusing on” affordability, but the fact is, most of these red-state senators staked out a view or two on cultural issues that would have gotten them canceled just a year earlier.

For the most part, the groups seem to have held their fire on this stuff, hoping that vague remarks don’t necessarily commit anyone to anything specific on policy. But I think policymakers should look at representing their constituents’ authentic views on guns, or on who plays on which sports team, or on how many refugees we let into the country. There is such a thing as a fundamental question of human rights, but most of the specifics on this stuff genuinely come down to judgment calls, and voters in places like South Carolina and Mississippi deserve to have their values represented in Congress without being forced to support thuggish authoritarians or corrupt plutocrats to get that. And I think part of stabilizing the democratic system is giving voters less polarized options.

The genuinely hard part of democratic politics, I think, is that you need to navigate around ideas that people like but that would backfire if you implemented them.

I’m sure a lot of people think they love the idea of price controls to bring down the price of beef. But if you implemented them and beef vanished from supermarket shelves, they’d be mad about that.

Alternatively, sometimes there’s an idea that really would accomplish a popular goal, like variable pricing of electricity to bring down average bills, but voters hate the idea. I’m not sure there’s a simple rule about how to think of these dilemmas — figuring out how to strike the right balance is where true statesmen make their bones.

Broadly speaking, though, I don’t think politicians or their staffs or journalists who cover them should view a Mayhew-like focus on securing re-election as ignoble or cowardly. Americans liked the relatively unprincipled midcentury political parties a lot more than they like today’s polarized, highly ideological ones. Real political courage is trying to be a genuine steward of your constituents’ interests rather than acting as a proxy for intense policy demanders or the preferences and priorities of the staffer class.

title: Why the New Right is failing

Why the New Right is failing

To be clear, I’m glad it’s failing.

Noah Smith
Nov 23
 
READ IN APP
 

Sometime in the mid-2010s, just as liberalism was getting replaced by “progressivism”, the conservatism that I had grown up with was getting replaced by something we then called the “alt-right”. Whereas the old conservatism was based on Christian faith, libertarian economics, and flag-waving patriotism, the alt-right saw America as a white racial nation-state, rejected the idea of free markets, and was basically irreligious and isolationist.

Over the course of two Trump presidencies and one Biden interregnum, the alt-right matured and grew into what I now call the New Right. In doing so, it basically took over from conservatism as the guiding ideology of the GOP base — though not (yet) of the GOP as a whole. Whereas the alt-right was a naked white-power movement, the New Right sees things in broader “civilizational” terms. It has embraced the idea of Christianity, not as a faith or a lifestyle, but as a tribal affiliation defining ingroup and outgroup. Its foreign policy matured into something concrete — a desire to wield American policy on behalf of “Western Civilization”.

At the grassroots level, the New Right also added some new components. It merged with the Covid antivax movement to become skeptical of modern medicine, public health, and life science in general. It partially merged with the incel movement, telling young men that their sexual frustration was the fault of progressivism. It veered even more strongly into antisemitism, probably feeling liberated to do so by rising antisemitism on the left in the wake of the Gaza war. And it added a strong component of anti-Indian hatred, seeing Indians as a uniquely vulnerable target among recent immigrant groups.

Anyway, it’s too early to say that this movement has failed. Yes, the Democrats won one midterm election, but Trump is still the President, and he has shown zero inclination to reverse course on any of his most New Right-aligned policies. He has made Stephen Miller, the ultimate anti-immigration crusader, his chief of staff, and posted a picture of himself hugging Vladimir Putin with the caption “My Friend”. Meanwhile, the New Right still has a fairly robust online presence.

But it’s impossible to deny that the winds have shifted. The midterms made it clear that even if the New Right sticks around for the long term, it won’t have a monopoly on power. That will make it essentially impossible for it to follow through on its long-term agenda. Basically, the notion that wokeness and internal disputes would cause the Democrats to permanently collapse as a party has been falsified.

Already, some prominent figures are backing away from the New Right. Elon Musk, who once stood on a stage and declared himself “Dark MAGA”, now says he’s not even MAGA at all, and is instead a political moderate:

What enthusiasm still does exist on the New Right tends to be concentrated on the movement’s most extreme fringe, which focuses on getting attention by bashing Trump and MAGA and saying ridiculous, extremist stuff. For example, Politico reports on the “Christ is King” conference, run by a guy named Joel Webbon:

[F]or Webbon, the problem was also that MAGA hadn’t gone far enough. He wanted even harsher deportation policies. He wanted a total repudiation of Israel. He wanted to curtail women’s right to vote, to criminalize abortion and homosexuality, and to expel Jews and non-Christians from public office…The event attracted a notorious set of online agitators, including conspiracist Alex Jones and Nick Fuentes, the 28-year-old white nationalist and antisemite, who made a rare public appearance as a guest speaker…

There are, in Webbon’s telling, few “guys” capable of leading this faction…He did put forward a few “guys” who might fit the bill, naming electoral losers like [James] Fishback, one of the weekend’s main draws, who recently lost [a gubernatorial primary] to a MAGA-backed candidate by 37 points in Florida…Webbon also went on to name Bo French, the far-right candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner who ultimately lost by some 670,000 votes to a Democrat after making anti-immigration a centerpiece of his campaign.

(There are also various loonies from overseas.)

These are all signs of a movement that’s on the way down. It may return someday — communism sort of did, after all — but its hopes of transforming America over the next few decades are fading. It’s not over yet, but it’s looking more and more that way.

A big part of the reason for that failure, of course, is that Americans simply do not buy what the New Right wants to sell them. Regular Americans generally like (legal) immigration, and they don’t see racial and religious heritage as an important determinant of who is a real American. It’s very hard to sell people a product they don’t want.

But there are also various strategic errors that the New Right made. To be clear, I’m glad these mistakes were made; I have zero desire to see a movement like the New Right hold power in my country. I just think it’s interesting and instructive to think about what the mistakes were.

One choice that wasn’t a mistake was to hitch the movement to Donald Trump. A lot of people in the New Right are going to blame their failure on Trump’s mistakes — his Iran War, his corruption, and his reluctance to do anything about inflation. But without the assistance from Trump’s personal charisma and idiosyncratic broad appeal, it’s doubtful that the New Right would ever have escaped the basement of the internet in the first place; the Republican establishment would have kept it locked in a box, the way they did with similar insurgencies from Pat Buchanan and the John Birch Society in past eras. Trump was actually the most effective leader the New Right could have chosen.

Instead, the New Right’s weakness mostly sprang from the fact that it was an online movement.

Reactionary impatience

Rightists will tell you that American culture has been completely captured by the left. And when you ask how this was accomplished, they’ll tell you about the “long march through the institutions” — a strategy that a German leftist described in the 1960s. Basically, the idea was for leftists to infiltrate universities, the media, the bureaucracy, and every other institution. Rightists believe, rightly or wrongly, that this plan was actually put into effect, and that this explains why university professors, media elites, civil servants, and so on tend to be left-wing today.¹

One might imagine that the New Right would try to execute a similar long-term strategy to win back the culture. Indeed, right-wing movements have been known to do something like this — the Federalist Society has been able to keep the American judiciary in rough ideological balance.

But the Federalist Society is part of the old conservative movement; the New Right has not shown much interest in executing a long-term strategy of institutional capture. Instead, they put most of their eggs in the basket of the Trump presidency, apparently hoping that either Trump would win the whole culture for them in a few years, or that he’d turn America into some kind of quasi-dictatorship that allowed his successors to continue the project of culture war and race war into the indefinite future. In terms of direct cultural appeal, the New Right mostly limited themselves to shouting online.

This demonstrates the extreme impatience of the New Right. Part of this is probably just inherent to rightist movements in general — there’s a reason that they’re called “reactionary”. Rightism tends to be strongly motivated by fear — the conceit is usually that if extreme measures are not taken right now, everything good in the world will be destroyed. The belief in imminent destruction doesn’t exactly lend itself to a patient long-term strategy of institutional takeover.

But part of the reason has to be the movement’s online roots. For people whose defining cultural expression consists of memes and Twitter mobs, the strategy of patiently infiltrating PhD programs over the course of 30 years must sound like hell. Virality and online conflict give instant gratification; winning a presidential election is only slightly less instantaneous. Institutional takeover requires a patience that was definitely present in 1985 among sad-sack leftist grad students with nothing to lose, but is in short supply among today’s online politics junkies.

This is why when Trump fades from the political scene and fails to be replaced by an eternal dynasty of rightist caudillos, the New Right will feel like they have nothing.

The New Right couldn’t make alliances

Politics is the art of making strategic alliances. The old conservative movement was very effective at this. Uniting the interests of Christian conservatives and libertarians took some doing. And conservatives worked heroically to include Catholics in a movement once dominated only by Protestants, leading to the Reagan Revolution and the exodus of Italian, Polish, and Irish voters from the Democrats to the GOP.

MAGA itself made strategic alliances in its successful 2024 comeback campaign. Co-opting RFK, Jr. — formerly a well-known progressive — into the fold was detrimental to the nation, but was also a stroke of political genius. Trump even allied with Tulsi Gabbard, using their shared fondness for Russia.

Trump’s 2024 campaign also offered the GOP its chance for the biggest ethnic realignment since Reagan. Trump won primarily thanks to the exodus of large numbers of Hispanic and Asian voters from the Dems to the GOP. These voters were frustrated by “woke” progressive attitudes toward race, and swayed by Trump’s promises to tame inflation.

But no sooner had these nonwhite voters handed Trump the presidency than the New Right started attacking them. From Bo French’s anti-Indian rants to Stephen Miller’s encouragement of racial profiling in ICE raids, rightists in power spit on the very people they needed in order to build long-lasting support. Meanwhile, rightist intellectuals continued to say dismissive and mean things about minority voters:

The Right will never do well with minority voters again if the GOP’s attitude toward them (as expressed in this post) is: “All minorities care about is receiving race-based preferences & hating white people.” Not only is this false, but it is no better than what the racialists of https://t.co/yBd1O0MwCK
