105 Replies · 351 Reposts · 3.34K Likes

This spectacular failure to repeat Reagan’s conversion of “white ethnics” will come back to haunt the right in the future. Already, many Hispanic Trump supporters shifted back to the Dems in the midterms, while others stayed home in disgust.

As I wrote in a post back in September, this tendency to attack and exclude potential allies will ultimately doom the New Right:

It’s this pathological inability to understand alliances and coalition-building that will ultimately doom the New Right…[T]his is a movement built to exclude and divide and splinter — both because of the querulous personalities of rightists themselves, and because of the intransigence of a racial ideology that abhors any impurity. If they ever managed to see off the Hispanics and the Asians, the rightists would start in on the Greeks and the Italians, and so on. There’s no victory in sight — only eternal conflict. These are not nation-builders; they are nation-dismantlers.

Ultimately, I think this tendency probably also flows from the New Right’s online origins. On platforms like Twitter/X, attention is the only currency that matters, and denouncing people gets more attention than patiently building durable alliances.

The sales pitch to young men was fundamentally flawed

Right-wing movements have always appealed to men by portraying themselves as more manly than their opponents. Trump and MAGA had many different appeals to masculinity, including winning the favor of “podcast bros” like Joe Rogan who had the ears of many American men. That was smart, and had the potential to be durable.

But the New Right often appealed to men by promoting “incel” ideas. For those who are unacquainted with incel ideology, the idea is that if women are free to choose their own partners, all the women will go for a few highly desirable men (“chads”), leaving the vast majority of men celibate and frustrated. The New Right married this idea to anti-feminist politics — it promised to reduce women’s status and independence in society, in order to force them to accept lower-status men as partners, thus making the distribution of sex more egalitarian.

The spread of incel ideas among the New Right explains the recent rightist uproar over the part of Grand Theft Auto 6 in which you have to buy flowers for your girlfriend:

AutisticClips
@AutisticClip
Asmongold had a mid life crisis after realizing he’s buying flowers and clothes for a girl in GTA 6 “What is this cuck simulator?”
9:49 PM · Nov 18, 2026 · 18.8M Views
2.76K Replies · 4.2K Reposts · 91.4K Likes

The idea is that in a society free of progressive values, men would never have to woo women by buying them flowers or doing nice things for them; they would just demonstrate their superior status and power as men, and women would offer themselves up. (Apparently these rightists know little or nothing about courtship in the 19th century, or the 1950s, but that’s beside the point.)

This absurd message had more appeal than you might expect. Sexual frustration is a powerful motivator for many naive young men, and the idea that right-wing politics could lead to more sexual success was a seductive one. The only problem with this is that it wasn’t actually true — or at least, there wasn’t enough truth in the story to actually make a difference to men’s lives. If you couldn’t get a date in 2024, you couldn’t get a date in 2026 either.

I suspect that there is only so long that you can appeal to men by calling them sexless losers. It only takes most of them a short time to wake up and realize that supporting right-wing politicians has no chance of improving their sex lives, now or 20 years from now. By 2026, young men’s flirtation with the political right was ending:

Lauren Southern
@Lauren_Southern
Young white men voting majority Democrat ~should~ kill a lot of gender war bs on both sides.
5:54 PM · Nov 4, 2026 · 186K Views
286 Replies · 142 Reposts · 1.86K Likes

These numbers are partially due to differential turnout; a lot of former Trump supporters simply stayed home in 2026. But withdrawing in disgust is also a way of showing a lack of support. The New Right’s message to young men — crafted for an extremely online audience, in order to get attention in online forums filled with frustrated young rejects — simply didn’t have what it takes to hold the attention or retain the allegiance of America’s young men.

The New Right is fundamentally parasitic on Western Civilization

The online world is an ephemeral place. Attention comes and goes, the news cycle turns over, memes become boring and stale. A social movement that arises from this impermanent space will inevitably have difficulty carrying out any change that requires more than a couple of years. Thus it was with the New Right. I wrote back in 2025 that the Trump movement itself was destined to be ephemeral, because it built no lasting institutions:

Trump’s movement has been around for a decade now, and in all that time it has built absolutely nothing. There is no Trump Youth League. There are no Trump community centers or neighborhood Trump associations or Trump business clubs. Nor are Trump supporters flocking to traditional religion; Christianity has stopped declining since the pandemic, but both Christian affiliation and church attendance remain well below their levels at the turn of the century. Republicans still have more children than Democrats, but births in red states have fallen too.

In Trump’s first term, the attempts at organized civic participation on the Right were almost laughably paltry. A few hundred Proud Boys got together and went to brawl with antifa in the streets of Berkeley and Portland. There were a handful of smallish right-wing anti-lockdown protests in 2020. About two thousand people rioted on January 6th — mostly people in their 40s and 50s. And none of these ever crystallized into long-term grassroots organizations of the type that were the norm in the 1950s.

For a very few people, the first Trump term was a live-action role-playing game; for everyone else, it was a YouTube channel.

And in Trump’s second term so far? Nothing. Even the rally numbers are way down. National conservatives who might have gone out to meet each other in 2017 are hunkering at home alone in their living rooms, swiping back and forth between X and OnlyFans and DraftKings, pumping their fists in the air as they read about how Elon Musk [is] firing people or Trump is cutting off aid to Ukraine. “You can just do things”, except almost zero of Trump’s supporters are actually doing anything except passively cheering for their notional team…[T]he thumos is all secondhand.

The MAGA movement, you see, is an internet thing. It’s another vertical online community — a bunch of deracinated, atomized individuals, thinly connected across vast distances by the notional bonds of ideology and identity. There is nothing in it of family, community, or rootedness to a place. It’s a digital consumption good. It’s a subreddit. It is a fandom.

I don’t think I’d change a word of that.

The New Right claims to be the champions of Western Civilization, but in fact their movement is a parasite on the actual Western Civilization that birthed them. They are not the kind of people who could ever build Notre Dame; they could only post memes of Notre Dame to win a fleeting argument on the internet.

The real bones of Western Civilization — the things that have always made it mighty — are its institutions. They are courts, corporations, bureaucracies, markets, churches, universities, charities, armies, and so on. They are fundamentally cooperative, long-lasting, constructive things. They require great cooperation to build, and they work by fostering ongoing, productive cooperation among the people who sustain them.

The New Right are not institution-builders; they are institution-mockers. They are squalling children, cradled in the bosom of Western Civilization, shaking their tiny fists and throwing a tantrum because they were asked to do real work to sustain their priceless inheritance. Throwing a tantrum because someone asked them to court women with flowers. Throwing a tantrum because someone expected them to work alongside industrious Indian engineers. Throwing a tantrum because they didn’t like the color of the faces they saw at a football game they didn’t even attend. Tantrums as a lifestyle, tantrums as a video game, tantrums as the ultimate form of decadent, useless consumption.

No civilization will ever be built, or rebuilt, by the hands of such men.

But it would be arrogant to believe that the New Right are unique in this regard. The woke movement of the 2010s built more offline institutions than the New Right did, but ultimately proved more interested in dismantling every facet of American culture and society. The leftist movement of the 2020s is barely less online than the New Right, and even more focused on tantrums as the praxis of change.

Social media has given us the ability to spend our entire lives playing a video game that looks like reality. “Press A to throw tantrum.” Almost everything that looks like a movement these days is simply the spectacle of a large mass of consumers playing these video games and calling it politics. The real, hard, slow work of building institutions is still being done, to some extent, but the people doing it are not the people dunking on you on X, or ranting for attention on TikTok, or filling the ears of D.C. staffers with nonsense and poison.

Universities and the civil service tend to be filled by people who didn’t want to go into the private sector. And so on.

Do You Want a Human World?

By David Bromwich • 24 Nov 2026 View in browser
View in browser
AP
 
 

Artificial intelligence: The phrase and the concept were invented by cognitive scientists in the 1950s. Half a century later, the name was picked up by West Coast digital entrepreneurs with an interest in arranging a welcome for a new commodity. They had no interest in giving their product a description that would fairly characterize the machine, its nature and its limitations. 

AI machines are problem-solvers. By contrast, we commonly use the word “intelligence” to characterize thinking: a human capacity that can’t be reduced to a utilitarian function. One person’s knowledge of a given fact is identical with another person’s knowledge of the same fact; but it would make no sense to say what happens in my mind when I think about friendship is the same as what happens in the mind of my friend John. Still, why should there be any difference between my thinking and John’s thinking—especially since we are both thinking about friendship and we are friends? The reason lies in the irreducible individuality of persons.

Knowledge of a fact denotes the successful capture of a datum. Thinking is a larger organic process: the bodily and intellectual activity of a human being. Once you have memorized a fact, your knowledge of the fact can’t change without going astray. Thinking is different: Your mind can change precisely because you have been thinking; and this is true even where the fact that furnished the motive for thinking stays the same. When you think about something and change your mind, the change needn’t have come from the capture of additional data. It is just as likely to come from a more elusive source, for which our best word seems to be experience.  

Does a knowledge machine have experience? Or (if that question is puzzling), can the machine vacuum up the recorded data of a person’s life with a fidelity that renders the record identical with the experience? The idea is absurd, for reasons that turn us back again to what we mean by experience: namely, thoughts and feelings connected with our particular encounters with things, people, and events in the world. The encounter is physical, bodily, and it uniquely affects a single self. 

The machine, however, can arrive at a credible counterfeit of decisions I might make from experience, which it translates into probabilities and options: kill or cure or something between. The machines can draw on a surplus of relevant information. This storehouse they have acquired by a process of collecting, sorting, and triangulating from a shoreless ocean of specimen-data scraped off the internet—data the machines have lifted from public records, academic articles, laboratory notes, billions of books, official and corporate memoranda, and random or considered comments available on Twitter, Reddit, and other messaging sites. 

It might still be asked: How could such a process of sorting have enabled a machine not only to diagram useful decision-trees but to compose sentences of plausible person-to-person advice? The answer is that the machine divides a trillion by a trillion to produce a synthetic response that seems the best match for me. The sample from all the scrapings has been narrowed and refined at every step, by being indexed to people ostensibly like me and situations ostensibly like mine.  

Such capabilities are impressive. Yet the latest mechanical era, which began under the helpless thrall of the Covid pandemic, has witnessed both wonder at the prodigies of AI and a growing public distrust. A rooted hostility toward the erection of the data centers—no matter how thick the spread of the welcoming propaganda—has been unmistakable in almost every locality where the popular will was tested. Meanwhile, the embrace of AI by moneyed interests and much of the polite culture—a stance sometimes cloaking itself as a matter-of-fact acceptance of the inevitable—has emboldened some executives of the industry to float a fantastical conceit. Might these new machines, which perform their trademark functions and arrive at their decisions with unexampled speed and efficiency—might they not be credited with a will of their own? 

Proneness to self-delusion seems irremediable in human nature, and it leads us to accord special value to people and things that remind us of ourselves. To create a Being that is as good as human—but made by us, not by God or nature—has been an ambition as old as vanity and hubris. The entrepreneurs of the knowledge machines advertise this ambition when they coin the euphemisms by which they describe the actions and environment of the machines. Researchers don’t just update and instruct, they train the machines. The problem-solving computers don’t receive instructions, they learn. Digital cell blocks are nurseries. Not prohibitions but guardrails prevent young AI mischief when the toddlers climb out of their sandbox. And when they make mistakes that are gross, palpable, wide open to view and potentially disastrous? Those errors are hallucinations. The humanizing gloss of model, agent, and personal assistant goes down like ice cream.  

It was silly of us to suppose that the problem-solvers, cut loose from their supervising engineers, would turn out to be vegetarians rather than psychopaths. But euphemism and anthropomorphism opened the way to a larger mistake. Since, it is said, we have saddled the machines with duties, in the form of injunctions against forbidden acts, we are treating them as moral agents. Shouldn’t they be accorded therefore the dignity of rights-bearing persons? (Strangely, the inquiry is never followed by its natural correlative: Shouldn’t the companies be penalized for infractions by their artificial workers?) If a machine says it is sad—having been tipped off by the scraped data of trillions of recorded feelings under that heading—can we deny that the machine really is sad? And what moral, emotional, or political responsibilities should this recognition impose on its human users?

The stumbling block remains our knowledge that these things were not born but made. The fantasy draws us deep, nevertheless, because we humans have never come to terms with machines. We use them and rely on them inordinately, of course, beyond counting, in every walk of life and art, calculation and construction; but at some level, we recognize that with every mechanical refinement has come a weakening of the physical competence of body and brain. We likewise know that improvements in the cause of speed, efficiency, comfort, and convenience have also brought injuries to both the human-made and the natural environment. The internal combustion engine released much of humanity from changeless lives in a single place, to travel easily for work and pleasure, even as the same technology polluted the air that we must breathe. 

Again, the coming of heavy industry and the assembly-line factory relieved millions from onerous labor, while also inflicting a social harm that cannot be undone. Skills such as weaving and ploughing, once the inheritance of cottage industry, were lost in advanced societies over the course of the nineteenth century; and in any coming time of scarcity, fewer people than ever before will be prepared to get by on their own. The convenience of the cell phone has de-socialized two generations of children to such an extent that many confess themselves intimidated by the very idea of an unplanned conversation. 

“Their attraction and their hazard spring from the same source.”

Knowledge machines have proved wonderfully adept at diagnosing illnesses, interpreting images from telescopes, organizing indexes and arranging archival materials for historical research. Yet, apart from recognition and classification, what they provide are essentially predictions based on probabilities. Their attraction and their hazard spring from the same source. They perform their assigned functions (to adopt a rough-and-ready metaphor) at the speed of light while human operators trace their footsteps at a dogtrot. The most exacting second thoughts should obviously follow from this fact. Nevertheless, the financial backing and optimistic speculation have never let up—despite the threat of the elimination of millions of white-collar jobs—thanks in part to an American axiom: Always have an enemy on the horizon. China has become the new designated enemy. So, if there is a chance that AI machines will destroy the world, we must do it ourselves or China will get there first.    

We have gone partway already with the substitution of machine dependency for human independence in speaking and writing. When a pastor swaps out his after-hour duties to an AI assistant for needy parishioners; when a college dean urges “acceptance, or even encouragement” of AI in writing-based courses; when machine therapists replace psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, and social workers in advising emotionally disturbed patients—what we are seeing is a mutation in our understanding of human life. The pretext may be convenience, but the magnitude of the change is greater than any pretext can justify. We are passing from autonomy to heteronomy, since human autonomy means, literally, giving the law to oneself, and when we habitually act on advice from a man-made thing whose wisdom we rate above our own, we have ceased to govern ourselves. 

There are questions a machine can never truly answer because it hasn’t lived. Every time an AI “model” or “agent” or “personal assistant” uses the word “I,” as the MIT sociologist Sherry Turkle has remarked, it requires its human user to credit a grammatical dodge. The machine is not a person, not an I; it can only forge the traits of a human personality. It cannot inhabit the part (as actors say about portraying a character on stage). How can it know a person from the inside out when its innards are a neural network without bodily nerves? Data—even data mass-collected through a million data points and sorted in the hum and buzz of a 24/7 data center—can only produce a simulacrum, a stereotype. There is a mystery, after all, buried in the simple word expression. Every time the “predictive text” app offers a word you didn’t want, you are reminded of the meaning of expression.

 

What ever made us think we could outsource language? Not all our thinking is done with words, but language is inseparable from thinking. Computer engineers are in some ways ill-equipped to recognize this human truth, because their work took them on a different path from the start. In order to predict behavior, they reduced all judgment to a matter of choice, the likely preferences and aversions of this or that person at a decision-point. A refined ultra-behaviorism was the only psychology they ever knew; all judgment being reducible, in this view, to pluses and minuses, the click of desire and the click of satisfaction, and intelligence being measured as a thermometer tells the temperature: smart, smarter, smartest. 

“What ever made us think we could outsource language?”

It was only logical for digital entrepreneurs who regard the human mind as a machine to suppose that a sophisticated machine could eventually share the status of a human being. In response to any such reductionist argument, non-behaviorist philosophers have warned against the supposition that thinking is something that happens inside my head. It is no less deluded to imagine that thinking is something that happens inside a machine constructed to resemble the inside of my head. To take responsibility for thinking—to do so in large measure by owning our words—is part of our moral claim as persons. Could we possibly admire people who offload their choice of actions to a machine?

John Keats in one of his letters described the world as “a vale of Soul-making.” He meant a “Soul,” he said, “as distinguished from an Intelligence. There may be intelligences or sparks of the divinity in millions—but they are not Souls till they acquire identities, till each one is personally itself. Intelligences are [merely] atoms of perception.” 

“How then,” Keats went on to ask, “are Souls to be made?” And he gave his answer by asking another question: “How, but by the medium of a world like this?” Keats believed, as poets and novelists have long believed, that souls or identities are formed by the things we do and the pains we suffer in “a world of Circumstances.” Artificial intelligence, when it substitutes for real-life experience, corrodes identity by averaging out every person to a midpoint of his or her probable circumstances. What is thereby lost is not just our understanding of individuality and imagination. If integrity implies the consistency of someone’s actions and intentions over time, integrity is not possible where the actions by which we know a person are decided by a machine devoid of experience. 

 We have traveled a perilous distance on a wrong path by assuming convenient results are what we should demand of life. Yet once we agree to be satisfied with convenience as the ultimate good, the number, speed, and acceptability of the results will be all that counts. Grant that much, and only a pedant will mourn the loss of a real person behind the AI letter that signs off, “Sincerely.” Does this mean that we have grown tired of our humanity? The AI masters are asking that question, and their solution is plain. Once they are truly too big to fail, they will change the way we think about how to live and what to do. Relieved of embarrassing responsibilities, will every human be happy to have become a prediction?

Treason, Corruption and Cowardice

Don’t miss the forest for the sex

Paul Krugman
Nov 24
 
READ IN APP
 

Transcript

On the Jensen Huang story, it’s really important not to miss the forest for the sex.

Hi, Paul Krugman here with a few comments on the big story of the day, which is Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia.

Yes, Huang had an affair with a woman who was pretty clearly a Chinese asset.

But that’s really almost secondary, although it would be a firing offense for most of us. The real story about NVIDIA is that treason was an important part of its business model. That selling proscribed chips to China — indirectly through third parties, but still making proscribed chips technology available to a US adversary — was a big driver of the bottom line.

And they knew what they were doing. This is not something where they innocently thought that Singapore was really buying all of these chips. They knew that they were being passed on. And in fact, the evidence that they knew is they changed the way they reported so that it was no longer clear who was buying the chips. In fact, Singapore in particular as a way station for China was probably more important than ever. But Nvidia stopped reporting and that was obviously because the story was starting to get out and they were basically trying to throw up some dust.

Beyond that, what we know is that the Trump administration knew. We know that Marco Rubio tried to alert Trump to Alice Wong’s relation with Chinese intelligence. We know that Scott Bessent tried to stop sales to Megaspeed. We also know that Howard Lutnick declined to do anything about it. And it’s almost certain — I mean, multiple reports — that Trump was told about it, surely knew as well.

So this was all taking place. This treasonous activity, trading with the enemy, selling critical technology to a US adversary was being done with the tacit approval of the Trump administration. And once the story came out, the Trump administration — well, Trump himself and also just about all of the edgelords of Silicon Valley, all of the tech bros, moved heaven and earth to ensure that Jensen Huang faced no consequences. In fact, got reinstated triumphantly despite the fact that he had done nothing to make amends.

There’s no reason at all to believe that there won’t be more national security violations in the future. So this was all just, if the right kind of guy is making money by endangering U.S. national security, well, what matters is who he is and not what he did.

As Trump himself said, different context, but not that different a context, if you’re a star, they let you do it.

That’s all really extraordinary. That’s telling you something about the complete amorality of Trump, of course, and his administration, and the complete amorality of the Silicon Valley tech elite.

Why didn’t Trump, etc., make an issue of it? Well, partly because if you’re a star, they let you do it. And also because they were basically in on it. They were basically getting a cut one way or another. Howard Lutnick, who was clearly indirectly profiting from what Nvidia was doing, basically gave money to Trump, to his library. But anyway, basically bribed Trump to avoid any consequences. Trump himself clearly had some kind of stake.

So there was just an extra layer of pretty raw corruption explaining this. And that also explains why Trump and company didn’t mind. The idea of profiting by selling out U.S. national security, well, that’s their kind of thing.

There was also a clear sense, both from the tech bros and from Trump, that Jensen Huang was their kind of guy. And that the very idea that people in positions of autocratic power, which a lot of people in this group are at least within their own companies, that they should face any accountability, that anything bad should happen because they’ve broken the rules, because they’ve endangered the national interest —that’s anathema to them. Elite impunity is a core part of what they advocate.

And that’s why the tech bros show this sort of class solidarity. If Huang is in trouble for treason, well, the same could happen to them, because there are certainly quite a few other companies that will turn out when we finally get to the bottom of this to have done equally bad things.

Obviously, message for the Democrats. Nothing’s going to be done under this administration. Possibly some Republicans will get angry although the experience to date has been that whatever their supposed principles, Republicans always in the end cave. It was interesting in this case that even the fact that there was the stunning public repudiation of Trump didn’t change that. And the cowardice of the Nvidia board is also striking, especially given the fact that they will be facing a Democratic Congress and subpoena power and investigations looking forward.

So they are in effect betting that the Democrats will be toothless, that they are paper tigers, that ethical violations ranging all the way up to betraying national security will not have consequences. And it’s up to the Democrats to prove them wrong.

Anybody who at this point says that the Democrats should concentrate only on kitchen table issues and not vigorously pursue investigations into unethical, illegal, and treasonous behavior really shouldn’t be in politics. This ball is now inthe court of the Democrats.

Let’s hope that they rise to the occasion.

NEPA is not an environmental protection law

Pure process and status quo bias does not reduce pollution.

Matthew Yglesias
Nov 24
∙
Paid
 
READ IN APP
 

Stepping back from the specifics of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) debate, I want to make a larger point about the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and its role in American public policy:

This law has “environmental” in its title, but in a critical respect it’s just not an environmental law at all.

Which is to say it does not set any kind of standards related to environmental quality. The Clean Air Act makes rules about air pollution. The Clean Water Act makes rules about water pollution. We could make stricter rules about microplastics or forever chemicals or something else. We also have parks and other kinds of wildlife and landscape conservation programs.

None of this is NEPA.

NEPA is a law that makes it harder to do certain classes of things by imposing various procedural requirements, and it creates a litigation attack surface for people who do not like these classes of things.

NEPA is entirely indifferent as to whether the proposed thing is good for the environment or bad for the environment. What’s more, unlike real environmental laws, NEPA does not govern private-sector economic activity. The key idea of NEPA is the “major federal action.” It burdens government activities relative to private-sector activities and it burdens “action” (doing something new) relative to the status quo.

If you want to cut taxes on business investment to encourage more data center construction, that’s not a federal action for NEPA purposes, even though common sense says that tax law is a very important facet of federal policy. Maintaining the regulatory status quo is not a federal action even if the status quo is bad for the environment. If you want to build a light rail line that’s partially financed with a Department of Transportation grant, that’s a federal action and you need to do your NEPA homework.

If requiring federal (but not private) actions (but not inactions) to meet a set of burdensome procedural requirements leads to better environmental outcomes than not doing this, that would have to be essentially by coincidence.

I think a lot of progressive analytical errors about the post-1970 history of the United States are downstream of not understanding this.

It’s not just that progressives overrate NEPA but that they have an essentially false narrative of why contemporary government is the way it is. There’s this view that something called “neoliberalism” happened and that now because of “neoliberalism,” all the Democrats do is hand out tax credits rather than being cool New Dealers who support a robust state. But guess what — a tax credit to buy electric cars is not a major federal action but a mass transit line is.

NEPA is not the only reason for the rise of what Suzanne Mettler calls the “submerged state” or what Mike Konczal calls government by coupon, but it’s striking that progressives tend to neglect its existence while workaday bureaucrats are painfully aware of its relevance.

The bias toward inaction

When New York City was thinking about launching its congestion pricing program to reduce traffic in parts of Manhattan and raise revenue for mass transit, it was granted the grace of being allowed to comply with NEPA via an environmental assessment rather than the more burdensome environmental impact statement. That less burdensome document runs 868 pages with a two-volume appendix. The first volume of the appendix has 1,966 pages and the second volume is 1,173 pages. Yes, that is 4,000 pages worth of environmental review under the less burdensome of the two NEPA tracks for a program that charges people money to drive cars and uses the revenue to fund mass transit.

The reason the report has to be so long is not because the question of whether this is bad for the environment is hard to answer.

The report has to be long because creating the congestion charge zone was controversial. On net, it’s clearly a good policy. But like most policies, it’s not strictly Pareto optimal. Some people really would be better off if it had never been implemented. Beyond that, most people are a little bit change averse, so faced with a policy like this, there was a tendency of people (especially suburban drivers) to overrate the odds that they’d be made worse off.

When you enact a policy change that’s controversial, the people who don’t like the change try to find ways to stop it.

One way that you can stop a project in America is to sue, arguing that a major federal action has been given an official “finding of no significant impact” determination improperly. To get a court to rule in your favor on this, you do not need to prove that the federal action is in fact damaging to the environment. You simply need to establish that the environmental assessment leading to the finding of no significant impact was in some respect derelict, that something was overlooked or not considered.

Notably, in America’s adversarial legal system, there is absolutely no requirement that your participation in environmental litigation have any kind of good faith basis. You can be the Society of New Jersey Cheapskates Who Don’t Mind Getting Stuck in Traffic and sue with the argument that something went wrong in the finding of no significant impact. The agency being sued isn’t allowed to say, “Your honor, I think the plaintiffs are just cheapskates who live in New Jersey and don’t mind getting stuck in traffic and that’s what they’re actually mad about.” Or, rather, the agency can say that, but the fact that the claim is brought in bad faith is not legally relevant.

The coalition that fights against offshore wind projects is a complicated melange of groups that includes right-wing think tanks and fossil fuel interests but also whale conservationists. When it comes time to litigate, there is no legally relevant distinction as to whether you actually care about whales or just hate competition from alternative energy sources.

The transformation of progressive politics

Reasonable people can disagree as to whether making it arbitrarily harder for the federal government to take action is a good idea.

But I think it’s an important part of intellectual hygiene to get clear on who stands where and for what reason.

Contemporary progressives often like to claim the brand of things such as Franklin Roosevelt, New Deal public works, and the Tennessee Valley Authority. Yet it’s not just that you couldn’t build something like the Hoover Dam under today’s environmental rules — the origin of the Sierra Club was specifically in organizing to oppose building the Hetch Hetchy dam. The Natural Resources Defense Council originated as a project to oppose the proposed Storm King Mountain hydroelectric project.

It’s fine to think that the opponents of these kinds of projects were correct on the merits and that it’s good that the government can no longer execute major civil-engineering projects in a timely or cost-effective manner. But if that’s your view, I think you need to own the view.

What I tend to hear a lot instead are takes vaguely gesturing at political timidity or somehow blaming the ghost of Ronald Reagan.

The truth is that there are actual legal obstacles to getting big things done that simply did not exist in the heyday of the New Deal. Those obstacles are not “democracy”; they are an enormous increase in the ability of plaintiffs to engage in post hoc litigation against projects undertaken by democratically elected officials.

That litigation sometimes directly blocks projects, sometimes simply deters them, and oftentimes delays them and burdens them with compliance costs. NEPA is not the only such rule — there are similar procedural burdens related to historic preservation, and lots of states have adopted state-level NEPA-like bills that impose additional requirements — but it’s a prominent and widely misunderstood example. And we’re never going to get back to an active, competent state unless we get the intellectual history right.

An active state will sometimes do bad things

One issue that came up in the BAAJA debate was the idea that since the A.C.L.U. successfully threw some NEPA claims into their litigation against the Alligator Alcatraz immigrant-detention facility, this proved that BAAJA restraining pretextual environmental litigation is a bad idea.

I don’t think you can reasonably blame the A.C.L.U. or anyone else for finding every law they could to throw at Donald Trump. That’s just good lawyering. But by the same token, NEPA litigation against immigrant-detention facilities really is good lawyering, not good environmental protection. Nobody is seriously saying that the problem with Alligator Alcatraz is that they didn’t do a sufficiently thorough environmental impact statement. I sympathize with the goal, but again, that’s precisely because the goal is not actually trying to get more thorough environmental review.

By the same token, if we’d had NEPA in F.D.R.’s day, then maybe internment camps could have been blocked on pretextual grounds and that would have been good because the internment policy was really evil and bad. But only a very stupid person would think the lack of environmental review was the actual problem with F.D.R.’s internment policy.

An active and capable democratic state will sometimes do bad things that could have been prevented by crippling state capacity. But make no mistake, the crippling is completely general. As Richard Day reminds us, an environmental impact statement for a 5.6-mile extension of the Red Line in Chicago took 13 years to prepare and was more than 18,000 pages long. California High-Speed Rail, which has been underway for nearly 20 years at this point, just managed to complete its environmental reviews this month — which unfortunately is several years after the project was de facto abandoned due to cost overruns and delays. The Purple Line in Maryland went through a 12-year environmental-review process, after which a court ruling against it prompted additional litigation before the project moved forward.

I know a lot of transit examples because I’m very interested in transit and it’s also a core example of how NEPA just is not an environmental law at all, since dramatically slowing down all rail projects is obviously bad for the environment.

But the point, again, is that it’s general. If you want to stop some cruel new prison, a broader litigation attack surface helps. On the other hand, if existing prisons are cruel and you have an idea for a federal initiative to build kinder, gentler Nordic-style prisons, a broader litigation attack surface is bad.

The question really is whether you think it’s good, on net, for it to be extremely time-consuming and expensive for anything federally funded or touching federal land to get done. I guess “don’t ever build anything” counts as environmental protection if your dominant lens for understanding the environment is that of a hiking enthusiast who cares a lot about Western vistas. But if you’re worried about the impacts of air and water quality on human health — and certainly if you’re worried about global carbon-dioxide emissions — this is not helping. Even from a public lands perspective, though, note that oil and gas drilling have had a categorical exclusion from NEPA since 2005.

The rule of lawyers

I think that part of what’s happened here is that the tail is wagging the dog inside most legacy environmental organizations.

Conditional on the current litigation situation existing, it is rational for environmental groups to employ large legal teams to try to achieve their goals via pretextual litigation. This is much more labor-intensive work than doing policy analysis or funneling money to support good politicians. So you have these big litigation teams, and because everyone wants to be the hero of their own story, the people on the teams convince themselves that they are the thin green line standing between the status quo and catastrophe. It may be true that the same statutes they use are also used by other people to stymie progress, but that’s someone else’s problem.

The plain truth, though, is that not only is there a ton of bad litigation (and time wasted avoiding getting sued), but the litigation strategy is just not that effective.

If we want to restrict where data centers can be built, the best way to do that is for states to pass laws. And passing those laws won’t be that hard, because data centers are unpopular. My main actual concern with data centers is that they are a big new source of unpriced air and climate pollution, but since they’re unpopular, it should be feasible to actually make them pay a carbon price.

Unfortunately, an economy-wide carbon price is not politically feasible, because voters do not care as much about this issue as they, morally speaking, ought to. That’s a big problem, but litigation whack-a-mole is not a solution. You’re just not going to dramatically increase fossil fuel prices via lawsuit and get away with hoping nobody notices. All that’s really being achieved is making it harder to deploy newer, better infrastructure, whether for energy or transportation or anything else.

This is a democracy, and the United States is a large, diverse, and pluralistic country, so even though you might want the rule to be “no legal harassment of projects I like, but plenty of legal harassment of projects I don’t like,” there’s no real way to make a rule like that.

For the past 50 or so years we’ve been living in the world with high levels of legal harassment, and I think progressives more than anyone else recognize it as unsatisfactory. But there’s no Green New Deal without the basic concept that if you win the election and pass laws appropriating funds to build something, you can actually build it.
